Trump to sign women’s health executive order Monday
text:
WASHINGTON (CNN) - President Donald Trump is scheduled to sign an executive order spearheaded by First Lady Melania Trump Monday.
The order will establish a women’s health arm of the National Institutes of Health.
It will focus on doing more research on women’s issues and translating that into treatments and cures.
The order will also set up a White House task force, to include Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Dr. Mehmet Oz.
This action marks the second executive order spearheaded by Melania Trump during the administration, following her 2025 “Fostering the Future” child welfare initiative.

title: Man stabbed, struck with brass knuckles in Lewiston
text:
A man was injured and another was arrested in connection with a stabbing in Lewiston on Saturday afternoon, according to a news release.
Around 3:30 p.m., Lewiston Police responded to reports of a fight near Dunkin’ Donuts at 420 Main Street. Officers found a 20-year-old man suffering from a single stab wound to the back, and other wounds apparently caused by being hit with brass knuckles.
The victim, whose name has not been released by authorities, was transported to Central Maine Medical Center to be treated for serious but not life-threatening injuries.
Officers arrested 18-year-old Alexander Keith at the scene in connection with the stabbing. Keith was transported to the Androscoggin County Jail and is not eligible for bail because he was already on deferred disposition.
Derek St. Laurent, a spokesperson for the Lewiston Police Department, said Sunday morning that investigators believe the two men know each other, and that the stabbing was not random.
Authorities are still investigating the incident.

title: Cooper Flagg’s new coach one of 3 first-timers in NBA this season
text:
Dusty May is new to the NBA. He’s not new to the NBA stage.
Thanks in large part to a Final Four run at Florida Atlantic in 2023 and leading Michigan to the NCAA title last season, May has coached plenty of big games in plenty of NBA arenas and knows what it’s like when those buildings are filled to the rafters.
And that means when he makes his regular-season debut as coach of Cooper Flagg and the Dallas Mavericks in a few days, May will have a real sense of what’s coming — at least from an surroundings standpoint.
“I’ve been in that environment,” May said. “Not at the level, obviously, but I’m someone who’s big on visualization. I see myself there. … But I have a real unique ability to, once the game starts, for 48 minutes to have 100% of my focus on the court and our bench.”
In other words, the coach of last season’s NCAA champion truly believes he’s ready for the NBA challenge. And he’s not alone, with six teams under new coaching management this season.
May is one of three first-time NBA coaches, along with Orlando’s Sean Sweeney (former San Antonio assistant) and Portland’s Micah Nori (former Minnesota assistant).
Another trio of coaches got new jobs in the league — former Memphis coach Taylor Jenkins has taken over in Milwaukee, former Orlando coach Jamahl Mosley has taken over in New Orleans, and former interim Portland coach Tiago Splitter (who coached for basically the entirety of last season) is the new coach in Chicago.
“I think just in general, the way we’re approaching things is, ‘What do we need to do today? Where are we at? How did we do with it? What do we need to improve on?’” Sweeney said. “We’ve done a good job of trying to set high standards for ourselves and lay down expectations for each other and live up to that.”
It is possible to win somewhere in Year 1 as a coach — just ask New York’s Mike Brown, who led the Knicks to last season’s NBA championship in his inaugural season on that team’s sideline. The coach of the reigning Western Conference champions, San Antonio’s Mitch Johnson, got to the finals in his second season as coach of the Spurs (which, technically, was his first full season as head coach).
Sweeney and Nori were widely considered as being ready to become head coaches for a few years before getting their current chances. May had taken two schools, one of them a mid-major, to the Final Four in a four-season span, more than proving his ability to win. Splitter did such a good job under awkward circumstances in Portland last season that he was a coach of the year candidate, and both Jenkins and Mosley had some success at their previous stops.
Nori essentially accepted a one-year contract with the Trail Blazers, an extremely rare move, especially for a first-time head coach. He’s betting on himself, saying that if he does the job, the options for future seasons on the existing contract will take care of itself.
“I’ve been around a lot of — I think it’s 13 — head coaches, so you start to see what you would do and what you’d like to do,” Nori said. “I guess the biggest difference, and they always talk about sliding over that one seat, is that it ends with you. … It’s your program now. That’s been the biggest adjustment.”
Mosley was living in Florida a few months ago, never thinking he’d be in Louisiana now. But when the Magic decided to change coaches, the Pelicans didn’t wait long before pouncing — knowing that Mosley would be a hot commodity. And Mosley says a change of scenery gave him an opportunity for what essentially is a reawakening.
“You get to do a lot of reflecting quick, right? You get to see exactly what worked, what didn’t work, how you can balance out what you do, the roster you have, you get to reflect on a lot of things that were successful and things that you need to work on,” Mosley said. “That’s what it gave me. And now look at the group of guys that we have here — young, energetic, wanting to learn, wanting to figure it out, hungry to get better. There’s so much of it here that it’s easy to pour into an organization like this.”

title: Gross coffee, a surprise candidate and a staring contest with a chicken
text:
There ought to be a special coffee aisle for imbeciles
So there I was at Shaw’s the other day, just looking to pick up a bag of coffee to brew at home. Just a nice medium roast, nothing fancy, thank you. So easy, a simpleton could do it. So, you can imagine my level of horror and self-loathing when I discovered later that what I had brought into my house was not regular coffee, but some caramel flavored monstrosity. Caramel! You’re looking at a guy who can’t stand any kind of flavored coffee or beer. Adding flavors to coffee or beer is just unnatural, in my book. But being the good sport I am, I decided to give caramel coffee a try. Who knew? Maybe I’d love it and be completely converted! But no. The very first sip of this cold brewed poison I took, I spat out into the sink before proceeding to call myself every terrible name you can imagine. I may as well have brought lice or termites or diseased rats into my house, such is the extent of my loathing for flavored coffee. I could have died drinking that, you know. I could have died!
By and by …
If you’re one of those weirdos who actually LIKES caramel flavored things, I have a whole batch of ghastly coffee you can have. Although, don’t mind me if I pretend to not know you when I make the handoff. You people are just loony.
One cool candidate
Got this note from a clearly drunken reader the other day. “As you probably are aware every street corner has tons of political signs. My question is: who is this ‘Frost Heave?’ Is he or she a republican, a democrat and what office are they running for?”
I wish I could help, but you KNOW I don’t follow politics.
Bok! Bok!
I totally got stared down by a rooster the other day while I was riding my motorcycle on the edge of the Lewiston downtown. It’s been a lot of years since I went head-to-head with a chicken, but I thought for sure I could ruffles this guy’s feathers. Nope. No matter how loudly I twisted my throttle and no matter how hard my steely gaze, that badass bird just kept staring back with those black little eyes and refused to move an inch. This is just terrible for my street cred. If a guy can’t intimidate a stupid chicken, I don’t know how he’s going to handle himself in the hood.
Your secret is safe
I declined to disclose the location of this man-bird standoff because if someone is secretly keeping fowl in the area, I don’t want to get him or her in trouble with city stuffed shirts. I may be a chicken, bro, but I ain’t no rat.
Mark LaFlamme is an award-winning Sun Journal reporter and columnist. He’s covered the nighttime police beat since 1994, which is just grand because he doesn’t like getting out of bed before noon. He is the author of eight published novels and rides a dual sport motorcycle everywhere he goes. Unless it’s winter, in which case he just sulks a lot.

LEWISTON — A celebration of Somali culture drew hundreds of people to the Agora Palace Event Center on Bates Street for a celebration of culture, community, and belonging. The event was called Midnimo, a Somali word that translates to unity, solidarity or peace.
The two headliners were Ilkacase Qeys, widely known as the “King of Somali Hip-Hop,” and Dalmar Yare. The event was hosted by the Community Organizing Alliance and Coffee By Design, alongside local community partners, including event organizer Mohamed Khalid.
“Beyond the music, we also incorporated nonpartisan civic engagement, a core part of COA’s work. title: Mount Desert Island hosts annual marathon, half, & relay
text:
MOUNT DESERT ISLAND, Maine (WABI) - The chilly autumn weather didn’t slow down the runners on Mount Desert Island as they participated in this year’s “Run MDI” marathon.
MDI’s Marathon, Half & Relay, hosted by Crow Athletics, takes runners through a scenic route against the backdrop of Acadia National Park: starting in Bar Harbor and ending in Southwest Harbor.
All runners received a “crusher claw” medallion after completing the race, with the 1st overall male and female runner in the full marathon taking home cash prizes of $1,000 each.

Vassalboro man seriously injured in Maine Turnpike crash
text:
Three people were hospitalized following a multi-vehicle crash on the Maine Turnpike in Falmouth late Saturday night, according to a news release from a Maine State Police spokesman.
Officials say 24-year-old Devon Thomas of Vassalboro was critically injured when he lost control of his Hyundai Elantra, hitting several guardrails before coming to a stop in the middle of the highway just before midnight.
Thomas’s vehicle also struck a car driven by 36-year-old Pruxelles Mujinga of Portland, and another driven by 22-year-old Madeleine Camaran-Moyers of Lewiston.
Traffic was diverted from exit 63 while the the injured drivers were treated by fire and EMS officials. All three were transported to Maine Medical Center in Portland.
Falmouth and Cumberland police also responded to the scene.

title: NASCAR building 80 cars for new movie starring Tom Cruise
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - NASCAR is reportedly building more than 80 race cars for an upcoming movie starring one of the most iconic American actors.
Tom Cruise announced in an Aug. 29 social media post that a “Days of Thunder” sequel is set to come out in the summer of 2028.
The original 1990 film became a favorite among race fans and was among the top-grossing films of that year at the box office.
NASCAR CEO Steve O’Donnell talked about the “Days of Thunder” sequel in a live podcast-style interview with Front Office Sports on Tuesday, Oct. 13.
“Tom’s message to us was, ‘I’m going to put you in front of an entirely new audience, and you need to be ready,’” O’Donnell said.
“And so there’s some things we’ll work together on. You know, do people understand the points system? How does The Chase work? How long are your races? All these things kind of to make sure that a new fan who may come out to the racetrack understands. Because for us, this is a whole new open door for us to bring new fans.”
O’Donnell said the original “Days of Thunder” showcased what NASCAR was in the 1990s. He suggested the new one would showcase what NASCAR is like now, and would embrace the technology and “everything that goes into the sport.”
The CEO also revealed an interesting request from Cruise.
Apparently, the legendary actor wanted to actually race in a real event to make the movie authentic.
O’Donnell said he was “shocked” by the request.
“I’m not sure that’s going to happen,” O’Donnell said of Cruise racing. “But he wants it to be as authentic as it can be. We’ll still see how the story lines, but all that’s playing out right now. I will tell you, we’re producing probably over 80 race cars that are going to be part of this. Some we don’t expect to be back; they’ll be wrecked.”
O’Donnell said the wrecked cars may be taken and left in places across the country and globe to help grow interest in NASCAR.
“You look at this long term of, OK, you’ve got race cars, some of them have been wrecked in the movie. Where can we leave these?” the CEO said in the Oct. 13 interview. “It’s an opportunity for us across the board.”
The new “Days of Thunder” is reportedly scheduled to start filming in March 2027. It is set to release in theaters on June 2, 2028.
Starring alongside Cruise, who will reprise his role as “Cole Trickle,” will be fellow acting icon Anne Hathaway. Cruise confirmed in an interview with Pat McAfee that Trickle’s character will return as a driver.
It is not yet clear where the movie will be filmed. The original included many locations around the Charlotte area and was filmed at multiple tracks across the Carolinas.

title: A.J. Brown struggles in return to Patriots in win over Jets
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — It was anything but smooth for A.J. Brown in his return to the New England Patriots on Sunday.
The prized offseason acquisition for the defending AFC champions finished with as many catches as dropped passes — three — and even drew a round of boos after a third-quarter drop in New England’s 26-19 win over the New York Jets.
His high ankle sprain might be in the past following a four-game stint on injured reserve, but the wide receievers hands were anything but a sure in his first game since New England’s season opener at Seattle.
The 29-year-old Brown was activated on Saturday after missing a minimum number of games after going on IR. He was in the starting lineup Sunday and finished with 27 yards receiving on 10 targets.
“No excuses. Ankle or not, I should make those plays,” said Brown, who spoke briefly while standing at his locker.
Brown’s first appearance on the Gillette Stadium video board came 48 minutes before kickoff. He received a nice applause from the crowd while he was warming up. Brown was also the final member of the Patriots’ offense to be introduced and received an extended ovation as he jumped and waved his arms in response.
By the third quarter, the good cheer from fans evaporated. One of the drops came in the second quarter when Drake Maye targeted him deep. Brown also let an onside kick by the Jets slip through his grasp, though the lapse didn’t hurt as tight end Eli Raridon fell on the ball and New England ran out the final 32 seconds.
Neither Brown’s coach or teammates expressed concern after the game. They said they know that a player with six 1,000-yard receiving seasons and three Pro Bowl nods will be fine in the long term.
“I know he wanted to do well for his football team,” said Patriots coach Mike Vrabel, who also coached Brown when the receiver broke into the NFL with Tennessee. “Unfortunately, it wasn’t his best effort. He knows that. We have all the confidence in the world in A.J. to be able to finish those plays. He has high expectations for himself, and we have high expectations for him.”
On the sideline, New England refrained from providing words of encouragement to Brown during his first game at Gillette Stadium as a Patriot.
“He’s been in the league a long time. He knows how to deal with things,” Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez said. “He’s been out for a while, so it’s different when you get out there and catch the ball when everyone is flying around. Everyone in the locker room and in this building, we have the utmost confidence in him.”

title: Ineffective Collins needs to go
text:
If Sen. Susan Collins was “one of the most powerful people in America,” as one of her ads claims, she would be able to build coalitions to effect change. She would be able to act on her “concerns” rather than just being an empty vote when it doesn’t matter.
She enables those who want to tear down the Constitution, rule by executive order, issue pardons to criminals, detain American citizens and throw them in camps, deny better healthcare and destroy our environment instead of making the polluters responsible. She votes for completely unqualified administrative leaders and judges who make the courts political.
If she is so powerful she should be able to push through meaningful legislation so that she wouldn’t have to keep running around putting out fires. After 30 years if the best she can do is wring her hands and be concerned then it’s time for change.
Lynn Irish
Hallowell

title: As an Oregon community mourns 4 killed in school shooting, 2 wounded survivors remain hospitalized
text:
BEND, Ore. (AP) — A special-needs teacher and student wounded in a deadly shooting at an Oregon elementary school remained hospitalized Saturday. But friends said their survival was a spot of hope in a community in mourning.
The youngest shooting survivor, 7-year-old Saylor Graham, is a feisty, vibrant fighter with a sweet nature whose story inspired other children, said Matt Sampson, executive director of Sparrow Clubs, where she was a member. She has a genetic disorder, usually uses a wheelchair and is non-verbal, but “she doesn’t even need words to connect with people,” he said.
“She’s just an amazing spirit who just immediately draws people to her and you just feel inspired by Saylor when you meet her,” Sampson said. “And she’s always wearing these iconic glasses, whether they’re pink or they’re red. She’s just such a cutie.”
Teacher Becky Drury, 54, is recovering in a Bend hospital with wounds to her arm and hand but hopes to go home soon, said Zack Hall, a family friend who is serving as her family’s spokesperson.
Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and a teacher were killed at the Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, Thursday when a former student there, 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, entered a special needs classroom and began firing with a shotgun.
One teacher was grappling with John for the weapon when the father of two students came in and shot him to death. They were credited with stopping the rampage and saving many people’s lives.
While police continued to investigate John’s motive, distraught parents, teachers and others gathered outside the school Saturday to leave flowers, pray and cry.
Savannah Patton, a mother who has a 1st and 4th grader at the school, sat on the grass Saturday across from a memorial of flowers, stuffed animals and balloons, and wiped tears from her eyes.
She told an Associated Press reporter that the teacher who died, Megan Lambert, 25, had been a substitute for her daughter’s class last year.
Patton said she has struggled to explain what happened to her daughter, who asked her, “Mommy, why would someone want to take a gun and kill us at school?” Patton said it was a question she didn’t know how to answer.
Physical challenges won’t keep her from “living with joy”
For several years, Saylor worked with students from Bend High School through the Sparrow Clubs, a volunteer group whose mission is to empower “kids to help kids in medical need” through kindness and community service, according to their website.
In a video on the Sparrow Clubs page, Saylor introduces herself, saying she loves watching Bluey and being around other kids, especially her brother. She said that while she is challenged by physical and cognitive issues, she can communicate with her eyes and a computer tablet.
“I prove every day that I’m a fighter who doesn’t give up,” she wrote in the video. ”Living with CASK-related challenges is full of unknowns, which can be very hard and scary for my whole family,” she said, “But it doesn’t keep me from smiling, laughing and living with joy!”
Some of the high school students who worked with Saylor said helping her gave them hope that there is still humanity in this world.
After the shooting, she was taken to a hospital in Portland. A GoFundMe for her family has raised almost $400,000.
“We will not let her name be forgotten”
Devon Johnson visited the memorial outside the school Saturday morning. Her husband teaches at Bend High School, and she is a volleyball coach at High Desert Middle School, so they are close with many of the staff at the elementary school.
“It’s just hard to take in,” she said. “I’m so glad to see that Bend is rallying and just wrapping their arms around this community, but it’s going to take a long time to get through this.”
Heidi Wood, the director of the Central Oregon Volleyball Club where Lambert coached, said in a social media post that she was “an amazing coach, ”an amazing teacher,” and “an amazing person who would do anything” for her students.
“To the shooter, she would have given you the shirt off her back,” Wood said. “But you didn’t give her a chance.”
Wood said that Lambert wouldn’t take her volleyball coaching pay in her first year so the money could be used for scholarships for players who couldn’t afford to play instead.
“That was her, and that is her,” Wood said. “We will carry on her love, her passion and we will not let her name be forgotten.”
___
Bellisle reported from Seattle. Associated Press writer Haven Daley contributed to his report.

title: Four for Lamoreau, 19 for Wisdom and a Huge Day at the PVC Championships
text:
The County Scoreboard: Four Goals for Lamoreau, Soccer Shutouts and PVC Championships Highlight Saturday
Saturday was a busy day for Aroostook County high school sports, with plenty of soccer action and an outstanding showing from County runners at the PVC Cross Country Championships.
Easton's Drew Lamoreau led the soccer highlights with four goals, Wisdom's boys and girls combined for 19 goals, and several County teams picked up shutout victories as the regular season approaches its final days.
Meanwhile, County runners brought home three team championships, two individual titles and both Coach of the Year honors at the PVC Championships in Old Town.
With Wednesday, October 21 marking the final countable day for soccer, the playoff picture is coming into focus, and there are still some important games left to play.
Boys Soccer
Lamoreau Scores Four in Easton's Win Over Southern Aroostook
Drew Lamoreau had a big afternoon for Easton, scoring four times as the Bears defeated Southern Aroostook 7-1.
Mason Pelletier added two goals, while Aaden Tibbetts scored once to round out the Bears' offense.
Josiah Ellis contributed two assists in the victory.
Caribou Blanks Hermon Again
Caribou continued its strong play with another 2-0 shutout victory over Hermon.
The Vikings also defeated the Hawks by the same score in their previous meeting, giving Caribou two shutout wins over Hermon in just over a week.
Wisdom Puts Up 11 Against East Grand
Wisdom had one of the biggest offensive performances of the day, defeating East Grand 11-0.
The Pioneers earned the shutout as they continued their final stretch of regular-season play.
Central Aroostook Shuts Out Woodland
Central Aroostook picked up a 2-0 victory over Woodland.
The Panthers added another win to their record as they prepare for the postseason.
John Bapst Defeats Presque Isle
Presque Isle dropped a 3-0 decision to John Bapst in Saturday's rematch.
The Wildcats had also fallen to the Crusaders earlier in the week, 4-2.
Orono Edges Fort Kent
Fort Kent came up just short against Orono, falling 2-1.
The Warriors were involved in one of Saturday's closest boys soccer matchups.
Girls Soccer
Lapierre Adds Another Hat Trick for Van Buren
Emily Lapierre continued her outstanding week with another hat trick as Van Buren defeated Easton 5-0.
Madelyn Marquis added a goal for the Lady Crusaders, who earned the shutout victory.
Lapierre also scored three times against Ashland on Thursday, including the overtime winner, giving her six goals over the two games.
Wisdom Spreads the Scoring Around Against East Grand
Wisdom rolled to an 8-0 victory over East Grand, with five different players finding the back of the net.
Ellie Cyr, Madi Cyr and Blake Pelletier each scored twice for the Lady Pioneers.
Peyton Roy and Hanna Martin added one goal apiece to complete the scoring.
Fort Kent Picks Up Close Win Over Orono
Fort Kent earned a 3-2 victory over Orono in one of Saturday's tighter girls soccer games.
The Lady Warriors picked up the one-goal win as the regular season enters its final days.
Presque Isle Battles John Bapst
Presque Isle played another close game against John Bapst but fell 3-2.
Hailey Plant and Peyton Boinske scored for the Lady Wildcats, with Lucy Cheney adding an assist.
It was the second competitive meeting between the two teams during the week, following John Bapst's 5-4 double-overtime victory on Monday.
Hermon Shuts Out Caribou
Hermon defeated Caribou 8-0 in Saturday's girls soccer matchup.
The Hawks also won the previous meeting between the two teams earlier in the month.
County Runners Bring Home PVC Championships
While soccer teams were busy across the region, Aroostook County runners were putting together an impressive afternoon at the PVC Cross Country Championships in Old Town.
Houlton/GHCA's boys captured the Small School championship, Presque Isle's girls won the Large School title, and Caribou's boys brought home the Large School championship.
Caribou's Pierce Gorneault and Emma Graves added individual titles, while the County also swept the conference coaching honors.
Caribou's Thomas Beckum was named PVC Large School Girls Coach of the Year, and Presque Isle's Dylan Marrero earned PVC Boys Large School Coach of the Year, and Houlton's Chris Rines earned PVC Small School Boys Coach of the Year honors.
Three team championships, two individual victories and two coaching awards made it quite a day for County cross country.
Soccer's Final Days Are Here
With the final countable day now set for Wednesday, October 21, County soccer teams are running out of opportunities to improve their postseason positions.
Saturday brought plenty of big performances, including Lamoreau's four-goal afternoon, another hat trick from Lapierre and shutout victories for several County teams.
There are still some important matchups ahead, but the focus is quickly shifting toward tournament soccer.
And with the success County runners enjoyed at the PVC Championships, championship season is already off to an impressive start across Aroostook County.

title: Obituary: Stephen “Steve” Thibodeau
text:
FAIRFIELD – Stephen “Steve” Thibodeau, 69, passed away on Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026. He was born on Aug. 16, 1957, to Maurice and Methyl (Haslam) Thibodeau.
Steve spent much of his life working with automotive parts and small engines. Known to many as “the parts guy,” he was the owner of DAC Distributors in Clinton. He took great pride in his work and was known for his incredible knowledge of the industry. His lifelong passion for cars and racing brought him tremendous enjoyment.
Above all, Steve will be remembered for his hard work, generous heart, and kind spirit. Those who knew him often described him as “the nicest guy in the world” and someone who “would give the shirt off his back to anyone.” He treasured his family and the relationships he built throughout his life.
Steve was predeceased by his beloved wife, Lucille “Lucy” Thibodeau; his parents, Maurice and Methyl; his brothers Larry, Mike, and Kevin, and his sister, Brenda.
He is survived by his daughter, Janneen King, and her husband, James; his beloved grandchildren, Kennedy, James, Makayla, Hunter and Takashi; his brother, Rick; his stepdaughters Kami Maheu and Kathy Alley; and many cherished nieces and nephews.
He shared a very special bond with his granddaughter, Savanna Fasulo, who was his sidekick until the very end. She was his devoted caretaker and protector, and their connection was a treasured part of his life.
Steve’s passing leaves a tremendous void in the lives of those who loved him. His generosity, kindness, and willingness to help others will never be forgotten. The memories he leaves behind will live on in the hearts of his family and all who had the privilege of knowing him.
A celebration of life will be held on Sunday, Oct. 25, at 1 p.m., at O’Brien’s in Waterville, to honor Steve and celebrate the life he lived.
The family would like to extend their heartfelt thanks to his doctor, Margaret and nurses Mary and Karen at MaineGeneral. For over a decade, you cared for Steve with compassion and kindness, making him feel like family.
He will be deeply missed, forever loved, and never forgotten.

title: Despairing at wealth concentration in a ‘post-government’ world
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Having voted since 1968, I find my election cynicism at a demoralizing level this year.
It’s hard to point to one thing that has hardened my cynicism, but the obscene concentration of wealth tops my list.
Our version of capitalism has given Elon Musk personal wealth greater than the GDP of 174 nations, while 86 million live in poverty or near poverty. There are many ultra-wealthy not far behind him and, with the carte blanche of Citizens United, that wealth has exponentially increased influence. We are now in a “post-government” world, where wealthy oligarchs make the decisions regardless of electoral outcomes. Who do they answer to?
We witnessed an example of “post-government” recently when President Trump had the AI billionaires to the White House to discuss AI regulation. The solution? No regulation. Let the geniuses regulate themselves. The most threatening technology since the atom bomb. But trust them.
Herb Fox
Limerick

Cumberland Fire Chief Daniel Small said three people were taken to the hospital. First responders had to extricate one person from a car, which took about half an hour.

title: American photographer attacked by Israeli settlers feels 'insulted' by Netanyahu's response
text:
American photographer attacked by Israeli settlers feels 'insulted' by Netanyahu's response
The photographer with The Washington Post who was attacked by Jewish settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank so badly that several vertebrae were broken said Sunday she was increasingly angry that Israel’s military seems to protect settlers more than the Palestinians they threaten.
The attack on Heidi Levine and Palestinians during the sensitive olive harvest — followed a day later by an attack on European diplomats in a Christian village — again highlights the rampant settler violence that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has blamed on a small number of troublemakers.
Levine, from her hospital bed, has told The Associated Press she was “shocked and insulted” that Netanyahu referred to the attack on her and others as alleged, adding that the prime minister “had all the evidence on the table.”
But she described the sharp condemnation of settler violence expressed to her in a call from Israel’s president, and in a letter signed by several of the country’s top former security and intelligence officials. All expressed shame over the attack.
Netanyahu, two weeks out from close elections that could end his time in power, is again confronted with an issue that has drawn growing international condemnation. Most of the world, under international law, considers the settlements in the West Bank illegal, and yet construction and expansion continue.
Hundreds of Palestinians have been attacked and multiple have been killed this olive harvest alone, which started in late September, rights groups have said. Olive trees, a central part of history and heritage and source of income for Palestinians, are regularly destroyed by Israeli settlers.
Levine blamed “Jewish terrorists” for Thursday's attack and added: “I’ve been covering this region for over 40 years, and I have never seen this country in such a state as it is today.”
Levine praises a call from Israel's president
Levine was recovering Sunday from injuries that included what appeared to be stab wounds in her buttocks, which required stitches. There was nothing new from police on the case, she said.
U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee, whose recent comments have condemned settler attacks on U.S. citizens but not on Palestinians overall, called the attack on Levine a “despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards” and said they should spend years in prison.
Separately, Israeli President Isaac Herzog called Levine, and Yair Golan, a former general and leader of the opposition Democrats party, visited. Netanyahu’s main rival in the elections, Gadi Eisenkot, said on X that “a handful of criminals is burning up the last shreds of legitimacy left to the state of Israel.”
Herzog was “actually very sweet,” Levine said Sunday. “Down to earth, calling them thugs, inviting me for a personal hug. He’s ashamed for what happened: ‘These people are a stain on Israeli society.’”
She said she has not heard from Netanyahu. She did receive, however, a letter signed by over a dozen former Israeli security, intelligence and other officials, including former Defense Minister Moshe Yaalon, former Mossad director Tamir Pardo and former Shin Bet director Ami Ayalon.
“We are deeply ashamed that Jewish terrorists in the West Bank continue to inflict suffering on innocent Palestinians, assault those who come to their defense, and target those who document and expose their despicable conduct,” said the letter, shared with the AP.
“Their brutality brings disgrace upon Israel and the Jewish people. Such acts undermine Israel’s security, its regional and international standing, and the moral fabric of our society. They represent a betrayal of everything we have devoted our lives to defending.”
The letter noted that “alas, with encouragement from the highest echelons of government,” only a fundamental change in policy can end the “disgraceful phenomenon.”
Levine says she plans to return to work
Levin told the AP that “I never wanted the story to be about me but about the people I’ve tried to document” over decades. She said she has sought to show how the violence is “increasing, becoming more and more dangerous.”
She has said the attackers — armed with bottles and slingshots — “were kicking me for like 10 minutes and I was trying to hold on to my cameras and my bag.” Her helmet and protective vest, which was marked “PRESS,” likely saved her from more serious injuries.
But she and others have openly wondered who will protect Palestinians. Rights groups have said few settlers are ever punished for the attacks that have surged in recent years.
“It’s about time you do something, Mr. Prime Minister,” Levine said.
As for herself, she plans to return to work.
“I’ve invested decades of blood, sweat and tears into this,” she said. “They cracked my bones, they haven’t cracked my spirit.”
Associated Press writer Sam Mednick in Tel Aviv, Israel, contributed to this report.

title: Ineffective Collins needs to go
text:
If Sen. Susan Collins was “one of the most powerful people in America,” as one of her ads claims, she would be able to build coalitions to effect change. She would be able to act on her “concerns” rather than just being an empty vote when it doesn’t matter.
She enables those who want to tear down the Constitution, rule by executive order, issue pardons to criminals, detain American citizens and throw them in camps, deny better healthcare and destroy our environment instead of making the polluters responsible. She votes for completely unqualified administrative leaders and judges who make the courts political.
If she is so powerful she should be able to push through meaningful legislation so that she wouldn’t have to keep running around putting out fires. After 30 years if the best she can do is wring her hands and be concerned then it’s time for change.
Lynn Irish
Hallowell

title: Death Notice: Danny Scott Goddard
Paris police report hundreds of arrests after violent clashes during protests
text:
France's Macron condemns those who 'sought to bring down the Republic' after rioting at nationwide protests
French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday voiced the public’s “anger” and “shame” over rioting and looting during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. At least 2,400 people were arrested.
Macron echoed other government officials in blaming much of the violence on far-left activists, accusing them of attacking police and public buildings to foment chaos.
“Those who looted will have to pay for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” Macron said in a televised address to the nation.
He denounced “unrestrained violence” by “insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals.”
Macron earlier held an emergency meeting with senior government officials, a day after masked groups set fires and attacked city halls in several cities. He said he had instructed prefects to work with mayors to protect public buildings and businesses in the coming weeks, including by banning protests when necessary.
Flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall in the city of Limoges, in central France, causing its roof to collapse and nearly destroying the building.
New tensions erupted in Paris on Sunday
In Paris, hundreds of protesters gathered again on Sunday at the Place de la République amid a heavy police presence. Officers used tear gas as tensions flared sporadically in the neighborhood, with small groups of people trying to set bicycles and trash bins on fire.
“The right to protest is a fundamental right. Deliberately and collectively sowing disorder through violence is not,” Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez wrote on X, citing the looting of hundreds of businesses across the country.
Authorities estimated Saturday's marches had a turnout of about 550,000, while organizers put it at 800,000. Demonstrators answered calls from a labor union, student organizations and activists hoping to revive the “yellow vest” movement, which emerged in 2018 to protest social injustice.
Mass protests in France are often marred by violence on the fringes of otherwise peaceful marches, leading to clashes with police. The arrest tally reported Sunday approached the nearly 2,000 recorded nationwide during a single day of yellow vest protests in December 2018.
Paris police said one person died of a heart attack, without providing details. The Paris prosecutor’s office said it was investigating.
Parisians deplore shattered shops and a damaged square
Dislodged cobblestones, shattered storefronts and broken glass littered the area around Paris’ Place de la République on Sunday. Looting and damage were also reported in other tourist and shopping districts.
Paris police said 855 people were arrested in the capital region. Prosecutors said 557 remained in police custody.
“I am actually stunned by the level of destruction and violence that was expressed,” said government employee Marie Peyreigne, 57, wondering what had led to the mayhem.
Parisians inspecting the damage photographed the partially dismantled base of the square’s central monument, a statue of Marianne, a symbol of France.
Jean Foissy, 74, said he had wanted to join the protest but encountered “a wall of riot police and fires everywhere” and returned home.
“I was very scared,” he said. “I’ve been a Parisian since I was born, so when I got here, it almost made me want to cry because I find it so bad, it hurts me.”
Margaux Eude, 26, said she supported the protest movement but “didn’t think it would escalate like this.”
“It’s the troublemakers who came, and it breaks my heart because it delegitimizes the movement,” she said.
Political leaders trade blame ahead of presidential election
Political leaders traded accusations over Saturday’s violence ahead of next spring’s presidential election.
Far-right leader and presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen criticized Macron's centrist government as “exhausted, disoriented and seemingly incapable of doing anything other than commenting on its own powerlessness,” in a video posted on social media.
Far-left contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu of “playing with fire,” alleging that “by banking on degradation, you have only succeeded in uniting all youths and workers’ unions.”
Mélenchon, who joined the Paris march Saturday, insisted that “my message is clear: those who share our fight have no business in looting or destruction.”
U.S. President Donald Trump posted “France is burning!” on his Truth Social platform, apparently linking the unrest to “the immigration of people from an entirely different world.”
“Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!” he wrote.
French authorities and police have not linked immigrants to the rioting. Macron, speaking about troublemakers, asked: "How can French people do this to France?”
Hundreds of businesses looted across the country
“The scale of the damage is considerable and unprecedented,” Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire wrote in an open letter. “Paris is a city of freedoms, debate and demonstrations. It must remain so. But it must also be a city where everyone can work and run a business safely.”
The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Lyon, the three largest cities, requested a meeting with the prime minister in the coming days “given the extent of the damage and the seriousness of the situation.”
In Marseille, some protesters briefly forced their way into City Hall's lobby and a group of people wearing hoods and masks damaged a police station. In Lyon, a fire broke out inside a tourist office.
In Limoges, the City Hall was ravaged by flames after “radical troublemakers” broke in while elected officials, employees, security personnel and members of the public were inside, Haute-Vienne prefect Maurice Barate said. “They deliberately set the building on fire. It is an extremely serious and unspeakable act,” he said.
In eastern France, the Mulhouse prosecutor’s office said an investigation has been opened after a 17-year-old girl was injured during the protests and lost an eye. On Saturday, another investigation was opened after a young protester lost a hand in Saint-Etienne.
The injuries come as police have drawn sharp scrutiny over their use of grenades and other riot-control weapons during recent demonstrations.

title: AP Top 25 live updates: A historic shake-up could be coming after 5 of the top 7 teams lose
text:
College football has never experienced a Saturday like this.
Five of the top seven teams in the AP Top 25 — No. 1 Georgia, No. 2 Notre Dame, No. 5 Indiana, No. 6 Alabama and No. 7 Texas — lost on the same day in the regular season for the first time in history.
That chaos is sure to shuffle the poll, starting at the top.
No. 3 Miami may have the clearest path to the top spot for the first time since 2002 after beating rival Florida State in a double-overtime thriller.
The biggest questions include how far Georgia, Notre Dame and Indiana might fall after close losses.
No. 1 Georgia lost 27-24 to Auburn and No. 2 Notre Dame lost 28-24 to BYU, marking the first time Nos. 1 and 2 lost on the same day in the regular season since 2012. And Indiana’s 22-game winning streak ended in gut-wrenching fashion against No. 4 Ohio State.
Here’s what to know:
Notre Dame-BYU could have unfolded differently
By MAURA CAREY
Notre Dame’s last chance to beat BYU fell incomplete in the end zone, but according to the Big 12, there was an officiating mistake and there was time for one last attempt in the 28-24 upset.
“Following the Big 12’s review of the final play of Saturday’s Notre Dame-BYU game, it was determined that time remained on the clock when the ball hit the ground and the play was incorrectly cleared by the replay officiating crew,” the Big 12 said in a statement. “The Conference will conduct a complete review of its end-of-game officiating process in advance of next week’s games.”
Who decides the rankings?
By THE ASSOCIATED PRESS
AP Top 25 voters are writers and broadcasters who cover college football.
AP employees do not vote, but they do choose the voters, and they seek wide representation from all over the country. This season, there are 69 voters.
The focus begins with voter representation in states with a Bowl Subdivision school, and the total number of voters from each state increases with the number of FBS teams. There are also spots reserved for national voters.
The AP allows broad latitude for voters to determine their rankings. They are urged to base their votes on performance, not reputation or preseason speculation (except, of course, for the always provocative preseason poll); to avoid regional bias, for or against; to pay attention to head-to-head results; and to make significant changes if desired.
A historic week in the Top 25
By ERIC OLSON
After a weekend never before seen for teams in The Associated Press Top 25, a major shake-up is on tap.
Five of the top seven teams in the rankings — No. 1 Georgia, No. 2 Notre Dame, No. 5 Indiana, No. 6 Alabama and No. 7 Texas — lost on the same day in the regular season for the first time in the history of the poll that began in 1936. It’s the first time Nos. 1 and 2 lost on the same day in the regular season since 2012 and eight Top 25 teams lost in all.

title: Woman saves future husband’s life after they were both struck by lightning while hiking
text:
TOWN OF EAGLE, Wis. (WTMJ) - A Chicago woman had to revive her future husband with CPR twice after they were both struck by lightning during a hiking trip.
Nick Broderick brought his then-girlfriend, Eva Broderick, to the Kettle Moraine State Forest in Wisconsin for a 10-mile hike last August. They were about two miles from their car when the weather changed.
“The rain just kept getting heavier and heavier as a really big rainstorm,” Nick Broderick said.
With nowhere to take shelter, the couple kept moving forward, but Eva Broderick was worried.
“She turned to me and said, ‘Nick, what if we get struck by lightning?’” Nick Broderick said.
Minutes later, that’s exactly what happened.
The rescue
Nick Broderick heard a boom, and it was the last thing he remembers. Firefighters say the tree next to the couple took a direct lightning hit, and they were struck by the ground current.
“All I remember was being curled in a fetal position with my hands over my ears, screaming, I think, and feeling what can only be described as electricity in my feet,” Eva Broderick said. “I was curled into Nick, and I looked over. He was laying on his back, his eyes were half open, glazed over, and he was blue and not breathing.”
Eva Broderick called 911 and immediately started CPR, but she couldn’t tell rescue crews where they were because the cell signal kept dropping. She also couldn’t remember where they had entered the forest or which path they were on.
“It’s pinging out a mile, a mile and a half into the forest area, but it’s not very specific. We just took our best guess and tried to send people everywhere we could,” Palmyra Fire Rescue Assistant Chief Dan Schiller said.
It took 50 minutes for crews to reach the couple on foot. In that time, Eva Broderick had to revive her boyfriend twice.
“That’s not something that normally happens,” Schiller said.
The proposal
Nick Broderick was taken to the hospital, where he spent three days recovering. He still has some hearing loss in one ear and tendon issues from the strike.
After he was released from the hospital, Nick Broderick proposed. The couple got married this August.
“We wanted to rewrite August and make it a better month,” Nick Broderick said.
“I’ve made the joke quite a few times that he can’t leave me. I brought him back from death, so he’s kind of stuck,” Eva Broderick said.
She will be honored with the Lifesavers Award at the Palmyra Fire Department in the coming weeks for her bravery in saving her boyfriend.

title: People killed, injured in incident at Canadian military base that caused major fire
text:
WAINWRIGHT, Alberta (AP) — Four Canadian service members were killed and 39 people injured, including 19 critically, when a fast-moving fire overtook soldiers conducting live-fire combat training at a military base in Alberta, officials said Sunday.
Maj. Gen. Wade Rutland said military officials knew about the fire for hours but believed it was sufficiently contained to allow training to continue before winds suddenly shifted, sending flames racing toward the soldiers.
“The fire was a kilometer away when the wind shifted. That is not normal for a fire to move a kilometer in 36 seconds,” he said at a news conference in Edmonton.
Rutland said a commander at the scene told him soldiers went from seeing no fire to having flames upon them in less than a minute.
The fire broke out Saturday during high-intensity combat training involving Charlie Company of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
About 84 soldiers were split between a grenade range and an area where they practiced attacks on simulated enemy positions. The fire swept into the second training area.
Rutland said investigators had not determined what ignited the grass fire.
He said the battalion was preparing for rapid deployment to global crises and a mission to reinforce Canadian troops in Latvia next spring.
The military identified those killed as Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton; Pvt. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; Pvt. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver, British Columbia; and Pvt. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, British Columbia. All four were serving with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, based in Edmonton.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said 39 people were receiving medical care. Sayeh Zielke, chief executive of Acute Care Alberta, said 19 were in critical condition, eight were stable and 12 were ambulatory and receiving treatment for less serious injuries.
Smith said some suffered severe burns and could face weeks or months of intensive treatment.
Prime Minister Mark Carney described the incident as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on domestic soil. He ordered flags lowered to half-staff on federal buildings nationwide.
Carney said the families of those killed had been notified. Those affected included regular forces personnel, reservists and soldiers from bases across Canada.
Hospitals respond to mass casualties
Alberta health officials said patients were transferred from Wainwright to four hospitals — the University of Alberta Hospital and Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton, Foothills Medical Centre in Calgary and Red Deer Regional Hospital.
Alberta officials said they had lifted the “Code Orange” emergency activated at several hospitals Saturday night to mobilize staff and beds for the casualties.
The response involved 22 ground ambulances, six airplanes and two helicopters, with assistance from neighboring Saskatchewan. Smith said all patients had been accounted for and no further patients were awaiting transport.
Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the town’s small hospital was not designed to handle a mass-casualty incident but praised local medical personnel.
Rutland confirmed that military search-and-rescue technicians parachuted into Wainwright to reinforce the emergency response. Pugh said their red parachutes were illuminated by flares as they descended shortly before midnight.
Cathy Keane, a mayoral candidate in Ontario, said her eldest son was among those critically injured. “As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family,” she wrote on Facebook, saying she was traveling to Alberta.
Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre, who represents the area in Parliament, visited Wainwright on Sunday and said he had heard accounts of people who ran toward the danger to help others and were now fighting for their lives in hospitals.
Military investigates fire
Rutland said the fire ignited in the military training area, where multiple exercises were underway, and spread rapidly in unusually strong winds.
He said winds had been within normal operating limits for much of Saturday, generally below 50 kph (31 mph), before intensifying rapidly. Range controllers rely on weather reports to determine whether training can safely continue, he said.
Rutland said investigators would examine whether the wind drove the fire toward the soldiers or whether flames spread unseen through vegetation before suddenly overtaking them.
The fire crossed established firebreaks before being contained with help from municipal firefighters.
The Canadian military said there were no indications of terrorism.
Rutland said military investigators would examine the circumstances, including whether safety protocols needed to change. “If our protocols need to change, then they’ll be updated,” he said.
The military typically convenes a formal board of inquiry after such incidents, Rutland said, cautioning that determining what happened would take time.
Rutland said Charlie Company had been withdrawn from the training area and the rest of the battalion suspended training Sunday.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4 p.m. Saturday following reports of a fire in the base’s training area.
Large areas of Alberta were hit by a windstorm Saturday, with gusts up to 100 kph (62 mph). The winds toppled trees, sent signs flying and pushed flames beyond the base into surrounding rural areas.
By late Saturday, the Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. No evacuation order was issued for residents.
CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations.
The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday’s referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada. Elections Alberta said the Wainwright Communiplex advance polling location closed early Saturday and election materials were transported securely.

title: Blaze at St. Petersburg oil sites as Kyiv launches more than 1,000 drones at Russia
text:
Blaze at St. Petersburg oil sites as Kyiv launches more than 1,000 drones at Russia
Ukrainian attacks set an oil export terminal ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday, as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones across Russia in one of its largest ever aerial bombardments.
Related video: Trump waives new sanctions on Russia under law named for late Sen. Graham
The attack comes amid deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington, with U.S. President Donald Trump criticizing Kyiv for its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
One person was killed and five more were wounded in the attack, which sparked fires at both the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city's Ruchi oil depot, said local Gov. Alexander Beglov. A logistics center belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data center for local tech giant VK were also targeted, both companies confirmed.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.
Meanwhile, a woman died and at least two other people were wounded, including a 6-year-old girl, after Russia launched two attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said.
Two apartment buildings, 18 cars and an educational institution were damaged as a result of the attack, head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration Mykhailo Semikin said.
U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.
Ukraine confirmed Thursday it had resumed attacks on Russian oil after a three-day hiatus.
Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of his country's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump's demand on Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government initially said that it was heeding the ceasefire.
In a post on X Sunday, Zelenskyy said that in the week since Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire, Russia had attacked Ukraine's energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times.
He also said that in the past night alone, energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions had been attacked and tens of thousands of families were still without power. He accused Russia of trying to cause a blackout.
"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," he wrote.
Zelenskyy also stressed that the war was continuing due to Russia's invasion — not because Ukraine was defending itself.
"It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance. Thank you to everyone who understands this and helps," he said.

title: Customers line up for last meal at Rockland restaurant
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ROCKLAND — As has been the case for nearly two decades, customers lined the parking lot awaiting the opening of the Home Kitchen Cafe.
On Sunday, customers lined up again for the final day of the popular Rockland restaurant.
Stephanie Cech said Home Kitchen has been her “go to” restaurant.
“All of the staff is so friendly and make you feel like home,” she said.
Cech’s favorite meal is breakfast fried rice. That meal consists of fried rice with two eggs, snow peas, carrots, roasted red pepper, fresh garlic, ginger, and other options.
Loren Beaver said he has been going to Home Kitchen since he moved to Rockland a few years ago. He lives in the neighborhood, so he walks to the restaurant at 650 Main St.
Beaver said Home Kitchen has a really good atmosphere and is a great place. He said he enjoys mixing with the other customers and the staff.
“Everybody is happy here,” he said.
He said he varies what he orders but that on a Sunday, it is often an eggs Benedict.
Penny York said she goes to Home Kitchen quite a bit. Penny was in line with her friend Renee who have been friends since school.
“This is our breakfast meet up spot. This is where we’ve been coming for years to get caught up every six months or so,” York said. “When people come from out of town and ask me where they should go to eat, where am I going to see real local people and with good food, I say Home Kitchen.”
For York, huevos rancheros is her favorite meal. Home Kitchen’s huevos rancheros is two poached eggs finished in its original spicy salsa roja topped with pepper jack cheese, house-made black beans over hand-made corn tortillas.
Her friend Renee said the make-your-own omelette is her favorite.
Owners James Hatch and Susan Schiro announced Oct. 3 in a Facebook post they would close the restaurant they have operated for the past 18 years. The bakery at the Rankin block is also closing.
“This place has always been about more than food. It’s been about doing things the right way, every single day. From scratch cooking to genuine hospitality, we set a standard for ourselves and worked hard to live up to it. This is not a post we ever thought we would make, but in today’s world, maintaining our level of quality has become increasingly challenging. Like many in our industry, we’ve faced a growing struggle to find and keep the skilled, dedicated team needed to consistently deliver the experience our customers expect and deserve. Rather than compromise what Home Kitchen Cafe stands for, we feel it’s the right time to step away,” the couple wrote.
“To our incredible employees, past and present, you are the heart of this story. Your commitment, resilience, and pride in your work carried us through every busy morning and every demanding season. Quite simply, we would not have made it this far without you.
And to our loyal customers and community, thank you for your unwavering support over the years. You filled our dining room, shared your lives with us, and made this journey deeply meaningful.”
The couple opened the business in February 2009. They initially leased the property from the Fish family but purchased the property in May 2011. The cafe underwent major renovations in late 2012 and reopened in February 2013.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Rangeley to explore snowmobile club park-and-ride
text:
The town of Rangeley will consider working with the Rangeley Snowmobile Club to construct a parking lot on Loon Lake Road, which would alleviate the strain on the downtown in winter.
Club member Dana Bowman and Brent West of the High Peaks Alliance presented updated information about the project to the board at an Oct. 5 meeting.
Rangeley Snowmobile Club applied for a $175,000 Maine Trail Bond grant to cover the construction of the park-and-ride, which would be up to two acres.
The club originally sought to use the funds to build a lot on Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust Land off Route 17, but wetlands there prevented the project from moving forward. They are now seeking a lot on town property next to the club’s groomer barn near the transfer station.
West said a new lot, for both vehicles and snowmobiles, would reduce strain on the five parking options in Rangeley, Oquossoc and Sandy River Plantation. He pointed to large trucks and trailers clogging up the downtown lots, as well as the unsanctioned parking on Morton Cutoff Road, as reasons for the request.
“This is trying to address some of those downtown problems,” West told the board.
A resident asked if the proposed space could impact future transfer station needs. Town Manager Joe Roach said there is cleared space within the 100-acre lot that would better suit any future expansion.
“I think we could reinvent the area that’s already cleared and make it more efficient,” Roach said. “That’s always been my vision for it. I don’t think you need more land there. I think the section next to the groomer barn is probably the best piece of land there because it does abut them.”
Bowman said that the club would be flexible to the town’s preference for ownership and upkeep, saying that either way, they would take care of the winter maintenance.
“We’d be willing to do the lease part of it,” he said. “Or if the town wanted to own the parking lot and we still did the maintenance, we wouldn’t have an issue with that either.”
West said he would like the construction completed by the end of 2027. Taking longer could impact the club’s ability to receive future grants.
The board voted unanimously to allow the town manager to send the grant to the town attorney and to draft a memorandum of understanding for review, not final approval. Members of the board also requested a site visit for this fall.

Authorities later posted a photo of the emu posing with police and its owner.

title: Despairing at wealth concentration in a ‘post-government’ world
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Having voted since 1968, I find my election cynicism at a demoralizing level this year.
It’s hard to point to one thing that has hardened my cynicism, but the obscene concentration of wealth tops my list.
Our version of capitalism has given Elon Musk personal wealth greater than the GDP of 174 nations, while 86 million live in poverty or near poverty. There are many ultra-wealthy not far behind him and, with the carte blanche of Citizens United, that wealth has exponentially increased influence. We are now in a “post-government” world, where wealthy oligarchs make the decisions regardless of electoral outcomes. Who do they answer to?
We witnessed an example of “post-government” recently when President Trump had the AI billionaires to the White House to discuss AI regulation. The solution? No regulation. Let the geniuses regulate themselves. The most threatening technology since the atom bomb. But trust them.
Herb Fox
Limerick

title: Brewers fan hopes 'Timeless Ticket' secures World Series seat
text:
Brewers fan redeems 12-year-old 'Timeless Ticket' for World Series game
A Brewers fan who bought a "Timeless Ticket" 12 years ago is finally using it to attend Game 1 of the World Series.
Brewers fan redeems 12-year-old 'Timeless Ticket' for World Series game
A Brewers fan who bought a "Timeless Ticket" 12 years ago is finally using it to attend Game 1 of the World Series.
Nate Holzman, a lifelong Milwaukee Brewers fan, is set to attend Game 1 of the World Series after redeeming a "Timeless Ticket" he purchased 12 years ago.
Holzman, originally from Oak Creek and now living in Los Angeles, was one of 1,000 people to buy the embossed "Timeless Ticket" from the Brewers more than a decade ago. The ticket, which cost $1,000, guaranteed a seat to any future game of his choice.
"Since that story ran on Friday, I've heard from a thousand of my closest friends. People I haven't heard from forever, social media, I guess it's all over social media," Holzman said.
After attending Game 3 of the National League Championship Series in Los Angeles, Holzman decided to cash in his ticket. He waited anxiously for a few days before the Brewers confirmed over the weekend that he would be attending Game 1 of the World Series.
"The Brewers are going to the World Series, and I'm going to the World Series! Doesn't get any better than that!" Holzman said.
Holzman, a new father, reflected on the significance of the moment, noting that his daughter is the same age he was the last time the Brewers made it to the World Series.
"Am I going to need to maybe transfer this ticket to my daughter's name because I die before the Brewers make it to the World Series, like, that seriously did cross my mind multiple times, but luckily I don't have to worry about that anymore," he said.
On Friday afternoon, Holzman will complete the final step by visiting the Will Call window at American Family Field, where he'll show his ID and ticket confirmation to claim his tickets.
Although Holzman did not have to pay extra for his own ticket, the ticket also allowed him to purchase three additional terrace seats at face value for $1,000 each. He said he was happy to pay the price so his parents and a friend could join him for the game.

I encourage all Freeport residents to vote in favor of the ordinance amendment to allow the Island Rover to be launched. It is unfortunate to need an ordinance to allow the Island Rover to be launched, but so far the obstructionists have prevented it from happening.
Opponents of the measure are afraid of all the things that could go wrong, but let’s not be afraid of this.
The language on the ballot for this question sounds like there are many extreme changes that the ordinance will create. It minimizes a very important fact: Section 10 of the proposed ordinance states that it is subject to review and approval of the Maine Department of Environmental Protection and that it shall only remain in effect for two years. Then it goes away.
Launching the Island Rover can be a safe and successful operation. It’s time to let it happen.

Freeport

title: Trump’s Russian diesel deal was the final straw for me
text:
Sam Patten has worked for Maine’s last three Republican senators, including Susan Collins’ first electoral campaigns, is a former managing editor of The Maine Wire and is the author of “Dangerous Company: The Misadventures of a Foreign Agent.”
When Donald J. Trump was again elected president in 2024, I figured he had earned his second chance. Regardless of whether I had voted for him that year, in 2020 or in 2016, he and I shared an experience that made me more open to him than anyone in my family or most of my friends.
At the time, I was the managing editor of the Maine Wire — the conservative voice in our state’s media. Covering his second administration to the extent it affects Maine from this perspective, I strained at times to understand and explain why he was doing the things he was. The flurry of executive orders at the very outset, for instance, suggested a new kind of energy. Some of his appointments, like Marco Rubio to his array of jobs and Tulsi Gabbard as director of national intelligence, struck me as promising.
It only took me until Feb. 28 of last year to get physically nauseated.
Trump’s jocks v. geek style beat-down session on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in the Oval Office punctured any Christian notions I had of redemption. It was disgusting. But I was also so very tired of Americans feeling their politics. I resolved to carry on trying the best I could to be objective — all the while hoping for better.
Due to his erratic and, at times, nonsensical behavior, I’ve come to think of Trump as mad. I would not be surprised if more than a few of my fellow Republicans think the same way.
“Should I be glad he didn’t throw spaghetti at the wall?” a now former GOP congresswoman asked me rhetorically in 2016 when, making small talk, I gamely asked if she didn’t agree Trump had made more sense at a recent media event than he had previously. She’d had enough. She went on to lose her seat that year to a Democrat Volvo salesman.
I hit that point this past weekend, on a flight back from Ukraine.
At the end of last year, I left my job at the Maine Wire to work full time on a Ukrainian consultancy project. So far this year, I’ve spent more than four months in Ukraine and over this period things have gotten worse in terms of the war.
After more than four years of a Russian invasion, Ukrainians have now begun deep strikes into Russia, primarily targeting its oil sector. So, the news that last Friday Trump moved to lift sanctions on Russian diesel and struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import nominal quantities of it into the U.S., allegedly to alleviate spiking fuel prices, was a lot to take on the back of a trip throughout which Russian shelling of civilian sites was constant.
My common experience with Trump goes back to 2018-19 during the Russia-gate probe. Then I was charged with, and pleaded guilty to, the charge of being an unregistered foreign agent for a Ukrainian politician.
Compared with a foreign power deciding who gets elected to Congress and who doesn’t, my crime — drafting talking points and op-eds for my client — could be considered risible or quaint, depending on your perspective. But, having been prosecuted as part of a broader investigation of whether Trump colluded with Russia in his first election, I remain a felon. I never sought a pardon.
There is no credible argument supporting Trump’s decision on Russian diesel. The amounts involved will not give much relief to U.S. consumers — at best 20 minutes of domestic demand, some calculate. The real problem is the fact that the Strait of Hormuz is effectively closed; that is what is driving today’s prices at the pump. And whatever revenues Russia gets will be spent on its war effort, murdering Ukrainian civilians.
So why on God’s green earth is he doing it?
Maine’s Sen. Susan Collins is right to join three other Senate Republicans in demanding the president reverse this decision. It doesn’t mean he’ll listen.
For Republicans, Trump’s insane decisions have a way of increasing in their tempo right up to consequential elections. His taking out the well-respected and highly effective Texas senator John Cornyn to run the toadying and corrupt Ken Paxton, now runs the risk of the Republican Party losing the Lone Star State for the first time in two generations. Zero sense, yet loyalists must put and shut up.
One of the reasons I once gave Trump the time of day was the seemingly insane behavior of his enemies. The “lawfare” exercised against him was real. I experienced it personally. Instead of fixing the system, however, he made it worse.
Now, Republicans who harbor any chance of withstanding the blue wave that’s coming in three weeks’ time must sidestep — or counter — the leader of their party. Ask Paul LePage about his deported in-law. Or placeholder Darline Graham about her brother Lindsey’s legacy: a hardline sanctions bill on Russia that Trump now flouts.
Whether it’s corruption, nuclear-powered narcissism or full-blown insanity, speculating about the “why” is no longer entertaining. Trump supporters are often forced to overlook the weirdness and remember the bigger objective. But when the betrayals knock with such manic insistence at your door, it becomes difficult, if not impossible, to see the larger benefit.
