title: Sunday Photos: October 18th, 2026
People killed, injured in an incident at a military base in Canada
text:
Four soldiers killed, 19 other people critically injured after grass fire at Canadian military
Four Canadian service members were killed and 39 people injured, including 19 critically, when a fast-moving fire overtook soldiers conducting live-fire combat training at a military base in Alberta, officials said Sunday.
Maj. Gen. Wade Rutland said military officials knew about the fire for hours but believed it was sufficiently contained to allow training to continue before winds suddenly shifted, sending flames racing toward the soldiers.
“The fire was a kilometer away when the wind shifted. That is not normal for a fire to move a kilometer in 36 seconds,” he said at a news conference in Edmonton.
Rutland said a commander at the scene told him soldiers went from seeing no fire to having flames upon them in less than a minute.
The fire broke out Saturday during high-intensity combat training involving Charlie Company of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
About 84 soldiers were split between a grenade range and an area where they practiced attacks on simulated enemy positions. The fire swept into the second training area.
Rutland said investigators had not determined what ignited the grass fire.
He said the battalion was preparing for rapid deployment to global crises and a mission to reinforce Canadian troops in Latvia next spring.
The military identified those killed as Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton; Pvt. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; Pvt. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver, British Columbia; and Pvt. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, British Columbia. All four were serving with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, based in Edmonton.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said 39 people were receiving medical care. Sayeh Zielke, chief executive of Acute Care Alberta, said 19 were in critical condition, eight were stable and 12 were ambulatory and receiving treatment for less serious injuries.
Smith said some suffered severe burns and could face weeks or months of intensive treatment.
Prime Minister Mark Carney described the incident as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on domestic soil. He ordered flags lowered to half-staff on federal buildings nationwide.
Carney said the families of those killed had been notified. Those affected included regular forces personnel, reservists and soldiers from bases across Canada.
Hospitals respond to mass casualties
Alberta health officials said patients were transferred from Wainwright to four hospitals — the University of Alberta Hospital and Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton, Foothills Medical Centre in Calgary and Red Deer Regional Hospital.
Alberta officials said they had lifted the “Code Orange” emergency activated at several hospitals Saturday night to mobilize staff and beds for the casualties.
The response involved 22 ground ambulances, six airplanes and two helicopters, with assistance from neighboring Saskatchewan. Smith said all patients had been accounted for and no further patients were awaiting transport.
Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the town’s small hospital was not designed to handle a mass-casualty incident but praised local medical personnel.
Rutland confirmed that military search-and-rescue technicians parachuted into Wainwright to reinforce the emergency response. Pugh said their red parachutes were illuminated by flares as they descended shortly before midnight.
Cathy Keane, a mayoral candidate in Ontario, said her eldest son was among those critically injured. “As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family,” she wrote on Facebook, saying she was traveling to Alberta.
Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre, who represents the area in Parliament, visited Wainwright on Sunday and said he had heard accounts of people who ran toward the danger to help others and were now fighting for their lives in hospitals.
Military investigates fire
Rutland said the fire ignited in the military training area, where multiple exercises were underway, and spread rapidly in unusually strong winds.
He said winds had been within normal operating limits for much of Saturday, generally below 50 kph (31 mph), before intensifying rapidly. Range controllers rely on weather reports to determine whether training can safely continue, he said.
Rutland said investigators would examine whether the wind drove the fire toward the soldiers or whether flames spread unseen through vegetation before suddenly overtaking them.
The fire crossed established firebreaks before being contained with help from municipal firefighters.
The Canadian military said there were no indications of terrorism.
Rutland said military investigators would examine the circumstances, including whether safety protocols needed to change. “If our protocols need to change, then they’ll be updated,” he said.
The military typically convenes a formal board of inquiry after such incidents, Rutland said, cautioning that determining what happened would take time.
Rutland said Charlie Company had been withdrawn from the training area and the rest of the battalion suspended training Sunday.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4 p.m. Saturday following reports of a fire in the base’s training area.
Large areas of Alberta were hit by a windstorm Saturday, with gusts up to 100 kph (62 mph). The winds toppled trees, sent signs flying and pushed flames beyond the base into surrounding rural areas.
By late Saturday, the Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. No evacuation order was issued for residents.
CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations.
The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday’s referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada. Elections Alberta said the Wainwright Communiplex advance polling location closed early Saturday and election materials were transported securely.

title: Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu for reelection 9 days before election
text:
Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu for reelection 9 days before election
President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu late in his reelection campaign, a coveted boost because of Trump’s popularity but one that the American had withheld for months as the vote neared and the leaders' strategies in the Middle East diverged.
Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu “has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
Israelis are set to vote Oct. 27, in the first national elections since Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
The absence of an endorsement was a setback for the Likud politician, who had billed his tight ties to the Republican president as a selling point for staying in power.
“Thank you, President Trump, for the tremendous support and work together,” Netanyahu said in a statement in Hebrew posted on X. “Together we will complete the mission!”
His Likud Party attached to the statement a 35-second video showing clips of the two leaders together and Trump praising Netanyahu.
It was not immediately clear what impact the endorsement would have on what is expected to be a tight race. Trump is still popular in Israel, but many Israelis, including leading commentators, have expressed disappointment over the inconclusive outcome of the Iran war and Trump’s ceasefire proposal, which fell short of many of the countries’ key goals when they jointly launched the war in February.
In his post, Trump again threatened to “soon finish the job” against Iran “unless they change their ways, rapidly,” but added he might not want to if Netanyahu loses the election. “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump said.
He said Netanyahu had been “Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.”
Trump endorsed Netanyahu in past elections and in November he sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog asking him to pardon Netanyahu on corruption charges.
But Trump's comments about Netanyahu in recent months had been much more subdued, and he repeatedly demurred when asking if he would back the prime minister. The president, when asked in a Time magazine interview published this month about backing the Israeli leader, said, ”I’m not involved in politics anymore,” despite his campaigning for and endorsing U.S. politicians.
Trump, especially in his second term, has sought to give his stamp of approval to candidates in foreign elections and claimed credit when they have been successful. He endorsed Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in his unsuccessful bid for a fifth term, as well as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Polish President Karol Nawrocki, and several Latin American leaders.
Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies and seemed more aligned than ever in the wake of the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities in 2025. But over the course of the nearly eight-month war with Iran this year, they have had disagreements.
Trump criticized Israel’s decision to attack a key Iranian gas field in the first weeks of the war. In June, he called Netanyahu “crazy." Trump also said that he was “a little bit perturbed” as Israel’s fighting with Hezbollah militants in Lebanon was holding back peace talks with Iran.
Beyond Iran, Netanyahu in August rejected Trump’s latest plan to advance a stalled ceasefire in Gaza, pushing back on the U.S. administration’s call for Israel to withdraw from territory it controls in Gaza until Hamas has been disarmed.

title: Coast to coast with Ford & Brinkley, part III
text:
In the historic portrayals of western expansion in our still young country, the Midwest was often portrayed as the “Wild West.” There remains a hint of envy, perhaps resentment, from the “outlier” states that were not the original 13 colonies. They were once-wild untapped resources, but are now the heartbeat of our country, with modern expansion evident everywhere due to their relatively flat topography and numerous natural resources, compared to the congested east and northeastern states.
After all, most of our food, energy and industrialized products all hail from the mid-west. Which is clearly evident by the massive warehouses, trucking depots and data centers we are passing daily as we drive along the commercial corridors of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois and into Missouri. Following the rivers that were the original routes of transportation, these places now carry expansive highways, railroads, and energy corridors.

title: ​Taste tests and ‘mac and trees’ rule as Lewiston-area schools buy local, cook from scratch
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUBURN — For the first time, fish tacos were on the lunch menu at Auburn Middle School.
Some students were weary of the fish, but others were gleeful for a new option.
At first glance, the tacos looked like any other school meal. But a closer look revealed nearly every ingredient — salsa, cabbage and the fish itself — came locally to the school and prepared there.
The meal was part of an ongoing four-year program by the school departments in Auburn, Lewiston and to encourage students to taste test new, local offerings. When successful, kid-popular meals, including fish tacos and “mac and trees,” end up permanently on a school menu.
Daily, students have at least two options for lunch, as well as a salad bar. Chris Piercey, Auburn’s nutrition director, admits that more often than not, students choose pizza over salad or fish.
Nonetheless, Piercey and his team are encouraged by students trying something new.
The local food initiative is called the School-Based Food Hub. It’s possible because of a four-year $623,970 grant from Full Plates Full Potential, a nonprofit working to end food insecurity in Maine. The grant is in its second year in the three school districts.
It’s the only School-Based Food Hub in the state, according to Anna Korsen, the co-executive director of Full Plates Full Potential, though other initiatives through the grant funding have similar goals.
Korsen’s group selected the trio of schools in 2024 as one of seven projects and two statewide initiatives funded through a $10 million federal grant.
“We were looking at the food system as a whole and how we can improve it in Maine,” Korsen said.
During the first two years, the three schools have spent $319,629 buying local food from 61 Maine farms, and the kitchen teams have processed over 10,000 pounds of local produce.
They’ve also purchased equipment through the grant to help streamline the process and hired more staff, which aligns with the goal of transforming local school nutrition programs.
What makes the Full Plates Full Potential program unique is that while several state and federal grants help school districts buy healthy, local food, the Full Plates program focuses on all that goes into a school system shifting to more locally sourced, healthy, homemade school recipes, and taste testing those offerings to become popular menu items.
SCHOOL-BASED FOOD HUB
Tucked back in the kitchen at the Auburn Middle School last week, Jen Roderick was preparing onions for some pasta sauce.
As part of the food hub program, Auburn, Lewiston and Lisbon buy and share production equipment, process food together and brainstorm ways to make the most of resources. In fact, Roderick was hired through the program.
As the processing manager, Roderick has time to focus just on food production, which is something the kitchen staff couldn’t do before, Piercey said. Often, school kitchens are not equipped with the staff, space or tools to create meals from scratch.
Because the schools are working with fresh produce, Roderick can freeze or store the food to optimize its use, as the nutrition directors prioritize purchasing fruits and vegetables that are in-season.
In total, the Auburn, Lewiston and Lisbon schools processed 685 pounds of zucchini, 637 pounds of summer squash, 4,976 pounds of potatoes and 173 pounds of green beans, according to a year-in-review by food hub Project Coordinator Kylie Welch.
All of that and more behind the scenes — including the purchase of new equipment — lead to the heart of the food hub program: taste testing, and ultimately getting more popular, healthy, local food on the schools’ menus.
TASTE TESTS
After lunch on a recent day at Auburn Middle School, students had the opportunity to taste test monkfish corn soup.
Jaxon Hill, 13, an eighth grader, was in charge of the taste-testing group. He already tried the soup when a representative from the Maine Coast Fishermen’s Association visited his classroom last month.
Because he was used to having a monthly taste test at the school, he asked if he could help out and test the soup for his classmates. He really wanted it to land on the lunch menu.
“My friend and I, we really liked it. We got like seven servings,” Hill said.
A taste test is preformed in each district monthly, with an effort made to highlight in-season produce.
The tests are run by the three schools’ FoodCorps members. FoodCorps is a nonprofit organization that encourages healthy food habits in schools and, most recently, introduced a school nutrition track for individuals hired by the organization to work in school districts.
Chloe Lendi, Auburn’s FoodCorps member, said getting kids to try new foods is challenging, but it helps to incorporate it in ways they might already be familiar with.
Lendi led an effort to incorporate broccoli into meals by testing some “Mac and Trees” — simply macaroni and cheese with broccoli. It had a 93% approval rating at Washburn Elementary School.
She also taste tested harissa chicken, a spicy North African dish, after a student suggested chicken shawarma in honor of National Arab American Heritage Month. By working with a local farm and catering company, they sourced the chicken locally and ensured that it met Halal standards.
In both instances, the food hub project allowed Lendi to be creative while not necessarily worrying about practicality around the school budget. It also allowed her to listen to students’ needs and wants in a way staff couldn’t have done as easily before. Both items Lendi tested with students were a success and made it onto the menu.
“We have a lot of kids to feed and that rely on school meals, so I think there’s a great opportunity here to make those meals the best that they can be,” she said.
BENEFITS OF HEALTHY MEALS
Carol Bilodeau has worked in the Auburn school district for 40 years and has been part of the effort to incorporate more fresh, local ingredients over the past two years. As she prepared lunches at Auburn Middle School earlier this month, she noted that students are better behaved, more courteous, respectful and engaged.
She thinks it may have to do with the food.
The offerings are healthier than in the past, and there is more variety, she said.
The Auburn School Department feeds over 3,500 students and 75% of them rely on the school lunch program instead of bringing their own, Piercey said, based on numbers for the current school year. Lewiston has just over 6,000 students, 80% of whom take school lunch; Lisbon has over 1,300 students with 51% eating school lunch, according to October figures from the Maine DOE.
Across Maine, around 100,000 students are fed daily through the free school food program, Korsen said. It’s often the only instance those children get to eat a healthy meal. A Maine law passed in 2021 made all school breakfast, lunch and snacks free for all students from pre-kindergarten through 12th grade.
“These programs are critical to make sure kids get healthy foods in schools and it’s often the most reliable source of healthy food across the state. We have such a high rate of food insecurity (in Maine) and it’s important to sustain programs like this,” Korsen said
In addition to the grant from Full Plates Full Potential, schools can purchase food through the state’s Local Food Fund. It gives schools $1 back for every $2 they spend on local produce, with a cap of $5,000. States such as Vermont and California have similar initiatives, she said.
Auburn has used around 60% of its $5,000 as of mid-October. Any other purchases past that must come out of the school budget. Despite the limits, Piercey said the grant is a great way to give back to the local economy while providing kids more healthy options.
Piercey said he will continue to purchase food locally once the funding runs out, but it will be from the school budget instead. This year alone, over the summer the schools purchased food from seven farms.
“I always want the opportunity to do something good …” Piercey said. “It’s helping the local economy, improving the quality of food we serve and educating students on where their food comes from. I’m a believer in farm-to-school.”
At the end of the four-year food hub grant, Piercey and the collaborators will create a guidebook for other school districts on how to optimize school nutrition departments through local foods.

title: Troy Jackson isn’t apologizing for telling Susan Collins to ‘shut up’
text:
In an interview Sunday on CNN, Maine Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson said he wouldn’t apologize for telling his opponent, Republican Sen. Susan Collins, to “shut up” during a debate last week.
The incident occurred after a protester opposing data centers began yelling as Collins spoke.
As the protester was being removed, Collins said the person was “obviously one of Troy’s supporters.”
Jackson responded, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.”
Speaking with CNN’s Dana Bash, Jackson said he felt like Collins was talking down to him.
“She accused me of setting that up. I had no idea who it was, and I was surprised whenever he jumped up out of there,” Jackson said.
“I’ve had four debates with Senator Collins. I’ve shook her hands afterward every time. But I’m not going to be talked down to by Senator Collins. I’m not going to be accused of things like that. I’m fighting for Mainers and I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me, and so I’m not going to apologize for that, no,” he said.
On Friday, Collins told Sean Hannity that Jackson’s “shut up” remark felt almost automatic.
“I was struck by how reflexive the response ‘Oh shut up’ was, but then I thought about the reputation that Troy Jackson has in Augusta, particularly when he is dealing with women with whom he disagrees. So in some ways it didn’t surprise me and the fact that it seemed like such an automatic quick reply was very telling,” she said.

title: Crews battling structure fire in Lisbon.
text:
Building a complete loss in Lisbon structure fire
Building a complete loss in Lisbon structure fire
A two story residential building was completely destroyed by a fire that started early Sunday morning in Lisbon.
Deputy Chief Robert Robitaille said that the call came in shortly after 3 a.m. after someone driving by spotted the fire at 51 Gould Road. When fire crews arrived, the building was about 80% involved.
Robitaille said no one was inside at the time because the building was under renovations.
"It's a very large and old residential structure. There was still a lot of belongings from the previous owners. Books, papers, that kind of stuff," said Robitaille.
According to a Facebook post from An Angel's Wing, the building was its new recovery home. "This property represented so much hope, hard work, and planning for the future, and seeing it damaged this way is heartbreaking. We are still processing the loss and determining what comes next," the nonprofit said.
There is a garage located behind the main building that fire crews were able to cut off the flames from. Robitaille said the main building is a total loss but there was no damage to the garage.
Officials said no injuries were reported.
"The only real difficulties was establishing water supply, and those difficulties were very short lived. We never ran out of water the whole time we were here," Robitaille said. "This is really the first day it was below freezing so there was no slip injuries or anything. We did have one hazard at the beginning of the fire was the power line that came down from the structure that was energized until CMP arrived."
Robitaille said it took about an hour for crews to bring the fire under control. Around 9 a.m., fire crews were still on scene putting water on the building. 
The State Fire Marshal's Office is assisting with the investigation. The cause of the fire is still unknown.

title: Oregon community mourns 4 killed in school shooting as 2 survivors remain hospitalized
text:
Oregon community mourns 4 killed in school shooting as 2 survivors remain hospitalized
A special-needs teacher and student wounded in a deadly shooting at an Oregon elementary school remained hospitalized Saturday. But friends said their survival was a spot of hope in a community in mourning.
Previous video: 3 students and a teacher dead after Oregon school shooting (Thursday)
The youngest shooting survivor, 7-year-old Saylor Graham, is a feisty, vibrant fighter with a sweet nature whose story inspired other children, Matt Sampson, executive director of Sparrow Clubs, where she was a member, said.
"She has a genetic disorder, usually uses a wheelchair and is nonverbal, but she doesn’t even need words to connect with people,” Sampson said.
“She’s just an amazing spirit who just immediately draws people to her and you just feel inspired by Saylor when you meet her,” Sampson said. “And she's always wearing these iconic glasses, whether they’re pink or they’re red. She’s just such a cutie.”
Teacher Becky Drury, 54, is recovering in a Bend hospital with wounds to her arm and hand but hopes to go home soon, said Zack Hall, a family friend who is serving as her family's spokesperson.
Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and a teacher were killed at the Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, Thursday when a former student there, 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, entered a special needs classroom and began firing with a shotgun.
One teacher was grappling with John for the weapon when the father of two students came in and shot him to death. They were credited with stopping the rampage and saving many people's lives.
While police continued to investigate John's motive, distraught parents, teachers and others gathered outside the school Saturday to leave flowers, pray and cry.
Savannah Patton, a mother who has a 1st and 4th grader at the school, sat on the grass Saturday across from a memorial of flowers, stuffed animals and balloons, and wiped tears from her eyes.
She told an Associated Press reporter that the teacher who died, Megan Lambert, 25, had been a substitute for her daughter’s class last year.
Patton said she has struggled to explain what happened to her daughter, who asked her, “Mommy, why would someone want to take a gun and kill us at school?” Patton said it was a question she didn’t know how to answer.
Physical challenges won't keep her from “living with joy”
For several years, Saylor worked with students from Bend High School through the Sparrow Clubs, a volunteer group whose mission is to empower “kids to help kids in medical need” through kindness and community service, according to its website.
In a video on the Sparrow Clubs page, Saylor introduces herself, saying she loves watching Bluey and being around other kids, especially her brother. She said that while she is challenged by physical and cognitive issues, she can communicate with her eyes and a computer tablet.
“I prove every day that I’m a fighter who doesn’t give up," she wrote in the video. "Living with CASK-related challenges is full of unknowns, which can be very hard and scary for my whole family,” she said, “But it doesn’t keep me from smiling, laughing and living with joy!”
Some of the high school students who worked with Saylor said helping her gave them hope that there is still humanity in this world.
After the shooting, she was taken to a hospital in Portland. A GoFund Me for her family has raised almost $400,000.
“We will not let her name be forgotten”
Devon Johnson visited the memorial outside the school Saturday morning. Her husband teaches at Bend High School, and she is a volleyball coach at High Desert Middle School, so they are close with many of the staff at the elementary school.
“It's just hard to take in,” she said. “I'm so glad to see that Bend is rallying and just wrapping their arms around this community, but it's going to take a long time to get through this.”
Heidi Wood, the director of the Central Oregon Volleyball Club where Lambert coached, said in a social media post that she was “an amazing coach, an amazing teacher” and “an amazing person who would do anything” for her students.
“To the shooter, she would have given you the shirt off her back,” Wood said. “But you didn’t give her a chance.”
Wood said that Lambert wouldn’t take her volleyball coaching pay in her first year so the money could be used for scholarships for players who couldn’t afford to play instead.
“That was her, and that is her,” Wood said. “We will carry on her love, her passion, and we will not let her name be forgotten.”
___
Bellisle reported from Seattle. Associated Press writer Haven Daley contributed to his report.

title: Man stabbed, struck with brass knuckles in Lewiston
text:
A man was injured and another was arrested in connection with a stabbing in Lewiston on Saturday afternoon, according to a news release.
Around 3:30 p.m., Lewiston Police responded to reports of a fight near Dunkin’ Donuts at 420 Main Street. Officers found a 20-year-old man suffering from a single stab wound to the back, and other wounds apparently caused by being hit with brass knuckles.
The victim, whose name has not been released by authorities, was transported to Central Maine Medical Center to be treated for serious but not life-threatening injuries.
Officers arrested 18-year-old Alexander Keith at the scene in connection with the stabbing. Keith was transported to the Androscoggin County Jail and is not eligible for bail because he was already on deferred disposition.
Derek St. Laurent, a spokesperson for the Lewiston Police Department, said Sunday morning that investigators believe the two men know each other, and that the stabbing was not random.
Authorities are still investigating the incident.

title: Does Maine want its elderly on the streets?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A legislative change is urgently needed in Maine.
Example: a homeowner allowing an elderly mother to remain in house after relocating elsewhere in Maine. There is no Homestead Exemption, as the requirement is owner residency in-home. In this case, it amounts to 10 years of exemption denial and highly increased chance that the house will have to be sold due to doubling of taxes, leaving the elderly parent homeless. Both parties moved in in 2006.
The home was unoccupied for two nights in 26 years. And the homeowner continues with all insurance, local and state taxes and municipal services. Legislators have been unresponsive, yet claim concern for the elderly.
Maggie Trout
Rockland

title: Latino voters helped put Trump back in the White House. What's their next move?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
CASA GRANDE, Ariz. (AP) — Chris Martinez feels like Donald Trump has made a fool of him.
The 28-year-old maintenance technician from Casa Grande, Arizona, voted for the Republican president expecting to get a thriving economy and no wars.
Instead, gas prices are so high that Martinez returned one of his vehicles to the lender, he shifted his food shopping to a discount grocer and he has watched as the United States has spent months in conflict with Iran.
“He’s doing nothing for us, to benefit us,” Martinez said. “And it kind of sucks because I got duped and I feel like a dummy.”
As a group, Latinos shifted toward Trump two years ago, helping return him to the White House with a Republican-controlled Congress. Now, many like Martinez are souring on the president and his party, which could upend the balance of power in Washington in the Nov. 3 elections.
“I went right for a while, but I’m back to the middle,” Martinez said.
The path to a U.S. House majority runs through heavily Latino districts in states such as Arizona, Colorado and Texas, where Democrats are counting on disaffected Trump supporters to swing back their way. It is unclear, however, whether Democrats have sealed the deal with voters who lack strong allegiance to either party.
Martinez, for one, is not sure if he is going to vote at all in the midterms.
An Arizona farming town faces a transition
Casa Grande, the town of 70,000 people where Martinez lives, sits at a crossroads between Phoenix and Tucson, an hour’s drive from each. There is a quaint downtown surrounded by master-planned developments offering affordable housing for people priced out of larger cities. Gated golf-course communities attract retirees.
Much of the town sits at the northern tip of Arizona’s 6th Congressional District, historically one of the most closely matched in the country. Republican Juan Ciscomani is seeking a third term. Two years ago, Ciscomani won by 2.5 percentage points and Trump won by less than 1 point.
This time, Ciscomani is subtly creating distance from Trump without directly criticizing the president or his policies. The congressman talks up his immigrant story — he was born in Mexico and moved to the U.S. as a kid — and frames himself as independent and bipartisan.
“I’m not a rubber stamp for anyone,” he says in one advertisement.
If Ciscomani retains his seat, it will be thanks to people like Chris Durant, 61, who has been voting for Republicans in recent elections and will probably do so again next month.
“We really don’t worry about gas and prices and what not,” Durant said as he and his wife loaded their pickup with groceries for his mother-in-law.
Ciscomani’s Democratic opponent is JoAnna Mendoza. The former Marine emphasizes her own hardscrabble upbringing as the daughter of immigrant farmworkers who worked the fields close to Casa Grande.
“People trust you if they know that you came from the community and understand their way of life,” Mendoza said in an interview earlier this year.
Most Hispanic voters disapprove of Trump
Trump made broad gains among Hispanics during the 2024 campaign that returned him to the White House.
Back then, about 7 in 10 Hispanic voters were “very concerned” about the cost of food and groceries, slightly more than about two-thirds of voters overall, according to AP VoteCast, a survey of more than 120,000 voters nationwide. Trump had a clear advantage among those voters.
Now, about 6 in 10 Hispanic voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of the presidency, according to an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll from October. More than 7 in 10 disapprove of his performance on the economy.
An AP-NORC poll conducted in September showed that Hispanic voters are more concerned than voters overall about the cost of groceries and housing, and 70% blame Trump’s policies more than factors outside his control for higher prices.
Their potential shift away from Republicans this year would be driven by anti-Trump sentiment, not a love of Democrats, said Mike Madrid, a political consultant who wrote “The Latino Century,” a book about Latino voters, and co-hosts “The Latino Vote” podcast.
Latinos are in the midst of a “dealignment,” rejecting strong associations with both parties because neither is speaking effectively to working class economic concerns, he said.
“The Latino electorate is moving from a racial-and-ethnic voting bloc to an economic, pocketbook, class-based voter,” Madrid said. “And the party that figures that out first is the party that will probably dominate for the next generation.”
Hispanics are about evenly split on their view of the Democratic Party, according to the October AP-NORC poll. Their views of the Republican Party are more negative, with 55% having an unfavorable view and 38% having a favorable one.
The economy is at the center of a Colorado contest
On a recent morning in Denver, Democratic state lawmaker Manny Rutinel stood before a crowd of union carpenters and rolled up his sleeve to show off a scar. The mark is from when he sold his blood more than 100 times to make ends meet.
“I’m the son of a single mom. She came to America to give me the American Dream. We worked hard for this country,” Rutinel told the boisterous crowd that fanned out to canvas for him in one of the country’s most-watched races.
Rutinel is challenging Republican Rep. Gabe Evans in Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, which stretches from blue-collar Denver suburbs to energy-rich farm and ranchland in the northern stretch of the state. Latinos are the district’s single largest ethnic group, and both the incumbent and challenger are Hispanic. Evans won by less than 1 percentage point while Trump won by 2 points.
Rutinel has focused relentlessly on the economy since winning the nomination.
“The folks around the district feel they’ve been lied to and betrayed,” he said in an interview.
Evans, a 40-year-old former police lieutenant, has portrayed Rutinel as having a record as a left-wing activist and liberal lawmaker.
“Go ask any Hispanic in the district, do you think we should secure the border? Do you think we should get rid of the bad guys? Do you think we should help the good guys? They’ll say yes,” Evans, whose grandfather was a Mexican immigrant, said in an interview.
Jose Montalvo, a 47-year-old trucker, voted for Evans even though he supported Democrat Kamala Harris for president in 2024. He likes to split his ticket between the parties but does not think he will do that this year after he needed to change insurers and cellphone providers to save money.
Montalvo is frustrated by Trump’s handling of gas prices, saying “I blame him for the fuel side of things.” That is a criticism he extends to all Republicans.
Maria del Carmen Rojas, a naturalized citizen who has lived in the United States for 36 years, said she is shocked that any Latinos could back Trump and a modern Republican Party that she thinks regularly denigrates immigrants.
She has four children who are U.S. citizens, including a son who served in the war in Afghanistan. She has spent her life working in factories and serving as a nanny to raise her children. Now she struggles to buy groceries.
“We Latinos contribute very much to this country, the taxes we pay, the service we provide,” she said.
Frustration mounts in Texas’ Rio Grande Valley
A wooden sign that said “need prayer?” sat on a table with free Bibles along a busy suburban walking trail in Edinburg, Texas, on a hot October evening.
The town is part of the state’s 15th Congressional District, which Trump carried by 18 percentage points but is now viewed as a top Election Day battleground.
Standing behind the table, Thomas Centrella, 42, said he has grown disillusioned with politics and finds himself fast-forwarding through campaign advertisements. Even though he tends to vote Republican, he might not in the future.
During Trump’s first term, Centrella said, “I feel like he was going in a good direction, but I think now that it’s just gotten weird.” He doubts he would ever vote for a Democrat but said he might skip elections or turn independent in the future.
Maria Elsa Gonzalez, who is retired, said she will again support the district’s Republican congresswoman, Monica de la Cruz, instead of Democrat Bobby Pulido, a Tejano music star. Speaking in Spanish, Gonzalez said Pulido “doesn’t have any preparation other than a pretty face and the fame of singing pretty.”
Priscilla Olivarez, 46, a public education teacher who was walking the trail is undecided in the midterms. She grew up as a Democrat and voted Republican in the last presidential election. Today, she is disappointed with an economy where costs seem to be growing faster than wages and she often digs into her own pocket to help pay for things in the classroom.
“I stand independent right now because I don’t agree with either side right now,” she said.
___
Riccardi reported from Denver and Gonzalez from Edinburg, Texas.

title: Death Notice: Ronald Ellis Sr.

She enables those who want to tear down the Constitution, rule by executive order, issue pardons to criminals, detain American citizens and throw them in camps, deny better healthcare and destroy our environment instead of making the polluters responsible. She votes for completely unqualified administrative leaders and judges who make the courts political.
If she is so powerful she should be able to push through meaningful legislation so that she wouldn’t have to keep running around putting out fires. After 30 years if the best she can do is wring her hands and be concerned then it’s time for change.

title: Police identify boy, man killed when pickup drove onto Kansas soccer fields
text:
Police identify boy, man killed when pickup drove onto Kansas soccer fields
Child and adult dead, 11 injured after vehicle drove through Wichita soccer game, police say
Police identify boy, man killed when pickup drove onto Kansas soccer fields
Child and adult dead, 11 injured after vehicle drove through Wichita soccer game, police say
Police in Wichita, Kansas, have identified the two people killed when a pickup truck drove onto soccer fields at a youth sports complex Saturday afternoon.
The victims were 6-year-old Cole Adrian and 35-year-old Nicholas Schafer, both from McPherson, Kansas. Police said the two were not related.
Previous coverage in the player above: Officials speak after two were killed when a vehicle drove through a youth soccer game
Ten other people were injured in the crash at Stryker Sports Complex in northeast Wichita, including five children younger than 10.
Police said Sunday that a 34-year-old woman was parked near the soccer fields before her Chevrolet pickup drove onto one of the fields, striking several children and adults.
Two of the driver's children were inside the pickup at the time. Another of her children was playing soccer on a different field.
The crash happened around 3:25 p.m. Saturday.
Both victims died at the scene. Ten people were taken to area hospitals with injuries described as noncritical. Another person was hospitalized for medical complications unrelated to traumatic injuries.
Police interviewed more than 30 witnesses, including the two children inside the pickup.
The driver was released following interviews with investigators and consultation with the Sedgwick County District Attorney's Office.
No charges have been filed yet.
Police are awaiting toxicology results and a mechanical examination of the pickup as they work to determine what caused the crash.
"Our hearts are with the families of Adrian and Nicholas as they face an unimaginable loss. What should have been a day of children playing soccer and families spending time together ended in tragedy," Wichita Police Chief Joe Sullivan said. "We are also thinking about those who were injured, their loved ones and everyone who witnessed what happened. We know this tragedy has affected many people throughout our community, and we want those families to know they are not alone. Our officers and investigators will continue working to understand exactly what happened."
McPherson, Kansas, mayor Jim Loving issued this statement on Sunday afternoon:
"On Saturday afternoon, two of our own — a 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man — were killed at a youth soccer game in Wichita. Eleven more were taken to hospitals, several of them children.
There is nothing I can say that makes that right.
To the families who lost someone: this whole town is grieving with you, and we will stand with you for as long as it takes. To the injured and their families: we are praying for your recovery.
Thank you to the bystanders who stepped in before the first ambulance arrived, and to the first responders in Wichita and here at home. Wichita Mayor Lily Wu has reached out to express her condolences to our community, and we are grateful for her support.
In the days ahead, give these families their privacy.
McPherson Public Schools (USD 418) has communicated directly with families. Counselors and support staff will be in every building Monday.
McPherson takes care of each other. We will get through this together."
Anyone with information is asked to contact Wichita police at 316-268-4407 or Crime Stoppers at 316-267-2111.

title: Growing up in Maine exposes the folly of party politics
text:
Jack Brogan of Freeport is studying political science at the University of Rhode Island.
This fall, I will vote in my first general election. Growing up in Maine has given me an unusual idea of politics.
We have an independent senator who caucuses with Democrats. We repeatedly reelected a Republican senator with support from voters who choose Democrats elsewhere on the ballot. This year, a former chairman of the Maine Republican Party is running for governor as an independent.
None of that seems strange to me. What seems stranger is the expectation that once I decide which party better represents me, an entire package of beliefs should follow. My positions on abortion, immigration, policing, climate change, guns and foreign policy are all supposed to become predictable from the letter beside the candidate I support.
I don’t think politics should work that way.
Political independence is often treated as an ideology somewhere between liberalism and conservatism: take the Democratic position, take the Republican position, split the difference and call yourself a moderate.
But that misunderstands independence. Political independence is not an ideology. It is a method of thinking.
Maine has provided plenty of examples. Sen. Angus King caucuses with Democrats because, as he explained when he entered the Senate, refusing to join either caucus would reduce his effectiveness. He also said that choice would not place him in “automatic opposition” to Republicans. His independence was never supposed to mean neutrality. It meant cooperation without ownership.
Susan Collins represents another version of Maine’s resistance to neat political categories. In 2020, Joe Biden won Maine while Collins also won statewide. In my previous op-ed (“The suburban trap: Why Troy Jackson’s path to victory runs through Scarborough, not Allagash,” Aug. 30) , I looked at those voters mainly as an electoral problem for Democrats.
But I have been thinking about them differently since then. Maybe there is something healthy about the fact that they exist.
Rick Bennett raises the same question. He chaired the Maine Republican Party before leaving it and running for governor as an independent. He has broken with Republicans on some issues while retaining positions rooted in his conservative background. Both parties have tried to define what Bennett “really” is.
Maybe both descriptions can contain some truth.
A former Republican can agree with Republicans on some things, Democrats on others, and decide neither party describes his politics well enough to belong to it.
Look at Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania. He remains a Democrat, but his breaks with the party on immigration and Israel have drawn criticism from fellow Democrats. The reaction raises a broader question: What does it mean to be a “big tent” party?
The public is less ideologically tidy than politics makes it appear. Someone can favor stronger unions and tougher enforcement against violent crime. Someone can support abortion rights and want a secure border.
Those voters are not confused. Our categories sometimes are.
Once politics becomes identity rather than judgment, disagreeing with your own side can feel less like changing your mind and more like betraying a group.
Maine has not escaped that trend. But our history is a reminder that things do not have to work that way.
King can caucus with Democrats without becoming one. Collins can win voters who reject Republican presidential candidates. Bennett can leave the Republican Party without automatically becoming a Democrat. Voters can do the same thing.
Independence does not mean every issue has two equally valid sides or that the answer always sits in the middle. Sometimes one party will make the better argument. It means reaching that conclusion yourself.
At 18, that is the kind of voter I want to become. I do not want voting for someone to mean inheriting every one of that candidate’s opinions, or recognizing a good argument from the other side to feel like disloyalty.
Maybe that is what Maine’s independent tradition is worth preserving: not a state without Democrats or Republicans, but a state where neither party owns the people who vote for it.

title: Cold morning followed by sunshine
text:
Cold morning followed by sunshine
Cold morning followed by sunshine
Sunday morning started off cold, with many areas recording temperatures below freezing, some even in the 20s. But high pressure is dominating the area today, so we will have more than enough sunshine to warm us back towards average. Temperatures for Sunday will still be slightly cooler than seasonable in the mid 50s, but conditions will feel warmer now that the wind chill is not as prominent as yesterday.
Tonight will be another cool night, with temperatures dipping into the 30s and upper 20s. Monday will have partly cloudy skies and another day of mid 50s for the high temperatures. Our high temperatures will peak on Tuesday with most areas getting closer to 60 degrees or higher.
We are watching a nor'easter forming off the coast of the mid-Atlantic but impacts to New England from the storm will be minimal. Maine will have gusty conditions and building nearshore waves, but rainfall is not expected out of the storm system. We have a dry and seasonable week ahead with no rainfall in the forecast.

title: 2-year-old put loaded gun in their mouth at daycare, state report says
text:
RICHMOND, Va. (WWBT/Gray News) - A 2-year-old Virginia child allegedly put a daycare administrator’s loaded gun in their mouth, according to a report from the state’s Department of Social Services.
The report alleges an administrator at Thrive Learning Center East, a daycare in Richmond, brought a gun onto the campus in a fanny pack on Sept. 25. A 2-year-old child got the loaded gun out of the fanny pack and put the barrel in their mouth, according to the report.
“[The toddler] walked over to a table with the firearm in their mouth, placed the firearm on a table where five other children were sitting on the floor, and then picked up the firearm from the table,” the report states.
Social Services said the toddler had the gun for about 15 seconds before any adults realized.
The toddler was able to get to the gun because the fanny pack was unzipped and placed on top of a “low stack of cots” inside the classroom, according to the report.
Social Services said the administrator regularly brought this gun to work with them and routinely left the fanny pack accessible to the children.
Around 30 seconds before the toddler grabbed the gun, the report alleges the administrator and another staff member were looking down at their phones, while a different staff member had their back turned to the 2-year-old, putting socks on another child.
Social Services says the administrator and the staff failed to report the incident to the department within 24 hours and instead waited four days before reporting it on Sept. 29.
The gun was removed from the immediate area where the children were, put in a lock box and removed from the building.
This is just one of several violations found at Thrive Learning Center East during an Oct. 8 inspection. Other violations found included leaving children unsupervised and not keeping up with vaccination records.
Social Services gave the daycare the following plan of correction:
“All staff will be trained/retrained on understanding mandated reporting requirements and what is included under the definition child abuse and neglect. Staff will be trained to report offenses to 911, the Department of Social Services, and/or Child Abuse and Neglect Hotline. Staff will be given information for reporting as well as be posted at the daycare in each classroom. Thrive Learning Center East will adhere to and train all staff regarding “Zero Tolerance” for firearms or other weapons on daycare property. Thrive Learning Center East has reached out to the Richmond Police Department for safety training and defense in the case of an intruder and will seek to partner with the Richmond Police Department on an annual training."

title: Celebrate bats, our unsung heroes of the night
text:
Ethan Gilardi is a wildlife biologist, bat specialist and the mammal program field coordinator for the Portland-based Biodiversity Research Institute.
On a cool and breezy night at a campsite in the Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument, a team of wildlife biologists crowds around the tailgate of a truck. After precisely 10 minutes, an alarm rings, and the team splits up to check a series of large mist nets stretched across dirt roads and the river’s edge, searching for nocturnal visitors that may have been caught by the nearly invisible mesh.
For hours, the nets remain empty. But as midnight approaches, headlamps illuminate the unmistakable silhouette of a small flying mammal: a bat. And not just any bat. Its multicolored coat of yellows, browns and blacks, with white frosted tips, reveals a rare sighting of a migratory tree species known as the hoary bat.
Working quickly, the team untangles the animal, records its measurements and releases it into the night. Buzzing with excitement, the biologists settle back into their chairs, flip their headlamps back to red and reset the timer for another 10 minutes.
Oct. 24 marks the beginning of International Bat Appreciation Week, a yearly celebration of an often-misunderstood group of animals that concludes, appropriately, on Halloween. Bats have long been linked to the holiday, likely because of their presence at ancient autumn bonfires that attracted insects. Their dark, swooping silhouettes were reminiscent of spirits, and bats became woven into medieval folklore.
Bat Week, which was founded by a coalition of conservation organizations and government agencies across North America, taps into this moment when bats are already on our minds, to help educate the public about these incredible and ecologically important animals.
Bats are an astonishingly diverse group of animals, with over 1,500 known species across the globe and 47 species in the U.S. Maine is home to eight species of bats — five of which live here year-round, hibernating in caves, mines, fallen rock piles and sometimes even barns and attics — along with three species of tree bats, which migrate south for the winter.
All of the bats in Maine are insectivorous, and they play a vital ecological role. Their appetite for moths, beetles, mosquitoes and other small flying insects enables them to help regulate Maine’s ecosystems and prevent the spread of insects that damage forests and crops, as well as those that affect human health. It is estimated that a single little brown bat can eat almost 1,000 mosquito-sized insects in an hour, while a nursing mother consumes almost 4,500 insects every night.
Yet bats face serious threats. Chief among them is white-nose syndrome, a fungal disease first documented in Maine in 2011. The fungus lives in the soils of caves and mines where bats hibernate, damaging their skin and rousing them mid-winter, which depletes their energy stores too early. White-nose syndrome has killed millions of bats across North America, with some areas losing 90 to 100% of cave-hibernating populations. Northern long-eared, little brown and tricolored bats are among the hardest hit species.
Habitat loss adds to the pressure on these populations, making the preservation of natural lands paramount to the future of these animals.
Better understanding bats is the first step to protecting them. Scientists across dozens of governmental agencies, academic institutions and research firms are studying white-nose syndrome and testing methods to prevent and treat it. These include using UV-C light to kill the fungus in caves, modifying airflow in areas where bats hibernate to inhibit fungal growth and testing vaccines to prevent or decrease the severity of infections.
Meanwhile, bat biologists across the continent have joined forces behind the North American Bat Monitoring Program (NABat), which standardizes the way we collect data about bats while pooling these data in a centralized hub. This allows researchers to better track bat population trends, inform conservation methods and develop new ways to support bats.
The Biodiversity Research Institute’s Mammal Program studies bats year-round, from collecting blood and hair samples for heavy metals testing in Colombia, to recording bat vocalizations for behavioral studies in Kenya, to performing the first bat captures in Katahdin Woods and Waters.
Additionally, through the Gulf of Maine Bat Research Program, scientists are studying how bats utilize offshore environments by placing echolocation recording detectors on islands, boats and buoys across the Gulf of Maine.
How can you help these ecologically valuable creatures? Put up a bat house, plant a native, pollinator-friendly garden and avoid disturbing hibernating bats by steering clear of caves and mines in the winter. And share what you’ve learned about bats to help correct misinformation and ensure these animals receive the protection and support they need.
“Nature Connects” is a monthly column showcasing conservation stories from people and organizations across Maine. To learn more or suggest story ideas, email [email protected].

Joey and Felicity, brown pelicans at the Pittsburgh Zoo, recovered safely after escaping their habitat Saturday morning.

Joey and Felicity, brown pelicans at the Pittsburgh Zoo, recovered safely after escaping their habitat Saturday morning.
Two pelicans have returned to the Pittsburgh Zoo Saturday night after escaping their habitat in the morning, leading to a day-long search.
The Pittsburgh Zoo & Aquarium said the two brown pelicans, Joey and Felicity, are safely back at the zoo with no injuries.
The zoo said teams monitored both animals until they could be safely approached and recovered. Neither animal was injured, but both will be monitored by the zoo's health team.
More than a dozen members of the public called a zoo hotline established to help monitor the birds.
Zoo officials thanked Pittsburgh River Rescue, Three Rivers Waterkeeper, the Army Corps of Engineers and the National Aviary for helping in the recovery effort.

title: A.J. Brown struggles in return to Patriots in win over Jets
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — It was anything but smooth for A.J. Brown in his return to the New England Patriots on Sunday.
The prized offseason acquisition for the defending AFC champions finished with as many catches as dropped passes — three — and even drew a round of boos after a third-quarter drop in New England’s 26-19 win over the New York Jets.
His high ankle sprain might be in the past following a four-game stint on injured reserve, but the wide receievers hands were anything but a sure in his first game since New England’s season opener at Seattle.
The 29-year-old Brown was activated on Saturday after missing a minimum number of games after going on IR. He was in the starting lineup Sunday and finished with 27 yards receiving on 10 targets.
“No excuses. Ankle or not, I should make those plays,” said Brown, who spoke briefly while standing at his locker.
Brown’s first appearance on the Gillette Stadium video board came 48 minutes before kickoff. He received a nice applause from the crowd while he was warming up. Brown was also the final member of the Patriots’ offense to be introduced and received an extended ovation as he jumped and waved his arms in response.
By the third quarter, the good cheer from fans evaporated. One of the drops came in the second quarter when Drake Maye targeted him deep. Brown also let an onside kick by the Jets slip through his grasp, though the lapse didn’t hurt as tight end Eli Raridon fell on the ball and New England ran out the final 32 seconds.
Neither Brown’s coach or teammates expressed concern after the game. They said they know that a player with six 1,000-yard receiving seasons and three Pro Bowl nods will be fine in the long term.
“I know he wanted to do well for his football team,” said Patriots coach Mike Vrabel, who also coached Brown when the receiver broke into the NFL with Tennessee. “Unfortunately, it wasn’t his best effort. He knows that. We have all the confidence in the world in A.J. to be able to finish those plays. He has high expectations for himself, and we have high expectations for him.”
On the sideline, New England refrained from providing words of encouragement to Brown during his first game at Gillette Stadium as a Patriot.
“He’s been in the league a long time. He knows how to deal with things,” Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez said. “He’s been out for a while, so it’s different when you get out there and catch the ball when everyone is flying around. Everyone in the locker room and in this building, we have the utmost confidence in him.”

title: No black-footed ferrets found in Meeteetse, Wyoming, 40 years after a rescue saved the species
text:
No black-footed ferrets found in Meeteetse, 40 years after a rescue saved the species
Wyoming wildlife managers are reporting that no black-footed ferrets are being detected in the cradle of the species' conservation: the Absaroka Range foothills outside of Meeteetse, where the ferrets were saved after presumed extinction in the 1980s.
A tough combination of plague and drought — both big issues for the embattled western species — are suspected causes of a population collapse in the Meeteetse area, where wildlife managers returned ferrets to the wild in 2016 after a three-decade-long absence. It's not assured that the reintroduced population is completely gone, but it's not looking promising, Wyoming Game and Fish Department small carnivore biologist Andy Gygli said.
Related video above: Why do drought conditions linger, even after heavy rains?
"We spent a couple hundred hours of effort surveying 4,000 to 5,000 acres of the Meeteetse reintroduction area," Gygli said. "We didn't see any ferrets."
The complete absence of ferrets during the late August surveys wasn't wholly surprising. Sylvatic plague flared in the region in 2018 and 2019, and ferret numbers plunged to just one confirmed animal in 2020. Subsequent releases of captive-raised ferrets, including 18 animals in 2022, helped the small population temporarily recover, but plague struck again in 2023. By 2025, spotlighting surveyors again detected just a single ferret. This summer there were none.
Ferrets bottoming out and potentially disappearing struck Meeteetse rancher Allen Hogg as a big letdown.
"I'm really disappointed, of course," Hogg told WyoFile. "They might be gone. But just because they didn't find them doesn't mean they're not there, either. I'm not saying all hope is lost."
The Meeteetse rancher's family name became synonymous with black-footed ferrets 45 years ago, when a blue heeler owned by his parents brought a dead weasel-like critter home. Subsequently, biologists found more than 100 other black-footed ferrets — presumed extinct for the two years prior — on and near the family ranch.
The exact cause of the ferrets' absence during the surveys is unknown, but recently drought in the Bighorn Basin walloped their primary prey species, prairie dogs. In many corners of the West, there just hasn't been enough vegetation growth to sustain strong numbers of the grass-eating mammals.
"We've heard a lot about deer, elk, pronghorn and cattle having hard times," Gygli said. "It's the same with our other herbivores. Prairie dogs also have to eat, and lack of (vegetation) coverage can result in low recruitment, which can result in downstream effects."
For ferrets, those downstream drought effects are severe. They, too, haven't had enough to eat. Indirectly, drought caused the numbers of rare mustelids in the world's largest wild black-footed ferret population, in South Dakota's Conata Basin/Badlands, to plummet from 250 to 70 animals between 2024 and 2025, according to biologist and ferret expert Travis Livieri, who studies that population.
"In my 30 years of doing this, I've never seen (drought) this bad, where prairie dogs failed to reproduce at a high rate," Livieri said. "The prairie dogs don't do well, the ferrets won't do well."
Prairie dogs in the Meeteetse area also continue to struggle, Gygli said. After the 2023 bout of sylvatic plague, Game and Fish surveys mapped prairie dog colonies and found only 3,800 acres in active use — down from the 6,000-plus acres that were mapped around the time of the 2016 reintroduction. Densities of prairie dogs per acre aren't great, either.
The habitat conditions were bad enough for black-footed ferrets this summer that Gygli diverted 10 captive-raised animals that were going to be released in Meeteetse to the Shirley Basin, site of a rare ferret reintroduction success story. His rationale was that keeping ferrets out of the reintroduction area would relieve predation pressure on prairie dogs, helping them recover — and ultimately again support ferrets.
"There are prairie dogs there," Gygli said. "They just need some time and some good conditions to come back. Rodents reproduce. That's part of their strategy — they reproduce really quick."
Wildlife managers are also assisting the recovery with prophylactic insecticide treatments to kill fleas and guard against plague. On average, they treat roughly 4,000 acres annually — a roughly $100,000 expense, with the lion's share covered by the Bureau of Land Management, Gygli said.
For now, the Meeteetse reintroduction area might stay free of ferrets intentionally. The last time that happened, in 1986, there were wildly different circumstances. It was a rescue mission to save the species. Although the federal and state wildlife officials found 124 black-footed ferrets after Shep the ranch dog's remarkable rediscovery, the population plummeted in 1985 from a combination of plague and canine distemper.
Retired Game and Fish Nongame Wildlife Supervisor Bob Oakleaf was on the front lines at the time, and he helped develop a contingency plan that outlined when wildlife officials should step in and whisk the remaining animals from the wild. Taking every last ferret into captivity from their only stronghold was a controversial decision, he recalled.
"There was a lot of blockage in the Game and Fish," Oakleaf told WyoFile. "Back then, the Game and Fish really wasn't oriented towards captive breeding."
Then-Game and Fish Director Bill Morris halted the ferret capturing operation "halfway through," he said, leading to a series of meetings. Oakleaf and others talked him into allowing them to resume.
"Thank God for the agreement on the contingency plan, because it allowed us to catch a few more ferrets," Oakleaf said.
After the last known wild ferret, a male known as Scarface, was captured in early 1987, there were a total of 18 black-footed ferrets remaining in the world — all from Meeteetse. Ferrets didn't return to the area for another three decades. They went back into the wild on the same private ranchland where they were rediscovered.
"All of the releases and all of the recovery efforts have all been concentrated here on our ranch and the Pitchfork," Hogg said. "Lenox Baker, the current owner, was probably the most instrumental person in getting them brought back here — he really made the push."
Hogg's hopeful that the Meeteetse reintroduction area's prairie dogs stage a comeback and the black-footed ferrets reappear — even if it takes continuous intervention.
"It might be a situation where, to maintain it here for historical reasons, we have to keep supplementing that population," Hogg said. "Sometimes it just is what it is. You can only spend so much money on a project. If it doesn't work, it doesn't work, but we certainly hope it will work."
There are some skeptics that Meeteetse will ever be home to self-sustaining ferrets. Oakleaf, the Game and Fish retiree, says he understands the desire to restore the historically significant population, but he worries that it's just not the right place — it's too small and has too much plague, he said.
"Everybody involved feels obligated to put them back in Meeteetse." Oakleaf said, "But, man, I don't know how you do it. It just hasn't shown over the years that it could support a ferret population."
For now, the Wyoming Game and Fish Department is not giving up.
"This is a place that we're going to continue to work on," Gygli said. "It's the place where ferrets persisted."
In an ideal world, prairie dog populations would bounce back enough to support a captive-raised ferret release in 2027, he said.
__
This story was originally published by WyoFile and distributed through a partnership with The Associated Press.

title: Missing the local touch from Maine hospitals
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I love the columns that Victoria Hugo-Vidal writes. And I agree with her all the time. Her piece on the quickly dropping obstetrics services in rural Maine (“Maine’s rural maternity wards require a mindset shift,” Oct. 4) sheds light on an issue that is disastrous for families and women in those areas.
The problem was created by hospitals being grabbed up by corporations and conglomerates. It seems now that every hospital or medical center is owned by others from away and managed by accountants for maximum profit.
It wasn’t always this way, of course. Not too many decades ago, hospitals were run locally. Communities would bond together to raise money for hospitals. There would be a board of directors comprised of local leaders. Maybe they would be run with a modest profit or loss. Community groups like Kiwanis, Rotary or Lions would raise funds. The annual golf tournament would support the hospital and there would be regular bake sales.
It’s probably unlikely we can go back to those days. But something has to give if our communities are not well served by competent medical facilities.
Brian Nickerson
South Portland

title: $570K property tops list of Bangor home sales, Sept. 6-12
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
All but one of the residential properties in Bangor that changed hands during one week in September had sale prices under $280,000.
Eight of the nine homes in Bangor that sold during the week of Sept. 6 had sale prices well below the median sale price of $290,000 for Penobscot County last month, according to the Maine Association of Realtors.
A brick double house stationed in the city’s Broadway Historic District that held five units was the one outlier, as it sold for $570,000, tax records show.
Statewide, median sales prices reached $415,000 last month, marking a less than 3% uptick since the prior year, the Maine Association of Realtors reported.
The Bangor Daily News built a list of all the residential property sales that occurred in Bangor from Sept. 6 to 12 using information from state transfer tax documents, which are available to the public online. Here’s what we found.
— 65 Bunker Lane sold on Sept. 11 for $265,000.
