title: Death Notice: Geneva M. Parlin
Obituary: Samuel E. Black
text:
SWEDEN – Samuel E. Black, 88, passed away peacefully in hospice care on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026.
Sam was born in Kankakee, Ill., and grew up in Rockford, Ill. In 1955, he graduated valedictorian from Rockford West High School where he was a member of the school’s 1955 State Champion basketball team.
He attended the University of Wisconsin, Madison, on a Navy ROTC scholarship, earning degrees in mechanical engineering and naval science in 1959. The same year he was commissioned as a second lieutenant in the U.S. Marine Corps, married his high school sweetheart, fellow Badger Susan Swanson, and began a long and adventurous life as a military family together with daughter, Perri (1960) and son, Andrew (1961).
Both Sam and Sue loved nature and the outdoors. A former counselor at Camp Wyonegonic in Demark, Sue introduced Sam to the state through family vacations in Denmark, and in 1969 they purchased a nineteenth century farmhouse in Sweden.
Sam’s 20-year military career as an infantry officer spanned a range of duties over three continents. He commanded a rifle platoon in Camp Pendleton, Calif. and a mortar platoon in Okinawa, Japan, and competed on the Marine Corps Rifle Team in Quantico, Va. He was the adjutant at the Marine Barracks in Washington, D.C., and served with the 1st Marine Regiment in Viet Nam 1966-67. He became a distinguished counter-insurgency instructor at the Amphibious Warfare School in Quantico, later returning to Camp Pendleton and Okinawa as the operations officer of the 1st Marine Regiment. He served as commanding officer of the Marine barracks on the Naval Submarine Base in New London, Conn. In 1977, the family moved to Rome, Italy, where Sam attended the NATO Defense College and then on to Stuttgart, West Germany, where he served on a joint staff supporting allies in northern Africa. In 1980, Sam retired from the Marine Corps as a lieutenant colonel and was awarded the Legion of Merit.
Sam was the rock of his family—a devoted husband to Sue and a loving father to Perri and Andy. During his tours in Okinawa and Viet Nam he wrote daily letters to Sue and his children. Despite his military commitments, he always found time to play games, read bedtime stories, and participate in family activities
Sam and Sue retired to Sweden to embark on a new chapter. A talented woodworker, Sam lovingly restored their old farmhouse. He compiled a “house book” where he recorded detailed progress of his work for future historical reference. He also rebuilt nearly ¾ of a mile of stone walls around the farm and was a vigilant steward of the land, ensuring that the woods and fields on his property were conserved as natural habitat.
Sam served as a volunteer firefighter and chair of the Sweden Planning Board where he was instrumental in helping develop Sweden’s first comprehensive plan. He was also a volleyball coach and member of the First Congregational Church in Bridgton.
Sam and Sue continued to travel the globe, visiting 45 countries on five continents over their lifetimes.
Although Sam liked to travel, he loved being at home. He was a calm, steady, nurturing gentle giant who would go the extra mile to help those he loved. He supported his children along their divergent life paths and he was his grandchildren’s ultimate “superfan,” attending all their sporting events, performances and special occasions. He was very fond of animals, particularly his cats, who would often join him on long walks around his property.
Sam was able to live in his beloved home until February, 2026, when he moved to the Maine Veterans’ Home in South Paris where he was known for his big smile and friendliness towards staff and residents alike. Sam’s family extends deepest, heartfelt thanks to the MVH staff for their love and care of Sam and for providing him a safe and loving home. The family is also very grateful to the doctors, nurses, and staff at Stephens Memorial Hospital and the Andwell hospice providers who made Sam’s final hours as comfortable as possible.
Sam was predeceased by Sue in 2018. He is survived by his daughter, Perri of Bridgton, his son, Andrew and his wife Monica Bigley of Cumberland; grandson, Aidan and his fiancé Caroline in Washington, D.C., granddaughter, Lillian in Boston, Mass.; his brother, Bruce of Rockford, Ill.; and extended family across the country.
A memorial service will be held at the Sweden Community Church, 137 Bridgton Rd. (Route 93), Sweden, on Saturday, Oct. 24, at 2 p.m.
In lieu of flowers, memorial donations may be made to the Sweden Food Pantry.

title: Patriots hold off Jets for 3rd straight win
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — The thinking in New England’s locker room under Mike Vrabel has been to never apologize for a win. So no one was feeling bad after the Patriots improved to 2-0 in the AFC East after their victory over the New York Jets on Sunday.
They also know that mounting injuries will require much more from everyone if they want to keeping winning.
Drake Maye threw three touchdown passes, New England overcame losing three offensive linemen and Charles Woods came up with Geno Smith’s first interception of the season in the fourth quarter to help the Patriots hold on for a 26-19 win.
“It was sloppy. It wasn’t clean,” said Maye, who completed 18 of 32 passes for 235 yards in his third consecutive game with at least three TD passes. “It wasn’t football that we felt like (was) complementary.”
Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas and Hunter Henry had touchdown catches for the Patriots (4-2), who have won three in a row. Douglas had a team-high seven catches for 86 yards.
A.J. Brown had three catches for 27 yards for the Patriots in his return from injured reserve, but his timing was off and he had three drops on his 10 total targets.
“None of us were at our best today, but we were good enough,” Vrabel said.
New England won its fourth straight against the Jets and 19th in its last 21 meetings despite right tackle Morgan Moses (ankle), left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) and right guard Ben Brown (knee) leaving with injuries.
“Those guys are playing through injuries,” Maye said. “We (had) three go down today, so these guys are fighting hard. They’re fighting their butts off, and it goes through them.”
The Jets (2-4) had a chance to tie it in the third quarter, but the Patriots held them to a field goal. New York squandered another opportunity to cut the deficit to a field goal in the fourth quarter when Smith was picked off by Woods. It came on Smith’s 166th pass of the season, ending his longest opening stretch to a season without an interception.
“Finishing on offense and detail on defense is something we’ve got to get better at because I think we gifted two touchdowns that shouldn’t have happened,” Jets coach Aaron Glenn said.
Smith finished 20 of 30 for 252 yards and a touchdown to rookie Omar Cooper Jr., who had six catches for 103 yards in his return from IR after missing four games with an ankle injury.
New England’s defense, which got a boost from cornerback Christian Gonzalez returning from a two-game absence with a shoulder injury, held New York to 0 for 3 in the red zone. The Jets were also 3 of 10 on third down and were stopped on fourth-down runs on consecutive possessions in the second quarter.
“Those plays are huge for us. I’m just proud of the defense, how we stayed together,” Gonzalez said. “They got some momentum there late and we were just able to finish the game.”
Building the lead
The Patriots led 17-3 at the half, courtesy of Doubs’ diving 42-yard touchdown catch and a 9-yard scoring grab by Douglas.
The Jets trimmed the gap to 17-10 in the third quarter after Cooper got behind Patriots safety Craig Woodson and caught a 42-yard TD from Smith.
That remained the score when Jets edge rusher David Bailey stripped TreVeyon Henderson of the ball and Jamien Sherwood recovered at the New England 36. New York drove to 10, but Smith was sacked by Elijah Ponder, forcing the Jets to settle for a 36-yard field goal by Jason Sanders.
The Patriots responded on their next series, capping a 12-play, 68-yard drive with a 7-yard TD strike from Maye to Henry, but Andy Borregales missed the extra point.
Just four plays later and the Jets down 10, Smith overshot Kenyon Sadiq on a deep pass that was intercepted by Woods.
Injuries
Jets: LB Kiko Mauigoa left with a thigh injury in the first quarter.
Patriots: Doubs (shoulder) exited in the first quarter following his touchdown catch and didn’t return. … Moses favored his left ankle when he left early in the second quarter. … Vera-Tucker left in the second with a hamstring injury and was ruled out. … Brown had trouble putting weight on his left leg as he was helped off in the fourth quarter with a knee injury.
Up next
Jets: Host the Dolphins next Sunday.
Patriots: Visit the Bears on Thursday night.

title: Carney says 4 service members killed and dozens injured in fire at Alberta military base
text:
WAINWRIGHT, Alberta (AP) — Four Canadian service members were killed and 39 people injured, including 19 critically, when a fast-moving fire overtook soldiers conducting live-fire combat training at a military base in Alberta, officials said Sunday.
Maj. Gen. Wade Rutland said military officials knew about the fire for hours but believed it was sufficiently contained to allow training to continue before winds suddenly shifted, sending flames racing toward the soldiers.
“The fire was a kilometer away when the wind shifted. That is not normal for a fire to move a kilometer in 36 seconds,” he said at a news conference in Edmonton.
Rutland said a commander at the scene told him soldiers went from seeing no fire to having flames upon them in less than a minute.
The fire broke out Saturday during high-intensity combat training involving Charlie Company of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
About 84 soldiers were split between a grenade range and an area where they practiced attacks on simulated enemy positions. The fire swept into the second training area.
Rutland said investigators had not determined what ignited the grass fire.
He said the battalion was preparing for rapid deployment to global crises and a mission to reinforce Canadian troops in Latvia next spring.
The military identified those killed as Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton; Pvt. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; Pvt. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver, British Columbia; and Pvt. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, British Columbia. All four were serving with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, based in Edmonton.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said 39 people were receiving medical care. Sayeh Zielke, chief executive of Acute Care Alberta, said 19 were in critical condition, eight were stable and 12 were ambulatory and receiving treatment for less serious injuries.
Smith said some suffered severe burns and could face weeks or months of intensive treatment.
Prime Minister Mark Carney described the incident as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on domestic soil. He ordered flags lowered to half-staff on federal buildings nationwide.
Carney said the families of those killed had been notified. Those affected included regular forces personnel, reservists and soldiers from bases across Canada.
Hospitals respond to mass casualties
Alberta health officials said patients were transferred from Wainwright to four hospitals — the University of Alberta Hospital and Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton, Foothills Medical Centre in Calgary and Red Deer Regional Hospital.
Alberta officials said they had lifted the “Code Orange” emergency activated at several hospitals Saturday night to mobilize staff and beds for the casualties.
The response involved 22 ground ambulances, six airplanes and two helicopters, with assistance from neighboring Saskatchewan. Smith said all patients had been accounted for and no further patients were awaiting transport.
Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the town’s small hospital was not designed to handle a mass-casualty incident but praised local medical personnel.
Rutland confirmed that military search-and-rescue technicians parachuted into Wainwright to reinforce the emergency response. Pugh said their red parachutes were illuminated by flares as they descended shortly before midnight.
Cathy Keane, a mayoral candidate in Ontario, said her eldest son was among those critically injured. “As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family,” she wrote on Facebook, saying she was traveling to Alberta.
Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre, who represents the area in Parliament, visited Wainwright on Sunday and said he had heard accounts of people who ran toward the danger to help others and were now fighting for their lives in hospitals.
Military investigates fire
Rutland said the fire ignited in the military training area, where multiple exercises were underway, and spread rapidly in unusually strong winds.
He said winds had been within normal operating limits for much of Saturday, generally below 50 kph (31 mph), before intensifying rapidly. Range controllers rely on weather reports to determine whether training can safely continue, he said.
Rutland said investigators would examine whether the wind drove the fire toward the soldiers or whether flames spread unseen through vegetation before suddenly overtaking them.
The fire crossed established firebreaks before being contained with help from municipal firefighters.
The Canadian military said there were no indications of terrorism.
Rutland said military investigators would examine the circumstances, including whether safety protocols needed to change. “If our protocols need to change, then they’ll be updated,” he said.
The military typically convenes a formal board of inquiry after such incidents, Rutland said, cautioning that determining what happened would take time.
Rutland said Charlie Company had been withdrawn from the training area and the rest of the battalion suspended training Sunday.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4 p.m. Saturday following reports of a fire in the base’s training area.
Large areas of Alberta were hit by a windstorm Saturday, with gusts up to 100 kph (62 mph). The winds toppled trees, sent signs flying and pushed flames beyond the base into surrounding rural areas.
By late Saturday, the Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. No evacuation order was issued for residents.
CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations.
The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday’s referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada. Elections Alberta said the Wainwright Communiplex advance polling location closed early Saturday and election materials were transported securely.

title: A needle’s prick and everything after: Wiscasset family, school deal with Oct. 8 incident
text:
It’s been a normal Thursday. You plan to leave the house in about an hour for Wiscasset Middle High School, to pick up your seventh grader.
A Wiscasset student since kindergarten, he loves it at WMHS. He’s almost like the school mascot — everyone knows him and supports him. That is hugely important, because he has an intellectual disability; and because he’s a 13-year-old.
While you’re still home, the school calls. It’s an adult who works with your son. He explains, your son’s OK, he's in the nurse’s office, where he went to get his hair checked. There, he slid his fingers down a bed cushion and a needle, a diabetic lancet for testing blood sugar level, pricked him.
The next day, you and hospital staff hold down your confused and frightened son for a blood draw to test for HIV and Hepatitis B and C. As a precaution, at your pediatrician’s recommendation, your son starts on two HIV medications.
He can’t swallow a pill, and these can’t be chewed. He's choking them down, every morning.
If this was your Oct. 8 and everything that followed it, you're Jessica Guthro, and this is a part of your and your son’s life for now. More blood draws are ahead.
In an interview Friday night, hours after she and son Liam met with administrators and others at the school, Guthro shared with Wiscasset Newspaper her family’s experience, one week in: From her being dumbfounded that something like that, a prick from a wayward needle at the nurse’s office, could even happen; to being appreciative of the school’s response and hopeful that, between the measures the school has taken and her choice to go public with their experience, this will not happen again to any family here or elsewhere.
Friday's school visit was Liam's first time there in a week, while mother and son adjusted to the situation and its impacts.
Recalling the Oct. 8 call, Guthro said, "I didn't even process why Liam was in the nurse's office to begin with. My mind instantly went to, 'Why is my kid getting poked with a needle? What are you talking about?'"
For the blood draw at Mid Coast Hospital Oct. 9, Guthro said, "I had to hold Liam, pin his arm between my legs, lay across his chest, while two men outstretched and held his arm down while he was lifting them out of chairs, and another guy drew his blood. It was traumatic. It was awful. And we have to do it two more times."
Due to his disability, "he does not understand any of this," his mother said. "He doesn't understand why he's being hurt. He doesn't understand the two pills that he has to choke down every morning ..."
Guthro said the school didn't know how long the needle might have been in the nurse's office bed. "That's the scariest part," she said. She was told the entire room has been cleaned now.
She said Friday's conversation was with Superintendent of Schools Dr. Kim Andersson, WMHS Principal Chris Hennessey, Special Education Director Amanda Little and the staff member who works with Liam and called her after the incident.
"They're all so sorry. Nobody in that room had a smile on their faces. Everyone was upset. Everyone misses Liam. He's like the school mascot, almost. Everybody knows this kid wherever we go." She recalled of Friday's visit, "he walked right up to the principal and fist bumped him. He hugged Kim Andersson. He hugged his teacher. He hugged the special education director. He needs school. School is amazing for him. And his friends, the support that he has from his friends at that school are one of the main reasons" he attends Wiscasset, she shared.
Leaving the hospital Oct. 9, Liam wouldn't let his mother hug him. "That's not me and Liam. Anybody that knows Liam knows that we're each other's person, like, when he's sad, he wants Mama, and he wouldn't let me touch him," he was so upset and confused, Guthro recalled.
She said she was told Friday, the medical bills will be covered, which was good because one of the HIV medications was $2,900; the other, $1,800, she said.
First on Facebook and then accepting the interview, Guthro went public with her family's experience so people will be "aware that this is a situation that happened, but ... that the school is doing what they can to make it right." And she hoped parents of children with diabetes will read about what happened, "and they'll sit down and have a conversation, like 'This is why we pay attention to what we do with our needles.'"
Of this whole experience, she said, "It's really a hard situation to wrap your head around, honestly ... The fact that one of these needles was misplaced is just dumbfounding."
Guthro planned for her son to return to class Monday, Oct. 19.
"They have been so apologetic. There was concern on their faces today. While we were in there, they were apologizing to Liam ... I feel like the school can head in a good direction. They just need some help from the parents, too. Parents backing them, as opposed to gung ho, 'Let's fire everybody,' because firing everybody isn't going to get anything accomplished."
In public comments apart from the needle incident, school officials have said the nurse's office has been covered by multiple staff of late. School nurse Sommer Maybee was arrested in Wiscasset Sept. 22 under the last name of Harding on an OUI charge. She later resigned and a search for WMHS's next nurse began.
Wiscasset Newspaper asked Andersson via email about the needle incident, including had any protocol been in place to prevent such an incident; any steps being taken to prevent a recurrence; how long was the lancet believed to have been there; was the school department paying for the medical testing the student is undergoing; and "any comment on what the child and their family is having to go through and how it hit you when you learned of the incident."
"We are not legally able to discuss or disclose any student issues with anyone except the students' parents," Andersson responded.
She added later, "Every time there is an incident at school we do our best to resolve it immediately in the best interest of students and staff. When mistakes and accidents happen, our team reacts professionally and immediately to address it. Then we debrief and determine what changes we need to make to improve the situation for the future. Then we make the changes necessary.
"Our work is rooted in promoting growth and change for all learners, this is what guides our decision-making every day. As administrators and teachers, we model this reflective practice for our students. We have great students who care for each other deeply. Many of our students are together from kindergarten to 12th grade; they care about one another and it shows. They are kind, tough, and resilient. I’m proud of our staff, our students, and our school."

title: Fisherman, 71, dies after being attacked by 12-foot alligator
text:
Fisherman killed after being pulled into water, attacked by alligator
Authorities said a man, who was fishing from the shoreline of a retention pond, was dragged into the water and attacked.
Fisherman killed after being pulled into water, attacked by alligator
Authorities said a man, who was fishing from the shoreline of a retention pond, was dragged into the water and attacked.
A man was killed after police said he was attacked by an alligator while fishing on the shoreline of a retention pond in Florida.
VIDEO: Victim of Winter Garden alligator attack remembered as kind, generous
Authorities said the victim— a 71-year-old man from Winter Garden, Florida — was pulled from the water near Lake Apopka after being attacked. He was pronounced dead at the scene.
Winter Garden officials responded around 5 p.m. Friday to a 911 call out of Dr. Bradford Memorial Park, Winter Garden Fire Rescue Department Chief Jose Gainza and Winter Garden police Capt. Michael Mason confirmed to Hearst station, WESH 2 News.
According to Mason, the victim was fishing on the shoreline of a retention pond near the lake when he was attacked by a nearly 12-foot alligator.
The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission later identified the man as Steven Hamilton.
Gainza said alligators were active in the area and in the way of rescue efforts, adding rescue swimmers could not immediately enter the water.
"Lake Apopka has tons of alligators in it, so that's not uncommon to see alligators in this part of town at all," Mason said.
Officials were later seen pulling the alligator from the water. The alligator later appeared to be euthanized.
Winter Garden police are investigating the attack with the FWC.
According to CNN, this is the second fatal attack in Florida reported this year. In June, Brittany Clark, 31, was killed by a 13-foot alligator near her home.

title: BYU outlasts No. 2 Notre Dame following last-second controversy
text:
BYU outlasts No. 2 Notre Dame as 5 of top 7 teams lost in the regular season for the first time
Bear Bachmeier threw a go-ahead touchdown pass with 1:47 left and then No. 8 BYU stopped No. 2 Notre Dame at the goal line to preserve a riveting 28-24 victory Saturday night.
Bachmeier ran for two TDs, caught another and had 224 yards passing to help the Cougars (6-0) beat the Irish for the first time since 2004. Preston Rex added 66 yards on 10 carries to help BYU start 6-0 for the third consecutive season.
Video above: Big 12 investigates reports of 'inappropriate chants' from Oklahoma State student section during BYU game
After Bachmeier's go-ahead score, CJ Carr completed several clutch passes to drive the Irish (6-1) into Cougar territory, including a fourth-down pass to Micah Gilbert that put Notre Dame at the BYU 9 with four seconds left. His final pass fell incomplete in the end zone.
The Irish cut an 11-point halftime deficit to five going into the fourth quarter after scoring field goals following a muffed punt return and a failed fake punt by the Cougars. Jonaz Walton plowed across the goal line on a 3-yard run to put Notre Dame in front with 9:31 left.
Bachmeier led BYU into Notre Dame territory, but Jayden Sanders picked off a pass at the Irish 15 with 8:05 remaining.
After the Cougars forced a 3-and-out, Bachmeier drove BYU 55 yards in 10 plays and found Walker Lyons on a go-ahead 6-yard grab with 1:47 left.
Carr threw for 261 yards and Nolan James Jr. added 77 yards and a touchdown on the ground for the Irish. Notre Dame ended a 16-game winning streak.
Bachmeier used a combination of efficient passing and tough running to put the Irish on their heels early. He completed 72% of his passes in the first half.
BYU capped its opening drive with Bachmeier’s five-yard TD run up the middle.
Notre Dame took a 10-7 lead on an 8-yard run from James. Then Bachmeier punished the Irish defense on back-to-back drives. He caught a short pass from Kyler Kasper and rumbled 15 yards to put BYU back in front. Then Bachmeier dove over the goal line from a yard out to extend the Cougars’ lead to 21-10 going into halftime.
The Irish drove down to the BYU 5 in the final seconds of the first half. Carr fumbled while trying to spike the ball, and Isaiah Glasker pounced on it to help the Cougars maintain a two-score lead going into the locker room.
It was just the second turnover of the season for Notre Dame.
The game capped off a wild day in college football that has never been seen before.
The thriller capped a wild Saturday in which five of the top 7 teams in the AP Top 25 lost on the same regular-season day for the first time, per Sportradar. Paired with No. 1 Georgia’s 27-24 loss to Auburn, the top two teams in the country lost on the same day for the first time in the regular season since Nov. 17, 2012.
The last time anything even remotely close happened was on Jan. 2, 1989, according to Sportradar, when five of the top eight teams lost.
Shakeup Saturday was driven by the Southeastern Conference, with No. 1 Georgia, No. 6 Alabama and No. 7 Texas going down as touchdown or more favorites.
No. 2 Notre Dame (at No. 8 BYU) and fifth-ranked Indiana (against No. 4 Ohio State) also lost, although those were less shocking.
It's the first time Nos. 1 and 2 lost on the same day in the regular season since Oregon (to Stanford) and Kansas State (to Baylor) in 2012.
The chaos, which is sure to shuffle the poll and College Football Playoff seeding forecasts, cleared a path for No. 3 Miami to take over the top poll spot after beating rival Florida State 43-35 in a double-overtime classic that ended in controversy.
The Hurricanes can only hope to do better than the No. 1 team has the last two weeks; Texas and Georgia lost to unranked teams, the first time that's happened in consecutive weeks since Notre Dame (to Stanford) and Michigan (to Michigan State) in 1990.
Five of the top eight teams in the AP poll lost on the same day in 1989 when No. 3 West Virginia, No. 5 USC, No. 6 Nebraska, No. 7 Auburn and eighth-ranked Arkansas stumbled in bowl games.
It was nearly as rare for heavyweights Georgia, Alabama and Texas to lose on the same Saturday, which hadn't happened since Oct. 26, 1996, according to the SEC.
It showed why SEC coaches were so hesitant to give in to playing a nine-game league slate. And it might be fitting that the bloody Saturday came on the same week the SEC capitulated to the Big Ten to move closer to finalizing a 24-team playoff.
The Bulldogs (6-1, 4-1 SEC) had been the league’s last remaining team without a loss, but Gunner Stockton threw two interceptions and fumbled with less than a minute to play in a 27-24 stunner to unranked Auburn (4-2, 2-2). Georgia, which had won 53 in a row against unranked teams, was a 20 1/2 -point favorite in the game known as “the Deep South’s Oldest Rivalry.”
Alex McPherson’s 34-yard field goal on the final play sent the visiting sideline into a frenzy. It was Auburn’s first win in Athens since 2005 and the program’s first road win against the nation’s No. 1 team since winning at Florida in 1994.
“We’re just continuing to plug,” said Auburn coach Alex Golesh, whose team scored on a trick play and an amazing, one-handed catch. “We’re going to build Auburn back to where everybody wants it, one game at a time. Just hang with us.”
Auburn’s win meant the team ranked No. 1 in the AP Top 25 lost in consecutive weeks to unranked teams for the first time since Notre Dame and Michigan in October 1990, according to Sportradar. Then-No. 1 Texas lost last week to Oklahoma in the Red River Rivalry.
That setback seemed to have a carryover effect for the Longhorns.
Arch Manning had more late-game woes against Florida. He fumbled with less than two minutes to play — a week after throwing an interception that helped Oklahoma win a week ago — and the Longhorns (4-2, 1-2) lost 27-24 at home to the Gators (5-2, 3-2). Texas was a 10 1/2-point favorite.
Manning completed 14 of 20 passes for 173 yards and a touchdown. He was sacked five times as Texas lost consecutive regular-season games for the first time since 2021.
Like Auburn and Florida, No. 14 Tennessee delivered a defensive gem in the rivalry known as the “The Third Saturday in October.” The Volunteers (6-1, 3-1) held Alabama to 201 yards in a 26-10 win in Knoxville, shutting down dynamic quarterback Keelon Russell and breaking out cigars for the third consecutive year.
The Vols finished with five sacks and four takeaways.
“Phenomenal performance,” Tennessee coach Josh Heupel said.
Alabama (5-2, 3-2) was a 7 1/2-point favorite and played without leading receiver Ryan Coleman-Williams. Fans rushed the field afterward, and the Vols will gladly pay the SEC fine.
Tennessee won despite without quarterback Faizon Brandon (shoulder). George MacIntyre filled in and got plenty of help from DeSean Bishop, who ran for 159 yards and two touchdowns.
It was Alabama’s second straight loss.
In other ranked SEC action, Lane Kiffin’s former and current teams rolled. Kiffin and No. 22 LSU overwhelmed 16th-ranked Mississippi State 31-3. And No. 9 Ole Miss thumped 13th-ranked Missouri 31-3.
And No. 15 Kentucky beat Oklahoma 21-13 on the road, making first-year coach Will Stein the first Wildcats coach to win six of his first seven games in more than a century.
Indiana loses for the first time in 23 months
Indiana's 22-game winning streak ended in gut-wrenching fashion against No. 4 Ohio State.
The defending national champion and fifth-ranked Hoosiers looked like they were going to rally to beat the Buckeyes, but standout receiver Nick Marsh stepped out of bounds in the end zone and negated what would have been a 27-yard touchdown reception on a fourth-and-4 play in the final minute.
Ohio State (6-1, 4-0 Big Ten) ran out the clock from there, escaping with a 19-15 victory despite losing quarterback Julian Sayin to a right shoulder injury. Sayin left in the fourth quarter returned with his throwing arm in a sling. Coach Ryan Day said Sayin would miss “several weeks.”
It was Indiana's first loss since falling at Notre Dame in the 2024 College Football Playoff and ended a 19-game winning streak at home.
The Hoosiers (6-1, 3-1) turned the ball over twice and missed two field goals, the first one after quarterback Josh Hoover missed seeing a wide-open receiver streaking toward the end zone.

title: Man, 19, accused of drugging, raping college student in her dorm room before she died
text:
NEW YORK (WABC) - A 19-year-old New York man is facing federal charges for allegedly drugging two college students with fentanyl and raping one of them in her dorm room before she died.
Moises Freire, 19, is accused of raping Annabel Richter, a student at New York’s Fashion Institute of Technology, after giving her fentanyl back in March. The drug killed Richter and nearly killed her friend.
The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration is investigating alongside the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York and the New York Police Department.
“They had no chance. It was such a high potent hit of fentanyl. It was immediate,” said Special Agent in Charge Christopher Roberts with the DEA’s New York Task Force Division.
According to a newly unsealed indictment, Freire allegedly conspired with 18-year-old Brian Peralta Cabrera – neither FIT students – to procure fentanyl that would “last the entire night.”
The two victims let Freire into their all-female dorms March 18, where he allegedly told them he had cocaine, but authorities say he knew it was “poison.” After ingesting the substance, both victims immediately lost consciousness, the indictment says.
“The fact that he [Freire] knew he was providing them poison and masked it and made believe it was cocaine [when] it was fentanyl, that’s what’s alarming in this case,” Roberts said.
Authorities say Freire raped Richter while she unconscious and took photos of her that he sent to friends. He allegedly waited 45 minutes before alerting campus security, who administered Narcan to the victims.
Richter and her friend were taken to the hospital. The friend regained consciousness after lifesaving treatment, but tragically, Richter never woke up.
These details emerge as anger increases over Cornell University’s handling of an alleged gang rape involving drugs in 2024. Students at FIT feel angry and on edge, even as the university says it’s increasing its security presence and providing support resources.
“We come here to learn. Yeah, sure, there’s the student life aspect, but no one signs up for that to happen,” one FIT student said.
Both defendants pleaded not guilty to initial charges back in March and are still in federal custody. They face arraignment on the new charges later this month.

title: As an Oregon community mourns 4 killed in school shooting, 2 wounded survivors remain hospitalized
text:
BEND, Ore. (AP) — A special-needs teacher and student wounded in a deadly shooting at an Oregon elementary school remained hospitalized Saturday. But friends said their survival was a spot of hope in a community in mourning.
The youngest shooting survivor, 7-year-old Saylor Graham, is a feisty, vibrant fighter with a sweet nature whose story inspired other children, said Matt Sampson, executive director of Sparrow Clubs, where she was a member. She has a genetic disorder, usually uses a wheelchair and is non-verbal, but “she doesn’t even need words to connect with people,” he said.
“She’s just an amazing spirit who just immediately draws people to her and you just feel inspired by Saylor when you meet her,” Sampson said. “And she’s always wearing these iconic glasses, whether they’re pink or they’re red. She’s just such a cutie.”
Teacher Becky Drury, 54, is recovering in a Bend hospital with wounds to her arm and hand but hopes to go home soon, said Zack Hall, a family friend who is serving as her family’s spokesperson.
Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and a teacher were killed at the Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, Thursday when a former student there, 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, entered a special needs classroom and began firing with a shotgun.
One teacher was grappling with John for the weapon when the father of two students came in and shot him to death. They were credited with stopping the rampage and saving many people’s lives.
While police continued to investigate John’s motive, distraught parents, teachers and others gathered outside the school Saturday to leave flowers, pray and cry.
Savannah Patton, a mother who has a 1st and 4th grader at the school, sat on the grass Saturday across from a memorial of flowers, stuffed animals and balloons, and wiped tears from her eyes.
She told an Associated Press reporter that the teacher who died, Megan Lambert, 25, had been a substitute for her daughter’s class last year.
Patton said she has struggled to explain what happened to her daughter, who asked her, “Mommy, why would someone want to take a gun and kill us at school?” Patton said it was a question she didn’t know how to answer.
Physical challenges won’t keep her from “living with joy”
For several years, Saylor worked with students from Bend High School through the Sparrow Clubs, a volunteer group whose mission is to empower “kids to help kids in medical need” through kindness and community service, according to their website.
In a video on the Sparrow Clubs page, Saylor introduces herself, saying she loves watching Bluey and being around other kids, especially her brother. She said that while she is challenged by physical and cognitive issues, she can communicate with her eyes and a computer tablet.
“I prove every day that I’m a fighter who doesn’t give up,” she wrote in the video. ”Living with CASK-related challenges is full of unknowns, which can be very hard and scary for my whole family,” she said, “But it doesn’t keep me from smiling, laughing and living with joy!”
Some of the high school students who worked with Saylor said helping her gave them hope that there is still humanity in this world.
After the shooting, she was taken to a hospital in Portland. A GoFundMe for her family has raised almost $400,000.
“We will not let her name be forgotten”
Devon Johnson visited the memorial outside the school Saturday morning. Her husband teaches at Bend High School, and she is a volleyball coach at High Desert Middle School, so they are close with many of the staff at the elementary school.
“It’s just hard to take in,” she said. “I’m so glad to see that Bend is rallying and just wrapping their arms around this community, but it’s going to take a long time to get through this.”
Heidi Wood, the director of the Central Oregon Volleyball Club where Lambert coached, said in a social media post that she was “an amazing coach, ”an amazing teacher,” and “an amazing person who would do anything” for her students.
“To the shooter, she would have given you the shirt off her back,” Wood said. “But you didn’t give her a chance.”
Wood said that Lambert wouldn’t take her volleyball coaching pay in her first year so the money could be used for scholarships for players who couldn’t afford to play instead.
“That was her, and that is her,” Wood said. “We will carry on her love, her passion and we will not let her name be forgotten.”
___
Bellisle reported from Seattle. Associated Press writer Haven Daley contributed to his report.

title: Obituary: Linda Ann (Bell) Harris
text:
AUGUSTA – Linda Ann Bell Harris, 86, of Augusta, slipped away peacefully on Oct. 11, 2026. She was born on Dec. 27, 1939, the daughter of William and Thelma Bell of Auburn.
She graduated from Edward Little High School in 1958 and married Richard Harris in 1959. They made their home in Poland in the 160-year-old family homestead where they raised two children.
Linda was a traditional homemaker. She owned a craft shop named Harris Homestead Gift Shop, loved sewing, needlework, and painting, and was a member of the University of Maine Cooperative Extension for over 25 years. Talented and creative, she loved designing beautiful greeting cards on the computer, sharing a little bit of her heart with every card she made.
She is survived by her daughter, Jody Harris of Augusta and son, Brian Harris of Westford, Mass.; a sister, Kay-Lee Bell of Biddeford, sisters-in-law Elizabeth Bell of Auburn and Charlene Webster of Farmingdale; and beloved nieces and nephews.
She was predeceased by her husband of 61 years, Richard, who died in 2021.
There will be a graveside service at Lane Cemetery, Empire Road, Poland on Nov. 2 at 1 p.m.
Arrangements are under the care of Chandler Funeral Home and Cremation Services 26 W Dwinal St Mechanic Falls. To make an online condolence please visit http://www.chandlerfunerals.com

title: ‘It would be funny’: Man accused of stealing flamingo testifies he drank 30-40 beers that day
text:
LAS VEGAS (KVVU/Gray News) - A man accused of stealing a flamingo from its Las Vegas Strip habitat took the stand at his own trial, saying he now realizes how big of a mistake it was.
Mitchell Fairbarn, 34, is facing two counts of animal cruelty after he allegedly stole a flamingo named Peachy from the Flamingo Hotel and Casino while drunk in March.
Police say Fairbarn, a tourist from Ontario, Canada, was seen on security camera around 5 a.m. March 3 hopping a fence to get inside the flamingo habitat. Fairbarn is accused of taking Peachy from the habitat and carrying the bird to his hotel room.
Peachy was injured in the incident. The flamingo’s treating veterinarian said the bird had seven to eight missing feathers, broken shafts and blood loss that were consistent with trauma. She added that Peachy needed antibiotics, anti-inflammatories and weeks of pain medication.
Prosecutors opened the trial with surveillance video, photos and Snapchat clips showing Fairbarn smiling, laughing and grabbing Peachy by the neck with two friends. The flamingo’s veterinarian called the video of Fairbarn grabbing Peachy by the neck inappropriate and potentially fatal.
Suspect testifies he thought the incident would be ‘funny’
Fairbarn took the stand Friday in his animal cruelty trial, testifying he took Peachy as a drunken “silly pranky joke” after drinking 30 to 40 beers. He denied malicious intent to hurt or kill the flamingo.
“Did you ever, at any time, have any malicious intent or desire?” his attorney asked. “Did you intend to kill?”
“No,” Fairbarn said.
During his testimony, Fairbarn said he lives in central Ontario, runs an excavation business started in 2014, is married and has three children. He said he grew up on farms, owns dogs and a parrot named Sonny and once rescued an abandoned llama and six ducks.
He mentioned being in Las Vegas for ConExpo, “a global construction show that happens every three years,” where he was asked to be “one of the representatives from Canada.”
Fairbarn also added that his father had been diagnosed with cancer in December 2025, and he was “on the fence about coming at all.”
He said he spent March 2 gambling and drinking an estimated 30 to 40 beers. He then stopped at the flamingo habitat around 5 a.m. – drunk, sleep-deprived and on a call. He mentioned entering the habitat to look at a bird with “uneven” wings while also acknowledging he shouldn’t go in.
Inside, he said he sat with one flamingo (not Peachy) then grabbed Peachy as a “silly pranky joke” to photograph, carried the bird to his room for “two or three minutes” put it in the hallway and was arrested changing to return it.
Fairbarn also mentioned being on house arrest. He has not been able to return to Canada since.
Under cross examination, he later admitted that the video “doesn’t look good,” and Peachy was hurt, saying “I’m taking responsibility” but claimed “I have no idea” how the feathers were lost.
The trial resumes Monday morning with closing arguments before jury deliberation.
Jury questions
The jury had several questions for Fairbarn.
Q: At the beginning of the video of the island, the birds are asleep and aren’t falling down. So the question is, if you know, do flamingos naturally, physically lay down?
A: They can, or when they’re doing the building nests and stuff.
Q: If the birds were in a resting, sleeping position, how could you tell the wings were uneven?
A: From where I was standing on the platform, on the main fence, one of their wings, one looked higher than the other.
Q: I just wanted clarification about the reasoning behind going into the exhibit initially. Was it because you saw a bird potentially in distress? Or was it to create a lasting memory of the trip?
A: The very intentional moment was to go see the bird that I thought looked funny. Ended up being to make it a funny trip while I was already there.
Q: At any point during your interacting with Peachy, did you notice his injuries or bleeding slash blood on your shirt or wall?
A: No.
Q: If someone hops your fence and enters your farm and hurts an animal that you own, what is your expectation of local law enforcement?
A: That’s a good question. I would say a proper investigation to ensure that an individual that took it actually is the one who harmed it.
Q: Is being intoxicated an excuse to hurt anything, either a man, a woman, an animal, regardless of intent?
A: No.
Q: What happened to the rescue ducks?
A: We got them in 2018, I believe. We had them for three years. We sold the property and the homeowners took them. Because they were living in one.
Q: How much do you drink on a typical day?
A: Not a lot. Nowhere near what I drank here.
Q: When you noticed a bird with its wings tucked, how did you know which bird to head for when you were on the island? Or how did you know it was the right bird?
A: From what I’d seen, once I got in there and walked up to it, that’s the one that I thought was the same one that I’d seen on the other side of the pink fence.
Q: When did you take off your shirt to wrap around Peachy’s body?
A: When I was leaving the exhibit, there’s waist-height hedges. That’s when I took my shirt off to wrap around the birds so the birds didn’t get bricked because they’re all perked.
Q: You stated you walked through the bushes. Did you sustain any scratches to your arms or your body?
A: Not that I remember. I don’t believe so.
Q: Can you clarify if you walked through the bushes while holding the bird?
A: Yes, I did.
Q: Was the bird healthy when you took it out of its habitat?
A: I did not see anything wrong with it when I took it.
Q: When the flamingo tucks its head under its wings to sleep, couldn’t that cause the wings to look uneven or could that cause the wings to look uneven?
A: For sure, yes.

6-year-old boy, 35-year-old man identified as victims killed when truck drove through soccer game
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (Gray News) - A child and an adult who were killed after a truck drove through a youth soccer game in east Wichita have been identified, authorities said.
Wichita police identified the victims as Cole Adrian, 6, and Nicholas Schafer, 35, both of McPherson. The two were not related.
The crash happened around 3:25 p.m. on Saturday. Sedgwick County 911 received multiple calls reporting that a vehicle had driven onto soccer fields at Stryker Sports Complex, striking several people.
Officials said a Chevrolet pickup driven by a 34-year-old woman was parked near the fields before it drove onto one of the fields, striking several people.
Emergency personnel responded and treated the injured. Despite lifesaving efforts, Adrian and Schafer died at the scene.
Eleven other people were taken to the hospital with traumatic injuries. They include a 5-year-old girl, a 5-year-old boy, two 8-year-old boys, a 9-year-old girl, a 28-year-old woman, a 32-year-old man, a 59-year-old woman, a 65-year-old woman and a 68-year-old man. A 61-year-old woman was taken to the hospital for medical, non-traumatic treatment.
The driver was taken into custody and later released pending toxicology testing and a mechanical examination of the vehicle, officials said. No charges have been filed.
Officials said two children, both children of the driver, were also inside the pickup at the time of the crash. The driver also had another child who was playing soccer on another field at the complex. It was not immediately clear if the children were injured in the crash.
Investigators are working to determine the circumstances that led to the crash.
Wichita Police Chief Joe Sullivan expressed his condolences to the families and everyone affected by the tragedy.
“Our hearts are with the families of Adrian and Nicholas as they face an unimaginable loss. What should have been a day of children playing soccer and families spending time together ended in tragedy,” Sullivan said. “We are also thinking about those who were injured, their loved ones and everyone who witnessed what happened. We know this tragedy has affected many people throughout our community, and we want those families to know they are not alone. Our officers and investigators will continue working to understand exactly what happened.”

title: Judith Ann “Judy” Berry Wilkie (1947-2026)

The truth about the Collins family and The County
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sam Collins of Caribou is the president of S.W. Collins Co. and the brother of Sen. Susan Collins.
I read Tommy Pinette’s op-ed concerning Sen. Susan Collins, the Collins family and Aroostook County with a mixture of dismay and disbelief (“Susan Collins has scant claim to ‘County roots,’” Sept. 6).
Mr. Pinette is certainly entitled to his political opinions. He is free to support Troy Jackson, oppose Susan Collins, criticize our family, question our politics and offer his own interpretation of Aroostook County’s history. He is not, however, entitled to his own facts.
Nor should the Maine Sunday Telegram have published a piece containing numerous assertions that could have been disproved with basic fact-checking. This is particularly troubling. Facts matter, including in politics.
Without having ever met anyone in my family to our knowledge, Mr. Pinette incorrectly claimed that Collins family members are “shipped to private, $60,000-per-year schools” over the Caribou public school system, “fly in private jets and chum around with the children of billionaires,” and implied that we have home theaters.
He asserted that every Collins family member in politics has been a Republican and accused the family of using political influence to block resources and community food programs.
This is simply false. Mr. Pinette presents a caricature of an imagined Aroostook County aristocracy. My siblings and I all attended Caribou High School. My brother Gregg and I remained in Caribou, and all seven of our children also graduated from Caribou High School. The 20-year-old partially rusted car that my daughters drove to school hardly classifies as a private jet. And our “home theater” is a 10-year-old iPad.
Like many Maine families, political views within ours are not monolithic. My great-great-grandfather S.W. Collins served as a Democrat in the Maine Legislature, and my great-grandfather H.D. Collins was initially a Democrat before later serving in the Legislature as a Republican, as well as current family members who identify as Democrats.
There are more falsehoods I could address, but I am even more disappointed by the picture painted of Aroostook County and the people who live here. The op-ed described Northern Maine as a “deindustrialized borderland” dominated by oligarchs and portrayed our farmers as a privileged owner class responsible for the region’s economic problems.
That bears little resemblance to the Aroostook County I know.
Our farmers, like other people from Aroostook County, are among the hardest-working people in Maine. Farmers operate businesses subject to changing weather, labor constraints and international competition. Calling Aroostook County families “oligarchs” may align with popular political rhetoric, but it does little to illuminate the realities of living here today. The County people work hard to make a living in a rural area that has its challenges.
The community, including schools, public organizations, nonprofits and economic development groups, works hard to secure government and private funding to improve our area and enable services and infrastructure that would be otherwise unaffordable.
Members of our family have joined our neighbors to serve on numerous boards and organizations spanning education, healthcare, veterans and economic development.
For generations, our family and company like many other County families have contributed financial support to improve life here and throughout Maine. Our company’s mission is “to be an active positive influence in the communities in which we live and work.” We take that responsibility seriously.
Mr. Pinette may disagree with Sen. Collins politically. He may disagree with members of our family. He may believe Aroostook County should pursue different economic or social policies. Those are legitimate subjects for vigorous debate which I would encourage.
The issue here is larger. Disagreement does not justify fabrication. A telephone call would have corrected the op-ed’s false claims. Newspapers play an essential role in our democracy precisely because readers expect them to distinguish fact from fiction. An opinion page should provide broad latitude for argument and criticism, but attaching the word “opinion” to an article should not relieve a newspaper of responsibility for verifying claims, especially those easily checked.
Before publishing allegations, a newspaper should make a reasonable effort to determine whether those assertions are true. When a paper relaxes its standards for fact-checking, it forfeits the unique authority and trust that separates professional journalism from internet noise, at a time when newspapers can least afford it.
After growing up and spending my life here, I know something about The County: people may disagree strongly, but they generally expect you to look them in the eye, tell the truth and stand behind what you say. That is how you maintain trust. The Maine Sunday Telegram should expect the same standard in what it chooses to publish.

title: Pope Leo tells faithful in St. Peter's Square he will gradually resume duties after cancer surgery
text:
Pope Leo tells faithful in St. Peter's Square he will gradually resume duties after cancer surgery
Pope Leo XIV thanked thousands of faithful in St. Peter's Square on Sunday for their prayers while he was hospitalized for an operation to remove a malignant tumor, and said he plans to gradually return to his usual duties.
Related video: Pope Leo's cancer diagnosis sparks push for more screenings
The crowd erupted in cheers when the pontiff showed himself in the window overlooking the square, where a week ago on the same occasion of the traditional Angelus blessing he revealed that a nodule had been located on his lung, and that it would be surgically removed.
’’Now that this delicate phase is behind me, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God’s help and your prayers," Leo said, his voice sounding strong four days after the lower lobe of his right lung was removed.
The pontiff said the experience of the last week “has made me feel especially close to those facing illness and infirmity.” He told the faithful that he had ‘’truly felt your support,'' and expressed ‘’particular gratitude to the doctors, nurses and all the staff at Gemelli hospital'' where he was treated.
The pope paused for a moment and waved to the crowd before retreating into his apartment in the Apostolic Palace.
A delegation from Africa in Rome for a congress danced and ululated after the pope’s blessing.
‘’He was always in our prayers when he was sick, and we are happy to see him today,″ said Alain Kalembu of the Democratic Republic of Congo. ″This is an expression of our joy.″
The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
He told a reporter in English that he was doing ‘’much better’’ as he drove away from Rome’s Gemelli hospital to return to the Vatican, after a shorter hospital stay than had initially been anticipated.
“I don’t believe it, because he was just operated on the other day,” Cosimo Mastrocinque, a retired factory worker visiting the Vatican from the southern region of Puglia, said. “It is a miracle that he recovered already.”
American tourists were especially eager to pray alongside the first pope born in the United States. Marla Marsala of Michigan was supposed to attend a Mass with the pope last week that was canceled due to his hospitalization.
‘’I am just happy that we are praying with him today instead of for him, like we were before,’’ Marsala said. "It was a tough week for all of the people who love him, which are many. He seems like a very strong soul. So I think he will pull through and fight it, and succeed and keep doing the wonderful work he is doing.''
Claire Holland from Jacksonville, Florida, said she felt “very blessed” to be present for the pope’s return to his flock.
“I’m so happy that he has recovered so quickly. I think there have been millions and millions of prayers. And he is a strong, determined man, and I am so happy that he is feeling well enough to do this,” Holland said.
Leo's next major engagement is an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that "there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place.”
“The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery,” Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery “in another 10 days or so.”
Histological testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumor’s molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumor’s genetic characteristics.

title: Patriots hold off Jets for 3rd straight win
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — The thinking in New England’s locker room under Mike Vrabel has been to never apologize for a win. So no one was feeling bad after the Patriots improved to 2-0 in the AFC East after their victory over the New York Jets on Sunday.
They also know that mounting injuries will require much more from everyone if they want to keeping winning.
Drake Maye threw three touchdown passes, New England overcame losing three offensive linemen and Charles Woods came up with Geno Smith’s first interception of the season in the fourth quarter to help the Patriots hold on for a 26-19 win.
“It was sloppy. It wasn’t clean,” said Maye, who completed 18 of 32 passes for 235 yards in his third consecutive game with at least three TD passes. “It wasn’t football that we felt like (was) complementary.”
Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas and Hunter Henry had touchdown catches for the Patriots (4-2), who have won three in a row. Douglas had a team-high seven catches for 86 yards.
A.J. Brown had three catches for 27 yards for the Patriots in his return from injured reserve, but his timing was off and he had three drops on his 10 total targets.
“None of us were at our best today, but we were good enough,” Vrabel said.
New England won its fourth straight against the Jets and 19th in its last 21 meetings despite right tackle Morgan Moses (ankle), left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) and right guard Ben Brown (knee) leaving with injuries.
“Those guys are playing through injuries,” Maye said. “We (had) three go down today, so these guys are fighting hard. They’re fighting their butts off, and it goes through them.”
The Jets (2-4) had a chance to tie it in the third quarter, but the Patriots held them to a field goal. New York squandered another opportunity to cut the deficit to a field goal in the fourth quarter when Smith was picked off by Woods. It came on Smith’s 166th pass of the season, ending his longest opening stretch to a season without an interception.
“Finishing on offense and detail on defense is something we’ve got to get better at because I think we gifted two touchdowns that shouldn’t have happened,” Jets coach Aaron Glenn said.
Smith finished 20 of 30 for 252 yards and a touchdown to rookie Omar Cooper Jr., who had six catches for 103 yards in his return from IR after missing four games with an ankle injury.
New England’s defense, which got a boost from cornerback Christian Gonzalez returning from a two-game absence with a shoulder injury, held New York to 0 for 3 in the red zone. The Jets were also 3 of 10 on third down and were stopped on fourth-down runs on consecutive possessions in the second quarter.
“Those plays are huge for us. I’m just proud of the defense, how we stayed together,” Gonzalez said. “They got some momentum there late and we were just able to finish the game.”
Building the lead
The Patriots led 17-3 at the half, courtesy of Doubs’ diving 42-yard touchdown catch and a 9-yard scoring grab by Douglas.
The Jets trimmed the gap to 17-10 in the third quarter after Cooper got behind Patriots safety Craig Woodson and caught a 42-yard TD from Smith.
That remained the score when Jets edge rusher David Bailey stripped TreVeyon Henderson of the ball and Jamien Sherwood recovered at the New England 36. New York drove to 10, but Smith was sacked by Elijah Ponder, forcing the Jets to settle for a 36-yard field goal by Jason Sanders.
The Patriots responded on their next series, capping a 12-play, 68-yard drive with a 7-yard TD strike from Maye to Henry, but Andy Borregales missed the extra point.
Just four plays later and the Jets down 10, Smith overshot Kenyon Sadiq on a deep pass that was intercepted by Woods.
Injuries
Jets: LB Kiko Mauigoa left with a thigh injury in the first quarter.
Patriots: Doubs (shoulder) exited in the first quarter following his touchdown catch and didn’t return. … Moses favored his left ankle when he left early in the second quarter. … Vera-Tucker left in the second with a hamstring injury and was ruled out. … Brown had trouble putting weight on his left leg as he was helped off in the fourth quarter with a knee injury.
Up next
Jets: Host the Dolphins next Sunday.
Patriots: Visit the Bears on Thursday night.

title: Trump’s Russian diesel deal was the final straw for me
text:
Sam Patten has worked for Maine’s last three Republican senators, including Susan Collins’ first electoral campaigns, is a former managing editor of The Maine Wire and is the author of “Dangerous Company: The Misadventures of a Foreign Agent.”
When Donald J. Trump was again elected president in 2024, I figured he had earned his second chance. Regardless of whether I had voted for him that year, in 2020 or in 2016, he and I shared an experience that made me more open to him than anyone in my family or most of my friends.
At the time, I was the managing editor of the Maine Wire — the conservative voice in our state’s media. Covering his second administration to the extent it affects Maine from this perspective, I strained at times to understand and explain why he was doing the things he was. The flurry of executive orders at the very outset, for instance, suggested a new kind of energy. Some of his appointments, like Marco Rubio to his array of jobs and Tulsi Gabbard as director of national intelligence, struck me as promising.
It only took me until Feb. 28 of last year to get physically nauseated.
Trump’s jocks v. geek style beat-down session on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in the Oval Office punctured any Christian notions I had of redemption. It was disgusting. But I was also so very tired of Americans feeling their politics. I resolved to carry on trying the best I could to be objective — all the while hoping for better.
Due to his erratic and, at times, nonsensical behavior, I’ve come to think of Trump as mad. I would not be surprised if more than a few of my fellow Republicans think the same way.
“Should I be glad he didn’t throw spaghetti at the wall?” a now former GOP congresswoman asked me rhetorically in 2016 when, making small talk, I gamely asked if she didn’t agree Trump had made more sense at a recent media event than he had previously. She’d had enough. She went on to lose her seat that year to a Democrat Volvo salesman.
I hit that point this past weekend, on a flight back from Ukraine.
At the end of last year, I left my job at the Maine Wire to work full time on a Ukrainian consultancy project. So far this year, I’ve spent more than four months in Ukraine and over this period things have gotten worse in terms of the war.
After more than four years of a Russian invasion, Ukrainians have now begun deep strikes into Russia, primarily targeting its oil sector. So, the news that last Friday Trump moved to lift sanctions on Russian diesel and struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import nominal quantities of it into the U.S., allegedly to alleviate spiking fuel prices, was a lot to take on the back of a trip throughout which Russian shelling of civilian sites was constant.
My common experience with Trump goes back to 2018-19 during the Russia-gate probe. Then I was charged with, and pleaded guilty to, the charge of being an unregistered foreign agent for a Ukrainian politician.
Compared with a foreign power deciding who gets elected to Congress and who doesn’t, my crime — drafting talking points and op-eds for my client — could be considered risible or quaint, depending on your perspective. But, having been prosecuted as part of a broader investigation of whether Trump colluded with Russia in his first election, I remain a felon. I never sought a pardon.
There is no credible argument supporting Trump’s decision on Russian diesel. The amounts involved will not give much relief to U.S. consumers — at best 20 minutes of domestic demand, some calculate. The real problem is the fact that the Strait of Hormuz is effectively closed; that is what is driving today’s prices at the pump. And whatever revenues Russia gets will be spent on its war effort, murdering Ukrainian civilians.
So why on God’s green earth is he doing it?
Maine’s Sen. Susan Collins is right to join three other Senate Republicans in demanding the president reverse this decision. It doesn’t mean he’ll listen.
For Republicans, Trump’s insane decisions have a way of increasing in their tempo right up to consequential elections. His taking out the well-respected and highly effective Texas senator John Cornyn to run the toadying and corrupt Ken Paxton, now runs the risk of the Republican Party losing the Lone Star State for the first time in two generations. Zero sense, yet loyalists must put and shut up.
One of the reasons I once gave Trump the time of day was the seemingly insane behavior of his enemies. The “lawfare” exercised against him was real. I experienced it personally. Instead of fixing the system, however, he made it worse.
Now, Republicans who harbor any chance of withstanding the blue wave that’s coming in three weeks’ time must sidestep — or counter — the leader of their party. Ask Paul LePage about his deported in-law. Or placeholder Darline Graham about her brother Lindsey’s legacy: a hardline sanctions bill on Russia that Trump now flouts.
Whether it’s corruption, nuclear-powered narcissism or full-blown insanity, speculating about the “why” is no longer entertaining. Trump supporters are often forced to overlook the weirdness and remember the bigger objective. But when the betrayals knock with such manic insistence at your door, it becomes difficult, if not impossible, to see the larger benefit.

title: Celebrate bats, our unsung heroes of the night
text:
Ethan Gilardi is a wildlife biologist, bat specialist and the mammal program field coordinator for the Portland-based Biodiversity Research Institute.
On a cool and breezy night at a campsite in the Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument, a team of wildlife biologists crowds around the tailgate of a truck. After precisely 10 minutes, an alarm rings, and the team splits up to check a series of large mist nets stretched across dirt roads and the river’s edge, searching for nocturnal visitors that may have been caught by the nearly invisible mesh.
For hours, the nets remain empty. But as midnight approaches, headlamps illuminate the unmistakable silhouette of a small flying mammal: a bat. And not just any bat. Its multicolored coat of yellows, browns and blacks, with white frosted tips, reveals a rare sighting of a migratory tree species known as the hoary bat.
Working quickly, the team untangles the animal, records its measurements and releases it into the night. Buzzing with excitement, the biologists settle back into their chairs, flip their headlamps back to red and reset the timer for another 10 minutes.
Oct. 24 marks the beginning of International Bat Appreciation Week, a yearly celebration of an often-misunderstood group of animals that concludes, appropriately, on Halloween. Bats have long been linked to the holiday, likely because of their presence at ancient autumn bonfires that attracted insects. Their dark, swooping silhouettes were reminiscent of spirits, and bats became woven into medieval folklore.
Bat Week, which was founded by a coalition of conservation organizations and government agencies across North America, taps into this moment when bats are already on our minds, to help educate the public about these incredible and ecologically important animals.
Bats are an astonishingly diverse group of animals, with over 1,500 known species across the globe and 47 species in the U.S. Maine is home to eight species of bats — five of which live here year-round, hibernating in caves, mines, fallen rock piles and sometimes even barns and attics — along with three species of tree bats, which migrate south for the winter.
All of the bats in Maine are insectivorous, and they play a vital ecological role. Their appetite for moths, beetles, mosquitoes and other small flying insects enables them to help regulate Maine’s ecosystems and prevent the spread of insects that damage forests and crops, as well as those that affect human health. It is estimated that a single little brown bat can eat almost 1,000 mosquito-sized insects in an hour, while a nursing mother consumes almost 4,500 insects every night.
Yet bats face serious threats. Chief among them is white-nose syndrome, a fungal disease first documented in Maine in 2011. The fungus lives in the soils of caves and mines where bats hibernate, damaging their skin and rousing them mid-winter, which depletes their energy stores too early. White-nose syndrome has killed millions of bats across North America, with some areas losing 90 to 100% of cave-hibernating populations. Northern long-eared, little brown and tricolored bats are among the hardest hit species.
Habitat loss adds to the pressure on these populations, making the preservation of natural lands paramount to the future of these animals.
Better understanding bats is the first step to protecting them. Scientists across dozens of governmental agencies, academic institutions and research firms are studying white-nose syndrome and testing methods to prevent and treat it. These include using UV-C light to kill the fungus in caves, modifying airflow in areas where bats hibernate to inhibit fungal growth and testing vaccines to prevent or decrease the severity of infections.
Meanwhile, bat biologists across the continent have joined forces behind the North American Bat Monitoring Program (NABat), which standardizes the way we collect data about bats while pooling these data in a centralized hub. This allows researchers to better track bat population trends, inform conservation methods and develop new ways to support bats.
The Biodiversity Research Institute’s Mammal Program studies bats year-round, from collecting blood and hair samples for heavy metals testing in Colombia, to recording bat vocalizations for behavioral studies in Kenya, to performing the first bat captures in Katahdin Woods and Waters.
Additionally, through the Gulf of Maine Bat Research Program, scientists are studying how bats utilize offshore environments by placing echolocation recording detectors on islands, boats and buoys across the Gulf of Maine.
How can you help these ecologically valuable creatures? Put up a bat house, plant a native, pollinator-friendly garden and avoid disturbing hibernating bats by steering clear of caves and mines in the winter. And share what you’ve learned about bats to help correct misinformation and ensure these animals receive the protection and support they need.
“Nature Connects” is a monthly column showcasing conservation stories from people and organizations across Maine. To learn more or suggest story ideas, email [email protected].

Service member killed in rappelling accident before college football game
text:
SAN ANTONIO, Texas (Gray News) - An airman from the Nellis Air Force Base was killed in a rappelling incident at a college football game.
A Nellis spokesperson did not release the service member’s name, but said they were assigned to the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2.
They were attempting to rappel from the rafters as part of a demonstration before the University of Texas at San Antonio and U.S. Naval Academy football game on Saturday, The New York Times reported. The game was the university’s annual Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans event.
“Our hearts are heavy following the tragic incident at the Alamodome prior to Saturday’s UT San Antonio football game against the U.S. Naval Academy,” UTSA President Taylor Eighmy wrote in a statement. “What was intended to be a day of camaraderie, tradition and celebration has been marked by profound sadness. I want to extend my deepest and most heartfelt sympathies to the service member’s family, his fellow airmen, squadron and all those whose lives have been touched by this heartbreaking tragedy. “
The service member was taken to an area hospital and later died, the spokesperson said.
The incident is under investigation.

title: Four for Lamoreau, 19 for Wisdom and a Huge Day at the PVC Championships
text:
The County Scoreboard: Four Goals for Lamoreau, Soccer Shutouts and PVC Championships Highlight Saturday
Saturday was a busy day for Aroostook County high school sports, with plenty of soccer action and an outstanding showing from County runners at the PVC Cross Country Championships.
Easton's Drew Lamoreau led the soccer highlights with four goals, Wisdom's boys and girls combined for 19 goals, and several County teams picked up shutout victories as the regular season approaches its final days.
Meanwhile, County runners brought home three team championships, two individual titles and both Coach of the Year honors at the PVC Championships in Old Town.
With Wednesday, October 21 marking the final countable day for soccer, the playoff picture is coming into focus, and there are still some important games left to play.
Boys Soccer
Lamoreau Scores Four in Easton's Win Over Southern Aroostook
Drew Lamoreau had a big afternoon for Easton, scoring four times as the Bears defeated Southern Aroostook 7-1.
Mason Pelletier added two goals, while Aaden Tibbetts scored once to round out the Bears' offense.
Josiah Ellis contributed two assists in the victory.
Caribou Blanks Hermon Again
Caribou continued its strong play with another 2-0 shutout victory over Hermon.
The Vikings also defeated the Hawks by the same score in their previous meeting, giving Caribou two shutout wins over Hermon in just over a week.
Wisdom Puts Up 11 Against East Grand
Wisdom had one of the biggest offensive performances of the day, defeating East Grand 11-0.
The Pioneers earned the shutout as they continued their final stretch of regular-season play.
Central Aroostook Shuts Out Woodland
Central Aroostook picked up a 2-0 victory over Woodland.
The Panthers added another win to their record as they prepare for the postseason.
John Bapst Defeats Presque Isle
Presque Isle dropped a 3-0 decision to John Bapst in Saturday's rematch.
The Wildcats had also fallen to the Crusaders earlier in the week, 4-2.
Orono Edges Fort Kent
Fort Kent came up just short against Orono, falling 2-1.
The Warriors were involved in one of Saturday's closest boys soccer matchups.
Girls Soccer
Lapierre Adds Another Hat Trick for Van Buren
Emily Lapierre continued her outstanding week with another hat trick as Van Buren defeated Easton 5-0.
Madelyn Marquis added a goal for the Lady Crusaders, who earned the shutout victory.
Lapierre also scored three times against Ashland on Thursday, including the overtime winner, giving her six goals over the two games.
Wisdom Spreads the Scoring Around Against East Grand
Wisdom rolled to an 8-0 victory over East Grand, with five different players finding the back of the net.
Ellie Cyr, Madi Cyr and Blake Pelletier each scored twice for the Lady Pioneers.
Peyton Roy and Hanna Martin added one goal apiece to complete the scoring.
Fort Kent Picks Up Close Win Over Orono
Fort Kent earned a 3-2 victory over Orono in one of Saturday's tighter girls soccer games.
The Lady Warriors picked up the one-goal win as the regular season enters its final days.
Presque Isle Battles John Bapst
Presque Isle played another close game against John Bapst but fell 3-2.
Hailey Plant and Peyton Boinske scored for the Lady Wildcats, with Lucy Cheney adding an assist.
It was the second competitive meeting between the two teams during the week, following John Bapst's 5-4 double-overtime victory on Monday.
Hermon Shuts Out Caribou
Hermon defeated Caribou 8-0 in Saturday's girls soccer matchup.
The Hawks also won the previous meeting between the two teams earlier in the month.
County Runners Bring Home PVC Championships
While soccer teams were busy across the region, Aroostook County runners were putting together an impressive afternoon at the PVC Cross Country Championships in Old Town.
Houlton/GHCA's boys captured the Small School championship, Presque Isle's girls won the Large School title, and Caribou's boys brought home the Large School championship.
Caribou's Pierce Gorneault and Emma Graves added individual titles, while the County also swept the conference coaching honors.
Caribou's Thomas Beckum was named PVC Large School Girls Coach of the Year, and Presque Isle's Dylan Marrero earned PVC Boys Large School Coach of the Year, and Houlton's Chris Rines earned PVC Small School Boys Coach of the Year honors.
Three team championships, two individual victories and two coaching awards made it quite a day for County cross country.
Soccer's Final Days Are Here
With the final countable day now set for Wednesday, October 21, County soccer teams are running out of opportunities to improve their postseason positions.
Saturday brought plenty of big performances, including Lamoreau's four-goal afternoon, another hat trick from Lapierre and shutout victories for several County teams.
There are still some important matchups ahead, but the focus is quickly shifting toward tournament soccer.
And with the success County runners enjoyed at the PVC Championships, championship season is already off to an impressive start across Aroostook County.
