title: Obituary: Jean Ellen Emmons
text:
PORTLAND – Jean Ellen Emmons, a beloved mother, grandmother, great-grandmother, sister, and friend, passed away on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, at the age of 91. Her life was filled with love, family, cherished traditions, and countless memories that will live on in the hearts of all who knew her.
A lifelong resident of Portland, Maine, Jean also enjoyed several wonderful years in Port Charlotte, Fla., where she made special memories with dear friends. In her final months, she was cared for by the wonderful team at Freeport Place Assisted Living, whose kindness and compassion brought comfort during this time. A special thank you to the staff at Northern Light Home Care and Hospice.
Jean’s own love story began at a dance at the Stevens Avenue Armory, where she met the love of her life, Carl. They danced the night away as though they had known each other forever. They married on Oct. 20, 1956, in Portland and honeymooned in the beautiful mountains of New Hampshire. Together, they built a life and a family, sharing 38 years of marriage until Carl’s passing on Aug. 31, 1994.
Their love was a special part of Jean’s life, and it is comforting to imagine them reunited in heaven, dancing together once more as their wedding anniversary approaches on Oct. 20. Some love stories never truly end; they simply wait for the day they can begin again.
Family was the heart of Jean’s world. Such a generous woman and a great role model, as she loved family and her faith.
Jean is survived by her beloved sister, Carol; her five children, Debbie, Mark, Diane, Kelley, and Jen; her 13 grandchildren, Joe, Michelle, Andrew, Crystal, Corey, Meredith, Austin, Melanie, Carlene, Benjamin, Meghan, Holly and Erin; and her 14 great-grandchildren, William, Nora, Mia, Sophia, Max, Landon, Jayce, Luca, Masha, Olivia, Leo, Madison, (with another soon to arrive) and Theo and Wesley.
Jean devoted much of her working life to Mercy Hospital in Portland, where she worked as an EKG technician. Mercy held a particularly special place in her heart, as it was also where she welcomed all five of her children into the world.
Beyond her family, Jean found happiness in the simple pleasures that made life special. She loved the ocean, especially Higgins Beach in Scarborough, where she could enjoy the beauty and peacefulness of the Maine coast. She looked forward to listening to the Boston Pops’ Fourth of July music, enjoyed the big band sounds she once danced to with Carl, and remained a devoted fan of the Boston Red Sox and Boston Celtics. She also loved a bowl of haddock chowder from DiMillo’s, a favorite that brought a little taste of home and happiness.
Rest peacefully, Mom. May you and Dad dance together again, just as you did that very first night. Until we meet again, you will forever be in our hearts.
Memorial services will be held on Nov. 5, from 11 a.m. to 12 p.m. at St. Pius X Catholic Church, 492 Ocean Ave. in Portland, followed by a burial at Forest City Cemetery at 12:30 p.m. in South Portland. A gathering of friends and family will follow at Bruno’s Restaurant on Allen Avenue in Portland.

title: Community leaders say foiled Illinois mass shooting was result of surge in anti-Hindu hate online
text:
A thwarted mass shooting targeting a large Hindu temple in suburban Chicago was fueled by years of hateful rhetoric on social media against Hindus and Indians, community leaders say.
Authorities on Wednesday arrested Alexandros Paporakis, 19, who they said drove to the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora, Illinois, on Sunday afternoon, armed with a rifle and body armor. Officials said he remained in the parking lot for several minutes, but left after his weapon jammed. Paporakis was arrested later that day near his home in Palatine, Illinois, after a co-worker at a Taco Bell alerted authorities to his plan to “kill Indian people.”
The temple, the largest in Aurora, was crowded Sunday with thousands observing the first day of Navaratri, a nine-night celebration of Shakti -- the divine feminine energy believed to be foundational to all creation.
U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, who represents Illinois’ 8th congressional district, said he and his parents were inside the temple Sunday afternoon.
“Little did we know there was an attacker outside with sinister intent,” he said Thursday. “This has really shaken us.”
During a news conference Friday morning in Chicago, Krishnamoorthi stood with several other faith and civic leaders calling for the attempted mass shooting to be investigated as a hate crime. Speakers also called for an organized community response to prevent hate and extremism targeting all communities.
Hindus face online hate and real-world threats
Pushpita Prasad, a spokesperson for the Coalition of Hindus of North America, said attacks against Hindus and Indians have been escalating in recent years. She said the racial slurs are increasingly visible online.
“You see vitriolic posts associating Indians with dirt and creating disgust about their appearance, food and cultural practices,” she said. “Sooner or later, all that online hate is going to migrate to the real world.”
Over the past two years, the rising wave of anti-Hindu hate has included a rash of vandalism and attacks across the country. Most recently, on Oct. 3, vandals hurled bricks at a Hindu temple in Richmond Heights, Ohio, shattering several windows while devotees were praying inside.
In June 2025, a gunman fired bullets into the Sri Sri Radha Krishna Temple in Spanish Fork, Utah, causing thousands of dollars in damage. In Sugar Land, Texas, a 90-foot statue of the deity Hanuman, consecrated in 2024 at a temple complex, continues to draw disparaging comments, including one YouTube personality who recently urged its demolition.
In Frisco, Texas, where people of Indian origin make up about one-third of the population, speakers have used public comment periods during city council meetings to label the Indian community as “invaders,” characterize Hindu temples as a threat and accuse H-1B work visa holders of stealing American jobs or committing fraud.
Leaders call for resources to combat hate and extremism
Temple administrators in Aurora issued a statement Thursday assuring the community that they value the safety of devotees, employees and volunteers, and have implemented additional security measures including an “armed security presence.”
Krishnamoorthi said the temple, situated on 20 acres, is a cultural hub for the community in the Chicago area. It has been his family’s home away from home for about 40 years, he said.
“For people who were newly immigrated, this became their connection to the homeland,” Krishnamoorthi said.
The temple serves as a venue for concerts, dance performances, birthdays and weddings, and the cafeteria that serves South Indian cuisine is popular, he said.
Krishnamoorthi called for the FBI to prosecute this incident as a hate crime, and for social media companies to end the hateful rhetoric online.
“The FBI also needs to redirect resources to combat domestic violent extremism,” he said. “Election fraud and immigration are not the biggest threats facing our country.”
Joel Finkelstein with the New Jersey-based Network Contagion Research Institute, which tracks cyber-social threats, said in 2025, anti-Indian content on X tripled in weekly volume. The administration’s changes in immigration policies, particularly relating to the H1-B visa, corresponded with measurable surges in racial slurs and deportation rhetoric targeting Indians, he said.
Amid the increase in online hate, Finkelstein said the South Asian community in the U.S., despite significant resources, lacks the ability to advocate for itself with strength and unity.
“There is nothing to stop it from getting worse,” he said.
Advocates say xenophobia has fueled hate
Sravya Tadepalli, executive director of Hindus for Human Rights, says her organization has formed strong coalitions with Muslim, Sikh and other organizations whose members also face hate.
“It’s important to understand that rhetoric is not just rhetoric,” she said. “It is harmful and can result in violence.”
Manjusha P. Kulkarni, co-founder of Stop AAPI Hate, said her organization’s research showed that online slurs targeting South Asians rose 109% from 2023 to 2025. Statistics aside, Kulkarni said she was personally shaken by the threat in Illinois.
“It hits all of us who are temple goers,” she said. “Seeing how going to my house of worship can put me and my children at risk is very scary.”
AAPI Hate pointed to “xenophobic policies and rhetoric” that depict Indian people as a demographic threat — including Vice President JD Vance calling H1-B workers “indentured servants” and Bo French, the Republican candidate for Texas’ Railroad Commission calling South Asian students at a Longhorns football game “a problem.” French’s post led to a flurry of other posts on social media calling for violence against Indian communities, including desecrating Hindu temples and statues.
Last month, a Sikh truck driver was stabbed in Wyoming, days after the Department of Homeland Security published a derogatory social media post about Sikh truck drivers.
Sikh temple shooting survivor stresses need for meaningful dialogue
Pardeep Kaleka’s father, Satwant Singh Kaleka, was one of six people killed in 2012 in a mass shooting at their gurdwara in Oak Creek, Wisconsin – the deadliest anti-Sikh attack in the U.S. The shooter, Wade Michael Page, was a self-proclaimed white supremacist.
After Paporakis’ arrest in Illinois, authorities said they recovered weapons, ammunition, a gas canister labeled with a slur referring to South Asians and several items depicting Nazi symbols. Officials said Paporakis wrote a manifesto in which he fantasized about mass murder and expressed his desire to kill as many non-white people as he could.
Kaleka, who co-wrote a book with a former white supremacist about his own journey of forgiveness after the Sikh temple shooting, said the young men who perpetrate these attacks don’t pop up suddenly.
“Most people who do this have lost hope, and their motivation is also to have you and society lose hope,” he said. “Their belief is if you can attack people in the space they hold most sacred, it plants a deep terror in communities.”
The solution is to have candid conversations across racial and religious boundaries so people can understand each other at a human level, Kaleka said. “Unless that happens, we’re more likely to see division rather than a collective spirit that joins us together.”

title: Lifestyle influencer shares new details on 4-year-old son's death
text:
'Hard to fathom my life without him': Lifestyle influencer shares new details on 4-year-old son's death
Lifestyle influencer Jennifer Burnham is grieving the loss of her four-year-old son.
The influencer announced her son's passing via Instagram, saying, "Heaven welcomed our angel, Baxter, last Monday, Oct. 5th."
Related video: Family remembers Dolly Parton’s lasting gift to dying fan
She continued, saying, "Baxter, from the moment you were born, you have always been our dream come true. You have the most perfect angelic face and the sweetest personality. You are always kind to everyone and always love holding a car in each hand or a bag of them with you everywhere you go... We love you always and forever."
Jennifer later shared in a video posted on Oct. 15 that her son had been diagnosed with a brain tumor in April after he’d begun crossing his left eye.
While doctors initially diagnosed him with strabismus, which is not unusual for someone of Baxter’s age, a pre-surgery MRI revealed a diffuse midline glioma.
“Which, in the brain tumor world, is essentially the worst type of brain tumor that you can have, unfortunately,” Jennifer said in the updated video. “Because it's in the brainstem and that's inoperable, meaning it's incurable.”
Doctors were able to perform surgery to remove part of the tumor that was on Baxter’s cerebellum. In addition, Jennifer and her husband Bryce tried several other treatments, including proton radiation.
Jennifer shared how her son had been strong through all the treatments, saying no child or parent should ever go through this type of pain.
“I know he's in heaven and just playing with his cars and trucks and eating cookies and ice cream and having the best time,” she said. “And that gives me comfort as a mom, just knowing that he's no longer in pain.”
Though “it doesn't change the fact that my heart is broken,” she added. “I'm just, like, not sure how to continue living every day. It's so hard to just fathom my life without him, because he is such a big, full part of it.”
Jennifer and her husband also share another son, 1-year-old Barron.
Jennifer has over 104,000 followers on Instagram and is known for sharing lifestyle, motherhood, and cooking content.

title: Obituary: Cheryl Sydney Miller
text:
ARLINGTON, Mass. – Cheryl Sydney Miller, “Sherry”, passed away on Oct. 5, 2026, at the Sunrise Senior Living Center in Arlington, Massachusetts, where she was a resident for the last two years. Prior to moving to Sunrise, she lived at Colonial Village in Arlington, Massachusetts, for over 45 years where she was an active member of the condo association.
Sherry was born on March 16, 1952, to Sue (Cohen) and Harold M. Miller in Lewiston, the youngest of three daughters. She graduated from Lewiston High School in 1970 and went on to Lasell Junior College earning an associate degree. Subsequently she attended Lesley University where she earned her bachelor’s and master’s degrees in education. Her employment history included working for Computer Vision, MITRE Corporation, and the Massachusetts Department of Unemployment Assistance prior to her retirement. In her retirement she became a substitute teacher in the Arlington Public Schools, a job she thoroughly enjoyed.
Sherry was a significant presence in the lives of her nephews and nieces and enjoyed spending time with them as they grew up.
Sherry cultivated and maintained close friendships with people from every facet of her life. She stayed connected to high school friends, college friends, work friends and new friends she met along the way.
She was always willing to be there for the people in her life. She treasured these lifelong relationships. Sherry was a life member of Hadassah and enjoyed the fellowship of the group’s Supper Club. She volunteered with the Jimmy Fund and was a member of the Arlington Garden Club, Arlington Friends of Drama, The League of Women Voters and played the piano at Sunrise in Arlington as a volunteer before she became a resident.
Sherry enjoyed many things including her love of Maine and the ocean, the Red Sox, playing the piano, embellishing stories and spending time with her family and friends.
She is survived by her two sisters, Marta Frank of Charlestown Massachusetts and Harpswell, and Roberta Hirshon of South Portland; her nephews Todd Hirshon of Boxford, Massachusetts and Jason Hirshon of Portland, Oregon and her nieces Sara Hirshon of Cape Elizabeth, Miriam Hirshon of Danville, Kentucky, Elizabeth Frank of New York City and Heather Schofield of Winchester, Massachusetts, as well as 11 great nieces and nephews.
She will be greatly missed and often remembered by many. A celebration of life will be held in the spring.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made in Sherry’s memory to Hadassah at http://www.donate.hadassah.org, the Shriner’s Hospital or the Jimmy Fund.

title: Box Office: Elizabeth Holmes movie ‘You Can See Everything’ is now a hit in theaters too
text:
North American movie theaters were flooded with new films this weekend, including a video game reboot, a big budget survival thriller and a Jane Austen adaptation.
While Paramount’s “Street Fighter” took the first-place spot, earning $31 million from 3,575 theaters according to studio estimates on Sunday, most of the attention and cultural discourse was elsewhere: On the nearly three-hour Elizabeth Holmes documentary, “You Can See Everything.”
‘You Can See Everything’ had thousands of sellouts
Buzz and box office don’t always line up, but “You Can See Everything” made an extraordinary $15 million from only 855 screens, with over 2,000 sellout showings over the weekend, according to A24. It also had the biggest opening for a film playing on under 1,000 screens since “Borat” opened to $26.5 million in 2006, and the biggest nonmusic documentary opening in two decades, since “Fahrenheit 9/11” made nearly $24 million from 868 theaters. Those numbers do not account for inflation.
Like other hits this year, like the Gen-Z driven “Backrooms” and “Obsession,” ticket sales for “You Can See Everything” were driven by a largely younger audience. Over 70% of the opening weekend crowd was under 35.
The film, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, was made in secret over three years. Fielder spent over a month with the disgraced Theranos founder and her family, including two young children and partner Billy Evans, in her final days before reporting to federal prison. The reviews have been extremely positive, with 99% on Rotten Tomatoes and 99 on Metacritic. It also got an unprecedented 91% “definite recommend” from audiences, according to PostTrak exit polls.
“You Can See Everything” reportedly cost under $7 million to make and less than $10 million to market.
“Everybody underestimated the movie, because on paper this is like, wait, a three-hour documentary?” said Paul Dergarabedian, the head of marketplace trends for Rentrak. “But he (Fielder) is a huge draw, and he has a huge following on social media, and then Elizabeth Holmes is just a character that you couldn’t even make up. It’s stranger than fiction, and that’s really compelling.”
‘Street Fighter’ knocks out ‘Whalefall’
“Street Fighter” topped the charts as expected with a $51 million global opening, including $20 million from international showings. The movie starring Callina Liang, Noah Centineo and Andrew Koji cost a reported $82 million to make, not accounting for marketing and promotion. Audiences were 69% male.
Both “Street Fighter” and “You Can See Everything” may have contributed to “Whalefall’s” relative failure this weekend. The $60 million survival thriller starring Austin Abrams and Josh Brolin made $8 million from 3,065 locations in the U.S. and Canada, despite being better reviewed than “Street Fighter.” With $9.5 million from international showings, the Disney release had a $17.5 million global launch.
“Whalefall” opened in fourth place, behind the Jessica Chastain horror “Other Mommy.” The Universal Pictures release added $8.4 million in its second weekend, bringing its domestic total to $44.9 million.
Fifth place went to “Sense and Sensibility,” which earned an estimated $7.3 million from 2,545 theaters. The well-reviewed Austen adaptation starring Daisy Edgar-Jones drew a predominantly younger (58% between the ages of 14 and 18) and female crowd (84%). It also got the strongest CinemaScore of the week (A-).
Warner Bros. Clockwork also released a restored presentation of Ken Russell’s 1971 film “The Devils” in 350 locations, where it made $1.6 million. It’s the first release from the studio’s specialty label.
‘Musk’ documentary facing advertising blocks
Alex Gibney’s Elon Musk documentary “Musk” also expanded to 472 screens in the U.S. and Canada, where it made $306,702. The film, which runs nearly four hours, has faced issues advertising on major social media platforms including X, which Musk owns, and TikTok, according to distributor Bleecker Street, who said TikTok this weekend permanently suspended the film’s ad account.
According to Rentrak, the weekend overall generated about $101.6 million in ticket sales, up 45% from the same weekend last year. The year to date stands at $8.2 billion, which is up almost 20% from 2025.
Top 10 movies by domestic box office
With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak:
1. “Street Fighter,” $31 million.
2. “You Can See Everything,” $15 million.
3. “Other Mommy,” $8.4 million.
4. “Whalefall,” $8 million.
5. “Sense and Sensibility,” $7.3 million.
6. “Verity,” $6.2 million.
7. “Resident Evil,” $5.5 million.
8. “Heart of the Beast,” $4.8 million.
9. “Jailer 2,” $3.2 million.
10. “Forgotten Island,” $2.3 million.

title: Past dust explosions in Maine failed to spark change. Will Searsmont?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Nine years ago, in the small central Maine town of Detroit, a foreman climbed to the top of a high-capacity fertilizer silo at Northeast Agricultural Sales. It was early October. The harvest season had wound down, and he was scraping off the residual chemical crust with a metal shovel.
As the man worked, he struck an exposed electrical wire, according to a U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration report. The resulting spark was small, but it happened in a dark, tightly enclosed cylinder filled with suspended particles of micro-pulverized sulfur.
The cloud ignited, severely injuring the foreman, Anthony Tower, and two others, federal records show.
Corporate leadership said the disaster was a result of human error, claiming Tower violated internal safety protocols by taking a metal tool into a confined space. Federal safety inspectors, however, saw systemic problems and fined the company $48,000 for mishandling dust hazards.
The blast was a warning: when fine particulate matter — whether it’s chemical sulfur, pulverized grain, microscopic aluminum or sawdust — is suspended in an enclosed space, it ceases to be mere waste. It becomes an explosive vapor waiting for a spark.
In the decade that followed, Maine’s regulatory infrastructure operated as if the Detroit explosion had been an anomaly: the state didn’t start tracking how many facilities have dangerous amounts of combustible dust, instead relying on companies to self-report the hazard; it also didn’t address loopholes that left private industrial sites largely uninspected for dust risks. Meanwhile, federal safety inspectors lacked a comprehensive standard and managed dust-related problems through reactive, piecemeal citations.
On May 15, those regulatory gaps culminated in another disaster, this time at a pine mill in Searsmont. There, on the grounds of Robbins Lumber, stood a concrete and steel silo designed to store kiln-dried sawdust and wood shavings.
When volunteer firefighters arrived at the mill that morning, they were responding to a routine call of a smoldering fire near the base of the silo, where workers bagged wood shavings. The crew directed a steady stream of water into the lower hatch, a tactic that had worked on previous small fires in the facility’s top-vented silo, according to an investigation by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health.
This particular silo, a used Harvestore installed in 1993, was an airtight, oxygen-limited model.
The water did not suffocate the ember. Instead, according to NIOSH, the high-pressure stream likely acted as a mechanical pump, driving fresh oxygen into the sealed upper vault. The force blasted microscopic wood dust off the interior walls, churning it into a cloud. When oxygen hit the hot fuel, the mixture detonated. The pressure spike lifted the silo off its foundation, and it blew apart in a violent fireball.
Andrew Cross, a volunteer firefighter from Morrill, died at the scene. Searsmont Assistant Fire Chief Wayne Woodbury and mill co-owner Alden Robbins were severely burned and died weeks later. A dozen others were injured.
NIOSH, which issues reports when firefighters are injured or killed on the job, concluded that officials at the state, local and company levels could have better identified and trained for the specific mechanics of combustible dust explosions, a hazard that the agency had been warning about for decades.
“I don’t know that the state understood the severity of combustible dust hazards, including myself,” said Maine State Fire Marshal Shawn Esler. He used to be the fire chief in Waterville, home to lumber yards, repair shops, plastic fabricators and other sites that could be at risk.
Without reform, experts say it’s only a matter of time before another explosion.
PHYSICS OF A DUST BOMB
A standard fire requires three elements: fuel, oxygen and heat. An explosion requires two extra variables: dispersion and confinement.
At Robbins Lumber, the fine pine dust was the fuel; the fire hose provided both the dispersion force and the oxygen surge; the embers provided the heat source; and the airtight silo provided the sealed pressure vessel. Once ignited, the expanding combustion gases had nowhere to go but out — destroying the vessel holding them.
“It is far from just a sawmill problem,” said Guy Colonna, a chemical engineer who helped draft the National Fire Protection Association’s combustible dust and confined space standards. “If people get just one thing out of my instruction, I hope it’s that.”
For years, Colonna has traveled the country trying to educate industrial operators on dust hazards, which extend from plastic recycling centers to flour mills. Federal data show more than 200 major combustible dust incidents across the U.S. since 1980, killing more than 100 people and injuring 700. Yet convincing small-town industrial enterprises to pay attention has historically proven difficult.
Last year, Colonna, who lives in Blue Hill, said he was forced to cancel a seminar in Maine because almost no one registered. Last month, when he returned to teach a two-day workshop, the 40-person class filled up within days, and the waiting list was long enough to fill two more classrooms, according to a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Labor.
“Now it’s on everyone’s front burner,” said Jeff Lewis, a risk management specialist at Cross Insurance, which covers many of Maine’s independent lumber mills and helped fund the cost of the combustible dust training course.
WHO OVERSEES DUST HAZARDS?
The regulatory framework is a patchwork of jurisdictional carve-outs.
At the state level, the Bureau of Labor Standards oversees safety strictly within public institutions, like town fire stations, public works facilities, churches or schools. Private industry falls under the federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration.
At the federal level, no single binding regulation governs combustible dust in general industry.
After fatal industrial dust catastrophes in the mid-2000s, Congress tried to pass a law forcing OSHA to create a comprehensive safety standard for particulate hazards. Rulemaking began in 2009, and heavy lobbying by manufacturers delayed the effort until it was dropped in 2017.
When a dust explosion occurs, OSHA must rely on the “General Duty Clause,” a broad provision requiring a workplace free from recognized hazards. Federal inspectors cite voluntary, third-party guidelines to prove a company ignored “recognized industry knowledge.”
Experts have characterized it as post-disaster prosecution rather than pre-disaster prevention.
Colonna is now advocating for updates to the NFPA code that would mandate signs on all sealed or oxygen-limited silos warning firefighters and workers never to inject air or water directly into a smoldering hatch.
State officials rely on voluntary safety reviews rather than mandatory enforcement. Maine offers free workplace safety reviews through the Bureau of Labor Standards, sending inspectors into private facilities to identify OSHA violations without issuing fines. The reviews temporarily shield that workplace from federal inspection.
State safety consultants toured nine sawmills in 2023, one in 2024, four in 2025 and two so far in 2026, state records show. Because those consultations are confidential, however, the public has no way to know if they analyzed dust levels.
Under Maine emergency planning rules, a private facility storing more than 10,000 pounds of combustible dust must report it to the state and their local fire departments. The 60 companies that did, according to records obtained by the Portland Press Herald, ranged from aerospace part makers to milk carton recyclers to composting facilities.
Only four of those were sawmills: Hammond Lumber in Belgrade, Louisiana-Pacific in New Limerick, PalletOne in Livermore Falls and Woodland Pulp in Baileyville. Robbins disclosed risks for its diesel fuel and sulfuric acid but not its sawdust silo.
On the morning of the disaster, federal regulators say the Searsmont silo was about 20% full. That means it held at least 36,000 pounds of fine, dry wood dust, which is almost four times the legal reporting threshold.
The public often assumes the Office of the State Fire Marshal conducts routine safety audits of industrial facilities like Robbins Lumber, but Esler said state law only gives him the authority to review building plans and inspect daycares, hospitals and public buildings.
“There are a lot of buildings built in Maine that do not require a permit from our office,” he said.
The Fire Marshal’s sole interaction with Robbins Lumber occurred during a routine paperwork review of blueprints for the mill’s sprinkler system, he said. With a small staff, the office cannot inspect every private business in Maine or check its hazard documentation.
While safety experts recommend red warning placards on airtight silos, state fire code does not mandate them, Esler said. Maine operates under the 2018 edition of NFPA code, which contains minimal references to combustible dust and imposes no labeling requirements on sealed silos.
The Maine Forest Products Council, the primary lobbying arm for the state’s timber and wood products industry, offered no statement regarding sector-wide dust safety protocols. But fire chiefs have told Esler that some mills are organizing walk-throughs of their high-risk areas.
Robbins Lumber management did not respond to questions about why a formal dust hazard analysis was never performed, why local fire departments were never briefed on the oxygen-limited mechanics of the silo or why the vessel did not have warning signs on it.
In August, the company issued a statement about its rebuilding plans on its website.
“Our objective is not simply to meet current industry standards, but to exceed them,” Catherine Robbins-Halsted, a co-owner and vice president, wrote. “We are committed to learning from this event and to doing everything we can to help prevent anything like this from happening again.”
WHAT CAN BE DONE?
In the aftermath of the explosion, a group of fire officials, sawmill operators, elected leaders and insurers formed to discuss a response to Searsmont. They must wait, however, until Mainers go to the polls next month before deciding what reforms to pursue, Esler said.
“I can’t give you the answers about the solutions that I feel may be warranted without consulting with the next governor,” Esler said.
Esler expressed skepticism toward creating a state-mandated inventory of privately owned silos to determine if combustible dust risks are documented and notified. His office cannot inspect a private workplace without statutory authority, a complaint or corporate invitation.
His office is wrapping up a statewide inventory of hazardous firefighting foam, but most of that material is stored in public buildings, where his office has more pull and more authority. He was also able to secure public funding to hire someone to conduct the survey.
He pointed to recent progress in equipping volunteer fire departments with mapping software that allows crews to view documented hazards on their way to a call. But that requires companies to accurately report their hazards and local fire departments to input the data.
The urgency for reform is compounded by an impending workforce collapse in the Maine fire service and the need for more training, Esler said.
For now, policy reforms are being vigorously debated behind closed doors but remain on hold. When asked what he would tell a Maine citizen asking how the state plans to prevent another Searsmont explosion, Esler’s answer was brief: “Wait and see.”

title: Early voting push ramps up amid ballot-counting legal battle
text:
Early voting push ramps up amid ballot-counting legal battle
The Trump administration is asking a judge to pause the counting of mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizens in California until their immigration status can be verified.
Early voting push ramps up amid ballot-counting legal battle
The Trump administration is asking a judge to pause the counting of mail-in ballots from alleged noncitizens in California until their immigration status can be verified.
The race is on to get out the vote in the final stretch of the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.
President Donald Trump continued his campaign travel blitz on Saturday with a rally in Kentucky aimed at boosting Republican turnout.
Meanwhile, organizers planned hundreds of "No Kings" rallies across the country this weekend. Many attendees held signs opposing Trump's policies, but organizers framed the events as a nonpartisan effort to encourage early voting. The national movement is also mobilizing to prepare for "mass nonviolent action in rapid response to election disruption or subversion if needed."
The rallies come amid an escalating legal battle in California, where the Trump administration is asking a judge to pause the counting of mail-in ballots from suspected noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed as part of a broader effort to prevent fraud.
California's Secretary of State Shirley Weber says the federal government hasn't provided evidence to support its allegations and warns that these "unprecedented measures" could threaten voting rights.
The Justice Department upped the stakes, warning in a letter addressed to the Los Angeles County Counsel’s office that local election officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters may be at risk of prosecution.
"They will all go to jail for a long period of time," Trump said on social media.
Meanwhile, Democratic Senators Alex Padilla, Dick Durbin and Sheldon Whitehouse are urging the Justice Department in a letter to reaffirm that it won't interfere in the election and rule out any attempt to seize ballots before the midterm results are certified.
The DOJ didn't immediately respond to requests for comment on the letter.

title: Foot and Paddle: Cranberry Peak – At Peak Color
Celebrate bats, our unsung heroes of the night
text:
Ethan Gilardi is a wildlife biologist, bat specialist and the mammal program field coordinator for the Portland-based Biodiversity Research Institute.
On a cool and breezy night at a campsite in the Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument, a team of wildlife biologists crowds around the tailgate of a truck. After precisely 10 minutes, an alarm rings, and the team splits up to check a series of large mist nets stretched across dirt roads and the river’s edge, searching for nocturnal visitors that may have been caught by the nearly invisible mesh.
For hours, the nets remain empty. But as midnight approaches, headlamps illuminate the unmistakable silhouette of a small flying mammal: a bat. And not just any bat. Its multicolored coat of yellows, browns and blacks, with white frosted tips, reveals a rare sighting of a migratory tree species known as the hoary bat.
Working quickly, the team untangles the animal, records its measurements and releases it into the night. Buzzing with excitement, the biologists settle back into their chairs, flip their headlamps back to red and reset the timer for another 10 minutes.
Oct. 24 marks the beginning of International Bat Appreciation Week, a yearly celebration of an often-misunderstood group of animals that concludes, appropriately, on Halloween. Bats have long been linked to the holiday, likely because of their presence at ancient autumn bonfires that attracted insects. Their dark, swooping silhouettes were reminiscent of spirits, and bats became woven into medieval folklore.
Bat Week, which was founded by a coalition of conservation organizations and government agencies across North America, taps into this moment when bats are already on our minds, to help educate the public about these incredible and ecologically important animals.
Bats are an astonishingly diverse group of animals, with over 1,500 known species across the globe and 47 species in the U.S. Maine is home to eight species of bats — five of which live here year-round, hibernating in caves, mines, fallen rock piles and sometimes even barns and attics — along with three species of tree bats, which migrate south for the winter.
All of the bats in Maine are insectivorous, and they play a vital ecological role. Their appetite for moths, beetles, mosquitoes and other small flying insects enables them to help regulate Maine’s ecosystems and prevent the spread of insects that damage forests and crops, as well as those that affect human health. It is estimated that a single little brown bat can eat almost 1,000 mosquito-sized insects in an hour, while a nursing mother consumes almost 4,500 insects every night.
Yet bats face serious threats. Chief among them is white-nose syndrome, a fungal disease first documented in Maine in 2011. The fungus lives in the soils of caves and mines where bats hibernate, damaging their skin and rousing them mid-winter, which depletes their energy stores too early. White-nose syndrome has killed millions of bats across North America, with some areas losing 90 to 100% of cave-hibernating populations. Northern long-eared, little brown and tricolored bats are among the hardest hit species.
Habitat loss adds to the pressure on these populations, making the preservation of natural lands paramount to the future of these animals.
Better understanding bats is the first step to protecting them. Scientists across dozens of governmental agencies, academic institutions and research firms are studying white-nose syndrome and testing methods to prevent and treat it. These include using UV-C light to kill the fungus in caves, modifying airflow in areas where bats hibernate to inhibit fungal growth and testing vaccines to prevent or decrease the severity of infections.
Meanwhile, bat biologists across the continent have joined forces behind the North American Bat Monitoring Program (NABat), which standardizes the way we collect data about bats while pooling these data in a centralized hub. This allows researchers to better track bat population trends, inform conservation methods and develop new ways to support bats.
The Biodiversity Research Institute’s Mammal Program studies bats year-round, from collecting blood and hair samples for heavy metals testing in Colombia, to recording bat vocalizations for behavioral studies in Kenya, to performing the first bat captures in Katahdin Woods and Waters.
Additionally, through the Gulf of Maine Bat Research Program, scientists are studying how bats utilize offshore environments by placing echolocation recording detectors on islands, boats and buoys across the Gulf of Maine.
How can you help these ecologically valuable creatures? Put up a bat house, plant a native, pollinator-friendly garden and avoid disturbing hibernating bats by steering clear of caves and mines in the winter. And share what you’ve learned about bats to help correct misinformation and ensure these animals receive the protection and support they need.
“Nature Connects” is a monthly column showcasing conservation stories from people and organizations across Maine. To learn more or suggest story ideas, email [email protected].

title: Gorham’s Orchard Ridge Farm for sale months after devastating fire
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gorham’s Orchard Ridge Farm is up for sale just over nine months after a fire destroyed a family home on the property, the owners wrote in an Instagram post Sunday.
Erica Gottshalk and her husband Will Gottshalk have owned the farm on Sebago Lake Road since 2021, and lived in the 1858 home with their two young children until it burned down on Jan. 2. The fire closed the farm for six days, sparing a farm market and a barn on the property.
“We are lucky to have walked away physically unharmed, and remain deeply grateful for the outpouring of support we received, but life-altering events force a deep reflection on the future, on where to invest precious time and energy,” the post said, adding that the family no longer has the bandwidth to keep the farm running.
The decision to sell the farm — which hosts community events like live music and yoga sessions — will also allow the Gottshalks to spend more time with family, the post read.
The Gottshalks wrote that the farm is in an ideal position for a “seamless transition” to new owners, complete with a brand new home that’s under construction on the property.
“One of the hardest parts of this decision is feeling like we might be letting down the community that has continuously lifted us up,” the Gottshalks wrote, expressing gratitude for the support the family received after the fire. “Our greatest hope is to find buyers who will honor what this space means to the community and keep it open for everyone to enjoy.”

Catholic priest killed by falling cross during livestreamed Mass in Ecuador
text:
(AP) - A Roman Catholic priest celebrating an evening Mass in southwestern Ecuador has died after a crucifix fell on him during the livestreamed service.
The Archdiocese of Guayaquil, a coastal city 265 kilometers (164 miles) southwest of the capital, Quito, identified the priest as Patricio Sánchez of Perpetuo Socorro Church.
Footage of the service on Saturday night shows a heavy crucifix detaching from the wall above the altar and striking Sánchez on the head as he celebrated Mass. He did not appear to see it falling.
Worshippers cried for help as the social media broadcast continued.
Local authorities have not commented on the incident.
Sánchez belonged to the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, a Roman Catholic religious order founded in 1732 with a presence in 80 countries.

title: Maine wildlife that has vanished or nearly disappeared
text:
This was originally published Oct. 10, 2025.
Maine looks different today than it did before Europeans arrived. Its wildlife has changed, with some species suffering heavily from hunting and habitat loss. In recognition of Indigenous Peoples’ Day, let’s explore these changes.
A few changes happened naturally, but most resulted from cultural differences between immigrants who began arriving 600 years ago and Native Americans, who have lived here for millennia.
Native peoples coexisted with nature. European settlers saw things differently: nature was to be subdued and bent to the will of those who could profit from it. Wildlife existed to be harvested by humans, and woe to any predator that competed with that harvest.
Overharvesting of game species and the elimination of predators were inevitable, almost expected — a classic example of the “tragedy of the commons.” This economic principle was understood during European settlement and has been around since at least Aristotle, more than 300 years before Christ. It holds that if everyone has equal access to a finite resource, those who take the most will benefit the most — until the resource is gone.
Wolverines lived in Maine prior to statehood but disappeared soon after. A bounty was placed on wolves in 1838, and they were extirpated within five decades. Maine loggers prized caribou meat; the last one was shot on Katahdin in 1908. The last known eastern cougar was shot in 1938.
Birds had it especially tough.
The great auk was the largest member of the puffin family. Like unrelated penguins, it was flightless and thus easy to hunt. The last known pair was shot on an island off the coast of Iceland on July 3, 1844.
The same fate befell Atlantic puffins. By the end of the 19th century, there was only one pair of Atlantic puffins left in Maine, nesting on Matinicus Rock. Not until the late 1970s did restoration efforts begin to bring them back.
The Labrador duck was the first species unique to North America to go extinct. Never very common, the last Canadian bird was shot on Grand Manan in 1874. The last American bird was reported in Elmira, New York, in 1878. Supposedly, it didn’t taste very good. It disappeared anyway.
Common eiders nearly followed the same path. They were prized for their feathers, and their eggs were easy to harvest. They teetered on extinction off the New England and Maritime Canada coastlines but recovered somewhat after hunting limits were enacted in the early 20th century.
Heath hens were once among the most abundant game birds in eastern North America, but they were easy to hunt. Throughout colonization, these small, chicken-like birds were hunted so heavily that household servants demanded they not be served heath hens more than two or three times a week. By 1850, all of Maine’s heath hens were gone. Today, none remain on the planet.
Likewise, Maine’s original population of wild turkeys was eliminated by the 1870s.
Birds disappeared across the country for similar reasons. The passenger pigeon was the most abundant bird in North America, numbering in the billions. Market hunters could harvest an entire tree full of roosting birds and carry them off to be sold for dinner in Boston and New York. By the turn of the 20th century, they were extinct.
Ivory-billed woodpeckers were already scarce in the 19th century, which made them valuable to collectors. Heavy logging in the river bottomlands of the American Southeast devastated the rest. The last known nesting pairs were found in the Singer Tract in Louisiana, but despite conservation efforts to protect the land, the trees were cut down in 1944.
And so it went. Attractive birds, including puffins, became fashion accessories for adornment on hats. Waterfowl and shorebirds, which migrate in large groups, were harvested with punt guns — enormous shotguns mounted on boats that could reap 50 birds at a time.
Hawk Mountain Sanctuary in Pennsylvania is famous for hawk migration along the ridgeline. Until the 1930s, hunters climbed the mountain to shoot raptors just for sport. At one point, there was even a $5 bounty for every goshawk killed. It was turned into a sanctuary in 1934.
Eventually, the wanton destruction of so much wildlife shocked Americans into action. Laws prohibited market hunting. Treaties protected migrating birds. In 1973, President Richard Nixon signed the Endangered Species Act.
History turned on its head: sportsmen and landowners became some of the strongest advocates for conservation.
Many of these protections are currently being rolled back in Washington. It seems we haven’t quite learned our lesson after all.

title: ‘It would be funny’: Man accused of stealing flamingo testifies he drank 30-40 beers that day
text:
LAS VEGAS (KVVU/Gray News) - A man accused of stealing a flamingo from its Las Vegas Strip habitat took the stand at his own trial, saying he now realizes how big of a mistake it was.
Mitchell Fairbarn, 34, is facing two counts of animal cruelty after he allegedly stole a flamingo named Peachy from the Flamingo Hotel and Casino while drunk in March.
Police say Fairbarn, a tourist from Ontario, Canada, was seen on security camera around 5 a.m. March 3 hopping a fence to get inside the flamingo habitat. Fairbarn is accused of taking Peachy from the habitat and carrying the bird to his hotel room.
Peachy was injured in the incident. The flamingo’s treating veterinarian said the bird had seven to eight missing feathers, broken shafts and blood loss that were consistent with trauma. She added that Peachy needed antibiotics, anti-inflammatories and weeks of pain medication.
Prosecutors opened the trial with surveillance video, photos and Snapchat clips showing Fairbarn smiling, laughing and grabbing Peachy by the neck with two friends. The flamingo’s veterinarian called the video of Fairbarn grabbing Peachy by the neck inappropriate and potentially fatal.
Suspect testifies he thought the incident would be ‘funny’
Fairbarn took the stand Friday in his animal cruelty trial, testifying he took Peachy as a drunken “silly pranky joke” after drinking 30 to 40 beers. He denied malicious intent to hurt or kill the flamingo.
“Did you ever, at any time, have any malicious intent or desire?” his attorney asked. “Did you intend to kill?”
“No,” Fairbarn said.
During his testimony, Fairbarn said he lives in central Ontario, runs an excavation business started in 2014, is married and has three children. He said he grew up on farms, owns dogs and a parrot named Sonny and once rescued an abandoned llama and six ducks.
He mentioned being in Las Vegas for ConExpo, “a global construction show that happens every three years,” where he was asked to be “one of the representatives from Canada.”
Fairbarn also added that his father had been diagnosed with cancer in December 2025, and he was “on the fence about coming at all.”
He said he spent March 2 gambling and drinking an estimated 30 to 40 beers. He then stopped at the flamingo habitat around 5 a.m. – drunk, sleep-deprived and on a call. He mentioned entering the habitat to look at a bird with “uneven” wings while also acknowledging he shouldn’t go in.
Inside, he said he sat with one flamingo (not Peachy) then grabbed Peachy as a “silly pranky joke” to photograph, carried the bird to his room for “two or three minutes” put it in the hallway and was arrested changing to return it.
Fairbarn also mentioned being on house arrest. He has not been able to return to Canada since.
Under cross examination, he later admitted that the video “doesn’t look good,” and Peachy was hurt, saying “I’m taking responsibility” but claimed “I have no idea” how the feathers were lost.
The trial resumes Monday morning with closing arguments before jury deliberation.
Jury questions
The jury had several questions for Fairbarn.
Q: At the beginning of the video of the island, the birds are asleep and aren’t falling down. So the question is, if you know, do flamingos naturally, physically lay down?
A: They can, or when they’re doing the building nests and stuff.
Q: If the birds were in a resting, sleeping position, how could you tell the wings were uneven?
A: From where I was standing on the platform, on the main fence, one of their wings, one looked higher than the other.
Q: I just wanted clarification about the reasoning behind going into the exhibit initially. Was it because you saw a bird potentially in distress? Or was it to create a lasting memory of the trip?
A: The very intentional moment was to go see the bird that I thought looked funny. Ended up being to make it a funny trip while I was already there.
Q: At any point during your interacting with Peachy, did you notice his injuries or bleeding slash blood on your shirt or wall?
A: No.
Q: If someone hops your fence and enters your farm and hurts an animal that you own, what is your expectation of local law enforcement?
A: That’s a good question. I would say a proper investigation to ensure that an individual that took it actually is the one who harmed it.
Q: Is being intoxicated an excuse to hurt anything, either a man, a woman, an animal, regardless of intent?
A: No.
Q: What happened to the rescue ducks?
A: We got them in 2018, I believe. We had them for three years. We sold the property and the homeowners took them. Because they were living in one.
Q: How much do you drink on a typical day?
A: Not a lot. Nowhere near what I drank here.
Q: When you noticed a bird with its wings tucked, how did you know which bird to head for when you were on the island? Or how did you know it was the right bird?
A: From what I’d seen, once I got in there and walked up to it, that’s the one that I thought was the same one that I’d seen on the other side of the pink fence.
Q: When did you take off your shirt to wrap around Peachy’s body?
A: When I was leaving the exhibit, there’s waist-height hedges. That’s when I took my shirt off to wrap around the birds so the birds didn’t get bricked because they’re all perked.
Q: You stated you walked through the bushes. Did you sustain any scratches to your arms or your body?
A: Not that I remember. I don’t believe so.
Q: Can you clarify if you walked through the bushes while holding the bird?
A: Yes, I did.
Q: Was the bird healthy when you took it out of its habitat?
A: I did not see anything wrong with it when I took it.
Q: When the flamingo tucks its head under its wings to sleep, couldn’t that cause the wings to look uneven or could that cause the wings to look uneven?
A: For sure, yes.

title: NASCAR building 80 cars for new movie starring Tom Cruise
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - NASCAR is reportedly building more than 80 race cars for an upcoming movie starring one of the most iconic American actors.
Tom Cruise announced in an Aug. 29 social media post that a “Days of Thunder” sequel is set to come out in the summer of 2028.
The original 1990 film became a favorite among race fans and was among the top-grossing films of that year at the box office.
NASCAR CEO Steve O’Donnell talked about the “Days of Thunder” sequel in a live podcast-style interview with Front Office Sports on Tuesday, Oct. 13.
“Tom’s message to us was, ‘I’m going to put you in front of an entirely new audience, and you need to be ready,’” O’Donnell said.
“And so there’s some things we’ll work together on. You know, do people understand the points system? How does The Chase work? How long are your races? All these things kind of to make sure that a new fan who may come out to the racetrack understands. Because for us, this is a whole new open door for us to bring new fans.”
O’Donnell said the original “Days of Thunder” showcased what NASCAR was in the 1990s. He suggested the new one would showcase what NASCAR is like now, and would embrace the technology and “everything that goes into the sport.”
The CEO also revealed an interesting request from Cruise.
Apparently, the legendary actor wanted to actually race in a real event to make the movie authentic.
O’Donnell said he was “shocked” by the request.
“I’m not sure that’s going to happen,” O’Donnell said of Cruise racing. “But he wants it to be as authentic as it can be. We’ll still see how the story lines, but all that’s playing out right now. I will tell you, we’re producing probably over 80 race cars that are going to be part of this. Some we don’t expect to be back; they’ll be wrecked.”
O’Donnell said the wrecked cars may be taken and left in places across the country and globe to help grow interest in NASCAR.
“You look at this long term of, OK, you’ve got race cars, some of them have been wrecked in the movie. Where can we leave these?” the CEO said in the Oct. 13 interview. “It’s an opportunity for us across the board.”
The new “Days of Thunder” is reportedly scheduled to start filming in March 2027. It is set to release in theaters on June 2, 2028.
Starring alongside Cruise, who will reprise his role as “Cole Trickle,” will be fellow acting icon Anne Hathaway. Cruise confirmed in an interview with Pat McAfee that Trickle’s character will return as a driver.
It is not yet clear where the movie will be filmed. The original included many locations around the Charlotte area and was filmed at multiple tracks across the Carolinas.

title: Catholic priest killed by falling cross during livestreamed Mass in Ecuador
text:
(AP) - A Roman Catholic priest celebrating an evening Mass in southwestern Ecuador has died after a crucifix fell on him during the livestreamed service.
The Archdiocese of Guayaquil, a coastal city 265 kilometers (164 miles) southwest of the capital, Quito, identified the priest as Patricio Sánchez of Perpetuo Socorro Church.
Footage of the service on Saturday night shows a heavy crucifix detaching from the wall above the altar and striking Sánchez on the head as he celebrated Mass. He did not appear to see it falling.
Worshippers cried for help as the social media broadcast continued.
Local authorities have not commented on the incident.
Sánchez belonged to the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, a Roman Catholic religious order founded in 1732 with a presence in 80 countries.

title: Let’s launch the Island Rover in Freeport
text:
I encourage all Freeport residents to vote in favor of the ordinance amendment to allow the Island Rover to be launched. It is unfortunate to need an ordinance to allow the Island Rover to be launched, but so far the obstructionists have prevented it from happening.
Opponents of the measure are afraid of all the things that could go wrong, but let’s not be afraid of this.
The language on the ballot for this question sounds like there are many extreme changes that the ordinance will create. It minimizes a very important fact: Section 10 of the proposed ordinance states that it is subject to review and approval of the Maine Department of Environmental Protection and that it shall only remain in effect for two years. Then it goes away.
Launching the Island Rover can be a safe and successful operation. It’s time to let it happen.
Albert Presgraves
Freeport

title: Community leaders say foiled Illinois mass shooting was result of surge in anti-Hindu hate online
text:
A thwarted mass shooting targeting a large Hindu temple in suburban Chicago was fueled by years of hateful rhetoric on social media against Hindus and Indians, community leaders say.
Authorities on Wednesday arrested Alexandros Paporakis, 19, who they said drove to the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora, Illinois, on Sunday afternoon, armed with a rifle and body armor. Officials said he remained in the parking lot for several minutes, but left after his weapon jammed. Paporakis was arrested later that day near his home in Palatine, Illinois, after a co-worker at a Taco Bell alerted authorities to his plan to “kill Indian people.”
The temple, the largest in Aurora, was crowded Sunday with thousands observing the first day of Navaratri, a nine-night celebration of Shakti -- the divine feminine energy believed to be foundational to all creation.
U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, who represents Illinois’ 8th congressional district, said he and his parents were inside the temple Sunday afternoon.
“Little did we know there was an attacker outside with sinister intent,” he said Thursday. “This has really shaken us.”
During a news conference Friday morning in Chicago, Krishnamoorthi stood with several other faith and civic leaders calling for the attempted mass shooting to be investigated as a hate crime. Speakers also called for an organized community response to prevent hate and extremism targeting all communities.
Hindus face online hate and real-world threats
Pushpita Prasad, a spokesperson for the Coalition of Hindus of North America, said attacks against Hindus and Indians have been escalating in recent years. She said the racial slurs are increasingly visible online.
“You see vitriolic posts associating Indians with dirt and creating disgust about their appearance, food and cultural practices,” she said. “Sooner or later, all that online hate is going to migrate to the real world.”
Over the past two years, the rising wave of anti-Hindu hate has included a rash of vandalism and attacks across the country. Most recently, on Oct. 3, vandals hurled bricks at a Hindu temple in Richmond Heights, Ohio, shattering several windows while devotees were praying inside.
In June 2025, a gunman fired bullets into the Sri Sri Radha Krishna Temple in Spanish Fork, Utah, causing thousands of dollars in damage. In Sugar Land, Texas, a 90-foot statue of the deity Hanuman, consecrated in 2024 at a temple complex, continues to draw disparaging comments, including one YouTube personality who recently urged its demolition.
In Frisco, Texas, where people of Indian origin make up about one-third of the population, speakers have used public comment periods during city council meetings to label the Indian community as “invaders,” characterize Hindu temples as a threat and accuse H-1B work visa holders of stealing American jobs or committing fraud.
Leaders call for resources to combat hate and extremism
Temple administrators in Aurora issued a statement Thursday assuring the community that they value the safety of devotees, employees and volunteers, and have implemented additional security measures including an “armed security presence.”
Krishnamoorthi said the temple, situated on 20 acres, is a cultural hub for the community in the Chicago area. It has been his family’s home away from home for about 40 years, he said.
“For people who were newly immigrated, this became their connection to the homeland,” Krishnamoorthi said.
The temple serves as a venue for concerts, dance performances, birthdays and weddings, and the cafeteria that serves South Indian cuisine is popular, he said.
Krishnamoorthi called for the FBI to prosecute this incident as a hate crime, and for social media companies to end the hateful rhetoric online.
“The FBI also needs to redirect resources to combat domestic violent extremism,” he said. “Election fraud and immigration are not the biggest threats facing our country.”
Joel Finkelstein with the New Jersey-based Network Contagion Research Institute, which tracks cyber-social threats, said in 2025, anti-Indian content on X tripled in weekly volume. The administration’s changes in immigration policies, particularly relating to the H1-B visa, corresponded with measurable surges in racial slurs and deportation rhetoric targeting Indians, he said.
Amid the increase in online hate, Finkelstein said the South Asian community in the U.S., despite significant resources, lacks the ability to advocate for itself with strength and unity.
“There is nothing to stop it from getting worse,” he said.
Advocates say xenophobia has fueled hate
Sravya Tadepalli, executive director of Hindus for Human Rights, says her organization has formed strong coalitions with Muslim, Sikh and other organizations whose members also face hate.
“It’s important to understand that rhetoric is not just rhetoric,” she said. “It is harmful and can result in violence.”
Manjusha P. Kulkarni, co-founder of Stop AAPI Hate, said her organization’s research showed that online slurs targeting South Asians rose 109% from 2023 to 2025. Statistics aside, Kulkarni said she was personally shaken by the threat in Illinois.
“It hits all of us who are temple goers,” she said. “Seeing how going to my house of worship can put me and my children at risk is very scary.”
AAPI Hate pointed to “xenophobic policies and rhetoric” that depict Indian people as a demographic threat — including Vice President JD Vance calling H1-B workers “indentured servants” and Bo French, the Republican candidate for Texas’ Railroad Commission calling South Asian students at a Longhorns football game “a problem.” French’s post led to a flurry of other posts on social media calling for violence against Indian communities, including desecrating Hindu temples and statues.
Last month, a Sikh truck driver was stabbed in Wyoming, days after the Department of Homeland Security published a derogatory social media post about Sikh truck drivers.
Sikh temple shooting survivor stresses need for meaningful dialogue
Pardeep Kaleka’s father, Satwant Singh Kaleka, was one of six people killed in 2012 in a mass shooting at their gurdwara in Oak Creek, Wisconsin – the deadliest anti-Sikh attack in the U.S. The shooter, Wade Michael Page, was a self-proclaimed white supremacist.
After Paporakis’ arrest in Illinois, authorities said they recovered weapons, ammunition, a gas canister labeled with a slur referring to South Asians and several items depicting Nazi symbols. Officials said Paporakis wrote a manifesto in which he fantasized about mass murder and expressed his desire to kill as many non-white people as he could.
Kaleka, who co-wrote a book with a former white supremacist about his own journey of forgiveness after the Sikh temple shooting, said the young men who perpetrate these attacks don’t pop up suddenly.
“Most people who do this have lost hope, and their motivation is also to have you and society lose hope,” he said. “Their belief is if you can attack people in the space they hold most sacred, it plants a deep terror in communities.”
The solution is to have candid conversations across racial and religious boundaries so people can understand each other at a human level, Kaleka said. “Unless that happens, we’re more likely to see division rather than a collective spirit that joins us together.”

title: American journalist injured in settler attack in Israeli-occupied West Bank
text:
(AP) - The U.S. ambassador to Israel condemned a settler attack on an American journalist that left her needing surgery, in the latest incident of such violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
Meanwhile, two helicopter pilots were killed Sunday in Saudi Arabia near the border with Yemen, which a Saudi military spokesperson said was due to a technical malfunction.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East. Read our full coverage here.
US ambassador condemns settler attack on American journalist
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee sharply condemned settler violence during an olive harvest in the West Bank that injured several Palestinians and Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine as “a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards.” In a post late Saturday on X, he called for “a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this.”
Levine was seriously injured in the attack Friday in the West Bank village of Abu Falah. Israeli police are also investigating an attack by Israeli settlers on European diplomats Saturday in another West Bank village. Settler violence against Palestinians has soared this year and spiked further in recent weeks as Israel plans to hold elections Oct. 27.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was ambiguous in addressing Levine’s assault, condemning “violence against anyone” but referring to the attack as “alleged” and saying its circumstances remain unclear. Huckabee said Levine’s assault was “vicious” and “dishonorable,” and noted that she was clearly identified as a journalist when she was attacked.
Levine, an award-winning photojournalist who has covered conflict zones around the world for more than four decades, remains hospitalized in Tel Aviv as she recovers from hand surgery, broken ribs and other injuries she sustained in the attack. She said she was forced to the ground and beaten for more than 10 minutes by the settlers, who also stole her camera, passport and phone.
The Washington Post reiterated its call for a full and transparent investigation, though Israel rarely investigates settler violence fully. Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group, says around 94% of investigations into settler violence since 2005 have ended without an indictment, with just 3% leading to full or partial convictions.
Saudi helicopter crashes near border with Yemen, killing pilots
A Saudi helicopter gunship crashed in southwestern Saudi Arabia, killing its two-member crew in an area close to the border with Yemen, due to a technical malfunction, a Saudi military spokesperson said Sunday. The helicopter crashed near the city of Najran, close to the Yemen border, in an area that has been caught up in fierce fighting between the Iran-backed Yemeni Houthi militants and a Saudi-led coalition attempting to contain them.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki made the statement hours after the Houthis claimed to have downed the Saudi helicopter.
The Houthis, a Shiite religious and political movement rooted in northern Yemen, are attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government in the civil war. The Saudis have struggled to counter the latest attacks, even with far superior U.S.-supplied arms.
Egypt agrees to provide defense support for Saudi Arabia
Egypt’s National Defense Council, which decides on the country’s high-level military and security affairs, has agreed to support its close ally Saudi Arabia in a major escalation of fighting between the kingdom and the Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen.
Chaired by President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi, the council decided in a Sunday meeting to provide “all possible forms of support” to enable Saudi Arabia to defend its security and stability, according to a statement from the Egyptian presidency.
The statement didn’t provide further details, but the council said it will also continue diplomatic efforts with regional and international parties to de-escalate the conflict.
El-Sissi said Saturday that his government will implement “any measure” to defend Saudi Arabia, and called for parliament to grant him the authorization to deploy troops and military equipment abroad. Parliament is set to meet later Sunday.
Tugboat near UAE damaged by projectiles
Two projectiles hit a vessel transiting off the United Arab Emirates early Sunday, wounding one person, a British military agency reported.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said the tug sustained damage but is continuing its journey. The UKMTO did not identify the vessel and no group claimed responsibility for the attack. The tug was attacked in the Gulf of Oman, south of the narrow Strait of Hormuz, which has faced blockades and attacks in recent months.
Iran approves new defense minister, vows to defend itself
Iran appointed Mehrdad Akhlaghi, a longtime official in Iran’s defense industry, as the new defense minister on Sunday.
His predecessor, Aziz Nasirzadeh, was killed on the first day of U.S.-Israeli attacks Feb. 28, along with Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and several senior Iranian military commanders.
During a confirmation hearing, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian vowed that Iran would not yield to pressure or demands from other countries.
“We will resolutely defend our land and country and will not allow our enemies to covet our beloved homeland, just as we have no designs on anyone else’s territory,” Pezeshkian said.
Akhlaghi vowed that any miscalculation from Israel or the U.S. would prompt a “surprising and extensive” response.
___
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.
