title: Driver in deadly Kansas soccer field crash released while investigation continues
text:
WICHITA, Kansas (AP) — A woman who drove a pickup truck onto a soccer field during a weekend youth game in Kansas, killing two people and injuring 10 others, has been released without charges as the investigation continues, police said Sunday.
The 34-year-old woman was released pending results of toxicology tests and a mechanical examination of the vehicle in the aftermath of Saturday’s crash. Her name hasn’t been made public.
“Our officers and investigators will continue working to understand exactly what happened,” Wichita Police Chief Joe Sullivan said, noting that no charges have been filed to date.
The woman had one child playing soccer on another field at the Stryker Sports Complex in northeast Wichita when Saturday’s crash occurred, a police statement said. The statement said two of her other children were with her in the pickup truck when it struck multiple children and adults.
According to a preliminary investigation, the Chevrolet pickup was parked in a parking space near the soccer fields before it drove onto one of the fields.
Police identified those killed at the scene as Cole Adrian, 6, and Nicholas Schafer, 35, both of McPherson, Kansas. They were not related.
Ten others ranging from 5 years old to 68 were taken to area hospitals with injuries described as non-serious.
Investigators say they have interviewed more than 30 witnesses, including the driver and her two children who were her inside the pickup at the time of the crash.

title: Cows roam downtown Kansas City after truck overturns, killing dozens of them
text:
Cows roam downtown Kansas City after truck overturns, killing dozens of them
Dozens of cattle spilled onto a street in Kansas City, Missouri, when a semitractor-trailer plunged off a highway overpass in the city’s downtown area and onto a car early Sunday, shutting down some roads and setting off a search for the traumatized animals that survived.
The accident occurred shortly before 3 a.m., and the roundup of surviving cattle continued into the early afternoon, authorities said.
The driver of the truck and the driver of a vehicle the truck landed on sustained minor injuries and were treated at local hospitals.
Kansas City Police Sgt. Phil DiMartino said that between 45 and 60 of the 120 to 130 cattle carried by the truck were killed when the tractor trailer overturned and fell from the westbound I-70 curve over SB I-35.
Dozens of other cows fled the crash scene, resulting in other crashes and more calls to the police from the public, he said.
“It is believed all cows have now been accounted for,” DiMartino said in an updated press release Sunday afternoon.
Some of the cattle had walked several miles before they were captured, said Kansas City Fire Battalion Chief Michael Hopkins.
“It was a pretty nasty accident,” Hopkins said.
Immediately after the accident, city authorities launched drones to track the cattle before a private company working together with the trucking company arrived with workers on horseback to round up the cattle, he said.
“More difficult has been getting the animals who did not survive,” he added.
The Associated Press contributed reporting.

title: Obituary: Ronald Ellis Sr.
text:
DIXFIELD – Ronald Ellis Sr., 83, died Tuesday Oct. 13, 2026, at Franklin Health in Farmington. He resided in Dixfield and was formally of Carthage.
Ronald was born in Rumford on May 26, 1943, the son of Morton and Grace (Virgin) Ellis. He served in the U.S. Navy and worked for the Department of Transportation as a truck driver for the State of Maine.
Ronald was married to Gloria White on Sept. 18, 1965, and she passed away on Nov. 19, 2016.
Survivors include sons Ronald Ellis Jr., and wife Gidget of Carthage and James Ellis of Bangor, a daughter, Kathy Robbins and husband Bobby of Livermore Falls; grandchildren, Jonathan Robbins and wife Samantha, Kayla Robbins and fiancé Luke Myers, Asia Ellis and fiancé Mike Kotredes, Dylan Ellis, and Alyssa Ellis; and great-grandchildren Kayson and Tanner Kotredes, and Hayden Robbins, Hailee Robbins Landon Myers.
He was predeceased by his parents; his wife, Gloria White; a sister, Elizabeth Ellis and a brother, John Ellis.
Friends and family are invited to share memories of Ronald at http://www.meaderandson.com.

title: Trump dominated rural America. Iowa is testing whether Democrats can win them back
text:
NEW HAMPTON, Iowa (AP) — Standing in the doorway of his home near the corn and soybean fields that blanket this stretch of northeast Iowa, Dave Roethler doesn’t know what happened to the Donald Trump he supported during his first presidency.
Trump did a “heck of a good job” back then, the 70-year-old school custodian said. But now Roethler laments an economy in which “it’s the middle-class families that are taking the big hit” while Trump is “going to come out way ahead.” He scoffs at the Republican president’s effort to win accolades such as the Nobel Peace Prize or a spot on Mount Rushmore.
“I think he has delusions of grandeur,” said Roethler, who plans to support Democrats next month in a state that has become a midterm battleground after Trump carried it by 13 percentage points two years ago. The president will return to Iowa twice before the election to rally supporters.
Democrats face a steep challenge in winning rural communities like this one in Chickasaw County, a onetime party stronghold that swung sharply to the right in the Trump era as a broader realignment swept through much of the agricultural Midwest. But by simply narrowing their losses with appeals to voters such as Roethler, Democrats hope to become newly competitive from Iowa and Kansas to Nebraska and Ohio.
Josh Turek, the Democrat running for a U.S. Senate seat in Iowa, said his party has “looked at this math problem incorrectly.”
“You’ve got to go out there in these rural counties and trim the margins,” he said in an interview.
Competitive races in states that usually aren’t
Republicans know they are on defense in these states. Trump recently held a rally in Nebraska to boost U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts and will do the same for U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas on Monday. Republicans are pumping money into both states before the Nov. 3 election.
Few places represent the party’s challenge like Iowa, where Democrats are mounting spirited campaigns for governor, U.S. Senate and several U.S. House seats, including the 2nd Congressional District, which encompasses much of the state’s northeast and was considered reliably Republican until recently.
With tariffs disrupting the agricultural economy and the war in Iran driving up gas prices — diesel surpasses $6 a gallon in Iowa — U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., swung through the district to ask voters to keep his fragile majority in place.
“This state is so important to us,” Johnson said in Cedar Falls.
The Republican erosion was evident about 45 miles north in New Hampton. A few houses away from Roethler, 69-year-old Bill Stonecypher voted for Trump in 2016, expecting him to apply his business acumen to governing. Now Stonecypher plans to vote for every Democrat on the ballot for the first time in his life.
“I just know it’s a mess and it’s going to take years to fix,” he said.
Another neighbor, 70-year-old Deb Thorne backed Trump in 2024 but said he hasn’t followed through on his pledge to lower costs.
“He lied to us,” she said. “I’m looking more at Democrats for everything.”
How a candidate for governor is reaching beyond the party base
Democrats in Iowa are buoyed by Rob Sand, the state auditor whose campaign for governor is built on explicit overtures to independents and disaffected Republicans.
A few dozen people gathered recently in an American Legion hall in St. Ansgar, a square-mile town near the Minnesota border. Sand opened by describing a “pretty standard upbringing” centered on hunting, fishing and church.
He distanced himself from the fighting over cultural issues that has bogged down the national party. A few heads in the room nodded as he spoke of opposition to transgender girls playing on female sports teams.
“All that stuff was stuff that nobody was talking about back when we were in high school,” said Sand, whose opponent is Republican Zach Lahn, a political newcomer.
The only reason he was a Democrat at all, Sand said, was that he had to pick a party to participate in primaries and he thought Democrats were stronger on issues like clean water and protecting public land.
Jim Wherry, a Republican member of the Mitchell County Board of Supervisors, attended the event and said Sand “has a pretty good chance.”
“My big thing is sometimes things get focused on urban areas,” he said. “So I like that he’s actually incorporating rural Iowa.”
Sand, who has won two statewide elections as state auditor, said he’s received support from voters who also backed Trump.
“One of the things that people who vote for both of us find in common is that we say what we think and we’re dissatisfied with the political system,” he said.
Democrats are boosting rural investments
Democrats are stepping up their rural investments. The Democratic Governors Association has directed $10 million each to campaigns in Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Wisconsin and could spend elsewhere ahead of the election.
“What I see is a map that has grown and grown and grown and that is good for Democrats,” Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who leads the DGA, said in an interview.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which is focused on retaking the House, launched a rural engagement program for the first time this election cycle, including polling, paid media and staff. The group has made a six-figure investment in television advertising in Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District alone.
Democratic candidate Lindsay James, a chaplain who often speaks of her faith to connect with voters, could see a boost because the district includes Sand’s hometown of Decorah. She’s competing against Republican Joe Mitchell, a former state representative who worked in the Trump administration.
In an interview, James said she was “committed to showing up everywhere.” When asked why Democrats lost rural voters in previous elections, she was blunt in her assessment.
“Democrats in Washington have left the Midwest behind,” she said.
Economic concerns could give Democrats an opening
The economic headwinds in Iowa could give James and other Democrats an opening.
A poll conducted in August by The Associated Press, in partnership with KFF, found that rural voters in the United States are economically frustrated with Trump. About half of rural voters believe the national economy is “worse off” than when Trump returned to office in January 2025. The survey found about 6 in 10 rural voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of the war with Iran.
Still, the survey found that rural voters were unlikely to support Democrats on a large scale in November.
Mark DeVries, a 64-year-old farmer in Franklin County, Iowa, said he does not agree with everything Trump does and acknowledged the president’s tariffs have hurt his business. But he said he was sticking with Trump and Republicans.
“He’s doing stuff that needs to get done,” DeVries said of Trump.
Campaigning with Mitchell, Johnson drew on that loyalty to Trump to warn of the consequences of Democrats regaining control of Congress. A Trump impeachment, he said, “is the first thing that would happen.”
But the Democrats hoping to go to Congress avoided being drawn into that fight.
Turek said he had “no interest” in impeachment and that Democrats “need to look forward, not back.”
James, who has made fighting corruption a campaign theme, said she’s “not interested in political theater.”
“I’m certainly interested in accountability,” she said. “But I’m singularly focused on policies that are going to provide, immediately, relief for families.”

title: Maine house destroyed by fire after being sold
text:
An unoccupied house in Lisbon that recently had been sold was destroyed by fire Sunday morning.
Firefighters with the Lisbon Fire Department responded to a reported structure fire at 51 Gould Road at approximately 3:00 a.m. on Sunday, according to the Maine Department of Public Safety. Upon arrival, firefighters found the residence fully engulfed in flames and beginning to collapse.
Investigators with the Maine State Fire Marshal’s Office responded to try to determine the cause. The cause of the fire remains undetermined and under investigation.
Anyone with information about this incident is asked to contact the Maine State Fire Marshal’s Office tip line at 1-888-870-6162.

title: Private jet skids off runway, hits fence at Las Vegas airport
text:
(AP) - A private jet went off the end of a runway during a planned takeoff at Las Vegas’ main airport Sunday and hit a perimeter fence, officials said.
No injuries were reported in the 11 a.m. mishap at Harry Reid International Airport, said airport spokesperson Monika Bertaki. She didn’t say what caused the plane, a Dassault Falcon 50, to go off the runway.
Two runways were closed for inspection after the incident and the Federal Aviation Administration temporarily paused planned flights to the airport, causing delays.
As of August, the airport had over 370,000 operations and more than 34 million passengers so far in 2026.

title: The truth about the Collins family and The County
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sam Collins of Caribou is the president of S.W. Collins Co. and the brother of Sen. Susan Collins.
I read Tommy Pinette’s op-ed concerning Sen. Susan Collins, the Collins family and Aroostook County with a mixture of dismay and disbelief (“Susan Collins has scant claim to ‘County roots,’” Sept. 6).
Mr. Pinette is certainly entitled to his political opinions. He is free to support Troy Jackson, oppose Susan Collins, criticize our family, question our politics and offer his own interpretation of Aroostook County’s history. He is not, however, entitled to his own facts.
Nor should the Maine Sunday Telegram have published a piece containing numerous assertions that could have been disproved with basic fact-checking. This is particularly troubling. Facts matter, including in politics.
Without having ever met anyone in my family to our knowledge, Mr. Pinette incorrectly claimed that Collins family members are “shipped to private, $60,000-per-year schools” over the Caribou public school system, “fly in private jets and chum around with the children of billionaires,” and implied that we have home theaters.
He asserted that every Collins family member in politics has been a Republican and accused the family of using political influence to block resources and community food programs.
This is simply false. Mr. Pinette presents a caricature of an imagined Aroostook County aristocracy. My siblings and I all attended Caribou High School. My brother Gregg and I remained in Caribou, and all seven of our children also graduated from Caribou High School. The 20-year-old partially rusted car that my daughters drove to school hardly classifies as a private jet. And our “home theater” is a 10-year-old iPad.
Like many Maine families, political views within ours are not monolithic. My great-great-grandfather S.W. Collins served as a Democrat in the Maine Legislature, and my great-grandfather H.D. Collins was initially a Democrat before later serving in the Legislature as a Republican, as well as current family members who identify as Democrats.
There are more falsehoods I could address, but I am even more disappointed by the picture painted of Aroostook County and the people who live here. The op-ed described Northern Maine as a “deindustrialized borderland” dominated by oligarchs and portrayed our farmers as a privileged owner class responsible for the region’s economic problems.
That bears little resemblance to the Aroostook County I know.
Our farmers, like other people from Aroostook County, are among the hardest-working people in Maine. Farmers operate businesses subject to changing weather, labor constraints and international competition. Calling Aroostook County families “oligarchs” may align with popular political rhetoric, but it does little to illuminate the realities of living here today. The County people work hard to make a living in a rural area that has its challenges.
The community, including schools, public organizations, nonprofits and economic development groups, works hard to secure government and private funding to improve our area and enable services and infrastructure that would be otherwise unaffordable.
Members of our family have joined our neighbors to serve on numerous boards and organizations spanning education, healthcare, veterans and economic development.
For generations, our family and company like many other County families have contributed financial support to improve life here and throughout Maine. Our company’s mission is “to be an active positive influence in the communities in which we live and work.” We take that responsibility seriously.
Mr. Pinette may disagree with Sen. Collins politically. He may disagree with members of our family. He may believe Aroostook County should pursue different economic or social policies. Those are legitimate subjects for vigorous debate which I would encourage.
The issue here is larger. Disagreement does not justify fabrication. A telephone call would have corrected the op-ed’s false claims. Newspapers play an essential role in our democracy precisely because readers expect them to distinguish fact from fiction. An opinion page should provide broad latitude for argument and criticism, but attaching the word “opinion” to an article should not relieve a newspaper of responsibility for verifying claims, especially those easily checked.
Before publishing allegations, a newspaper should make a reasonable effort to determine whether those assertions are true. When a paper relaxes its standards for fact-checking, it forfeits the unique authority and trust that separates professional journalism from internet noise, at a time when newspapers can least afford it.
After growing up and spending my life here, I know something about The County: people may disagree strongly, but they generally expect you to look them in the eye, tell the truth and stand behind what you say. That is how you maintain trust. The Maine Sunday Telegram should expect the same standard in what it chooses to publish.

title: 6-year-old boy, 35-year-old man identified as victims killed when truck drove through soccer game
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (Gray News) - A child and an adult who were killed after a truck drove through a youth soccer game in east Wichita have been identified, authorities said.
Wichita police identified the victims as Cole Adrian, 6, and Nicholas Schafer, 35, both of McPherson. The two were not related.
The crash happened around 3:25 p.m. on Saturday. Sedgwick County 911 received multiple calls reporting that a vehicle had driven onto soccer fields at Stryker Sports Complex, striking several people.
Officials said a Chevrolet pickup driven by a 34-year-old woman was parked near the fields before it drove onto one of the fields, striking several people.
Emergency personnel responded and treated the injured. Despite lifesaving efforts, Adrian and Schafer died at the scene.
Eleven other people were taken to the hospital with traumatic injuries. They include a 5-year-old girl, a 5-year-old boy, two 8-year-old boys, a 9-year-old girl, a 28-year-old woman, a 32-year-old man, a 59-year-old woman, a 65-year-old woman and a 68-year-old man. A 61-year-old woman was taken to the hospital for medical, non-traumatic treatment.
The driver was taken into custody and later released pending toxicology testing and a mechanical examination of the vehicle, officials said. No charges have been filed.
Officials said two children, both children of the driver, were also inside the pickup at the time of the crash. The driver also had another child who was playing soccer on another field at the complex. It was not immediately clear if the children were injured in the crash.
Investigators are working to determine the circumstances that led to the crash.
Wichita Police Chief Joe Sullivan expressed his condolences to the families and everyone affected by the tragedy.
“Our hearts are with the families of Adrian and Nicholas as they face an unimaginable loss. What should have been a day of children playing soccer and families spending time together ended in tragedy,” Sullivan said. “We are also thinking about those who were injured, their loved ones and everyone who witnessed what happened. We know this tragedy has affected many people throughout our community, and we want those families to know they are not alone. Our officers and investigators will continue working to understand exactly what happened.”

title: Invasive insect leads to Old Orchard Beach public park having to cut down more than 500 trees
text:
Invasive insect leads to Old Orchard Beach public park having to cut down more than 500 trees
Due to an infestation of Hemlock Woolly Adelgid, volunteers at Guild Park in Old Orchard Beach had to work toward cutting down more than 500 trees in the park.
The action was a part of the forest management plan, according to the Ocean Park Association Environment and Natural Resources Committee members.
The plan has the goal of making the area sustainable for the future by removing the impacted trees, most of which the committee says most were dead. The efforts opened the canopy in the area and allow the forest to regenerate itself more easily.
"I think even members of the committee, myself included, had to be kind of brought along that cutting down any tree was a good thing," said committee member Janet Anderson. "And so I became convinced over time that for the long-term health of the park, this is sort of a necessary thing to do."
According to the committee, the invasive insects are about the size of the ballpoint of a pen and their nests can be found in the spring, appearing like a white puff on tree branches.
"Each one of those white puffs has 100 woolly adelgids that come crawling out as larvae," commented committee member Mark Lauritano. "And then they attach themselves to the base of each needle on the branch. And just suck the sap right out of the tree."
Lauritano said that the goal of the Ocean Park Association as a whole is to make the public areas accessible not just for visitors now, but for generations to come.
The removal of the trees isn't the only way the group is doing that. Logged in to a database and tagged with a specific number were over 3,000 trees in the 20-acre park that have a diameter of 10 inches or more.
Several trees also have an orange ribbon representing those trees as a candidate to receive a pesticide that battles adelgid. Along with the release of 500 beetles this year and last year that have the sole purpose of feeding on adelgid, the group is trying to prevent future tree removal.
"Ocean Park has been a thriving summer community and turning into more of a year-round community within Old Orchard Beach since the 1880s," added Lauritano. "So, it's been around a while, and we want to keep that and continue to make it sustainable for future generations."
The group is hoping to even capitalize on the free space where tree removal equipment was placed in the park.
According to Anderson, a woodland garden could be coming to Guild Park. It would be the home to several native plants that will bring a variety of wildlife and add to the educational aspects of the space.

title: Bruins beats Kings for 5th straight victory
text:
LOS ANGELES — Marat Khusnutdinov scored in the third period and the Boston Bruins beat the Los Angeles Kings 4-1 on Saturday night for their fifth straight victory.
David Pastrnak had a goal, Elias Lindholm and JJ Peterka scored empty-netters, and Jeremy Swayman made 25 saves. The Bruins swept the three California teams as part of a four-game trip that ends in Dallas on Tuesday.
Alex Laferriere scored for Los Angeles, and Anton Forsberg made 24 saves. The Kings remained winless through six games to start the season and were held to one goal for the fourth straight contest.
Khusnutdinov put the Bruins ahead 2-1 with 6:24 remaining, scoring on a backhander after Forsberg failed to cover up Morgan Geekie’s shot and Matt Poitras kept the puck alive.
The Kings got off to a quick start, scoring 31 seconds into the game. Laferriere was at the top of the crease to put in Adrian Kempe’s pass for his second goal of the season, making the most of his promotion to first-line center.
But the Bruins responded early in the second period, with Pastrnak tying it at 2:43. He pounced on a loose puck in the neutral zone and took it the other way to beat Forsberg on a wrist shot from the right circle for his fourth goal.
It was Pastrnak’s 289th goal at even-strength, tying Phil Esposito for third-most in Boston history.
Bruins center Pavel Zacha did not play because of an upper-body injury he sustained in the third period against the Ducks on Friday. He is day-to-day, coach Marco Sturm said before the game.
Up next
Bruins: At Dallas on Tuesday night.
Kings: At Washington on Tuesday night.

title: Allegations by former tenant, Lewiston councilor roil legislative race
text:
Key Takeaways Key Takeaways are written by Maine Trust staff and highlight the most important points of this article so you can get the gist at a glance.
- City Councilor and state House District 94 Rep. Scott Harriman has been accused of entering his tenant’s bed, lending her money to buy drugs and providing his vehicle as a space to get high.
- Harriman said the allegations are untrue and that their amplification is politically motivated as he seeks to retain his House seat.
LEWISTON — A former tenant and her allegations of impropriety have put a city councilor running for reelection to the Legislature in the spotlight.
Ward 3 City Councilor and House District 94 Rep. Scott Harriman, also a landlord, is being accused by his former tenant, Karrah Knight, of inappropriate conduct and providing transportation to buy drugs in 2025.
Harriman has maintained the allegations are false and only surfaced after he was forced to evict Knight. He said the claims are politically motivated, and being amplified by a right-wing news organization as part of a coordinated effort to unseat him in his Nov. 3 legislative race.
Both spoke at length this week with the Sun Journal.
Details about the allegations first surfaced in a June email that Lewiston mayoral candidate Charles Soule sent to some City Council members, Mayor Carl Sheline and city officials. The matter become more public in mid-September when a resident read the email aloud at a council meeting.
The email alleged Harriman entered Knight’s bed uninvited on several occasions. It also alleged he provided money for her to buy drugs.
The Maine Wire, a media arm of the conservative Maine Policy Institute, interviewed Knight over the phone and later in person, during which she repeated the allegations.
As a result, some residents have called for Harriman’s resignation from City Council and the Maine Legislature.
Knight: ‘It’s nothing but the truth’
In an interview on Thursday, Knight said during her time as his tenant Harriman entered her apartment and her bed uninvited and on several occasions drove her to get drugs, often paying for them, and providing his car as a space to get high.
Knight provided no other details about the bedroom allegations other than to claim he got into bed with her and that he did not touch her.
“That I knew — that’s not normal,” Knight said, adding that she did not want any kind of intimate relationship while trying to get sober and leave prostituting.
“He did drive me to the methadone clinic, but when his girlfriend was at work, he let me borrow money and he knew it was for crack because I told him I can’t quit all at once, that I had to kind of ween down off one and then work on the other.”
Knight said Harriman lent her “a substantial amount of money,” about $800, to purchase drugs, about triple the amount she would need for rent.
Knight said she recognized that Harriman and his partner showed interest in her because they knew she needed a stable living arrangement to sort out her life. However, she suspects Harriman had other motives as well — she said his demeanor changed when she rebuffed advances and began hanging out with other men.
Knight questions why she was evicted over a small amount of rent due when Harriman had previously given her much more.
“A whole year and I was never even late for rent — I had to be pushed out in the cold on the street over $100, but he would give me $800 for drugs?” she said. “He knew I would have nowhere to go, that it would be life or death for me. “
While living in Harriman’s apartment building, Knight said she did get sober for about a seven-month period. She said she had to “learn how to be normal again,” and after kicking the heroin habit, she found she just wanted to move on.
“It’s just taken so much. My daughter thinks I messed up, my family thinks I messed up and I didn’t,” Knight said, adding that she has since relapsed. “I don’t want revenge, I just want to move on and get back to where I was. … It took me 10 years to do anything for myself and my addiction. I actually did it, and now I’m paying for it. It’s so exhausting.”
Knight said she would like to take a polygraph test to prove to the public, as well as her daughter, that her story is true and that she never gave up on her sobriety despite relapsing. She said she would answer any question posed to her.
“Coming into my bed, borrowing money for drugs. All of it. Because it’s nothing but the truth,” Knight said.
Knight said her goal in speaking out is to empower others to do the same, not for revenge against Harriman.
“Going to the news was not something I was prepared for … but I just want any female out there that’s ever been in prostitution or abused and don’t have the means to get out of it … to know they can.”
Harriman: ‘I would never do something like that’
In an interview Wednesday, Harriman said Knight’s description of their tenant/landlord relationship is untrue.
“I don’t know if she’s making it up completely to try to discredit me, if someone planted that with her or what,” he said, when asked whether he entered Knight’s bed. “But I would never do something like that.”
Harriman also said allegations of lending money for drugs and allowing Knight to smoke crack in his car are also untrue. He said he did provide Knight with transportation to a methadone clinic almost daily for a long period.
Eventually, Knight began missing trips to receive methadone “a day here and there,” then every couple days, he said. The rides to the clinic became sporadic. So did her rent payments, he said.
Knight would smoke in the building, Harriman said, and broke into his mailbox, the basement and the laundry room.
“I had to evict her, that part’s true,” he said. “She was a very challenging tenant. Her behavior affected other tenants in the building and things declined over several months.”
Harriman said he empathized with Knight when he originally agreed to rent his apartment to her. Sometimes he would see her on the street in what he described as mild crises, and it occurred to him that having a stable place to live would alleviate some of the pressures she was living with.
“Susan Longchamps, my colleague on the City Council, also knew her and had known her longer. I leaned on Susan for assistance at times, including talking to the tenant when her behavior was getting worse,” Harriman said. “Karrah’s a good person. She’s just got a lot of struggles and challenges, and unfortunately, it didn’t work out in that apartment.”
Knight’s allegations came initially as a surprise, but were not especially shocking considering the tumultuous landlord/tenant relationship, Harriman said.
When Knight was evicted, she made threatening statements — not violent in nature, but vindictive, Harriman said. Perhaps hoping he would change his mind about the eviction, Harriman surmised, Knight had not packed her belongings when the final day of her tenancy came up. He said he was forced to call the police to have her removed.
Knight came back to the apartment a week later to gather more belongings, Harriman said, but she again refused to leave. He had to call the police a second time.
“We had some contact by phone and text to coordinate when she could retrieve her belongings,” Harriman said. “After the first time, I told her she couldn’t come back into the building and that I’d bring her things outside. I put boxes on the porch, and she came and got them. That’s the only contact I’ve had with her.”
‘The political aspect’
Harriman said he believes the submission of the allegations to the council and The Maine Wire’s subsequent role in reporting on them are politically motivated.
A Democrat, Harriman said The Maine Wire is not a credible news organization but rather a propaganda arm of a right-wing think tank funded by out-of-state billionaires.
“I think it’s clear the allegations are false and that the way they’ve been brought into this campaign cycle is a last-ditch effort to swing the election in a certain direction,” Harriman said. “I think that lends them less credibility.”
Harriman has released several clips of home surveillance footage of Jon Fetherston, who reported on the allegations for The Maine Wire. The clips show Fetherston parked outside Harriman’s home speaking loudly on his cellphone to someone about Harriman and his campaign.
The videos, Harriman said, show that The Maine Wire is coordinating with Harriman’s House District 94 Republican opponent Janet Beaudoin in an effort to influence the election.
In one video, Fetherston is speaking on speakerphone to someone about wanting to get a statement from the Maine Republican Party for his story on Knight’s allegations.
“If it got picked up by one other news organization, why wouldn’t they?” Fetherston can be heard saying in the video. “Do they want you to win this seat?”
In another video, a voice on the other end of Fetherston’s call can be heard saying, “I think the more attention we can bring on this, the better. I mean, this could legitimately flip the seat. I’m with it.”
Referring to Knight’s allegations and the efforts to disseminate them some three weeks before the Nov. 3 election, Harriman said, “I find it hard to miss the political aspect, especially given the timing. It feels like a manufactured political hit.”

title: Obituary: Jean Claude E. Poulin
text:
LEWISTON – Jean Claude E. Poulin, 81, of Auburn, passed away peacefully on Monday, Oct. 12, 2026, at St. Mary’s D’Youville Pavilion.
He was born in St. Martin, Quebec, Canada, on May 20, 1945, the son of the late Emile and Fernande (Poulin) Poulin and had been a resident of this community for most of his life.

During his career as a truck tire salesman for Stratham and New England Truck Tire, he traveled over a million miles within his sales routes which he was very proud of.
He enjoyed time with his brothers playing golf and was very passionate about his Montreal Canadiens especially when they played against the Boston Bruins. He enjoyed summer cookouts where he was named “The Burger Master” and most of all he enjoyed spending time with his family and friends.

title: Nellis Air Force Base: Service member dies after rappelling fall at a UT San Antonio game
text:
Nellis Air Force Base: Service member who died after rappelling fall at UTSA-Navy game identified
A military service member has died after he fell hard as he rappelled from the ceiling to midfield before a University of Texas at San Antonio football game where the military was honored.
Related video: Trump waives new sanctions on Russia under law named for late Sen. Graham
Nellis Air Force Base Public Affairs said the service member assigned to the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2, was taken Saturday to a local hospital, where he later died.
Nellis Air Force Base later identified the service member as U.S. Air Force Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson.
An investigation was underway into what led up to the incident at UTSA’s annual Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans game against Navy.
A video of the fall that was posted on social media showed the man, in combat fatigues, quickly descending to the ground feet-first. The fall occurred with fans in the stands and a band assembled nearby on the field. He was treated on the field for several minutes and taken away on a gurney.
Following the incident, UTSA issued a post on Instagram, saying, "We are deeply saddened by the incident that occurred at the start of tonight’s football game. Our heartfelt thoughts and prayers are with the soldier who was affected, his family and his military colleagues."
The university said it was offering well-being services to support staff, faculty and students.
The game at the Alamodome in San Antonio, Texas, which UTSA won 38-34, was delayed for about 10 minutes.
Who was Tech Sgt. Ian Patterson?
The Air Force base said Patterson was from Fort Stewart, Georgia, and served for 15 years.
His decorations included the Air and Space Commendation Medal with three oak leaf clusters and the Army Commendation Medal Air, Air and Space Achievement Medal and Army Achievement Medal, each with one oak leaf cluster.
In 2022, he was named the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the Year at the Headquarters Air Force level.
Patterson had been one of four military service members scheduled to participate in the pregame rappelling demonstration.
According to an Air Force website, the service members who were participating in the rappelling demonstration were part of a team of specialists who embed with Army and Marine units and help to direct air and artillery strikes from forward ground locations.
Part of their training includes learning to rapidly drop by rope, sometimes from helicopters that are 100 feet (about 30 meters) or more above the ground.
Tributes pour in after tragedy
After the game, UTSA Coach Jeff Traylor told reporters that the accident was “heartbreaking” and “tragic.”
He said the team could see the effect that it had on the crowd of over 23,000 people as soon as players arrived on the field for the game, although Traylor had only been told there had been an “incident” that would delay the start of the game by about 10 minutes.
“You could tell the energy was just gone,” he said. “It just really puts things in perspective. It really does.”
U.S. Air Force Brig. Gen. Scott C. Mills, 57th Wing commander, also issued a statement, saying, "Tech. Sgt. Patterson and his service mattered immensely to our wing, and to the family, friends, and teammates who had the privilege of knowing and serving alongside him. Our team is now focused on standing beside Ian’s family, loved ones, and fellow Airmen as we navigate this profound loss together.”
He continued, saying, “Our relationship with local community partners is incredibly important to our Airmen, especially during difficult times like these. We are grateful to the San Antonio community and our mission partners at Joint Base San Antonio for the care, compassion and support they have shown.”

title: Obituary: Adah Jean (Patch) Ginn
text:
SCARBOROUGH – Adah Jean Patch Ginn, 96, passed away peacefully at her home in Scarborough on Oct. 4, 2026, following a period of declining health.
Adah was born Sept. 13, 1930, in Bangor, Maine, the daughter of Clifford and Jean Spruance Patch. She attended Bangor High School, where she was an outstanding student and athlete. She went on to attend Wellesley College, but left before graduating to marry Herb Ginn—the big brother of her best friend, Shirley Ginn, and the man who would remain her best friend and partner for the next 70 years.
Herb had recently returned from serving in the Navy in Japan and was headed to Boston University School of Law. Their first child, Mark, was born while they were living in Boston, Mass. Following Herb’s graduation from law school, the young family returned to Bangor, where Herb joined the family business, Fox & Ginn.
In 1955, Adah and Herb moved to Cape Elizabeth, where they welcomed two daughters, Jean and Tracey, and built the home and family life that would mean so much to them.
Adah was, in many ways, the quintessential mother of her generation. She was there for the ball games, concerts, dance recitals and countless other milestones of her children’s lives. But no one who knew Adah would ever describe her simply as a wife and mother. She was strong-willed, fiercely competitive and decidedly opinionated—and she was never particularly shy about letting you know what she thought. Those qualities stayed with her throughout her 96 years and were a large part of what made Adah, Adah.
Perhaps nowhere was her competitive spirit more evident than at the bridge table. Adah and Herb were nationally ranked duplicate bridge players, competing in tournaments throughout the country and playing several times a week for many years. Bridge brought them competition, friendships and more than a few adventures. After a ski injury once left Adah with her leg in a cast, they simply changed their plans: rather than fly to a bridge tournament in Cleveland, Ohio, they drove so she could keep her leg elevated along the way. Missing the tournament apparently wasn’t an option.
They were equally adventurous travelers. Adah and Herb saw much of the world together, sometimes arriving in a foreign country in the middle of the night, speaking not a word of the local language and armed with little more than a map pulled from the pages of National Geographic. Somehow, they always found their way.
Winter weekends were spent at Sugarloaf, where they skied and reconnected with lifelong Bangor friends and their families. Those friendships, like so many in Adah’s life, endured for decades.
Bridge remained part of Adah’s life well into her later years. She especially loved bringing her “bridge ladies” to the family’s Nonantum Resort in Kennebunkport for marathon games. Even in their 80s and 90s, they thought nothing of playing until midnight.
Above all else, Adah’s greatest joy was her family. She delighted in following the lives and accomplishments of her eight grandchildren and 19 great-grandchildren. Their activities, adventures and milestones gave her enormous pleasure and pride.
Adah was predeceased by her beloved husband of 70 years, Herb; her son, Mark; her brother, Clifford, and her sister, Jean.
She is survived by her daughter, Jean Ginn Marvin and her husband, Bob, of Scarborough, her daughter Tracey Ginn Guidi of Satellite Beach, Fla.; her grandchildren Clifford Ginn (Amanda), Dr. Jennifer Ginn Foy (Danial), Lt. Col. Adam Marvin (Shauna), Parker Marvin
(Kristina), Tanya Guidi Smith (Brandon), Stephanie Guidi, Daniel Guidi and Colby Marvin Bracy (Andrew); and 19 great-grandchildren.
Adah is also survived, in a very special sense, by the extraordinary group of caregivers who became part of her extended family. Their kindness, patience, companionship and devotion made it possible for Adah to remain in the home she loved until she drew her final breath. Her family will never forget what they did for her and will remain forever grateful to them.
Adah’s was a long life, richly lived—a life filled with family, friendship, competition, travel, laughter and adventure. She was fortunate to have nearly a lifetime with the man she loved, and generations of family who loved her in return. At the end of her life, she was exactly where she wanted to be: at home.
Funeral services will be held Saturday, Oct. 24, at 11 a.m. at Black Point Congregational Church in Scarborough.
In lieu of flowers, the family asks that those wishing to honor Adah’s memory consider a contribution to either the Ginn Family Scholarship at the Maine Community College System at https://www.maineccfoundation.org/ or the Adah Patch Ginn & Clifford Spruance Patch Scholarship at the University of Maine System http://umainefoundation.org/

title: I headed into the woods for one last shot at wild trout. I got more than I bargained for.
text:
The air is still, the temperature warmer than might be expected for October. While sipping tea from a favorite mug, my attention is drawn to a pair of cedar waxwings plucking dusty-blue berries from a red cedar tree beside our porch. The wooden deck feels cool under my bare feet, but not too cold. I remove a cushion from a redwood chair and lay it on the upper step to prevent moisture from seeping up from the floorboard. Taking a seat, I watch the day unfold like the last of summer’s morning glories.
A mist has dampened the lawn. Beads of moisture illuminate webs weaved by spiders. Daisies and Queen Anne’s lace growing along the edges of the lawn have withered, their simple beauty pressed into memory. It’s been a while since we’ve seen the silver-haired woodchuck waddle out from his den onto the earthen dam behind our pond.
The last few weeks have marked fall’s great hurrah. The biting wind and rain of November will inevitably give way to months of ice and snow, but not before the celebration of heartbreaking beauty proceeds to its conclusion.
Leaves need to be raked and stove wood stacked. Moss growing on the siding along the north-facing wall must be power-washed and the snowplow connected to our tractor, but I’m drawn, more than any other time of year, to Bonnie Brook. Perhaps there are still a few trout willing to play tag with a fly before giving themselves over to the icy shroud of winter.
It’s a few minutes past 10 when I park my pickup along the cracked macadam. I can hear the tick of leaves as they touch down between patches of summer grass turned the color of straw. Following a well-worn deer trail through a field, I cross under a grove of white pines. The previous week, remnants of a late-season hurricane disgorged 3 inches of rain.
The woodland surrounding this stretch of stream consists primarily of hemlock, spruce and white pine, with a lesser number of hardwood trees. Although the sun is strong, the temperature remains cool under the shade of the mature trees.
Suspended over the forest floor is an aromatic blend of damp bark, hemlock needles and fallen leaves that combines with the scent of decaying ferns and rotting mushrooms.
Bending on one knee, I scan the current for signs of fish. I’m looking for the flutter of a fin, the heave of a gill, a shifting shadow. The brown trout here are wild and have no use for me. Their backs bear dark green markings like sinuous worm trails that allow these secretive fish to blend in with a streambed dappled with sunken leaves over copper-and-flint-colored cobble.
Although the sides of each brown trout are covered with pumpkin-colored spots, their flanks are not visible. I have caught bigger trout in larger rivers, but none quite as comely as those that begin and end their secret lives in this little mountain brook.
There are no rises. Didn’t expect any. I knot a wet fly to my tippet. One I tied myself. Nothing special, a bit of hare’s ear dubbed along the shank of the hook, a few strands of brown hackle for a tail and a single turn of a grouse feather behind the eye for a collar.
Nothing on my first few casts, but then I come upon a familiar boulder. The soft-hackled fly ticks off its side and sinks before drifting down along the edge of the stream. And just like that, I’m into my first fish, a plump, not-so-pleased 9-inch brown trout.
I work upstream for at least a mile, maybe farther, while fooling a few more fish, spooking others. Clouds have rolled in, the wind picking up. There is good water above the bend, but my right knee has begun to ache. There’s always tomorrow, I tell myself, although at my age, that’s not nearly as certain as it might have once been.
Rain begins to spit down. With the sleeves of my flannel shirt lowered, the collar around my neck raised, I tramp back to the truck.
Through intermittent wipers, I spot a large black bear with three cubs rambling along the edge of the forest. The yearlings lope into the middle of the road. Their mother follows, advancing between her young and the truck. There’s a slight hitch in the bruin’s stride. I wonder if she, too, has a bum leg. The fur along her broad shoulders has a whisper of white, like the gray sweeping through my once-black beard.
The old sow watches the cubs shuffle up an embankment. Before lumbering into the forest, she turns to look in my direction. The only sound is that of the wipers as they sweep across the windshield. I notice the tan fur around her muzzle. Dignified, with a hint of a hump, her snout glistens with droplets of rain. Then my eyes catch hers, and I wonder what manner of brown trout might be found in those chestnut pools.

Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection
text:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu late in his reelection campaign, a coveted boost because of Trump’s popularity but one that the American had withheld for months as the vote neared and the leaders’ strategies in the Middle East diverged.
Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu “has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
Israelis are set to vote Oct. 27, in the first national elections since Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
The absence of an endorsement was a setback for the Likud politician, who had billed his tight ties to the Republican president as a selling point for staying in power.
“Thank you, President Trump, for the tremendous support and work together,” Netanyahu said in a statement in Hebrew posted on X. “Together we will complete the mission!”
His Likud Party attached to the statement a 35-second video showing clips of the two leaders together and Trump praising Netanyahu.
It was not immediately clear what impact the endorsement would have on what is expected to be a tight race. Trump is still popular in Israel, but many Israelis, including leading commentators, have expressed disappointment over the inconclusive outcome of the Iran war and Trump’s ceasefire proposal, which fell short of many of the countries’ key goals when they jointly launched the war in February.
In his post, Trump again threatened to “soon finish the job” against Iran “unless they change their ways, rapidly,” but added he might not want to if Netanyahu loses the election. “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump said.
He said Netanyahu had been “Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.”
Trump endorsed Netanyahu in past elections and in November he sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog asking him to pardon Netanyahu on corruption charges.
But Trump’s comments about Netanyahu in recent months had been much more subdued, and he repeatedly demurred when asking if he would back the prime minister. The president, when asked in a Time magazine interview published this month about backing the Israeli leader, said, ”I’m not involved in politics anymore,” despite his campaigning for and endorsing U.S. politicians.
Trump, especially in his second term, has sought to give his stamp of approval to candidates in foreign elections and claimed credit when they have been successful. He endorsed Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in his unsuccessful bid for a fifth term, as well as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Polish President Karol Nawrocki, and several Latin American leaders.
Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies and seemed more aligned than ever in the wake of the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities in 2025. But over the course of the nearly eight-month war with Iran this year, they have had disagreements.
Trump criticized Israel’s decision to attack a key Iranian gas field in the first weeks of the war. In June, he called Netanyahu “crazy.” Trump also said that he was “a little bit perturbed” as Israel’s fighting with Hezbollah militants in Lebanon was holding back peace talks with Iran.
Beyond Iran, Netanyahu in August rejected Trump’s latest plan to advance a stalled ceasefire in Gaza, pushing back on the U.S. administration’s call for Israel to withdraw from territory it controls in Gaza until Hamas has been disarmed.
___
Associated Press writer Josef Federman in Jerusalem contributed to this report.

title: Blaze at St Petersburg oil sites as Kyiv launches more than 1,000 drones at Russia
text:
(AP) - Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war.
The strikes came as tensions between Kyiv and Washington deepened, with U.S. President Donald Trump criticizing Kyiv’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure and the prospect of further U.S. sanctions against Moscow still uncertain.
Trump said Sunday that he decided to hold off on implementing new sanctions on Russia because he doesn’t “want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.”
In a social media post, the U.S. president defended his Friday order to issue a waiver to prevent new sanctions from being placed on Moscow from bipartisan criticism that he was favoring Russian President Vladimir Putin’s interests over those of Ukraine. Trump said he believed new sanctions would undermine negotiations to bring about a diplomatic end to the war in Ukraine.
“I can sign it later, or any time that I want!” Trump added of the sanctions.
Trump also lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has been critical of Trump’s recent outreach to Putin, for launching strikes on Russian energy infrastructure during the conflict, claiming Zelenskyy “doesn’t want to end this war.”
Zelenskyy: Waiving sanctions strengthens Russia
Speaking on NBC’s “Meet the Press” earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy said waiving sanctions against Russia would strengthen Putin’s war effort. He also said U.S.-Ukraine intelligence sharing had resumed after being “blocked for some period of time.”
Zelenskyy said that while he trusted Trump, siding with Moscow would be a tragedy and a “historic mistake” for Washington.
“People want to forget what’s going on. But we can’t give this possibility to forget, or to change reality, or to change the truth,” Zelenskyy said. “We can’t compare me and Putin. He’s (an) aggressor. He occupied us. He killed adults and children, his soldiers. He’s a terrorist. And that’s why I hope that President Trump will be very clear with this position.”
Later Sunday, Zelenskyy said on social media that he had spoken with U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the results of an Oct. 9 meeting between U.S. and Ukrainian negotiating teams in Miami, as well as “next steps in diplomacy.”
Two killed as Russia and Ukraine trade blows
One person was killed and five others were wounded in the St. Petersburg attack, which sparked fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot, local Gov. Alexander Beglov said. A logistics center belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data center operated by Russian tech giant VK were also targeted, the companies confirmed.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency Tass that Kyiv was “resisting” Moscow’s invasion but could not “change the current course of events.”
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a woman was killed and a 6-year-old girl was among at least two other people wounded in two Russian attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said Sunday.
Russia continues energy attacks, Kyiv says
Trump announced on Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” in the 4½-year-old war, but offered no details. Kyiv reported Russian attacks on energy sites continued after Trump’s announcement, and on Thursday said it had resumed strikes on Russian oil facilities after a three-day pause.
Zelenskyy wrote on X on Sunday that Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times in the week since Trump’s announcement. The Ukrainian government initially said it was observing the ceasefire.
Energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions were struck overnight, leaving tens of thousands of families without power, he said, accusing Russia of trying to cause a blackout.
“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting,” the Ukrainian president wrote.
Ukraine apology to Lithuania over drone alert
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry apologized on Sunday after a drone entered Lithuania’s airspace, prompting authorities to issue an air raid warning.
Russian electronic warfare may have diverted the drone during a Ukrainian operation against legitimate military targets in Russia, ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said in a statement.
Lithuanian authorities urged residents in two northern counties along the Latvian border to take cover early Sunday because of a possible drone incursion, public broadcaster LRT reported.
A drone entered the northern Pasvalys region and damaged a moving car, LRT said, citing Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Center. No injuries were reported.
___
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Bruins beats Kings for 5th straight victory
text:
LOS ANGELES — Marat Khusnutdinov scored in the third period and the Boston Bruins beat the Los Angeles Kings 4-1 on Saturday night for their fifth straight victory.
David Pastrnak had a goal, Elias Lindholm and JJ Peterka scored empty-netters, and Jeremy Swayman made 25 saves. The Bruins swept the three California teams as part of a four-game trip that ends in Dallas on Tuesday.
Alex Laferriere scored for Los Angeles, and Anton Forsberg made 24 saves. The Kings remained winless through six games to start the season and were held to one goal for the fourth straight contest.
Khusnutdinov put the Bruins ahead 2-1 with 6:24 remaining, scoring on a backhander after Forsberg failed to cover up Morgan Geekie’s shot and Matt Poitras kept the puck alive.
The Kings got off to a quick start, scoring 31 seconds into the game. Laferriere was at the top of the crease to put in Adrian Kempe’s pass for his second goal of the season, making the most of his promotion to first-line center.
But the Bruins responded early in the second period, with Pastrnak tying it at 2:43. He pounced on a loose puck in the neutral zone and took it the other way to beat Forsberg on a wrist shot from the right circle for his fourth goal.
It was Pastrnak’s 289th goal at even-strength, tying Phil Esposito for third-most in Boston history.
Bruins center Pavel Zacha did not play because of an upper-body injury he sustained in the third period against the Ducks on Friday. He is day-to-day, coach Marco Sturm said before the game.
Up next
Bruins: At Dallas on Tuesday night.
Kings: At Washington on Tuesday night.

title: A.J. Brown struggles in return to Patriots in win over Jets
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — It was anything but smooth for A.J. Brown in his return to the New England Patriots on Sunday.
The prized offseason acquisition for the defending AFC champions finished with as many catches as dropped passes — three — and even drew a round of boos after a third-quarter drop in New England’s 26-19 win over the New York Jets.
His high ankle sprain might be in the past following a four-game stint on injured reserve, but the wide receievers hands were anything but a sure in his first game since New England’s season opener at Seattle.
The 29-year-old Brown was activated on Saturday after missing a minimum number of games after going on IR. He was in the starting lineup Sunday and finished with 27 yards receiving on 10 targets.
“No excuses. Ankle or not, I should make those plays,” said Brown, who spoke briefly while standing at his locker.
Brown’s first appearance on the Gillette Stadium video board came 48 minutes before kickoff. He received a nice applause from the crowd while he was warming up. Brown was also the final member of the Patriots’ offense to be introduced and received an extended ovation as he jumped and waved his arms in response.
By the third quarter, the good cheer from fans evaporated. One of the drops came in the second quarter when Drake Maye targeted him deep. Brown also let an onside kick by the Jets slip through his grasp, though the lapse didn’t hurt as tight end Eli Raridon fell on the ball and New England ran out the final 32 seconds.
Neither Brown’s coach or teammates expressed concern after the game. They said they know that a player with six 1,000-yard receiving seasons and three Pro Bowl nods will be fine in the long term.
“I know he wanted to do well for his football team,” said Patriots coach Mike Vrabel, who also coached Brown when the receiver broke into the NFL with Tennessee. “Unfortunately, it wasn’t his best effort. He knows that. We have all the confidence in the world in A.J. to be able to finish those plays. He has high expectations for himself, and we have high expectations for him.”
On the sideline, New England refrained from providing words of encouragement to Brown during his first game at Gillette Stadium as a Patriot.
“He’s been in the league a long time. He knows how to deal with things,” Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez said. “He’s been out for a while, so it’s different when you get out there and catch the ball when everyone is flying around. Everyone in the locker room and in this building, we have the utmost confidence in him.”

title: Patriots hold off Jets for 3rd straight win
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — The thinking in New England’s locker room under Mike Vrabel has been to never apologize for a win. So no one was feeling bad after the Patriots improved to 2-0 in the AFC East after their victory over the New York Jets on Sunday.
They also know that mounting injuries will require much more from everyone if they want to keeping winning.
Drake Maye threw three touchdown passes, New England overcame losing three offensive linemen and Charles Woods came up with Geno Smith’s first interception of the season in the fourth quarter to help the Patriots hold on for a 26-19 win.
“It was sloppy. It wasn’t clean,” said Maye, who completed 18 of 32 passes for 235 yards in his third consecutive game with at least three TD passes. “It wasn’t football that we felt like (was) complementary.”
Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas and Hunter Henry had touchdown catches for the Patriots (4-2), who have won three in a row. Douglas had a team-high seven catches for 86 yards.
A.J. Brown had three catches for 27 yards for the Patriots in his return from injured reserve, but his timing was off and he had three drops on his 10 total targets.
“None of us were at our best today, but we were good enough,” Vrabel said.
New England won its fourth straight against the Jets and 19th in its last 21 meetings despite right tackle Morgan Moses (ankle), left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) and right guard Ben Brown (knee) leaving with injuries.
“Those guys are playing through injuries,” Maye said. “We (had) three go down today, so these guys are fighting hard. They’re fighting their butts off, and it goes through them.”
The Jets (2-4) had a chance to tie it in the third quarter, but the Patriots held them to a field goal. New York squandered another opportunity to cut the deficit to a field goal in the fourth quarter when Smith was picked off by Woods. It came on Smith’s 166th pass of the season, ending his longest opening stretch to a season without an interception.
“Finishing on offense and detail on defense is something we’ve got to get better at because I think we gifted two touchdowns that shouldn’t have happened,” Jets coach Aaron Glenn said.
Smith finished 20 of 30 for 252 yards and a touchdown to rookie Omar Cooper Jr., who had six catches for 103 yards in his return from IR after missing four games with an ankle injury.
New England’s defense, which got a boost from cornerback Christian Gonzalez returning from a two-game absence with a shoulder injury, held New York to 0 for 3 in the red zone. The Jets were also 3 of 10 on third down and were stopped on fourth-down runs on consecutive possessions in the second quarter.
“Those plays are huge for us. I’m just proud of the defense, how we stayed together,” Gonzalez said. “They got some momentum there late and we were just able to finish the game.”
Building the lead
The Patriots led 17-3 at the half, courtesy of Doubs’ diving 42-yard touchdown catch and a 9-yard scoring grab by Douglas.
The Jets trimmed the gap to 17-10 in the third quarter after Cooper got behind Patriots safety Craig Woodson and caught a 42-yard TD from Smith.
That remained the score when Jets edge rusher David Bailey stripped TreVeyon Henderson of the ball and Jamien Sherwood recovered at the New England 36. New York drove to 10, but Smith was sacked by Elijah Ponder, forcing the Jets to settle for a 36-yard field goal by Jason Sanders.
The Patriots responded on their next series, capping a 12-play, 68-yard drive with a 7-yard TD strike from Maye to Henry, but Andy Borregales missed the extra point.
Just four plays later and the Jets down 10, Smith overshot Kenyon Sadiq on a deep pass that was intercepted by Woods.
Injuries
Jets: LB Kiko Mauigoa left with a thigh injury in the first quarter.
Patriots: Doubs (shoulder) exited in the first quarter following his touchdown catch and didn’t return. … Moses favored his left ankle when he left early in the second quarter. … Vera-Tucker left in the second with a hamstring injury and was ruled out. … Brown had trouble putting weight on his left leg as he was helped off in the fourth quarter with a knee injury.
Up next
Jets: Host the Dolphins next Sunday.
Patriots: Visit the Bears on Thursday night.

title: Pope Leo tells faithful in St. Peter’s Square he will gradually resume duties after cancer surgery
text:
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV thanked thousands of faithful in St. Peter’s Square on Sunday for their prayers while he was hospitalized for an operation to remove a malignant tumor, and said he plans to gradually return to his usual duties.
The crowd erupted in cheers when the pontiff showed himself in the window overlooking the square, where a week ago on the same occasion of the traditional Angelus blessing he revealed that a nodule had been located on his lung, and that it would be surgically removed.
‘’Now that this delicate phase is behind me, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God’s help and your prayers," Leo said, his voice sounding strong four days after the lower lobe of his right lung was removed.
The pontiff said the experience of the last week “has made me feel especially close to those facing illness and infirmity.” He told the faithful that he had ‘’truly felt your support,’’ and expressed ‘’particular gratitude to the doctors, nurses and all the staff at Gemelli hospital’’ where he was treated.
The pope paused for a moment and waved to the crowd before retreating into his apartment in the Apostolic Palace.
A delegation from Africa in Rome for a congress danced and ululated after the pope’s blessing.
‘’He was always in our prayers when he was sick, and we are happy to see him today," said Alain Kalembu of the Democratic Republic of Congo. “This is an expression of our joy.”
The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
He told a reporter in English that he was doing ‘’much better’’ as he drove away from Rome’s Gemelli hospital to return to the Vatican, after a shorter hospital stay than had initially been anticipated.
“I don’t believe it, because he was just operated on the other day,” Cosimo Mastrocinque, a retired factory worker visiting the Vatican from the southern region of Puglia, said. “It is a miracle that he recovered already.”
American tourists were especially eager to pray alongside the first pope born in the United States. Marla Marsala of Michigan was supposed to attend a Mass with the pope last week that was canceled due to his hospitalization.
‘’I am just happy that we are praying with him today instead of for him, like we were before,’’ Marsala said. “It was a tough week for all of the people who love him, which are many. He seems like a very strong soul. So I think he will pull through and fight it, and succeed and keep doing the wonderful work he is doing.’’
Claire Holland from Jacksonville, Florida, said she felt “very blessed” to be present for the pope’s return to his flock.
“I’m so happy that he has recovered so quickly. I think there have been millions and millions of prayers. And he is a strong, determined man, and I am so happy that he is feeling well enough to do this,” Holland said.
Leo’s next major engagement is an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that “there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place.”
“The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery,” Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery “in another 10 days or so.”
Histological testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumor’s molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumor’s genetic characteristics.

title: Obituary: Cecile A. “CC” Baker
text:
WINTHROP – Cecile A. “CC” Baker, 74, passed away on Oct. 14, 2026, at the Balsam House in Readfield while surrounded by her family.
Cecile, known to many as “CC”, was born on May 9, 1952, the middle child of Everett and Agnes (Soucy) Weston. They grew up on a small family farm on Churchill Road in Augusta, where she learned the value of hard work at a young age. Following her education at Cony High School, CC began working and held a variety of jobs including waitressing, foreman at Hallowell Shoe, and lastly, working at Togus VA Medical Center from 1996 to 2018. CC was undoubtedly a hard worker, often taking on extra shifts in order to provide for her family.
CC was an avid gardener who enjoyed taking care of her property whether she was tending her gardens or mowing her lawn. She immensely enjoyed the holiday season, generously giving gifts to all of her family members, but she especially loved Halloween. CC decorated her home and workspace during Halloween, an won many costume competitions.
CC will be remembered for her determined spirit and caring heart.
She was predeceased by her parents; an infant grandson, Remi Baker; and a nephew, Travis Weston.
Cecile is survived by her children, Heather Lajoie and her husband Matt, Heidi Guiliano, Nathan Baker, and son-in-law, David Guiliano; grandchildren, Keyrah Powers, Konnor Powers, Kolby Lajoie, Kelsey Lajoie, Hayden Guiliano, and Benjamin Guiliano; siblings, Roger Weston and Helen Hall; and a nephew, Troy Weston.
The family wishes to thank the staff of the Balsam House and Andwell Hospice for the care provided to Cecile during her last months.
A period of visitation will be held on Thursday, Oct. 22, from 11 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. at Plummer Funeral Home, 16 Pleasant St., Augusta, ME 04330. A Mass of Christian Burial will follow at 1:30 p.m. at St. Mary of the Assumption Catholic Church, 41 Western Ave., Augusta.
Condolences, stories and photos may be shared by visiting http://www.plummerfh.com.
In lieu of flowers, memorial contributions in Cecile’s name may be considered to:
Kennebec Valley Humane Society at
pethavenlane.org/donate/

title: Obituary: Ruth Eleanor (Phinney) Gurney
text:
NORWAY – Ruth Eleanor Phinney Gurney, a remarkable woman, 95 years of age, left this world in peace on Oct. 11, 2026, at her home in Norway, Maine.
Ruth was born to Charles and Evelyn Tripp Phinney on April 17, 1931. She was a proud graduate of the Class of 1949 of Norway High School, now the Guy E. Rowe elementary school. It was a short walk to school from her family residence on Paris Street and to downtown Norway where she worked at Ashton Drug store.
Ruth and Bryant met each other when young, holding hands at the Rex movie theater when tickets were just 11 cents. They married and traveled extensively throughout the country during Bryant’s early working years. Eventually they returned to Norway, purchasing land on the hill overlooking the lake and building a home there. In August 2026, Ruth and Bryant celebrated their seventy-seventh wedding anniversary and will be together for eternity.
Ruth was a lifelong learner who was curious about the world and always ready for a conversation. She was intelligent, direct, and funny with a warmth that made it easy to become her friend. Ruth loved reading and baking, and you could always count on the cookie jar being full. Ruth had a heart of gold and a deep love for her community and knowing the local happenings. Over the years, she served as a Girl Scout leader, was a steady patron of the Norway Memorial Library, and volunteered with the American Legion Auxiliary.
Ruth and Bryant enjoyed dancing at local venues with dear friends, attending a few Patriots games, visiting family in the South, and trying their luck at blackjack in Las Vegas, Nev.
Ruth was truly one of a kind. She was blessed with treasured family members and friends throughout her life.
Ruth is survived by her husband, Bryant; and an extended family that includes her daughter, Jane (and Anselmo), son-in-law Raymond (and Jennifer); grandson Nathan (and Amy and daughters Rosa and Iola); grandson Kyle (and Mayra), and granddaughter Laura (and Sven); as well as nieces and nephews including Coleen Trask, Eric Donahue, and Joyce, Brian, Brent, and Beth Phinney, and their families. Many loved ones passed before her.
Those who visited with Ruth knew the coffee pot was always on, usually accompanied by a donut or a muffin, and always a good conversation. She had a way of making people feel welcome, whether stopping by for a quick visit or staying to catch up on life. In Ruth’s memory, we invite you to make time to share a cup of coffee with family and friends and talk about the little things that make life special.
Arrangements are in the care of Cliff Gray Cremation where condolences and tributes may be shared with Ruth’s family and friends at http://www.cliffgraycremations.com

title: Missing the local touch from Maine hospitals
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I love the columns that Victoria Hugo-Vidal writes. And I agree with her all the time. Her piece on the quickly dropping obstetrics services in rural Maine (“Maine’s rural maternity wards require a mindset shift,” Oct. 4) sheds light on an issue that is disastrous for families and women in those areas.
The problem was created by hospitals being grabbed up by corporations and conglomerates. It seems now that every hospital or medical center is owned by others from away and managed by accountants for maximum profit.
It wasn’t always this way, of course. Not too many decades ago, hospitals were run locally. Communities would bond together to raise money for hospitals. There would be a board of directors comprised of local leaders. Maybe they would be run with a modest profit or loss. Community groups like Kiwanis, Rotary or Lions would raise funds. The annual golf tournament would support the hospital and there would be regular bake sales.
It’s probably unlikely we can go back to those days. But something has to give if our communities are not well served by competent medical facilities.
Brian Nickerson
South Portland

title: Fire destroys unoccupied Lisbon home, cause undetermined
text:
LISBON, Maine (WABI) - Investigators are working to determine what caused a fire that destroyed an unoccupied home in Lisbon early Sunday morning.
At approximately 3 a.m. the Lisbon Fire Department responded to a reported structure fire on Gould Road.
Officials say that upon arrival, firefighters found the residence fully engulfed in flames and beginning to collapse.
The cause of the fire remains undetermined, and the investigation is ongoing.
Officials said the residence had recently been sold and was unoccupied at the time of the fire.
