title: Cindy Crawford shares first public statement on her son’s death
text:
Cindy Crawford shares first public statement on her son’s death
Actress and model Cindy Crawford made her first public statement on her son Presley Gerber's death Sunday.
"He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever," Crawford wrote on Instagram. "We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability."
Gerber, a model, died on Sept. 20 at age 27 while at a rehab facility. As of late September, the Santa Monica Police Department was investigating his death as a suspected overdose.
Born in California in 1999, Gerber was one of two children Crawford shared with businessman Rande Gerber. Like his sister, Kaia Gerber, he entered the modeling industry at a young age, making his runway debut for Italian label Moschino aged just 16.
Last December, Gerber posted a video to Instagram describing his use of prescription medication, including antidepressants and Xanax for panic attacks. “Unfortunately, I’ve had a lot of loss in many different forms recently,” he said in the since-removed video. “So that is not an excuse, but it’s the reason why I am where I’m at now.”
Commenting on the video at the time, Crawford had written “Presley — we love you and you are not alone.”
More recently, the 60-year-old supermodel had posted to Facebook to mark her son’s 27th birthday in July, writing: “I’m so proud of the man you’ve become, but I’ll always see you as my little boy!”
Crawford asked for privacy after Gerber's death."We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain," Crawford wrote Sunday. "Til we meet again our sweet boy. We love you forever, Mom, Dad and Kaia."
CNN contributed reporting.

title: Death Notice: Kim Marie (Alcantara) Mundee
Does Maine want its elderly on the streets?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A legislative change is urgently needed in Maine.
Example: a homeowner allowing an elderly mother to remain in house after relocating elsewhere in Maine. There is no Homestead Exemption, as the requirement is owner residency in-home. In this case, it amounts to 10 years of exemption denial and highly increased chance that the house will have to be sold due to doubling of taxes, leaving the elderly parent homeless. Both parties moved in in 2006.
The home was unoccupied for two nights in 26 years. And the homeowner continues with all insurance, local and state taxes and municipal services. Legislators have been unresponsive, yet claim concern for the elderly.
Maggie Trout
Rockland

title: 84-year-old Gorham man seriously burned after clothing catches fire, officials say
text:
GORHAM, Maine (WABI) - An 84-year-old man suffered serious burn injuries Sunday afternoon in what investigators say was an accidental fire, according to the Maine State Fire Marshal’s Office.
The Gorham Fire Department responded to a house on Barstow Road around 3 p.m. after receiving a report of a man with burns.
Responders found the man with extensive burns to multiple areas of his body. He was transported to Maine Medical Center for treatment.
A preliminary investigation indicates the man was burning paper on a stove when his clothing caught fire.
The Fire Marshal’s Office reminds residents to use caution when burning paper or other materials and to keep combustible items and clothing away from open flames and heat sources.

A private jet went off the end of a runway during a planned takeoff at Las Vegas’ main airport Sunday and hit a perimeter fence, officials said.

title: Growing up in Maine exposes the folly of party politics
text:
Jack Brogan of Freeport is studying political science at the University of Rhode Island.
This fall, I will vote in my first general election. Growing up in Maine has given me an unusual idea of politics.
We have an independent senator who caucuses with Democrats. We repeatedly reelected a Republican senator with support from voters who choose Democrats elsewhere on the ballot. This year, a former chairman of the Maine Republican Party is running for governor as an independent.
None of that seems strange to me. What seems stranger is the expectation that once I decide which party better represents me, an entire package of beliefs should follow. My positions on abortion, immigration, policing, climate change, guns and foreign policy are all supposed to become predictable from the letter beside the candidate I support.
I don’t think politics should work that way.
Political independence is often treated as an ideology somewhere between liberalism and conservatism: take the Democratic position, take the Republican position, split the difference and call yourself a moderate.
But that misunderstands independence. Political independence is not an ideology. It is a method of thinking.
Maine has provided plenty of examples. Sen. Angus King caucuses with Democrats because, as he explained when he entered the Senate, refusing to join either caucus would reduce his effectiveness. He also said that choice would not place him in “automatic opposition” to Republicans. His independence was never supposed to mean neutrality. It meant cooperation without ownership.
Susan Collins represents another version of Maine’s resistance to neat political categories. In 2020, Joe Biden won Maine while Collins also won statewide. In my previous op-ed (“The suburban trap: Why Troy Jackson’s path to victory runs through Scarborough, not Allagash,” Aug. 30) , I looked at those voters mainly as an electoral problem for Democrats.
But I have been thinking about them differently since then. Maybe there is something healthy about the fact that they exist.
Rick Bennett raises the same question. He chaired the Maine Republican Party before leaving it and running for governor as an independent. He has broken with Republicans on some issues while retaining positions rooted in his conservative background. Both parties have tried to define what Bennett “really” is.
Maybe both descriptions can contain some truth.
A former Republican can agree with Republicans on some things, Democrats on others, and decide neither party describes his politics well enough to belong to it.
Look at Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania. He remains a Democrat, but his breaks with the party on immigration and Israel have drawn criticism from fellow Democrats. The reaction raises a broader question: What does it mean to be a “big tent” party?
The public is less ideologically tidy than politics makes it appear. Someone can favor stronger unions and tougher enforcement against violent crime. Someone can support abortion rights and want a secure border.
Those voters are not confused. Our categories sometimes are.
Once politics becomes identity rather than judgment, disagreeing with your own side can feel less like changing your mind and more like betraying a group.
Maine has not escaped that trend. But our history is a reminder that things do not have to work that way.
King can caucus with Democrats without becoming one. Collins can win voters who reject Republican presidential candidates. Bennett can leave the Republican Party without automatically becoming a Democrat. Voters can do the same thing.
Independence does not mean every issue has two equally valid sides or that the answer always sits in the middle. Sometimes one party will make the better argument. It means reaching that conclusion yourself.
At 18, that is the kind of voter I want to become. I do not want voting for someone to mean inheriting every one of that candidate’s opinions, or recognizing a good argument from the other side to feel like disloyalty.
Maybe that is what Maine’s independent tradition is worth preserving: not a state without Democrats or Republicans, but a state where neither party owns the people who vote for it.

title: Family claims mother charged in Great Wolf Lodge murders ‘never wanted to get pregnant’
text:
(Gray News) - The family of a woman who is charged with killing her husband and 3-year-old son said she “never wanted to get pregnant” and resented her son because she lost time alone with her husband, according to WPVI.
Metallica Rose Harrison, 27, is accused of killing her husband, Charles Harrison, and her son at Great Wolf Lodge in Scotrun, Pennsylvania.
How the incident unfolded
Officials were notified of the “violent domestic tragedy” in a Great Wolf Lodge hotel room around 3 p.m. Monday.
Investigators said Metallica Harrison was suicidal when she called 911. Police found her at the resort with cuts on her wrists and neck. That is when they found Charles Harrison with several stab wounds to his chest. The couple’s son, who has not been identified, was found with a single stab wound through the chest.
A “large butcher kitchen knife” and a smaller knife were found in the bathroom, according to a criminal complaint. Great Wolf Lodge staff confirmed that the knives, which had teal handles, did not belong to the lodge, according to the complaint and WPVI.
Charges filed
The Monroe County District Attorney’s Office has charged Metallica Harrison with two counts of criminal homicide.
Harrison was taken to the hospital for self-inflicted injuries and is receiving treatment. She remains in police custody.
Investigation details
The family checked into the Great Wolf Lodge on Sept. 21, then on Oct. 5 they extended their stay with a checkout date of Oct. 13.
The Monroe County district attorney said this was just the start of a lengthy investigation. Investigators said they are still reviewing extensive evidence found at the scene. Autopsies will be done later this week.

title: Cooper Flagg’s new coach one of 3 first-timers in NBA this season
text:
Dusty May is new to the NBA. He’s not new to the NBA stage.
Thanks in large part to a Final Four run at Florida Atlantic in 2023 and leading Michigan to the NCAA title last season, May has coached plenty of big games in plenty of NBA arenas and knows what it’s like when those buildings are filled to the rafters.
And that means when he makes his regular-season debut as coach of Cooper Flagg and the Dallas Mavericks in a few days, May will have a real sense of what’s coming — at least from an surroundings standpoint.
“I’ve been in that environment,” May said. “Not at the level, obviously, but I’m someone who’s big on visualization. I see myself there. … But I have a real unique ability to, once the game starts, for 48 minutes to have 100% of my focus on the court and our bench.”
In other words, the coach of last season’s NCAA champion truly believes he’s ready for the NBA challenge. And he’s not alone, with six teams under new coaching management this season.
May is one of three first-time NBA coaches, along with Orlando’s Sean Sweeney (former San Antonio assistant) and Portland’s Micah Nori (former Minnesota assistant).
Another trio of coaches got new jobs in the league — former Memphis coach Taylor Jenkins has taken over in Milwaukee, former Orlando coach Jamahl Mosley has taken over in New Orleans, and former interim Portland coach Tiago Splitter (who coached for basically the entirety of last season) is the new coach in Chicago.
“I think just in general, the way we’re approaching things is, ‘What do we need to do today? Where are we at? How did we do with it? What do we need to improve on?’” Sweeney said. “We’ve done a good job of trying to set high standards for ourselves and lay down expectations for each other and live up to that.”
It is possible to win somewhere in Year 1 as a coach — just ask New York’s Mike Brown, who led the Knicks to last season’s NBA championship in his inaugural season on that team’s sideline. The coach of the reigning Western Conference champions, San Antonio’s Mitch Johnson, got to the finals in his second season as coach of the Spurs (which, technically, was his first full season as head coach).
Sweeney and Nori were widely considered as being ready to become head coaches for a few years before getting their current chances. May had taken two schools, one of them a mid-major, to the Final Four in a four-season span, more than proving his ability to win. Splitter did such a good job under awkward circumstances in Portland last season that he was a coach of the year candidate, and both Jenkins and Mosley had some success at their previous stops.
Nori essentially accepted a one-year contract with the Trail Blazers, an extremely rare move, especially for a first-time head coach. He’s betting on himself, saying that if he does the job, the options for future seasons on the existing contract will take care of itself.
“I’ve been around a lot of — I think it’s 13 — head coaches, so you start to see what you would do and what you’d like to do,” Nori said. “I guess the biggest difference, and they always talk about sliding over that one seat, is that it ends with you. … It’s your program now. That’s been the biggest adjustment.”
Mosley was living in Florida a few months ago, never thinking he’d be in Louisiana now. But when the Magic decided to change coaches, the Pelicans didn’t wait long before pouncing — knowing that Mosley would be a hot commodity. And Mosley says a change of scenery gave him an opportunity for what essentially is a reawakening.
“You get to do a lot of reflecting quick, right? You get to see exactly what worked, what didn’t work, how you can balance out what you do, the roster you have, you get to reflect on a lot of things that were successful and things that you need to work on,” Mosley said. “That’s what it gave me. And now look at the group of guys that we have here — young, energetic, wanting to learn, wanting to figure it out, hungry to get better. There’s so much of it here that it’s easy to pour into an organization like this.”

title: Ex-employee sues Bar Harbor glamping resort over alleged racial and gender discrimination
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A former housekeeper has filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against a popular Bar Harbor glamping resort, alleging her ex-employer discriminated against her on the basis of her race and gender.
Sharonda Boston, of Las Vegas, claims Terramor Outdoor Resorts retaliated against her — moving her in 2025 from a supervisory housing unit to a regular employee housing complex — after she filed repeated complaints regarding a contractor’s sex-based insult and various housing-related issues.
The lawsuit, centered around housemate drama and lack of managerial oversight, comes roughly a year after the alleged racial and gender discrimination occurred. Terramor is often cited by travel blogs and media outlets as one of the most unique glamping resorts in the United States.
Boston filed the civil rights lawsuit against Kampground of America, Inc., Terramor’s parent company, in federal court on Oct. 13, according to the United States District Court of Maine filing.
Boston, a Black woman who was Terramor’s lead housekeeper from mid-August through late October 2025, said she kept a detailed log of incidents she experienced at work and in her onsite housing that included “repeated disturbances, unusual staff presence around her work and living areas, concerns about privacy and conduct she perceived as intimidating and targeted.”
The former employee presented her concerns to Terramor management, who suggested she should move from her current supervisory living complex to other employee housing, according to the filing.
Boston, who is representing herself in the lawsuit, alleges Terramor’s management then failed to address an incident involving a landscaping contractor who called her a sex-specific expletive. Upon reporting the incident, Boston was instructed to “stay out of the contractors’ way and discouraged her from videotaping people,” according to her complaint.
Following her complaint regarding the contractor, management then ordered her to move out of the supervisory housing, immediately, according to the court filing. Management said Boston was “‘making everyone uncomfortable’ and causing others to ‘walk on eggshells.’”
Boston did not receive any formal disciplinary action related to the mandatory housing change, she said, adding that she also contacted KOA human resources on the matter.
“[The plaintiff alleges] that race and color were motivating factors in the manner in which she was singled out, removed from supervisor housing, treated in employee housing, and denied the level of protection and response she repeatedly requested from management and HR,” according to the lawsuit.
After the move, Boston continued to experience disruptions in her living space, including “repeated loud banging, door slamming, stomping and shared-wall disturbances,” the lawsuit says. The disruptions interfered with Boston’s sleep patterns and caused her emotional harm, according to the complaint.
She found her new room in disarray, with dust, trash, stagnant water and other cleanliness problems that weren’t addressed before her relocation, according to the lawsuit.
“[The] plaintiff alleges that the combined treatment in the workplace and employer housing, the gendered insult and management response, the removal from housing specifically tied to her supervisory position, the conditions after the move, the different housing-departure treatment she reported, and KOA’s response after repeated complaints caused significant anxiety, sleep disruption, hypervigilance, emotional distress, and impairment of her ability to rest and function normally,” according to the filing.
A Terramor spokesperson declined to comment Friday on the pending litigation.
Boston, who is requesting a jury trial, did not respond Friday to multiple inquiries from the Bangor Daily News.

title: The truth about the Collins family and The County
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sam Collins of Caribou is the president of S.W. Collins Co. and the brother of Sen. Susan Collins.
I read Tommy Pinette’s op-ed concerning Sen. Susan Collins, the Collins family and Aroostook County with a mixture of dismay and disbelief (“Susan Collins has scant claim to ‘County roots,’” Sept. 6).
Mr. Pinette is certainly entitled to his political opinions. He is free to support Troy Jackson, oppose Susan Collins, criticize our family, question our politics and offer his own interpretation of Aroostook County’s history. He is not, however, entitled to his own facts.
Nor should the Maine Sunday Telegram have published a piece containing numerous assertions that could have been disproved with basic fact-checking. This is particularly troubling. Facts matter, including in politics.
Without having ever met anyone in my family to our knowledge, Mr. Pinette incorrectly claimed that Collins family members are “shipped to private, $60,000-per-year schools” over the Caribou public school system, “fly in private jets and chum around with the children of billionaires,” and implied that we have home theaters.
He asserted that every Collins family member in politics has been a Republican and accused the family of using political influence to block resources and community food programs.
This is simply false. Mr. Pinette presents a caricature of an imagined Aroostook County aristocracy. My siblings and I all attended Caribou High School. My brother Gregg and I remained in Caribou, and all seven of our children also graduated from Caribou High School. The 20-year-old partially rusted car that my daughters drove to school hardly classifies as a private jet. And our “home theater” is a 10-year-old iPad.
Like many Maine families, political views within ours are not monolithic. My great-great-grandfather S.W. Collins served as a Democrat in the Maine Legislature, and my great-grandfather H.D. Collins was initially a Democrat before later serving in the Legislature as a Republican, as well as current family members who identify as Democrats.
There are more falsehoods I could address, but I am even more disappointed by the picture painted of Aroostook County and the people who live here. The op-ed described Northern Maine as a “deindustrialized borderland” dominated by oligarchs and portrayed our farmers as a privileged owner class responsible for the region’s economic problems.
That bears little resemblance to the Aroostook County I know.
Our farmers, like other people from Aroostook County, are among the hardest-working people in Maine. Farmers operate businesses subject to changing weather, labor constraints and international competition. Calling Aroostook County families “oligarchs” may align with popular political rhetoric, but it does little to illuminate the realities of living here today. The County people work hard to make a living in a rural area that has its challenges.
The community, including schools, public organizations, nonprofits and economic development groups, works hard to secure government and private funding to improve our area and enable services and infrastructure that would be otherwise unaffordable.
Members of our family have joined our neighbors to serve on numerous boards and organizations spanning education, healthcare, veterans and economic development.
For generations, our family and company like many other County families have contributed financial support to improve life here and throughout Maine. Our company’s mission is “to be an active positive influence in the communities in which we live and work.” We take that responsibility seriously.
Mr. Pinette may disagree with Sen. Collins politically. He may disagree with members of our family. He may believe Aroostook County should pursue different economic or social policies. Those are legitimate subjects for vigorous debate which I would encourage.
The issue here is larger. Disagreement does not justify fabrication. A telephone call would have corrected the op-ed’s false claims. Newspapers play an essential role in our democracy precisely because readers expect them to distinguish fact from fiction. An opinion page should provide broad latitude for argument and criticism, but attaching the word “opinion” to an article should not relieve a newspaper of responsibility for verifying claims, especially those easily checked.
Before publishing allegations, a newspaper should make a reasonable effort to determine whether those assertions are true. When a paper relaxes its standards for fact-checking, it forfeits the unique authority and trust that separates professional journalism from internet noise, at a time when newspapers can least afford it.
After growing up and spending my life here, I know something about The County: people may disagree strongly, but they generally expect you to look them in the eye, tell the truth and stand behind what you say. That is how you maintain trust. The Maine Sunday Telegram should expect the same standard in what it chooses to publish.

title: Visitors track down the perfect pumpkin at Seashore Trolley Museum
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
KENNEBUNKPORT — The wheels of a 125-year-old wooden trolley grated and scraped against aged tracks, skating along the heritage railway under a canopy of vibrant yellow and orange trees.
Don Stephenson turned the brakes and reached down to yank the pull cord of a yellow 1901 J.G. Brill Company streetcar — the Connecticut Co. 303. The car let out two loud hoots and lurched to a stop beside a small pumpkin patch at the Seashore Trolley Museum.
Dozens of visitors, some dressed in Halloween costumes, hopped off the trolley and dashed toward the pumpkins, ready to choose the best ones at the 28th annual Pumpkin Patch Trolley event on Sunday.
“It never gets boring,” Stephenson said, leaning on the rails of a streetcar he’s been operating for the last 40 years. “I mean, how many people can say they ran a 125-year-old trolley?”
The Seashore Trolley Museum hosts similar events year-round, attracting thousands of visitors. The proceeds help fundraise for the museum and give visitors a fun way to take in a slice of history, Executive Director Katie Orlando said.
The pumpkin patch trolley rides are a precursor to Trolleyween; the museum’s Halloween festival and its way of celebrating the end of its operating season. Guests come dressed in all sorts of costumes, from a family full of “Wizard of Oz” characters to kids dressed as hot dogs.
“We usually have kids dress up as the trolley,” Orlando laughed. “Either they or an adult paints the trolley on a box and they wear it with suspenders.”
When the Connecticut Co. 303 arrived back at the station, two tiny fairies fluttered off toward a pumpkin painting station. Trailing behind them were Peter Pan, Captain Hook and Tinker Bell.
“We dress up every year,” Tinker Bell — or the fairies’ mom Lauren Reidmann — said. “We were on the lookout for a place where everyone dresses up to have fun with our family.”
The pumpkin patch trolley was the perfect opportunity for Reidmann’s family to take their costumes out for a trial run before the big day. Later, she and her fairies will be in the running against a family of “Where’s Waldos” for a costume contest and an opportunity to win a free family membership at the museum.
Events like the pumpkin patch keep the place running. With more than 250 historic streetcars, cranes, wagons and other vehicles, upkeep gets expensive. Most of them are donated or “rescued,” Stephenson said, and preserving them is a constant task.
After a slow start to the season, Orlando wasn’t sure the museum would hit budget goals or surpass the 4,900 guests it hosted last year. She hypothesized that unstable economic conditions in recent years made it harder for members and visitors to contribute to the museum.
“We were really nervous because if we don’t hit budget goals with our admissions, that means we have to solicit additional donations from our donors,” Orlando said “Which, if they’re struggling too, it’s kind of a hard ask.
But by the fourth weekend of trolley season, the museum had already welcomed north of 6,000 attendees — a new record.
“Our guests this year have been incredible,” Orlando smiled.
Stephenson is also pleased with the turnout this year. He said he’s normally on the lookout for people that seem like they could be good trolley conductors, which he recognizes is a niche job. At the museum, it’s also a volunteer position.
“We we keep losing our volunteers to attrition and age and everything else,” Stephenson said. But it’s events like the pumpkin patch and Trolleyween that give him the opportunity to inspire the next generation of conductors.
Stephenson said by the time Trolleyween ends, he’s pretty exhausted. He operates hundreds of rides each season and has been for 30 years. He’s looking forward to a break, but he knows that feeling won’t last long.
“I get an itch at the end of December,” he smiled.

title: Cooper Flagg’s new coach one of 3 first-timers in NBA this season
text:
Dusty May is new to the NBA. He’s not new to the NBA stage.
Thanks in large part to a Final Four run at Florida Atlantic in 2023 and leading Michigan to the NCAA title last season, May has coached plenty of big games in plenty of NBA arenas and knows what it’s like when those buildings are filled to the rafters.
And that means when he makes his regular-season debut as coach of Cooper Flagg and the Dallas Mavericks in a few days, May will have a real sense of what’s coming — at least from an surroundings standpoint.
“I’ve been in that environment,” May said. “Not at the level, obviously, but I’m someone who’s big on visualization. I see myself there. … But I have a real unique ability to, once the game starts, for 48 minutes to have 100% of my focus on the court and our bench.”
In other words, the coach of last season’s NCAA champion truly believes he’s ready for the NBA challenge. And he’s not alone, with six teams under new coaching management this season.
May is one of three first-time NBA coaches, along with Orlando’s Sean Sweeney (former San Antonio assistant) and Portland’s Micah Nori (former Minnesota assistant).
Another trio of coaches got new jobs in the league — former Memphis coach Taylor Jenkins has taken over in Milwaukee, former Orlando coach Jamahl Mosley has taken over in New Orleans, and former interim Portland coach Tiago Splitter (who coached for basically the entirety of last season) is the new coach in Chicago.
“I think just in general, the way we’re approaching things is, ‘What do we need to do today? Where are we at? How did we do with it? What do we need to improve on?’” Sweeney said. “We’ve done a good job of trying to set high standards for ourselves and lay down expectations for each other and live up to that.”
It is possible to win somewhere in Year 1 as a coach — just ask New York’s Mike Brown, who led the Knicks to last season’s NBA championship in his inaugural season on that team’s sideline. The coach of the reigning Western Conference champions, San Antonio’s Mitch Johnson, got to the finals in his second season as coach of the Spurs (which, technically, was his first full season as head coach).
Sweeney and Nori were widely considered as being ready to become head coaches for a few years before getting their current chances. May had taken two schools, one of them a mid-major, to the Final Four in a four-season span, more than proving his ability to win. Splitter did such a good job under awkward circumstances in Portland last season that he was a coach of the year candidate, and both Jenkins and Mosley had some success at their previous stops.
Nori essentially accepted a one-year contract with the Trail Blazers, an extremely rare move, especially for a first-time head coach. He’s betting on himself, saying that if he does the job, the options for future seasons on the existing contract will take care of itself.
“I’ve been around a lot of — I think it’s 13 — head coaches, so you start to see what you would do and what you’d like to do,” Nori said. “I guess the biggest difference, and they always talk about sliding over that one seat, is that it ends with you. … It’s your program now. That’s been the biggest adjustment.”
Mosley was living in Florida a few months ago, never thinking he’d be in Louisiana now. But when the Magic decided to change coaches, the Pelicans didn’t wait long before pouncing — knowing that Mosley would be a hot commodity. And Mosley says a change of scenery gave him an opportunity for what essentially is a reawakening.
“You get to do a lot of reflecting quick, right? You get to see exactly what worked, what didn’t work, how you can balance out what you do, the roster you have, you get to reflect on a lot of things that were successful and things that you need to work on,” Mosley said. “That’s what it gave me. And now look at the group of guys that we have here — young, energetic, wanting to learn, wanting to figure it out, hungry to get better. There’s so much of it here that it’s easy to pour into an organization like this.”

title: Stampede at Hindu festival in India kills 19
text:
Stampede at a popular Hindu festival in eastern India kills 19
A stampede during a major Hindu festival in eastern India’s West Bengal state has left at least 19 people dead, officials said Sunday.
The stampede in the state capital of Kolkata happened Saturday night when a crowd near a pavilion ran for cover as it began raining during Durga Puja, an annual Hindu festival celebrating the goddess Durga. According to police, some worshippers fell on the road, triggering the stampede.
Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, who visited Kolkata Medical College and Hospital where victims were taken, said 19 people had died and 25 were receiving treatment. He announced an investigation by a Special Investigation Team to be headed by a judge of the state’s High Court.
Police detained some pavilion organizers, private security personnel and on-duty staff, and launched a probe into any crowd-control and safety lapses.
Around 3,500 Durga Puja pavilions, known locally as pandals, have been set up across Kolkata for the festival. Following the stampede, authorities advised several of Kolkata’s most heavily attended venues to temporarily close to visitors.
Crowd crushes are relatively common in India during religious festivals, as large crowds, sometimes in the millions, gather in confined areas with few safety or crowd control measures. In January of 2025, at least 30 people were killed as tens of thousands of Hindus rushed to bathe in a sacred river during the Maha Kumbh festival, the world’s largest religious gathering.
In 2013, pilgrims attending a Hindu festival at a temple in the central state of Madhya Pradesh panicked amid fears that a bridge would collapse. At least 115 people were crushed to death or drowned in the river below.

title: Obituary: Sidney H. Geller
text:
WATERVILLE – Sidney Herbert Geller, 89, of Waterville, Maine, passed away peacefully in his sleep on Oct. 15, 2026.
“Sid” was born in Portland on April 5, 1937, to Mary (nee Blumenthal) and Harry Geller. A proud Mainer, he was born and raised in Portland and spent his adult life living in Waterville. Upon retirement, he enjoyed winters in Boca Raton, Fla., and summers at “the camp” on East Pond in Oakland.
He graduated from Deering High School, attended Northeastern University, and earned his bachelor’s degree from Drake University. He later attended Boston University School of Law before earning his law degree from the University of Maine School of Law. True to his sense of humor, he always joked that he was never at the top of his class.
After passing the Maine Bar Exam, Sid moved to Waterville to pursue his career in law. He practiced law in Waterville for 63 years. Throughout his life, he remained deeply committed to giving back to his community. He was very philanthropic and particularly devoted to supporting his synagogue, Beth Israel in Waterville, and The Cedars in Portland.
Sidney was predeceased by his parents; his brother, Arnold; and many beloved aunts and uncles.
He is survived by his wife of 61 years, Elizabeth “Liz” Geller; his three sons, David, his wife Jenny of Waterville, Michael, his partner Clinton O’Dell of Rumford, R.I., and Stephen Geller of Cape Cod, Mass.; and his three grandchildren, Chloe Geller and her partner David Barre of York, and Ian and Ava Geller both of Waterville. He also leaves behind his beloved sisters-in-law Susan Goldberg and Barbara McPherson; along with many nieces, nephews, and cousins.
Sid leaves behind a legacy of family, community, loyalty, and laughter. He will be dearly missed and fondly remembered by all who had the privilege of knowing him.
A funeral will be held at the Levey Chapel in Portland, on Sunday, Oct. 18, at 12 p.m.
Visiting hours, Wednesday. Oct. 21, 1:30 to 4 p.m. and Shiva service at 6 p.m. at 50 Burleigh St., Waterville.
Memorial service, followed by a reception and shiva, Thursday, Oct. 22 at 1:30 p.m., Beth Israel Congregation, 291 Main St., Waterville.

title: Sunday Photos: October 18th, 2026
Despairing at wealth concentration in a ‘post-government’ world
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Having voted since 1968, I find my election cynicism at a demoralizing level this year.
It’s hard to point to one thing that has hardened my cynicism, but the obscene concentration of wealth tops my list.
Our version of capitalism has given Elon Musk personal wealth greater than the GDP of 174 nations, while 86 million live in poverty or near poverty. There are many ultra-wealthy not far behind him and, with the carte blanche of Citizens United, that wealth has exponentially increased influence. We are now in a “post-government” world, where wealthy oligarchs make the decisions regardless of electoral outcomes. Who do they answer to?
We witnessed an example of “post-government” recently when President Trump had the AI billionaires to the White House to discuss AI regulation. The solution? No regulation. Let the geniuses regulate themselves. The most threatening technology since the atom bomb. But trust them.
Herb Fox
Limerick

title: Obituary: Natalie Ann (Spinney) Murray
text:
FALMOUTH – Natalie Ann Spinney Murray died at home on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. She was creative, curious and kind all her life.
Natalie was born in Rochester, N.H. on Aug. 13, 1934 to Ernest O. and Ida L. (Cotton) Spinney. She grew up in North Wakefield, N.H.
Her schooling began in a one room schoolhouse in Wakefield, N.H. She graduated from Brewster Academy in Wolfeboro, N.H. in 1952. She studied nursing at the Eliot Hospital School of Nursing and graduated as an RN in 1955.
Natalie moved to Boston, Mass. with classmates and worked at the Beth Israel Hospital. Coming back to New Hampshire to help care for her mother, she worked at Huggins Hospital and a small nursing home, The Door Stop.
In 1960 she married David Murray and moved to Valhalla, N.Y. where she was on the nursing staff at Grasslands Hospital before moving back to Wolfeboro, N.H.
In 1962 they welcomed their daughter, Nancy Jane. After David joined the U.S. Air Force the family moved to Ohio, then San Antonio, Texas where they welcomed their son, John David in 1966. The family was stationed on several air bases, including Illinois, Arizona and Plattsburg, N.Y. before purchasing a home in Falmouth, Maine in 1971 where they have lived for the past 55 years. In 1991 they were thrilled to welcome their grandson, Andrew David Murray.
Natalie enjoyed many creative pursuits from embroidery, cake decorating and many handicrafts. One of her great passions was reading. She often had several books going at one time – one for waiting at appointments, one beside her bed and one for just enjoying.
Natalie joined the Maine Senior College at USM in 1997 which became the first Osher Lifelong Learning Institute (OLLI). She enjoyed learning writing, music, history, art, theater and poetry. It was there that she found her “poetic voice”. She was named the Maine Senior College Network Poet Laureate in 2012.
In 2014 her book “Lemon Drop Day” was published. It was the thrill of her life to know that her book is in the Library of Congress.
In 1985, for their twenty-fifth anniversary, David asked Natalie what she wanted to do. “Go to London”. That year they went to London and Scotland. They returned several times including in 2013 when they took their grandson, Andrew.
They also traveled to France, Italy, Spain. With OLLI they traveled to Greece, Ireland, Prague and four national parks in the western U.S. states. They enjoyed several cruises to Bermuda, the Caribbean and through the Panama Canal stopping in a few countries in Central and South America. During all the travels, Natalie loved learning about the history and art as well as the culture and food.
Natalie was predeceased by her parents; and older siblings, Leona McSorely of Anchorage, Alaska and her brother, Bruce Spinney of Wisconsin.
She is survived by her husband, David of 66 years; daughter Nancy, son John; grandson Andrew; and great-grandchildren Caellum, Zinnia, Maitreya and Veda.
A celebration of Natalie’s life will be held on Saturday Nov. 7 from 2 to 4 p.m. at Jones, Rich and Barnes Funeral Home.
Please visit http://www.jonesrichandbarnes.com to leave condolences for the Murray family and share a memory of Natalie.
In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to OLLI – Maine Senior College at University of Southern Maine.

Gorham man seriously burned when clothes catch fire
text:
An 84-year old Gorham man suffered serious burns Sunday afternoon when his clothing caught fire when he was burning paper on a stove.
The Gorham Fire Department was called to the incident on Barstow Road around 3 p.m., according to the Maine Department of Public Safety. First responders found the man with extensive burns on multiple areas of his body and then transported him to Maine Medical Center for treatment.
Investigators with the Maine State Fire Marshal’s Office have classified the incident as accidental, the department said in a release.
Officials with the fire marshal’s office stressed that people should exercise caution when burning paper or other items and to keep combustible items and clothing away from open flames or other heat sources.

title: Woman saves future husband’s life after they were both struck by lightning while hiking
text:
TOWN OF EAGLE, Wis. (WTMJ) - A Chicago woman had to revive her future husband with CPR twice after they were both struck by lightning during a hiking trip.
Nick Broderick brought his then-girlfriend, Eva Broderick, to the Kettle Moraine State Forest in Wisconsin for a 10-mile hike last August. They were about two miles from their car when the weather changed.
“The rain just kept getting heavier and heavier as a really big rainstorm,” Nick Broderick said.
With nowhere to take shelter, the couple kept moving forward, but Eva Broderick was worried.
“She turned to me and said, ‘Nick, what if we get struck by lightning?’” Nick Broderick said.
Minutes later, that’s exactly what happened.
The rescue
Nick Broderick heard a boom, and it was the last thing he remembers. Firefighters say the tree next to the couple took a direct lightning hit, and they were struck by the ground current.
“All I remember was being curled in a fetal position with my hands over my ears, screaming, I think, and feeling what can only be described as electricity in my feet,” Eva Broderick said. “I was curled into Nick, and I looked over. He was laying on his back, his eyes were half open, glazed over, and he was blue and not breathing.”
Eva Broderick called 911 and immediately started CPR, but she couldn’t tell rescue crews where they were because the cell signal kept dropping. She also couldn’t remember where they had entered the forest or which path they were on.
“It’s pinging out a mile, a mile and a half into the forest area, but it’s not very specific. We just took our best guess and tried to send people everywhere we could,” Palmyra Fire Rescue Assistant Chief Dan Schiller said.
It took 50 minutes for crews to reach the couple on foot. In that time, Eva Broderick had to revive her boyfriend twice.
“That’s not something that normally happens,” Schiller said.
The proposal
Nick Broderick was taken to the hospital, where he spent three days recovering. He still has some hearing loss in one ear and tendon issues from the strike.
After he was released from the hospital, Nick Broderick proposed. The couple got married this August.
“We wanted to rewrite August and make it a better month,” Nick Broderick said.
“I’ve made the joke quite a few times that he can’t leave me. I brought him back from death, so he’s kind of stuck,” Eva Broderick said.
She will be honored with the Lifesavers Award at the Palmyra Fire Department in the coming weeks for her bravery in saving her boyfriend.

title: Lewiston’s revered Virgin Mary medallion finds a ‘proper’ home
text:
LEWISTON — For nearly a hundred years, a large medallion of the Blessed Virgin Mary gazed down upon worshipers at St. Mary’s Church in the section of the city known as Little Canada.
The medallion was adored. Venerated. Revered.
“It was always there,” said Roger Caron, who was an altar server at the church in the mid-1960s. “It was beautiful. It was part of the church and it was part of us.”
And then for more than a decade, after the closing of St. Mary’s at 46 Cedar St. in 2000, the Blessed Virgin gazed down upon comedians cracking off-color jokes, Halloween parties, Broadway shows, rock bands and a host of other events that were decidedly non-Catholic in nature.
The events were being offered by the Franco American Heritage Center, which had taken over the church, and it was generally agreed that the Mother Mary, known officially as Our Lady of Perpetual Help, was out of place.
“Groups would come in from out of town,” said Paul Dube, whose late wife, Rita, took an interest in the medallion. “They were non-Catholic groups and they didn’t want that statue up there. Rita had a nice curtain that could be lowered over it when there was one of those groups coming in.”
The thought of the Blessed Mother being concealed in such a manner was appalling to some, including Rita, who was a founding member of the Franco Center board.
Almost everybody agreed that the grand medallion, carved of wood and roughly 5 feet tall and 3 feet wide, should be taken down from the spot it had occupied since St. Mary’s was built in the early 1900s.
But what to do with such a magnificent statue of such a sacred religious figure?
One member of the Franco board thought it should be taken down and shipped to a mission in Haiti.
“Rita was totally against that,” Paul said. The medallion “was part of the church; part of the history. She fought that for a year and won.”
Eventually Elaine Roop, then board president of what had become the Franco Center, reached out to the Very Rev. Daniel Greenleaf, pastor of the Prince of Peace Parish, to see if he was interested in taking possession of the medallion.
He was. Very interested, as it turns out.
“It was such a significant piece for the people who went to Mass down in Little Canada,” said Greenleaf, whose Prince of Peace Parish includes the Basilica of Saints Peter and Paul on Ash Street in Lewiston. “It was a central piece of the church. And so we had some discussions and I said, ‘We’ll take it.’”
The rest of the congregation felt the same. The medallion needed to be preserved no matter what it took.
“We said, ‘We will not let this thing go to waste,’” said Caron, a longtime parishioner at St. Mary’s and now the basilica. “‘We will not have it destroyed or cut into pieces. Somehow, we’re going to preserve it and find a place for it.”
And the will of those people was strong enough to see the matter through. In 2022, the medallion was moved out of the former St. Mary’s Church and brought to the basilica.
Not that it was as simple as it sounds.
‘Awe-inspiring’‘
The medallion is estimated to weigh at least 500 pounds. Moving it was delicate work and required special equipment.
Since then, the medallion has been propped on saw horses while awaiting its new home in the basilica’s chapel. That’s another five years of strange history for The Blessed Virgin, but that part is almost over.
On Wednesday, the medallion will be on full display in the chapel, placed lovingly within an altar hand carved by 22-year-old Dave Madore, of Gray, the same carpenter who carved an altar for a Nativity scene brought from The Holy Land in 2023 by Greenleaf and a group of his parishioners. Madore, who is a member of the parish, produced the ornate table in front of the medallion as well as the reredos — the ornamental wooden wall that displays the medallion.
And on that same Wednesday, the Most Rev. James Ruggieri, bishop of the Diocese of Portland, will be at the basilica to consecrate the medallion — a Catholic service in which the statue will be deemed holy.
After that, at 6 p.m., the altar and its medallion will be presiding over Mass in the basilica’s lower chapel, with the Blessed Virgin Mary once again gazing down upon those who adore her.
“I got a sneak peak of it last week,” said Caron. “And I was just taken aback by how beautiful it looked, and how awe-inspiring. It’s a perfect fit for the chapel. It’s going to be a great addition to the basilica, and the history of St. Mary’s is going to be maintained and preserved.”
The chapel wall needed to be reinforced to accept the weight of the medallion, but everybody involved in the process considers it a labor of the very deepest kind of love.
“Placing the Blessed Virgin medallion from the former St. Mary’s Church in the refurbished lower chapel of the basilica,” said parishioner Maura Murphy, “shows us where the past, present and future of Lewiston’s Catholic and cultural heritage come together in a most meaningful, lovely way.”
Origins unknown
The medallion features the carved figure of Mother Mary cradling a baby Jesus. The precise history of the piece is elusive — most of those familiar with it only know that it was part of St. Mary’s Church from the very beginning.
Construction of the church began 1907 and wasn’t completed until 20 years later, with worshipers gathering in a basement for services in the years between.
St. Mary’s had been established after the Saints Peter and Paul Parish was divided in 1907 to accommodate the quickly growing French-speaking mill-worker population. Located at the corner of Cedar and Oxford streets, the church would eventually become a cornerstone of the city’s Franco-American “Little Canada” neighborhood.
And the Blessed Virgin was the centerpiece of the church.
In 1930, a Boston newspaper published a photo of St. Mary’s and deemed it the most beautiful Church in New England. Until the day it closed in 2000, St. Mary’s continued to hold Masses in English and French.
The Norman-Gotchic-style church was designed by a pair of architects from Boston, according to historical sources. It is generally presumed that they also commissioned the creation of the grand medallion that became such an integral part of worship at St. Mary’s.
But who created the iconic medallion of Our Lady of Perpetual Help? Was it some studio, individual or an active member of the architectural firm O’Connell & Shaw?
Those details seem lost to history. But those who have adored the medallion for years are plenty happy that the Virgin Mother has a new home that is properly suited for her.
In fact, for some, the storied medallion features prominently in the best of their earliest memories.
“It had a lot of effect on me as a Franco-American boy growing up in Lewiston,” said Caron.
Elaine Roop, who spent 15 years trying to get the medallion into a proper home, said in a 2022 interview that it had always bothered her that the Virgin Mother had to be covered with a curtain for certain events at the Franco Center.
“It was such an important thing for me to see that she received the respect so rightfully deserved,” Roop said. “I wanted to find a proper place for her, not just some afterthought.
“I have been waiting for this moment,” she said, “since I made a promise to Mary that I would find her a proper place.”

title: Consumer apprehension grows as US retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
U.S. consumers aren’t just frustrated with high prices. They’re angry and confused about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting those prices.
Digital price tags are rapidly replacing paper ones in grocery aisles. Artificial intelligence tools help businesses decide what to charge by predicting how customers might respond. Terms like “dynamic pricing” and “surveillance pricing” are stirring anxiety on social media, where users wonder if different people are getting different prices for the same product.
Americans have grown accustomed to changing prices when booking flights, hotel rooms and rides, but the prospect of everyday spending shaped by algorithms they don’t understand and personal data they may not realize they’re sharing has touched a nerve.
“There are major tensions happening right now between who’s really going to have the power with some of these algorithms and usage of bots and AI: the companies or the shopper,” said Katie Thomas, who leads an internal consumer behavior think tank at the management consulting firm Kearney.
Companies using the technology say some concerns stem from misconceptions about how their pricing tools work. Walmart CEO John Furner said in a blog post last month that digital price tags save workers’ time and keep prices up to date. He said the labels aren’t used to raise prices based on the weather, time of day or individual shopper.
“We price the product, not the person,” Furner wrote.
But companies aren’t always transparent about the customer data they collect and how it’s used, which has made consumers suspicious and led to speculation. For example, social media posts falsely imply that electronic shelf labels Walmart plans to put in all its U.S. stores scan shoppers’ faces or cellphones to set individualized prices, Thomas said.
Lawmakers and regulators are taking action. Legislators in at least 30 states have considered pricing bills this year, including measures addressing algorithmic and personalized pricing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
The Federal Trade Commission has proposed an enforcement policy warning businesses that failing to disclose their use of personal data to set individualized prices could violate consumer protection law.
Here are some of the pricing practices and technologies drawing scrutiny.
Dynamic pricing can raise and lower prices
What it is: Dynamic pricing means adjusting prices in response to changing market conditions, including supply and demand. An airline that adjusts ticket prices as departures approach is using dynamic pricing. Uber’s practice of lifting fares when demand outstrips the supply of available drivers, such as during rush hour, is a type of dynamic pricing known as surge pricing.
Why it matters: Frequent price changes extend well beyond food. Decodo, a web data company, tracked price changes in 2025 across products ranging from electronics to clothing and home improvement supplies. About half the U.S. changes it recorded were decreases, contrary to consumers’ assumptions that dynamic pricing only raises prices, said Gabriele Vitke, a senior product marketing manager.
Digital price labels are coming to more US stores
What they are: Digital displays that let stores update shelf prices electronically instead of replacing paper tags.
Why it matters: Digital price labels, long used in Europe and Asia, are drawing more attention as they spread to major U.S. retailers like Walmart and Whole Foods. Consumer advocates have argued that digital labels could eventually be used for surge pricing or personalized pricing. Labor unions also have opposed the technology.
The electronic shelf labels make frequent changes easier but don’t necessarily lead to higher prices during periods of strong demand. Retailers typically update electronic shelf prices on a regular schedule, often weekly, because shoppers value consistency, said Asa Farquhar of Relex Solutions, a retail technology company. Researchers who tracked prices at an unnamed grocery chain found “virtually no surge pricing” after the labels were introduced.
“Changing prices throughout the day, the way airlines or rideshare apps do, is exceedingly rare in grocery and general merchandise today,” Farquhar said.
Personalized pricing, also called surveillance pricing, draws on customer data
What it is: Personalized pricing means offering customers different prices and discounts based on their locations, incomes, web-browsing habits and other information about individuals or groups of shoppers. Some advocacy groups and regulators use the term “surveillance pricing” for the same practice.
Why it matters: It’s unclear how widely businesses use personal information to customize prices. An FTC staff report released in January 2025 found that intermediaries offering tools that can tailor prices and promotions worked with at least 250 clients, including grocery and clothing retailers.
Lawmakers in Maryland, New Jersey and Connecticut recently enacted restrictions on using shoppers’ personal data to determine what they pay. The Maryland and New Jersey laws focus on groceries, with exceptions for certain loyalty discounts and other promotional offers. Connecticut’s legislation covers a broader range of retail purchases.
California prosecutors sued Target in 2022, alleging that the retailer’s app displayed lower prices before shoppers entered stores and raised them once they were inside.
Target agreed to a $5 million settlement and a ban on using so-called geofencing technology to increase prices.
Target said the app functionality at issue was used to “provide guests with accurate pricing, which can vary across stores and channels.” The retailer said it didn’t personalize prices based on a guest’s data or behavior and remains “committed to clear, transparent pricing.”
Different prices do not necessarily mean personal data was used. Last year, an investigation by Consumer Reports, Groundwork Collaborative and More Perfect Union found that shoppers on Instacart were shown different prices for identical products at the same stores. Instacart subsequently ended what it described as tests that randomly assigned shoppers to groups rather than setting prices based on their personal information.
Algorithmic pricing gets an assist from AI
What it is: Algorithmic pricing uses software to recommend or automatically set prices. Companies have used such systems for decades. AI can help the software identify patterns in sales, competitors’ prices and other information to predict demand and estimate how different prices would affect sales and profits. These tools can support both dynamic and personalized pricing.
Why it matters: It’s unclear how widely retailers use AI to help set prices, but research suggests businesses across industries are adopting it.
Simon-Kucher, a global consulting company, surveyed more than 2,200 business leaders in 28 countries and 39 industries last year, and 41% said they used AI software to gather market intelligence, including competitors’ prices. Another 28% said they used it for “real-time price optimization.” Price optimization means choosing prices that advance business goals, such as increasing profits, attracting shoppers or clearing unsold goods.
The National Retail Federation, which represents big and small stores, said algorithmic pricing is a new method of doing what retailers have always done: monitor and adjust prices depending on supply, demand, seasonality, competitors’ prices and other factors.
Some lawsuits have alleged companies used pricing algorithms to undermine competition.
A 2023 anti-monopoly lawsuit the FTC brought against Amazon challenged, among other practices, an algorithmic tool codenamed Project Nessie. The agency alleged Amazon used the tool to identify products whose prices it could raise with competitors likely to follow, generating more than $1 billion in excess profits.
A trial is scheduled for next year. Amazon said the FTC allegations “grossly mischaracterize” the pricing tool.
Project Nessie was intended to stop retail price-matching practices from creating unsustainably low prices, the e-commerce giant said. Amazon said it tested the tool for a few years but it didn’t work as intended and was scrapped before the federal agency’s lawsuit.
A recent consumer lawsuit against McDonald’s alleged that its pricing system use nonpublic sales data from competing locations to coordinate prices. The Chicago-based burger giant said the lawsuit was “filled with inaccuracies” and that the company makes the tool available to U.S. franchisees to help them set prices at their individual restaurants.

title: Week Ahead in Washington: Week of October 18
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance are campaigning across the country this week as Election Day approaches on Tuesday, November 3.
Trump will visit a new state each day as he campaigns for Republicans in key races. He holds a rally in Kansas on Monday before traveling to North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa and Florida by the end of the week.
Each stop represents an opportunity for Trump to hold a rally - campaigning for a continued Republican majority in Congress.
Trump is also scheduled to campaign next weekend in Georgia and Michigan, both states Democrats are targeting in hopes of a blue wave this election.
Vance will campaign separately, with a stop in Hendersonville, North Carolina, on Monday before traveling to Nebraska on Thursday.
The campaign push comes just over two weeks before Election Day, when control of Congress will be decided.
According to the latest polls, Democrats hold an edge over Republicans to become the majority party, a potential loss for the White House as Trump enters his final two years in office.

title: Maine Witch Walk’s annual costume walk and goblin market at Bangor Waterfront Park
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Maine Witch Walk held its annual costumed walk and Goblin Market at Bangor Waterfront Park today.
The event featured a vender market, food truck, and dance circle, along with a one-mile walk where participants could show off their witch-inspired costumes.
Vendors had a range of goods for sale, from original prints to fortune-telling sessions.
“This is my first year at this event. I’ve been tabling in general for about two or three years now, but I’ve been making art like my whole life.” said Clover, a vender at the Goblin Market.
“I practice witchcraft myself, so I’ve always felt connected to the witch community, and I feel like it just attracts a lot of people with similar views and just like weirdos like me,” said Clover.
The Witch walk has something for everyone, and you don’t have to consider yourself a witch to enjoy dancing, food, and original art.
To learn more about the event, visit www.mainewitchwalk.com

title: Visitors track down the perfect pumpkin at Seashore Trolley Museum
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
KENNEBUNKPORT — The wheels of a 125-year-old wooden trolley grated and scraped against aged tracks, skating along the heritage railway under a canopy of vibrant yellow and orange trees.
Don Stephenson turned the brakes and reached down to yank the pull cord of a yellow 1901 J.G. Brill Company streetcar — the Connecticut Co. 303. The car let out two loud hoots and lurched to a stop beside a small pumpkin patch at the Seashore Trolley Museum.
Dozens of visitors, some dressed in Halloween costumes, hopped off the trolley and dashed toward the pumpkins, ready to choose the best ones at the 28th annual Pumpkin Patch Trolley event on Sunday.
“It never gets boring,” Stephenson said, leaning on the rails of a streetcar he’s been operating for the last 40 years. “I mean, how many people can say they ran a 125-year-old trolley?”
The Seashore Trolley Museum hosts similar events year-round, attracting thousands of visitors. The proceeds help fundraise for the museum and give visitors a fun way to take in a slice of history, Executive Director Katie Orlando said.
The pumpkin patch trolley rides are a precursor to Trolleyween; the museum’s Halloween festival and its way of celebrating the end of its operating season. Guests come dressed in all sorts of costumes, from a family full of “Wizard of Oz” characters to kids dressed as hot dogs.
“We usually have kids dress up as the trolley,” Orlando laughed. “Either they or an adult paints the trolley on a box and they wear it with suspenders.”
When the Connecticut Co. 303 arrived back at the station, two tiny fairies fluttered off toward a pumpkin painting station. Trailing behind them were Peter Pan, Captain Hook and Tinker Bell.
“We dress up every year,” Tinker Bell — or the fairies’ mom Lauren Reidmann — said. “We were on the lookout for a place where everyone dresses up to have fun with our family.”
The pumpkin patch trolley was the perfect opportunity for Reidmann’s family to take their costumes out for a trial run before the big day. Later, she and her fairies will be in the running against a family of “Where’s Waldos” for a costume contest and an opportunity to win a free family membership at the museum.
Events like the pumpkin patch keep the place running. With more than 250 historic streetcars, cranes, wagons and other vehicles, upkeep gets expensive. Most of them are donated or “rescued,” Stephenson said, and preserving them is a constant task.
After a slow start to the season, Orlando wasn’t sure the museum would hit budget goals or surpass the 4,900 guests it hosted last year. She hypothesized that unstable economic conditions in recent years made it harder for members and visitors to contribute to the museum.
“We were really nervous because if we don’t hit budget goals with our admissions, that means we have to solicit additional donations from our donors,” Orlando said “Which, if they’re struggling too, it’s kind of a hard ask.
But by the fourth weekend of trolley season, the museum had already welcomed north of 6,000 attendees — a new record.
“Our guests this year have been incredible,” Orlando smiled.
Stephenson is also pleased with the turnout this year. He said he’s normally on the lookout for people that seem like they could be good trolley conductors, which he recognizes is a niche job. At the museum, it’s also a volunteer position.
“We we keep losing our volunteers to attrition and age and everything else,” Stephenson said. But it’s events like the pumpkin patch and Trolleyween that give him the opportunity to inspire the next generation of conductors.
Stephenson said by the time Trolleyween ends, he’s pretty exhausted. He operates hundreds of rides each season and has been for 30 years. He’s looking forward to a break, but he knows that feeling won’t last long.
“I get an itch at the end of December,” he smiled.

Martin's Point is discontinuing certain Medicare Advantage plans in Maine for plan year 2027.
Two viewers reached out to Maine's Total Coverage saying they had received letters from Martin's Point notifying them that their Medicare plan would not be offered in 2027. Both letters state their plans will expire on Dec. 31, 2026, and that they will have to switch to a different plan.
In a statement to Maine's Total Coverage, Martin's Point said it is changing its Medicare Advantage plan offerings.
"Each year, Medicare Advantage organizations evaluate their plan offerings and submit plans to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) for approval. As part of this annual process, organizations may discontinue certain plans and introduce new plans," according to a Martin's Point spokesperson.
The healthcare provider said it is discontinuing certain plans and introducing new plans in their place. It also clarified it will continue to offer plans in every county in Maine. Martin's Point said all current members have been notified of the changes and that it will work directly with those affected.

title: Death Notice: Ruth Eleanor (Phinney) Gurney
Bangor community programs team up for weekly park cleanups
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A grassroots effort in Bangor is working every weekend to help clean up trash and properly dispose of syringes.
Since August, more than a dozen volunteers have met up at Needlepoint Sanctuary at 1009 Ohio St. every Sunday before heading out to areas in Bangor in order to clean up trash and sharps.
During their 12th weekend of activity, volunteers took to cleaning Coe Park.
“As we clean up the parks, we make sure that our volunteers are all well-educated on sharp safety. We use our provided sharps containers here. All of the sharps that we find, including broken glass and things like that, might be dangerous to the public,” Wyatt Worster, Program Administrator with Needlepoint Sanctuary.
The weekly clean ups are a collaborative effort between Needlepoint Sanctuary, a syringe service program, and the volunteer led Quality of Life Maine.
“The four goals right now of Quality of Life Maine are to facilitate compassionate outreach to the unhoused, to pick up litter in public spaces, to reduce the stigma surrounding the issue of homelessness, and to be a part of the solution in Bangor,” said Program Director Bryce Badger
Badger, who founded Quality of Life Maine in April, started the organization to help out the Bangor community and to be part of a solution to Bangor’s struggle with homelessness.
“I was volunteering at a food bank, and they’re like, you can take two bags of food home with you. Well, I’m not food insecure, so I don’t think I need to. But then I was like, well, maybe I could find somebody who could use them,” said Badger, “That’s how it kind of started, by getting those two free bags of food for volunteering at the food bank.”
What started as a single idea has evolved into collaborative weekly clean-ups that allow many volunteers to get involved.
“I got more involved because I wanted to clean up my city and fight the narrative that’s been really been spreading at City Hall from some people, and just giving back and cleaning up my community,” said volunteer Adam Baker.
Organizers say that when winter arrives, the weekly clean ups will transition into an outreach program to help people get warm. Worster also says the series of events also helps to spread the word on other local resources.
“Unfortunately, I don’t think that there’s enough talk around the town of how important and how accessible these resources are. I wish that we could kind of like branch out a little bit more and get the community more involved and get the word spread. There’s the Mabel Wadsworth Center, there’s Maine Family Planning, there’s Wabanaki (Public Health),” said Worster.
Volunteers meet every Sunday at 11:30 a.m. at Needlepoint Sanctuary at 1009 Ohio St. You can learn more by visiting Quality Life of Maine and Needlepoint Sanctuary by visiting their social media pages.

title: Rangeley to explore snowmobile club park-and-ride
text:
The town of Rangeley will consider working with the Rangeley Snowmobile Club to construct a parking lot on Loon Lake Road, which would alleviate the strain on the downtown in winter.
Club member Dana Bowman and Brent West of the High Peaks Alliance presented updated information about the project to the board at an Oct. 5 meeting.
Rangeley Snowmobile Club applied for a $175,000 Maine Trail Bond grant to cover the construction of the park-and-ride, which would be up to two acres.
The club originally sought to use the funds to build a lot on Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust Land off Route 17, but wetlands there prevented the project from moving forward. They are now seeking a lot on town property next to the club’s groomer barn near the transfer station.
West said a new lot, for both vehicles and snowmobiles, would reduce strain on the five parking options in Rangeley, Oquossoc and Sandy River Plantation. He pointed to large trucks and trailers clogging up the downtown lots, as well as the unsanctioned parking on Morton Cutoff Road, as reasons for the request.
“This is trying to address some of those downtown problems,” West told the board.
A resident asked if the proposed space could impact future transfer station needs. Town Manager Joe Roach said there is cleared space within the 100-acre lot that would better suit any future expansion.
“I think we could reinvent the area that’s already cleared and make it more efficient,” Roach said. “That’s always been my vision for it. I don’t think you need more land there. I think the section next to the groomer barn is probably the best piece of land there because it does abut them.”
Bowman said that the club would be flexible to the town’s preference for ownership and upkeep, saying that either way, they would take care of the winter maintenance.
“We’d be willing to do the lease part of it,” he said. “Or if the town wanted to own the parking lot and we still did the maintenance, we wouldn’t have an issue with that either.”
West said he would like the construction completed by the end of 2027. Taking longer could impact the club’s ability to receive future grants.
The board voted unanimously to allow the town manager to send the grant to the town attorney and to draft a memorandum of understanding for review, not final approval. Members of the board also requested a site visit for this fall.

title: 84-year-old Gorham man seriously burned after clothing catches fire, officials say
text:
GORHAM, Maine (WABI) - An 84-year-old man suffered serious burn injuries Sunday afternoon in what investigators say was an accidental fire, according to the Maine State Fire Marshal’s Office.
The Gorham Fire Department responded to a house on Barstow Road around 3 p.m. after receiving a report of a man with burns.
Responders found the man with extensive burns to multiple areas of his body. He was transported to Maine Medical Center for treatment.
A preliminary investigation indicates the man was burning paper on a stove when his clothing caught fire.
The Fire Marshal’s Office reminds residents to use caution when burning paper or other materials and to keep combustible items and clothing away from open flames and heat sources.

title: Shopping in Freeport? Stop by the Camp Sunshine Pumpkin Festival
text:
Thousands of pumpkins on display as the Camp Sunshine Pumpkin Festival expands to three days
The festival will be open at L.L. Bean's Flagship store from noon to 8 p.m. on Sunday
Thousands of pumpkins on display as the Camp Sunshine Pumpkin Festival expands to three days
The festival will be open at L.L. Bean's Flagship store from noon to 8 p.m. on Sunday
This year, the Camp Sunshine Pumpkin Festival has expanded to three days, fitting in more live entertainment and activities to help raise money for the programming they provide to families with children facing life-threatening illnesses.
The event takes place on the campus of L.L. Bean's flagship store. More than 5,000 pumpkins are on display, including "glow heart pumpkins," which get displayed in a tower. A heart shape is carved out of the pumpkins, and each one is in honor of or in memory of a loved one. Schools helped to carve out the rest of the pumpkins on campus and each pumpkin featured a unique design.
The festival starts at noon and goes until 8 p.m. People can take home uncarved pumpkins for free, play mini golf, and eat at several different food trucks that will be parked.
One of the new events is The Pumpkin Festival Flannel 5K & Fun Run. It's taking place at Mast Landing School at noon. Registration is available online or in person and is $50. There is also a virtual option for people who aren't able to make it in-person.
While the festival is free, donations are encouraged. All of the money raised supports Camp Sunshine's mission to provide free sessions at its camp in Sebago Lake. Children that are facing life-threatening illnesses are invited to come with their families. This year, the goal is to reach $160,000 through the Pumpkin Festival. As of Sunday morning, $120,000 had been raised.

title: Blaze at St Petersburg oil sites as Kyiv launches more than 1,000 drones at Russia
text:
(AP) - Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war.
The strikes came as tensions between Kyiv and Washington deepened, with U.S. President Donald Trump criticizing Kyiv’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure and the prospect of further U.S. sanctions against Moscow still uncertain.
Trump said Sunday that he decided to hold off on implementing new sanctions on Russia because he doesn’t “want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.”
In a social media post, the U.S. president defended his Friday order to issue a waiver to prevent new sanctions from being placed on Moscow from bipartisan criticism that he was favoring Russian President Vladimir Putin’s interests over those of Ukraine. Trump said he believed new sanctions would undermine negotiations to bring about a diplomatic end to the war in Ukraine.
“I can sign it later, or any time that I want!” Trump added of the sanctions.
Trump also lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has been critical of Trump’s recent outreach to Putin, for launching strikes on Russian energy infrastructure during the conflict, claiming Zelenskyy “doesn’t want to end this war.”
Zelenskyy: Waiving sanctions strengthens Russia
Speaking on NBC’s “Meet the Press” earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy said waiving sanctions against Russia would strengthen Putin’s war effort. He also said U.S.-Ukraine intelligence sharing had resumed after being “blocked for some period of time.”
Zelenskyy said that while he trusted Trump, siding with Moscow would be a tragedy and a “historic mistake” for Washington.
“People want to forget what’s going on. But we can’t give this possibility to forget, or to change reality, or to change the truth,” Zelenskyy said. “We can’t compare me and Putin. He’s (an) aggressor. He occupied us. He killed adults and children, his soldiers. He’s a terrorist. And that’s why I hope that President Trump will be very clear with this position.”
Later Sunday, Zelenskyy said on social media that he had spoken with U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the results of an Oct. 9 meeting between U.S. and Ukrainian negotiating teams in Miami, as well as “next steps in diplomacy.”
Two killed as Russia and Ukraine trade blows
One person was killed and five others were wounded in the St. Petersburg attack, which sparked fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot, local Gov. Alexander Beglov said. A logistics center belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data center operated by Russian tech giant VK were also targeted, the companies confirmed.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency Tass that Kyiv was “resisting” Moscow’s invasion but could not “change the current course of events.”
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a woman was killed and a 6-year-old girl was among at least two other people wounded in two Russian attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said Sunday.
Russia continues energy attacks, Kyiv says
Trump announced on Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” in the 4½-year-old war, but offered no details. Kyiv reported Russian attacks on energy sites continued after Trump’s announcement, and on Thursday said it had resumed strikes on Russian oil facilities after a three-day pause.
Zelenskyy wrote on X on Sunday that Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times in the week since Trump’s announcement. The Ukrainian government initially said it was observing the ceasefire.
Energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions were struck overnight, leaving tens of thousands of families without power, he said, accusing Russia of trying to cause a blackout.
“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting,” the Ukrainian president wrote.
Ukraine apology to Lithuania over drone alert
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry apologized on Sunday after a drone entered Lithuania’s airspace, prompting authorities to issue an air raid warning.
Russian electronic warfare may have diverted the drone during a Ukrainian operation against legitimate military targets in Russia, ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said in a statement.
Lithuanian authorities urged residents in two northern counties along the Latvian border to take cover early Sunday because of a possible drone incursion, public broadcaster LRT reported.
A drone entered the northern Pasvalys region and damaged a moving car, LRT said, citing Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Center. No injuries were reported.

title: Man critically injured in multi-vehicle crash on Maine Turnpike in Falmouth
text:
FALMOUTH, Maine (WABI) - A man was critically injured after a crash on the Maine Turnpike in Falmouth overnight, according to Maine State Police.
