title: Obituary: Danny Scott Goddard
text:
LEWISTON – Danny Scott Goddard, also known as “Digger Dan,” passed away at 10 a.m., on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026, in Lewiston, surrounded by his loved ones. He was born on Dec. 10, 1960, to Milton Goddard and Alberta Perry of Auburn.
Danny leaves behind his loving wife, Lanette Goddard of Lewiston; his daughter, Sarah Krias and her husband John, of Turner, his son, Craig Goddard and his wife, Megan, of Turner, and his stepdaughter, Alanna Elwell and her husband, Thomas, of Auburn. He is also survived by his sister, Lisa Kaulbach, of Dixfield; and the mother of his children, Susan Goddard, of Lewiston.
Danny was a proud grandfather to Leo Goddard of Topsham, his firstborn grandson, and Jackson and Camden Goddard of Turner, whom he loved dearly. He also cherished his newest grandbaby, 2-year-old Miles Elwell of Auburn, whom he called “Boo-Boo.” His family also included six grand-dogs who adored him, along with his own fur babies, Jo Jo and Maxx, the cats who loved their dad. He is also survived by several nieces, nephews; aunts, uncles; and cousins; as well as his longtime close friend, Turk; and his brother-in-law, Kevin Mabry, of Auburn.
Danny was a well-liked man who made friends wherever he went. He enjoyed road trips, spending time by the ocean, drinking Pepsi, and listening to music, especially watching live concert DVDs. In his younger years, he also enjoyed being a DJ.
Danny had a special connection with animals. He was truly an animal whisperer, and it seemed that every animal he met was naturally drawn to him.
A true salesman through and through, Danny could sell just about anything. Throughout his career, he sold everything from cars and mobile homes to medical equipment. He even sold quality meats out of his truck, which had a freezer in the back. His unforgettable sales pitch was, “You can beat my prices, but you can’t beat my meat!” That was Danny – always ready with a laugh and a memorable one-liner.
Above all, Danny believed in not taking life too seriously. His great laugh, quick wit, and larger-than-life personality brought joy to those around him. He had a way of making people smile, and those who knew him will forever remember the laughter, stories, and memories they shared with him.
Danny was predeceased by his parents, Milton and Alberta; his brother, Michael, his sister and friend, Sandra; and his brother from another mother, best friend, and cousin, Kenny, also known as “Toasty.”
Danny leaves behind a lifetime of memories, countless friendships, and a family who loved him dearly. His presence will be deeply missed, but his laughter, humor, and reminder to enjoy life will live on in the hearts of all who knew him.
A celebration of life will be held at 4 p.m., on Friday, Oct. 23 at the American Legion on Washington Street in Auburn. A full bar will be available. All those that plan to attend are encouraged to wear their favorite Boston sports gear or favorite band t-shirt.
In accordance with Danny’s wishes, he will be cremated.
Rest easy, Digger Dan. You will be forever loved, deeply missed, and never forgotten.

title: Growing up in Maine exposes the folly of party politics
text:
Jack Brogan of Freeport is studying political science at the University of Rhode Island.
This fall, I will vote in my first general election. Growing up in Maine has given me an unusual idea of politics.
We have an independent senator who caucuses with Democrats. We repeatedly reelected a Republican senator with support from voters who choose Democrats elsewhere on the ballot. This year, a former chairman of the Maine Republican Party is running for governor as an independent.
None of that seems strange to me. What seems stranger is the expectation that once I decide which party better represents me, an entire package of beliefs should follow. My positions on abortion, immigration, policing, climate change, guns and foreign policy are all supposed to become predictable from the letter beside the candidate I support.
I don’t think politics should work that way.
Political independence is often treated as an ideology somewhere between liberalism and conservatism: take the Democratic position, take the Republican position, split the difference and call yourself a moderate.
But that misunderstands independence. Political independence is not an ideology. It is a method of thinking.
Maine has provided plenty of examples. Sen. Angus King caucuses with Democrats because, as he explained when he entered the Senate, refusing to join either caucus would reduce his effectiveness. He also said that choice would not place him in “automatic opposition” to Republicans. His independence was never supposed to mean neutrality. It meant cooperation without ownership.
Susan Collins represents another version of Maine’s resistance to neat political categories. In 2020, Joe Biden won Maine while Collins also won statewide. In my previous op-ed (“The suburban trap: Why Troy Jackson’s path to victory runs through Scarborough, not Allagash,” Aug. 30) , I looked at those voters mainly as an electoral problem for Democrats.
But I have been thinking about them differently since then. Maybe there is something healthy about the fact that they exist.
Rick Bennett raises the same question. He chaired the Maine Republican Party before leaving it and running for governor as an independent. He has broken with Republicans on some issues while retaining positions rooted in his conservative background. Both parties have tried to define what Bennett “really” is.
Maybe both descriptions can contain some truth.
A former Republican can agree with Republicans on some things, Democrats on others, and decide neither party describes his politics well enough to belong to it.
Look at Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania. He remains a Democrat, but his breaks with the party on immigration and Israel have drawn criticism from fellow Democrats. The reaction raises a broader question: What does it mean to be a “big tent” party?
The public is less ideologically tidy than politics makes it appear. Someone can favor stronger unions and tougher enforcement against violent crime. Someone can support abortion rights and want a secure border.
Those voters are not confused. Our categories sometimes are.
Once politics becomes identity rather than judgment, disagreeing with your own side can feel less like changing your mind and more like betraying a group.
Maine has not escaped that trend. But our history is a reminder that things do not have to work that way.
King can caucus with Democrats without becoming one. Collins can win voters who reject Republican presidential candidates. Bennett can leave the Republican Party without automatically becoming a Democrat. Voters can do the same thing.
Independence does not mean every issue has two equally valid sides or that the answer always sits in the middle. Sometimes one party will make the better argument. It means reaching that conclusion yourself.
At 18, that is the kind of voter I want to become. I do not want voting for someone to mean inheriting every one of that candidate’s opinions, or recognizing a good argument from the other side to feel like disloyalty.
Maybe that is what Maine’s independent tradition is worth preserving: not a state without Democrats or Republicans, but a state where neither party owns the people who vote for it.

title: No Kings rallies urge voters to cast ballots early ahead of midterms
text:
No Kings rallies across US urge voters to cast ballots early ahead of midterms
Rallies organized by the No Kings network opposed to President Donald Trump were being held Saturday in cities and communities across the U.S., with an aim of getting people out to vote early in the midterm elections.
The hundreds of planned events were being billed as nonpartisan, though they sought to build on nearly two years' worth of No Kings marches and demonstrations by people upset with Trump's presidency.
A band entertained what appeared to be a few hundred people in caps and coats Saturday at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C. Despite the chilly weather, many in the crowd danced to the tunes. "VOTE EARLY" and "HANDS OFF MY VOTE!" were among the many signs held aloft.
At an Atlanta rally, City Councilman Michael Julian Bond told the crowd to urge others to vote ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.
"The Constitution gives you one power, right? That is the power to vote. Are you gonna use that power?" he asked.
"You don't see Superman giving up his power," Bond continued. "You don't see Black Panther giving up his power. You don't see Wonder Woman giving up her magic lasso. So why would you give up your right, your power, your obligation to vote? Be a superhero, use your power. Go to the polls and vote."
Trump has long been suspicious of mail voting, and has claimed without evidence that voting fraud cost him the 2020 presidential election.
His administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for the midterm elections from people whom the federal government has identified as "likely" noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.
On Friday, the Justice Department warned that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution.
Earlier Friday, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Dick Durbin, D-Ill., wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding that the Justice Department commit to not seizing ballots or other election materials before the midterm elections are certified.

title: Steelers-Saints Paris game remains scheduled despite civil unrest, NFL says
text:
Paris game between Steelers and Saints still on despite civil unrest, NFL says
The game in Paris between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints remains scheduled as planned despite civil unrest in the French capital, the NFL said Sunday.
The teams are set to play next Sunday at Stade de France in what would be the NFL's first regular-season game in Paris, where events are also planned for football fans during the week.
Related video above: Saints fans heading to Paris urged to prepare for travel delays and protests
Rioting and looting have taken place during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.
"Preparations continue as scheduled for NFL events and the game at Stade de France next Sunday," the league said in a statement Sunday.
"We continue to work closely with local authorities and partners on all operational and security matters. We are also providing the two clubs with regular updates. There's been no disruption or impact at league sites."
The Saints were scheduled to arrive in Paris early Monday. The Steelers travel later in the week.
Hundreds of protesters gathered again on Sunday at the Place de la République amid a heavy police presence. Officers used tear gas as tensions flared sporadically in the neighborhood.
Dislodged cobblestones and broken glass littered the area. Looting and damage were also reported in other tourist and shopping districts.
Paris police said 855 people were arrested in the capital region.
French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday voiced the public's "anger" and "shame" over the rioting and looting.

title: Missing the local touch from Maine hospitals
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I love the columns that Victoria Hugo-Vidal writes. And I agree with her all the time. Her piece on the quickly dropping obstetrics services in rural Maine (“Maine’s rural maternity wards require a mindset shift,” Oct. 4) sheds light on an issue that is disastrous for families and women in those areas.
The problem was created by hospitals being grabbed up by corporations and conglomerates. It seems now that every hospital or medical center is owned by others from away and managed by accountants for maximum profit.
It wasn’t always this way, of course. Not too many decades ago, hospitals were run locally. Communities would bond together to raise money for hospitals. There would be a board of directors comprised of local leaders. Maybe they would be run with a modest profit or loss. Community groups like Kiwanis, Rotary or Lions would raise funds. The annual golf tournament would support the hospital and there would be regular bake sales.
It’s probably unlikely we can go back to those days. But something has to give if our communities are not well served by competent medical facilities.
Brian Nickerson
South Portland

title: Death Notice: Pamela A. Boyden
Obituary: Jean Ellen Emmons
text:
PORTLAND – Jean Ellen Emmons, a beloved mother, grandmother, great-grandmother, sister, and friend, passed away on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, at the age of 91. Her life was filled with love, family, cherished traditions, and countless memories that will live on in the hearts of all who knew her.
A lifelong resident of Portland, Maine, Jean also enjoyed several wonderful years in Port Charlotte, Fla., where she made special memories with dear friends. In her final months, she was cared for by the wonderful team at Freeport Place Assisted Living, whose kindness and compassion brought comfort during this time. A special thank you to the staff at Northern Light Home Care and Hospice.
Jean’s own love story began at a dance at the Stevens Avenue Armory, where she met the love of her life, Carl. They danced the night away as though they had known each other forever. They married on Oct. 20, 1956, in Portland and honeymooned in the beautiful mountains of New Hampshire. Together, they built a life and a family, sharing 38 years of marriage until Carl’s passing on Aug. 31, 1994.
Their love was a special part of Jean’s life, and it is comforting to imagine them reunited in heaven, dancing together once more as their wedding anniversary approaches on Oct. 20. Some love stories never truly end; they simply wait for the day they can begin again.
Family was the heart of Jean’s world. Such a generous woman and a great role model, as she loved family and her faith.
Jean is survived by her beloved sister, Carol; her five children, Debbie, Mark, Diane, Kelley, and Jen; her 13 grandchildren, Joe, Michelle, Andrew, Crystal, Corey, Meredith, Austin, Melanie, Carlene, Benjamin, Meghan, Holly and Erin; and her 14 great-grandchildren, William, Nora, Mia, Sophia, Max, Landon, Jayce, Luca, Masha, Olivia, Leo, Madison, (with another soon to arrive) and Theo and Wesley.
Jean devoted much of her working life to Mercy Hospital in Portland, where she worked as an EKG technician. Mercy held a particularly special place in her heart, as it was also where she welcomed all five of her children into the world.
Beyond her family, Jean found happiness in the simple pleasures that made life special. She loved the ocean, especially Higgins Beach in Scarborough, where she could enjoy the beauty and peacefulness of the Maine coast. She looked forward to listening to the Boston Pops’ Fourth of July music, enjoyed the big band sounds she once danced to with Carl, and remained a devoted fan of the Boston Red Sox and Boston Celtics. She also loved a bowl of haddock chowder from DiMillo’s, a favorite that brought a little taste of home and happiness.
Rest peacefully, Mom. May you and Dad dance together again, just as you did that very first night. Until we meet again, you will forever be in our hearts.
Memorial services will be held on Nov. 5, from 11 a.m. to 12 p.m. at St. Pius X Catholic Church, 492 Ocean Ave. in Portland, followed by a burial at Forest City Cemetery at 12:30 p.m. in South Portland. A gathering of friends and family will follow at Bruno’s Restaurant on Allen Avenue in Portland.

title: Man, 19, accused of drugging, raping college student in her dorm room before she died
text:
NEW YORK (WABC) - A 19-year-old New York man is facing federal charges for allegedly drugging two college students with fentanyl and raping one of them in her dorm room before she died.
Moises Freire, 19, is accused of raping Annabel Richter, a student at New York’s Fashion Institute of Technology, after giving her fentanyl back in March. The drug killed Richter and nearly killed her friend.
The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration is investigating alongside the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York and the New York Police Department.
“They had no chance. It was such a high potent hit of fentanyl. It was immediate,” said Special Agent in Charge Christopher Roberts with the DEA’s New York Task Force Division.
According to a newly unsealed indictment, Freire allegedly conspired with 18-year-old Brian Peralta Cabrera – neither FIT students – to procure fentanyl that would “last the entire night.”
The two victims let Freire into their all-female dorms March 18, where he allegedly told them he had cocaine, but authorities say he knew it was “poison.” After ingesting the substance, both victims immediately lost consciousness, the indictment says.
“The fact that he [Freire] knew he was providing them poison and masked it and made believe it was cocaine [when] it was fentanyl, that’s what’s alarming in this case,” Roberts said.
Authorities say Freire raped Richter while she unconscious and took photos of her that he sent to friends. He allegedly waited 45 minutes before alerting campus security, who administered Narcan to the victims.
Richter and her friend were taken to the hospital. The friend regained consciousness after lifesaving treatment, but tragically, Richter never woke up.
These details emerge as anger increases over Cornell University’s handling of an alleged gang rape involving drugs in 2024. Students at FIT feel angry and on edge, even as the university says it’s increasing its security presence and providing support resources.
“We come here to learn. Yeah, sure, there’s the student life aspect, but no one signs up for that to happen,” one FIT student said.
Both defendants pleaded not guilty to initial charges back in March and are still in federal custody. They face arraignment on the new charges later this month.

title: Gene therapy helps doctors restore hearing for children born deaf
text:
New gene therapy helps doctors restore hearing for children born deaf
A major medical triumph right here in Cincinnati: a new gene therapy is now giving some children born deaf the ability to hear.
One family seeing the benefits came all the way to Cincinnati from Central Asia.
Two young siblings were born with profound hearing loss caused by a genetic condition; a breakthrough at Cincinnati Children's is helping change their lives forever.
"I was literally at one of our outlying clinics, and this family came in with two cute and adorable kids and asked if I could help them hear," said Dr. John Greinwald, an otolaryngology attending at Cincinnati Children's.
Unable to get treatment back home for their two young children born deaf, this family from Uzbekistan researched options and found Greinwald in Cincinnati.
"Basically, looked me up, stalked me on the internet and saw that I'm an expert in the field of molecular genetics of deafness," Greinwald said.
Brother Abdu and sister Sumaya became patients in this breakthrough clinical trial.
Doctors here performed one of the world's first bilateral gene therapy injections.
Within weeks, both could hear without any implants or devices.
"This is groundbreaking. The genetic therapy is predicted to last a lifetime," Greinwald said.
Greinwald explaining their approach.
"The approach for this is very similar to a standard cochlear implant. We go from behind the ear through the bone, and we go down to the opening of the cochlea... And we dose them and give them a gene therapy product," Greinwald said. "There have been very, very few complications. And both of our patients did phenomenally well."
Not only did it work, but Greinwald also said the children's hearing shows signs of continued improvement.
"This has taken a village. This is hundreds of researchers working on this, hundreds of folks on the clinical side doing this kind of work. But it is a, it is kind of a medical miracle," Greinwald said.
It's important to know every case of hearing loss is different, and this treatment is only for a specific genetic condition.
However, Greinwald said he believes this breakthrough will lead to other gene therapies in our lifetime that could help treat a wide range of hearing loss.

title: Past dust explosions in Maine failed to spark change. Will Searsmont?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Nine years ago, in the small central Maine town of Detroit, a foreman climbed to the top of a high-capacity fertilizer silo at Northeast Agricultural Sales. It was early October. The harvest season had wound down, and he was scraping off the residual chemical crust with a metal shovel.
As the man worked, he struck an exposed electrical wire, according to a U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration report. The resulting spark was small, but it happened in a dark, tightly enclosed cylinder filled with suspended particles of micro-pulverized sulfur.
The cloud ignited, severely injuring the foreman, Anthony Tower, and two others, federal records show.
Corporate leadership said the disaster was a result of human error, claiming Tower violated internal safety protocols by taking a metal tool into a confined space. Federal safety inspectors, however, saw systemic problems and fined the company $48,000 for mishandling dust hazards.
The blast was a warning: when fine particulate matter — whether it’s chemical sulfur, pulverized grain, microscopic aluminum or sawdust — is suspended in an enclosed space, it ceases to be mere waste. It becomes an explosive vapor waiting for a spark.
In the decade that followed, Maine’s regulatory infrastructure operated as if the Detroit explosion had been an anomaly: the state didn’t start tracking how many facilities have dangerous amounts of combustible dust, instead relying on companies to self-report the hazard; it also didn’t address loopholes that left private industrial sites largely uninspected for dust risks. Meanwhile, federal safety inspectors lacked a comprehensive standard and managed dust-related problems through reactive, piecemeal citations.
On May 15, those regulatory gaps culminated in another disaster, this time at a pine mill in Searsmont. There, on the grounds of Robbins Lumber, stood a concrete and steel silo designed to store kiln-dried sawdust and wood shavings.
When volunteer firefighters arrived at the mill that morning, they were responding to a routine call of a smoldering fire near the base of the silo, where workers bagged wood shavings. The crew directed a steady stream of water into the lower hatch, a tactic that had worked on previous small fires in the facility’s top-vented silo, according to an investigation by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health.
This particular silo, a used Harvestore installed in 1993, was an airtight, oxygen-limited model.
The water did not suffocate the ember. Instead, according to NIOSH, the high-pressure stream likely acted as a mechanical pump, driving fresh oxygen into the sealed upper vault. The force blasted microscopic wood dust off the interior walls, churning it into a cloud. When oxygen hit the hot fuel, the mixture detonated. The pressure spike lifted the silo off its foundation, and it blew apart in a violent fireball.
Andrew Cross, a volunteer firefighter from Morrill, died at the scene. Searsmont Assistant Fire Chief Wayne Woodbury and mill co-owner Alden Robbins were severely burned and died weeks later. A dozen others were injured.
NIOSH, which issues reports when firefighters are injured or killed on the job, concluded that officials at the state, local and company levels could have better identified and trained for the specific mechanics of combustible dust explosions, a hazard that the agency had been warning about for decades.
“I don’t know that the state understood the severity of combustible dust hazards, including myself,” said Maine State Fire Marshal Shawn Esler. He used to be the fire chief in Waterville, home to lumber yards, repair shops, plastic fabricators and other sites that could be at risk.
Without reform, experts say it’s only a matter of time before another explosion.
PHYSICS OF A DUST BOMB
A standard fire requires three elements: fuel, oxygen and heat. An explosion requires two extra variables: dispersion and confinement.
At Robbins Lumber, the fine pine dust was the fuel; the fire hose provided both the dispersion force and the oxygen surge; the embers provided the heat source; and the airtight silo provided the sealed pressure vessel. Once ignited, the expanding combustion gases had nowhere to go but out — destroying the vessel holding them.
“It is far from just a sawmill problem,” said Guy Colonna, a chemical engineer who helped draft the National Fire Protection Association’s combustible dust and confined space standards. “If people get just one thing out of my instruction, I hope it’s that.”
For years, Colonna has traveled the country trying to educate industrial operators on dust hazards, which extend from plastic recycling centers to flour mills. Federal data show more than 200 major combustible dust incidents across the U.S. since 1980, killing more than 100 people and injuring 700. Yet convincing small-town industrial enterprises to pay attention has historically proven difficult.
Last year, Colonna, who lives in Blue Hill, said he was forced to cancel a seminar in Maine because almost no one registered. Last month, when he returned to teach a two-day workshop, the 40-person class filled up within days, and the waiting list was long enough to fill two more classrooms, according to a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Labor.
“Now it’s on everyone’s front burner,” said Jeff Lewis, a risk management specialist at Cross Insurance, which covers many of Maine’s independent lumber mills and helped fund the cost of the combustible dust training course.
WHO OVERSEES DUST HAZARDS?
The regulatory framework is a patchwork of jurisdictional carve-outs.
At the state level, the Bureau of Labor Standards oversees safety strictly within public institutions, like town fire stations, public works facilities, churches or schools. Private industry falls under the federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration.
At the federal level, no single binding regulation governs combustible dust in general industry.
After fatal industrial dust catastrophes in the mid-2000s, Congress tried to pass a law forcing OSHA to create a comprehensive safety standard for particulate hazards. Rulemaking began in 2009, and heavy lobbying by manufacturers delayed the effort until it was dropped in 2017.
When a dust explosion occurs, OSHA must rely on the “General Duty Clause,” a broad provision requiring a workplace free from recognized hazards. Federal inspectors cite voluntary, third-party guidelines to prove a company ignored “recognized industry knowledge.”
Experts have characterized it as post-disaster prosecution rather than pre-disaster prevention.
Colonna is now advocating for updates to the NFPA code that would mandate signs on all sealed or oxygen-limited silos warning firefighters and workers never to inject air or water directly into a smoldering hatch.
State officials rely on voluntary safety reviews rather than mandatory enforcement. Maine offers free workplace safety reviews through the Bureau of Labor Standards, sending inspectors into private facilities to identify OSHA violations without issuing fines. The reviews temporarily shield that workplace from federal inspection.
State safety consultants toured nine sawmills in 2023, one in 2024, four in 2025 and two so far in 2026, state records show. Because those consultations are confidential, however, the public has no way to know if they analyzed dust levels.
Under Maine emergency planning rules, a private facility storing more than 10,000 pounds of combustible dust must report it to the state and their local fire departments. The 60 companies that did, according to records obtained by the Portland Press Herald, ranged from aerospace part makers to milk carton recyclers to composting facilities.
Only four of those were sawmills: Hammond Lumber in Belgrade, Louisiana-Pacific in New Limerick, PalletOne in Livermore Falls and Woodland Pulp in Baileyville. Robbins disclosed risks for its diesel fuel and sulfuric acid but not its sawdust silo.
On the morning of the disaster, federal regulators say the Searsmont silo was about 20% full. That means it held at least 36,000 pounds of fine, dry wood dust, which is almost four times the legal reporting threshold.
The public often assumes the Office of the State Fire Marshal conducts routine safety audits of industrial facilities like Robbins Lumber, but Esler said state law only gives him the authority to review building plans and inspect daycares, hospitals and public buildings.
“There are a lot of buildings built in Maine that do not require a permit from our office,” he said.
The Fire Marshal’s sole interaction with Robbins Lumber occurred during a routine paperwork review of blueprints for the mill’s sprinkler system, he said. With a small staff, the office cannot inspect every private business in Maine or check its hazard documentation.
While safety experts recommend red warning placards on airtight silos, state fire code does not mandate them, Esler said. Maine operates under the 2018 edition of NFPA code, which contains minimal references to combustible dust and imposes no labeling requirements on sealed silos.
The Maine Forest Products Council, the primary lobbying arm for the state’s timber and wood products industry, offered no statement regarding sector-wide dust safety protocols. But fire chiefs have told Esler that some mills are organizing walk-throughs of their high-risk areas.
Robbins Lumber management did not respond to questions about why a formal dust hazard analysis was never performed, why local fire departments were never briefed on the oxygen-limited mechanics of the silo or why the vessel did not have warning signs on it.
In August, the company issued a statement about its rebuilding plans on its website.
“Our objective is not simply to meet current industry standards, but to exceed them,” Catherine Robbins-Halsted, a co-owner and vice president, wrote. “We are committed to learning from this event and to doing everything we can to help prevent anything like this from happening again.”
WHAT CAN BE DONE?
In the aftermath of the explosion, a group of fire officials, sawmill operators, elected leaders and insurers formed to discuss a response to Searsmont. They must wait, however, until Mainers go to the polls next month before deciding what reforms to pursue, Esler said.
“I can’t give you the answers about the solutions that I feel may be warranted without consulting with the next governor,” Esler said.
Esler expressed skepticism toward creating a state-mandated inventory of privately owned silos to determine if combustible dust risks are documented and notified. His office cannot inspect a private workplace without statutory authority, a complaint or corporate invitation.
His office is wrapping up a statewide inventory of hazardous firefighting foam, but most of that material is stored in public buildings, where his office has more pull and more authority. He was also able to secure public funding to hire someone to conduct the survey.
He pointed to recent progress in equipping volunteer fire departments with mapping software that allows crews to view documented hazards on their way to a call. But that requires companies to accurately report their hazards and local fire departments to input the data.
The urgency for reform is compounded by an impending workforce collapse in the Maine fire service and the need for more training, Esler said.
For now, policy reforms are being vigorously debated behind closed doors but remain on hold. When asked what he would tell a Maine citizen asking how the state plans to prevent another Searsmont explosion, Esler’s answer was brief: “Wait and see.”

title: 56th Annual Pumpkin Festival happening today!
text:

ANSWER: This will be a fun time for everyone. May it be a fine day with lots of sun, pumpkin spice, and apple goodies, and all the fall feels!

There will be food, candy, games, prizes and a hayride. Everyone is welcome and it’s free of charge. Come join the fun! — Laural, Lisbon Falls
ANSWER: I’m glad you’re still carrying on this tradition. Let us know if you need any donations of food and candy and I’ll put the word out for that as well. Have fun!

ANSWER: The Chapman House provides care to senior ladies who need assistance with tasks of daily living. As I was reading the newsletter, I also saw that the organization will hold their annual Holiday Craft Fair on Saturday, Nov. 14, from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. If you or someone you know would like to rent a space, please contact Sheryll at 783-0961 to RSVP. Each space will be $25. They’re hoping to have a great turnout this year.
In other news, the organization is also looking for volunteers. Go here if you’re interested in finding out more: https://chapmanhouse.org/about-chapman-house/volunteers/ and thank you for your continued support of The Chapman House.

ANSWER: I’m putting this out into Sun Spots Land and I’ll be keeping my eyes peeled and my ear to the ground. I’ve found that’s how news of these types of events spread. Sun Spotters, please share the info if you hear of any community gatherings for trick-or-treaters, and check out the event in the headline for pre-Halloween family fun!

title: Oxford residents to vote on cannabis business cap Nov. 3
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Among the questions that will be on the ballot Nov. 3, Oxford voters will be asked if they wish to cap the number of issued cannabis licenses at 14.
There are currently 16 active licenses, held by 13 business entities.
The Select Board held a public hearing for the proposed ordinance change in October.
During the hearing two residents fed up with the perception that Main Street/Route 26 has become a cannabis corridor thanked the board for its work to address the number of businesses, but also felt that 14 licenses is still too many.
When municipal officials amended Oxford’s cannabis ordinance five years ago to include adult recreational use, the consensus was that a free market approach, and demand, would naturally determine how many businesses in the space could exist and profit.
They also determined that based on the town’s commercial zone map and available spaces that no more than four could operate.
By 2022, the last time the ordinance was amended, there were seven cultivators and stores. At that time Oxford had collected $26,500.
So far this year the town has brought in $51,000 in licensing fees.
The license type breaks down as follows: one medical manufacturing and one recreational manufacturing operation; four recreational and two medical stores; and eight cultivation facilities, five of which are medical and three recreational.
Half of the licensees operate out of one warehouse at 7 Oxford Homes Lane, which was formerly a manufactured home facility.
Cultivation licenses are broken down into tiered categories. Tier one allows for 30 plants or 500 square feet of flowering canopy. Tier two allows up to 2,000 square feet of canopy. Tier three allows up to 7,000 square feet of canopy. Tier four allows up to 20,000 square feet of canopy, the maximum.
During the hearing, board Chair Dana Dillingham explained it was a board majority that settled on using 14 as maximum for cannabis businesses and if residents wanted to lower the maximum they would have to take it up at a future date.
Selectman Philip Richardson explained their approach was to make the decrease reasonable rather than too much at once for some voters.
“We’re starting at 14 to see how that goes,” Richardson said. “Potentially, if a lot of people are interested in reducing the number then maybe we’ll try that. It seemed like too big a swing to go from 16 to 10, or even cut it in half.”
The amended cannabis referendum will be decided by voters on Nov. 3. Polls will be open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. at Oxford Town Office, at 127 Pottle Road.

title: Trump’s Russian diesel deal was the final straw for me
text:
Sam Patten has worked for Maine’s last three Republican senators, including Susan Collins’ first electoral campaigns, is a former managing editor of The Maine Wire and is the author of “Dangerous Company: The Misadventures of a Foreign Agent.”
When Donald J. Trump was again elected president in 2024, I figured he had earned his second chance. Regardless of whether I had voted for him that year, in 2020 or in 2016, he and I shared an experience that made me more open to him than anyone in my family or most of my friends.
At the time, I was the managing editor of the Maine Wire — the conservative voice in our state’s media. Covering his second administration to the extent it affects Maine from this perspective, I strained at times to understand and explain why he was doing the things he was. The flurry of executive orders at the very outset, for instance, suggested a new kind of energy. Some of his appointments, like Marco Rubio to his array of jobs and Tulsi Gabbard as director of national intelligence, struck me as promising.
It only took me until Feb. 28 of last year to get physically nauseated.
Trump’s jocks v. geek style beat-down session on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in the Oval Office punctured any Christian notions I had of redemption. It was disgusting. But I was also so very tired of Americans feeling their politics. I resolved to carry on trying the best I could to be objective — all the while hoping for better.
Due to his erratic and, at times, nonsensical behavior, I’ve come to think of Trump as mad. I would not be surprised if more than a few of my fellow Republicans think the same way.
“Should I be glad he didn’t throw spaghetti at the wall?” a now former GOP congresswoman asked me rhetorically in 2016 when, making small talk, I gamely asked if she didn’t agree Trump had made more sense at a recent media event than he had previously. She’d had enough. She went on to lose her seat that year to a Democrat Volvo salesman.
I hit that point this past weekend, on a flight back from Ukraine.
At the end of last year, I left my job at the Maine Wire to work full time on a Ukrainian consultancy project. So far this year, I’ve spent more than four months in Ukraine and over this period things have gotten worse in terms of the war.
After more than four years of a Russian invasion, Ukrainians have now begun deep strikes into Russia, primarily targeting its oil sector. So, the news that last Friday Trump moved to lift sanctions on Russian diesel and struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import nominal quantities of it into the U.S., allegedly to alleviate spiking fuel prices, was a lot to take on the back of a trip throughout which Russian shelling of civilian sites was constant.
My common experience with Trump goes back to 2018-19 during the Russia-gate probe. Then I was charged with, and pleaded guilty to, the charge of being an unregistered foreign agent for a Ukrainian politician.
Compared with a foreign power deciding who gets elected to Congress and who doesn’t, my crime — drafting talking points and op-eds for my client — could be considered risible or quaint, depending on your perspective. But, having been prosecuted as part of a broader investigation of whether Trump colluded with Russia in his first election, I remain a felon. I never sought a pardon.
There is no credible argument supporting Trump’s decision on Russian diesel. The amounts involved will not give much relief to U.S. consumers — at best 20 minutes of domestic demand, some calculate. The real problem is the fact that the Strait of Hormuz is effectively closed; that is what is driving today’s prices at the pump. And whatever revenues Russia gets will be spent on its war effort, murdering Ukrainian civilians.
So why on God’s green earth is he doing it?
Maine’s Sen. Susan Collins is right to join three other Senate Republicans in demanding the president reverse this decision. It doesn’t mean he’ll listen.
For Republicans, Trump’s insane decisions have a way of increasing in their tempo right up to consequential elections. His taking out the well-respected and highly effective Texas senator John Cornyn to run the toadying and corrupt Ken Paxton, now runs the risk of the Republican Party losing the Lone Star State for the first time in two generations. Zero sense, yet loyalists must put and shut up.
One of the reasons I once gave Trump the time of day was the seemingly insane behavior of his enemies. The “lawfare” exercised against him was real. I experienced it personally. Instead of fixing the system, however, he made it worse.
Now, Republicans who harbor any chance of withstanding the blue wave that’s coming in three weeks’ time must sidestep — or counter — the leader of their party. Ask Paul LePage about his deported in-law. Or placeholder Darline Graham about her brother Lindsey’s legacy: a hardline sanctions bill on Russia that Trump now flouts.
Whether it’s corruption, nuclear-powered narcissism or full-blown insanity, speculating about the “why” is no longer entertaining. Trump supporters are often forced to overlook the weirdness and remember the bigger objective. But when the betrayals knock with such manic insistence at your door, it becomes difficult, if not impossible, to see the larger benefit.

title: Past dust explosions in Maine failed to spark change. Will Searsmont?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Nine years ago, in the small central Maine town of Detroit, a foreman climbed to the top of a high-capacity fertilizer silo at Northeast Agricultural Sales. It was early October. The harvest season had wound down, and he was scraping off the residual chemical crust with a metal shovel.

title: Obituary: David G. Hutchins
text:
LIVERMORE FALLS – David G. Hutchins of Livermore passed away on Oct. 13, 2026, from the long-term effects of Agent Orange. He was 79 years old.
Born on Sept. 27, 1947, to Donald and Betty Hutchins, David grew up in Harford.
As a young man, David felt a deep sense of duty to his country. In 1967, he enlisted in the United States Marine Corps and served three tours in Vietnam. He proudly served with the Ghost Battalion (2nd Battalion, 1st Marines), attaining the rank of sergeant before his discharge in 1969. His service to his country remained an important part of his life, and his commitment to helping others continued long after his military service ended.
In 1984, he married Cynthia Bell. They shared 33 years together before her passing. Together, they shared not only a life but also a deep commitment to helping others.
David continued to serve his community as a volunteer firefighter in South Paris. His dedication to service extended well beyond his time in the Marines. Whether helping someone face-to-face or contributing to numerous charitable organizations, he believed in doing what he could to make life a little easier for others. David also had a soft spot for all furry friends, especially his beloved dog, Izzy.
David enjoyed many hobbies and loved working with his hands, whether he was driving a tractor, building a garage, or adding to his train village. He also enjoyed MMA and NASCAR.
Some of his fondest memories were of roller skating at Bear Pond, where he skated and worked alongside his lifelong skating buddies, Steve and Rick. His love of skating continued over the years at the Rollodrome in Auburn, where he skated until health issues no longer allowed him to continue.
David’s life was one of compassion and quiet generosity. He gave of himself freely, loved deeply, and leaves behind a legacy that will not be forgotten. He will be dearly missed and lovingly remembered.
He is survived by his children, David W. Hutchins and his wife, Johnna, and Kim Ross her companion, Dave Johnson; his companion, Penny Brown; his grandchildren, Michael and Hailey Ross, Sam and Greta Ross, Dominique Dionne, and Kelsey Patten; and his seven great-grandchildren, Flora, Salem, Landon, Hadley, Enzo, Delia, and Daxton.
He is also survived by his siblings, Wesley Hutchins and his wife, Dana, Julie Stewart and her husband, James, and Jane Averill and her husband, Mike; as well as many nieces and nephews.
He was predeceased by his wife, Cynthia; his two brothers, Donald and Michael Hutchins, his sister-in-law, Kathy Hutchins; and his nephew, Michael Averill.
Family and friends are invited to David’s graveside service with Marine military honors on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 1 p.m., at Demerritt Cemetery, Peru. Visit David’s Book of Memories at http://www.wilesrc.com as Wiles Remembrance Center is honored to be caring for the family of David G. Hutchins.
In lieu of flowers please donate in David’s Memory to the American Cancer Society at http://www.cancer.org, or the Wounded Warrior Project at http://www.woundedwarriorproject.org

title: Obituary: Adrienne Strout
text:
CORINTH – Adrienne Strout, 88, passed away peacefully with her family by her side.
Adrienne was born in Patten, on Jan. 4, 1938, to Rex and Thelma (Stubbs) James. She graduated from Brewer High School in 1956. After high school, she attended Husson College.
In 1957, she married Barry Dale Strout, the love of her life. Together they raised their four children and ran the farm in Cornville. Being a homemaker made her proud. She worked part-time while the children were young and then worked at the Animal Clinic in Skowhegan.
After retirement, Barry and Adrienne opened Adrienne’s Attic in Dexter and traveled to Pennsylvania and Florida selling antiques. In her 80s, always by Barry’s side, she rode the drag, counting the loops, as they conditioned the draft horses. Together they attended horse pulling events. Barry kept time, and Adrienne recorded the results.
Our Mum loved her family, the cabin overlooking the lake, and camp. She was a wonderful hostess. Sharing her home and the camp with friends and relatives brought her tremendous joy. She had a gift for making everyone feel welcome. A nurturer and caregiver, she often opened up our home to kids who needed support, redirection, or just acceptance and love. She loved everyone unconditionally, and that love was reciprocated. Mum was caring and selfless. Her daily goal was to make people laugh. She enjoyed playing the role of “The Nosey Neighbor” at the Annual James Family Reunion, which she valued greatly. Entertaining others by performing skits for various groups and family was in her DNA. Adrienne also loved church, kayaking, reading, crafts, taking pictures, and writing.
Living with dementia for the last several years was hard, yet she never let it define her. She never lost her smile or the ability to bring laughter and joy to others.
She was a former member of the United Methodist Church in Skowhegan and the Christian Community Church in Dexter, an active member of Eastern Star, a member of Somerset County Extension, a 4-H leader, and a member of Maine Farm Bureau Women’s Association. She was a leader and never hesitated to take on any role she needed to.
Adrienne was predeceased by her husband, Barry; her parents; her brother and childhood pal, Boyd James, her sister, Brenda (James) Hogate; and granddaughter, Desiree Marie Strout and great-grandson, Gage Weeks.
She is survived by her children James Strout Sr. and wife Leanne, Kelly Burns and husband Jim, Jody Strout and wife Kelley, and Jeffrey Strout; sister, Wendy (James) Luce, brother, Kevin James; grandchildren Jamie Strout (Karen), Rob Strout, Jessica Strout, Brett Strout (Michelle), Greg Strout (Krissy), Haley Labrie (Mike), Jacob Burns, Jesse Strout (Tabby), Danica Strout (Zack); step-grandchildren Allison Pollock (Tyler) and Brittany Moon, Greg Burns, Laurie Flynn, and Heather Bingelis (Mark); 21 great-grandchildren; and nieces, nephews.
Visiting hours will be held on Thursday, Oct. 22, 4 to 6 p.m., at the Crosby Neal Funeral Home, 117 Main St., Newport. A service will be held on Friday, Oct. 23, at 11 a.m., at the Corinna Methodist Church, 16 Dexter Rd., Corinna. Immediately after the service, a committal service will be held at Mount Pleasant Cemetery in Dexter.
The family would like to thank the owners, staff, and residents of JEM Estates in Corinth for their wonderful care, compassion, and love for our mother.
We would also like to thank the Gentiva Hospice Team, especially Sarah, Morgan, and Eric, for the skilled care, compassion, love, and support for our Mum and the family.
In place of flowers, donations may be sent to Dementia/Alzheimer’s Assoc. (Maine Chapter).

title: ‘It’s a very dark time’: Inside Cornell’s homecoming weekend
text:
‘It’s a very dark time’: Inside Cornell’s homecoming weekend
Worlds are colliding at Cornell. On the football field, the men’s varsity team is practicing for its homecoming game, the flagship event of its season. Players are fine-tuning routes and dapping each other up after a well-executed play. The school mascot dances past, a seven-foot bear pumping its paws in the air, and alumni groups mingle in a neighboring parking lot. Open a Cornell brochure: this is what homecoming looks like.
But here’s what it sounds like: clanging cowbells, and angry yells, and the sudden blares of a police siren. A few feet beyond the football field, student protesters are locking eyes with p0lice across a makeshift barrier, screaming at the officers from three feet away. The crowd swells and placards bounce up and down, the noise and fury drifting to the football field and through campus.
It’s been a month since Cornell was rocked by a lawsuit, filed by a former student identified as Jane Doe in legal documents, alleging she was drugged and gang raped at a Chi Phi frat house in 2024. The ensuing scandal, and a reopened criminal investigation, have ruptured the feeling of serenity that this remote, idyllic campus provides. Little has felt normal since.
Suddenly, these students are part of one of the biggest stories in the nation, and it’s taking a toll.
“You can feel it all the time: the tension,” says Harrison Beckwith, a sophomore on the student committee that canceled this year’s homecoming concert after its headline act pulled out. “In all my classes, you just feel a lot of sadness. A lot of uncertainty everywhere. Anger.”
It is a surreal time here. An entire population of students has suddenly found itself under a national microscope. Many are tired of the scrutiny, and it’s easy to understand why. They expected college to be fun, and none of this is fun.
But there are bigger forces at play; an entire system is under inspection too, and on that, students here are sharply divided. Many are fired up, hoping to seize this rare moment of outrage to change the way this centuries-old institution works. Nearly everyone is weary of the continued media presence on campus. Fraternities, silenced for now by a university ban on parties at frat houses, are nervously watching each other’s actions, aware that one wrong move could doom Greek life here for good.
And amid it all, a homecoming weekend. The university has tried to make the event look and feel like it does on pamphlets. It hasn’t worked: the undercurrent of anger and suspicion is everywhere. For this story, CNN spoke to dozens of students, alumni and faculty members on campus this weekend, many of whom requested anonymity to avoid angering their fraternities, sororities or colleagues.
“It’s rough,” says Natalie, a senior who asked that her last name not be published, about the feeling on campus. “A lot of people are getting fingers pointed at them.” The school, she says, is “punishing victims and students instead of targeting what needs to be targeted.”
“A lot of us care deeply about making a better environment and community,” she says — but she knows that change won’t come easily. “This isn’t the first time this has happened. It’s not going to be the last.”
Late last month, when Jane Doe’s lawsuit first spurred national outrage, Beckwith and his friend Gustavo Ponzoa realized they had a problem.
The two sophomores said they had spent months working to arrange Cornell’s annual homecoming concert, a fixture of the school’s social calendar. They estimate 1,500 students attended last year. But both of their phones were blowing up from inside and outside Cornell, and they predicted the email several days before it arrived: Between Friends, the headline act, was pulling out.
This isn’t the Cornell that Beckwith arrived at last year: he was happy to be at that one. “You feel a lot of pride, a lot of excitement,” he says, recalling his first weeks on campus. Those feelings changed when he read Jane Doe’s complaint, especially the vulgar messages sent by a fraternity member about “free p---y” in the house. It left both men disgusted and ashamed of their school. “Every step of the way, there was a failure,” says Beckwith.
Video above: Attorney of the former student who alleges she was raped speaks to CNN
New York’s governor has since appointed state Attorney General Letitia James to re-examine the case, and Cornell has retained former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Q. Yates to review how the school “prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct on campus.”
“There’s definitely a notable change in the atmosphere,” Beckwith says. “You don’t feel pride … you almost feel betrayed.” The past month, Beckwith says, “was a revelation.” He didn’t believe the actions alleged by Doe could take place at Cornell — but now, he says, he realizes that behavior is “among us.”
“It makes you so much more paranoid and distrustful of other people.”
Ponzoa chimes in, describing it as a “super gloomy” few weeks. “Every single day — even going to class felt rough.”
And now, the Ivy League school these young men strived to attend is one that seemingly no one wants to be associated with.
“The next (concert) is straight up not happening. Who are we going to book?” asks Ponzoa. “Artists are worried about their safety (and) their brands.” He’s already heard “no’s” from musicians who were previously lined up, he says. “I don’t blame them. I would do the same.”
The canceled gigs include what would have been a celebratory 50th anniversary of a legendary Grateful Dead show at Cornell’s Barton Hall, a milestone in the histories of both the band and the school. Beckwith and Ponzoa both note that these are minor inconveniences in the face of much more serious issues. But they serve as reminders of just how far Cornell’s reputation has fallen.
Instead, the pair are looking to other pages of music history for inspiration. They are working to organize a show, featuring Cornell’s own student musicians, to raise money for the anti-sexual assault nonprofit RAINN. “There’s been so many instances of musicians fighting for what’s right, through concerts,” says Ponzoa, citing Joan Baez and the Live Aid concert among his lofty examples. “We want to be a part of that history.”
There are snippets of normalcy this weekend, if you look for them. Alumni receptions take place on campus, and Ithaca’s steakhouses and upmarket restaurants are booked through the night. In the Cornell store, Vickie Sparks cradles a pile of merch, including a mug reading “Cornell Mom,” her bashful son, a recent mathematics graduate, in tow.
“I was conflicted about coming back,” says Sparks, from Berea, Kentucky. “I didn’t know how well we would be received. I didn’t know how comfortable I would be wearing my Cornell gear.” But their trip had been booked for a year, and “this horrible thing that has transpired was not going to make me change my plans,” she says. “We can’t let an incident, as bad and horrible as this was, be the only thing that Cornell is known for.”
But right now, it’s the only thing many people are thinking about.
For many of Cornell’s female students, the events of the past month haven’t just been traumatizing: they’ve been re-traumatizing. They remember the gossip two years earlier, when they were freshmen or sophomores, that something awful had happened at the Chi Phi house. Cornell is a large university, but when rumor spreads, any school can become a small town.
“I was on campus when it happened,” says Natalie, the senior. “You assume that the admin’s going to do something about it and support the student that needs support. Instead, we hear about it two years later, and nothing has been really done.”
“How do you know where to go from there?”
She talks while selling baklava in the foyer of the student union. Above her head and all around her is an elaborate mural, painted a century ago to depict the character traits of noble men. In Latin, an inscription translates to: “Nothing in the realm of men is alien to me.”
“Every woman on campus definitely has been a victim (of sexual assault or harassment), or has a friend who needed support,” Natalie says. She adds that she has friends who have filed complaints through Title IX, the federal civil rights law prohibiting gender-based discrimination, that have gone nowhere.
“It’s systemic, and it’s not gonna change overnight,” she says. But like so many students here, she is angry at the school’s leadership, and its embattled president, Michael Kotlikoff. “I don’t know if I trust anything that they’re doing,” she says.
“We understand why members of our community are asking questions about the university’s response in 2024, particularly in light of the deeply troubling allegations that have now become public,” Cornell told CNN in a statement Sunday. “Cornell took the reports very seriously and moved promptly to initiate its Title IX process. The university conducted an extensive investigation and adjudication over several months and imposed different sanctions based on the findings and circumstances involving each student.”
Two of the students named in Doe’s complaint were expelled, while others received lesser punishments. Two students, including one who was found responsible for entering the room where Doe was allegedly assaulted but not attacking her, were punished with directed study and writing reflection essays.
Outside, as gray clouds unleash a torrent of rain, a protest begins to form. These have been near-daily exhibitions of anger and frustration. Beneath umbrellas, attendees join a call and response: “There are no excuses!” and “No cover-up, no lies!” and “Ban the frats!”
“There’s a lot of anger,” says Gabe Sekeres, a doctoral student at Cornell, of the protest that he helped organize. “This is something that has been brewing for a number of years.”
“It was so clear from those messages that these men in Chi Phi felt as though (Jane Doe) was not a human. They truly dehumanized her,” he says. “It’s something that is endemic in fraternity culture. The university tells them that they are better than everyone else. They give a lot of money. They bring in a lot of money for the university. And as a result, they get to act with impunity.”
The Chi Phi national fraternity has condemned the alleged assault, saying it took actions in 2024 that “went beyond anything the law or Cornell University required of us.” Cornell shut down Chi Phi in 2024, and the fraternity is still prohibited from operating on campus.
Sekeres has long questioned the purpose of Greek life, a system he considers elitist and exclusionary. And now, he sees an opportunity to end it.
His protest swells to several dozen people and then takes off across campus, the attendees marching and clanging cowbells as they go. Eventually, university police contain the group behind a barrier and stand sullenly as protesters direct their angst towards officers.
Eeshaan Chaudhuri didn’t prepare for this. When he ran for president of the student assembly, he gave speeches to half-empty rooms about dining policies and the lack of free parking at the student health center.
“If you were to ask me, even a month and a half ago, what I thought my senior year would look like, I wouldn’t say it would (involve) speaking to CNN.”
But Chaudhuri, dressed in a charcoal suit and blessed with a politician’s ability to filibuster, could easily pass as a first-time candidate for a state legislature seat. He’s a bridge between students and the Cornell administration, and it’s difficult to imagine a time when that relationship has been more strained.
“The student body’s upset,” he says. “Sexual violence is a huge problem here at Cornell. And what (the) admin is doing right now to combat it is clearly not enough.”
Chaudhuri’s parents emigrated from India to the East Coast. His father had hoped to go to Cornell himself, and Chaudhuri lights up when he describes the moment he told his parents of his acceptance to the school. “I was able to achieve something my dad couldn’t do,” he says. “It’s been very humbling.”
But when he talks about his role today, his exhaustion is obvious. “I haven’t been to class in three weeks,” he admits: he has a mountain of homework waiting for him tonight, and his lecturers’ patience is wearing thin.
We meet in the backroom at Collegetown Bagels, a lively bakery-turned-bar that doubles as the go-to meeting spot for many undergrads. He knows that the life of everyone around him has been impacted, too.
“There are students here on campus that just want to be normal students. They want to go to class without having the media filming them. They didn’t ask for any of this when they applied to Cornell in the first place.”
But the exhaustion and the anger live side by side, and many students are directing their fury towards Kotlikoff, who last week said he was “deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024” and announced a range of new measures to increase security and support on campus.
He has resisted calls to resign.
Asked whether he supports those calls, Chaudhuri takes a beat for the first time, mentally sifting through the complicated realities of his role. “I wouldn’t be comfortable commenting on that at the moment,” he says at first. Then he admits that “Eeshaan, as a student, would call for the president to resign … absolutely.”
But Eeshaan the student politician isn’t so sure: a transition would slow down policy changes, he warns, and the problem is deeper than one man.
“I don’t think replacing the president of the university stops sexual violence,” he says.
It’s nighttime, and the frat houses are dark. At Delta Kappa Epsilon, in the parking lot, a group of guys underdressed for the cold are playing a three-on-three football scrimmage. “Kill, kill, kill,” they yell into the cool air. Nearby, EDM blares from another frat house, in spite of the tension around parties. Silhouetted figures are visible through the windows, and rowdy conversation bleeds through the walls.
And across the road, at the foot of a cobblestoned hill that cars sigh and grumble as they traverse, is the empty Chi Phi house. Students, walking heavy-footed down the slope, throw the occasional glance through its windows. This is Cornell’s grimmest new landmark.
What happened inside that Tudor-style building in October 2024 is the subject of a civil complaint and now a fresh criminal investigation. The house has sat vacant since Cornell concluded its own Title IX investigation and shuttered the frat. But it remains a monument to a swelling movement against the closed-door nature of many Greek institutions.
Some feel that movement has gone too far. Sienna, a sorority sister who asked CNN not to publish her last name, is one of few students willing to provide a partial defense of the seven students named in Doe’s complaint.
“I think that they were bad apples in a bunch,” she says. But the case is “revealing another issue with the American public,” she adds: “We’re morally determining their guilt. It’s ‘innocent until proven guilty,’ and that’s not what’s happened here.”
In her sorority, the mood has been “glum.” She says many freshmen and sophomores are wondering: “This (alleged rape) happened two years ago. Why is this (scandal) happening now?”
“We don’t want negative backlash. We don’t want to be identified, and blasted all over TikTok,” she says. Greek life, she says, is supposed to be “a positive experience for everybody. That’s why we pay thousands of dollars to be a part of it.”
Now, she walks to her sorority building past protests calling for Greek life to be shut down.
“They’re misunderstanding the way college life functions,” she argues. “If Greek life got banned, these boys — they’re not going away. If there’s a lot of horse deaths happening, are you gonna be like, ‘ban horse stables’?”
“The issue is truly not frats,” Sienna says. “It’s just bad men.”
But according to many on campus, the issue is far more than that. They say a structure of secrecy operates within frats that protects bad behavior. That is a pattern that a frat member at Cornell, who spoke to CNN on the condition of anonymity, says he recognizes.
“Although it can be hurtful to hear people chanting ‘F--- the frats,’ I completely understand where their anger is coming from,” he says. “There definitely are problems with Greek life.”
“Everyone at elite institutions has the tendency to protect people in their circle,” he says. “Whatever happened in that house, the brothers were openly acting terribly, with so much malice, and I feel like if there was more public scrutiny, they would never have had the ability to commit the terrible things that they did.”
He feels the ban on frat parties is fair, and he’s willing to abide by it. But he’s not so sure about everyone else.
“I definitely have some concerns that other houses will not follow the rules, and essentially get Greek life banned on campus,” he says. Asked if someone, eventually, will slip up, the brother is unequivocal. “Oh, absolutely.”
Still, not everyone welcomes more scrutiny. Sienna argues there is a “good amount of oversight occurring” at frat and sorority houses. “It’s like, how much more oversight do you want on a college campus?” she asks. “At the end of the day, we’re teenagers and 21-year-olds … it’s not a secret that we wanna have fun.”
On Saturday, the chill rolls in. Winter here can be brutal, and this is its warning shot.
The mood on campus feels tense. Saturday is typically the biggest day of homecoming weekend, but today’s agenda is stripped down. Fraternities, which would usually throw crammed street parties in Ithaca’s Collegetown neighborhood, have been denied event permits by the city and urged instead to tailgate in the parking lot outside the 111-year-old Schoellkopf Field, surrounded by university police.
Already, fevered speculation has spread. A lengthy message, posted to the anonymous student message board app Sidechat, has gone viral: it warns that Cornell’s leadership has given frats one last chance, but “one f---up from any chapter and it is likely Greek life is gone for good.” (A fraternity president confirmed that the message was an accurate summation of the university’s position).
It’s a triumphant day on the football field, where Cornell beats undefeated Lehigh in an upset. But most fraternity brothers aren’t watching. They’re back in Collegetown, filling the streets despite the ban on public events. For a few minutes, it looks like a normal celebration, at a normal time: students are drinking and laughing. And then the police wade in to shut down the gathering. The crowds, so full of defiance and angst a moment ago, disperse in minutes.
Many just wanted to have fun. But instead, a reckoning has split Cornell’s students.
“The frats hold a lot of power,” Ponzoa tells CNN. “Greek life has a big place here.” Cornell’s protesters allege that power has remained unchecked for years.
But now, the power may be shifting.
For weeks, Beckwith has felt little pride in his university. But then, after the shock of the complaint wore off, he started to find it in new places.
“I see so many students, at the protest, at the (student paper) Cornell Daily Sun, who are rising up, standing up and advocating. That’s inspiring to see,” he said.
“It’s a very dark time,” he said. “But you see so much hope.”

title: American journalist injured in settler attack in Israeli-occupied West Bank
text:
(AP) - The U.S. ambassador to Israel condemned a settler attack on an American journalist that left her needing surgery, in the latest incident of such violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
Meanwhile, two helicopter pilots were killed Sunday in Saudi Arabia near the border with Yemen, which a Saudi military spokesperson said was due to a technical malfunction.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East. Read our full coverage here.
US ambassador condemns settler attack on American journalist
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee sharply condemned settler violence during an olive harvest in the West Bank that injured several Palestinians and Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine as “a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards.” In a post late Saturday on X, he called for “a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this.”
Levine was seriously injured in the attack Friday in the West Bank village of Abu Falah. Israeli police are also investigating an attack by Israeli settlers on European diplomats Saturday in another West Bank village. Settler violence against Palestinians has soared this year and spiked further in recent weeks as Israel plans to hold elections Oct. 27.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was ambiguous in addressing Levine’s assault, condemning “violence against anyone” but referring to the attack as “alleged” and saying its circumstances remain unclear. Huckabee said Levine’s assault was “vicious” and “dishonorable,” and noted that she was clearly identified as a journalist when she was attacked.
Levine, an award-winning photojournalist who has covered conflict zones around the world for more than four decades, remains hospitalized in Tel Aviv as she recovers from hand surgery, broken ribs and other injuries she sustained in the attack. She said she was forced to the ground and beaten for more than 10 minutes by the settlers, who also stole her camera, passport and phone.
The Washington Post reiterated its call for a full and transparent investigation, though Israel rarely investigates settler violence fully. Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group, says around 94% of investigations into settler violence since 2005 have ended without an indictment, with just 3% leading to full or partial convictions.
Saudi helicopter crashes near border with Yemen, killing pilots
A Saudi helicopter gunship crashed in southwestern Saudi Arabia, killing its two-member crew in an area close to the border with Yemen, due to a technical malfunction, a Saudi military spokesperson said Sunday. The helicopter crashed near the city of Najran, close to the Yemen border, in an area that has been caught up in fierce fighting between the Iran-backed Yemeni Houthi militants and a Saudi-led coalition attempting to contain them.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki made the statement hours after the Houthis claimed to have downed the Saudi helicopter.
The Houthis, a Shiite religious and political movement rooted in northern Yemen, are attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government in the civil war. The Saudis have struggled to counter the latest attacks, even with far superior U.S.-supplied arms.
Egypt agrees to provide defense support for Saudi Arabia
Egypt’s National Defense Council, which decides on the country’s high-level military and security affairs, has agreed to support its close ally Saudi Arabia in a major escalation of fighting between the kingdom and the Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen.
Chaired by President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi, the council decided in a Sunday meeting to provide “all possible forms of support” to enable Saudi Arabia to defend its security and stability, according to a statement from the Egyptian presidency.
The statement didn’t provide further details, but the council said it will also continue diplomatic efforts with regional and international parties to de-escalate the conflict.
El-Sissi said Saturday that his government will implement “any measure” to defend Saudi Arabia, and called for parliament to grant him the authorization to deploy troops and military equipment abroad. Parliament is set to meet later Sunday.
Tugboat near UAE damaged by projectiles
Two projectiles hit a vessel transiting off the United Arab Emirates early Sunday, wounding one person, a British military agency reported.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said the tug sustained damage but is continuing its journey. The UKMTO did not identify the vessel and no group claimed responsibility for the attack. The tug was attacked in the Gulf of Oman, south of the narrow Strait of Hormuz, which has faced blockades and attacks in recent months.
Iran approves new defense minister, vows to defend itself
Iran appointed Mehrdad Akhlaghi, a longtime official in Iran’s defense industry, as the new defense minister on Sunday.
His predecessor, Aziz Nasirzadeh, was killed on the first day of U.S.-Israeli attacks Feb. 28, along with Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and several senior Iranian military commanders.
During a confirmation hearing, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian vowed that Iran would not yield to pressure or demands from other countries.
“We will resolutely defend our land and country and will not allow our enemies to covet our beloved homeland, just as we have no designs on anyone else’s territory,” Pezeshkian said.
Akhlaghi vowed that any miscalculation from Israel or the U.S. would prompt a “surprising and extensive” response.
___
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.
