title: Aroostook farm “matchmaker” invents agriculture trading card game for schools
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Kids will soon be able to collect and trade farm game cards to run their own fantasy farm while making crop, livestock, planting, financing and transportation decisions that sometimes get foiled by rivals.
In the “Farm to Table” game, players gain and lose beans through their farm management decisions. Often saddled with obstacles like weather, infections and buyouts, they have to calculate how to offset such losses with insurance, grants or choosing less costly and more productive decisions. The first player to reach 200 beans in 20 turns wins and the farmer falling 200 beans into debt loses their farm to the Bean Counter.
In a time when budgets are tight and families struggle to put healthy food on the table, the farm game teaches kids and families new options.
Dr. Roxanne Bruce, in conjunction with Portland-based Standard Magic, created the game as part of a larger effort to link kids, schools, families and farmers to locally grown and created foods. The game and her other two related ventures, FarmFinder USA and the umbrella company, Cultivated Encounters, will get a first look on Wednesday, Oct. 21, during a panel presentation and launch of the live demonstration version at Tech Week in Portland.
“I will be looking for farms to participate in the beta testing of the new site that launches during tech week next week,” the Ludlow resident said. “The more connections we make in our communities between farmers and schools, the brighter the future.”
Cultivated Encounters, co-owned by Bruce, Victoria Gray and Steven Rose, serves the farm to school community. Working directly with farms, school nutrition directors and teachers, Bruce, who has a doctorate in business administration with a focus on agriculture and marketing, is a matchmaker of sorts. She links previously disparate groups – local farms and school nutrition procurement – while teaching them how to prepare the foods.
“Food security starts in your community,” she said. “When farmers connect with schools, we give the school nutrition directors access to fresh, local ingredients. Money spent at these local farms goes directly to supporting businesses in Maine and around the school district.”
As part of the farm game, kids can earn additional game cards in their school cafeteria if they scan a posted QR code related to the farm that provided items used in that day’s menu, Bruce said, adding that they will eventually be able to also trade cards with each other.
“I am building it like a Pokemon or Magic the Gathering,” she said.
Along with that will be the FarmFinderUSA maps, currently featuring 3,490 farms on the site, 671 mapped locations and 181 local food options. As part of the initiative, there will also be printable curriculum for teachers and YouTube video libraries for help with cooking farm fresh foods.
Additionally, Bruce has a Food is Medicine contract with Avec Community Action (formerly Aroostook Community Action Program) and she is working with MicMac Farm in their agricultural kitchen to cook and bake items that are sold through Cultivated Encounters sales site.
“The farms have been bringing me seconds that we don’t want to go to waste, and then I turn that into food items that we offer to the schools and the public,” Bruce said. “If I work with people and I’m teaching them, at the end of it, they shouldn’t need me anymore — and if they do still need me then I screwed up.”

title: Obituary: Geneva M. Parlin
text:
NORRIDGEWOCK – Geneva M. Parlin, 90, of Norridgewock, passed away peacefully on Sept. 8, 2026, at Cedar Ridge Nursing Home in Skowhegan.
Geneva spent much of her life taking care of everyone around her. Family was everything to her, and helping others was what she loved to do. She had a caring and generous heart and was happiest when she was doing something for someone else.
While raising her family, Geneva worked at Avian Farms. Later, she worked as a chef at a local restaurant and then in the kitchen at Woodlawn Nursing Home, continuing her lifelong tradition of caring for others.
Geneva is survived by her son, Brian Parlin and wife, Terrie, of Dexter, her daughter, Tammy King and husband, Jeff, of Norridgewock, and her son, Mark Parlin of Sidney.
She also leaves behind six grandchildren, Amanda Nichols and husband, Tom, Samantha Sidell and husband, Devin, Whitney Parlin, Brian Parlin, Jonathan Cayford, and Jenna Perkins.
Geneva was blessed with five great-grandchildren, Evan and Emilee Nichols, Liam Sidell, Mason Parlin, and Ryker Grant, who brought her much joy and happiness.
She also leaves behind her five siblings, Robert and wife, Dawn, Junior and wife, Linda, Sally Hanscom, Loretta Greene, and Cissy Bronn; as well as several nieces and nephews.
Geneva was predeceased by the father of her children, Royce Parlin; mother, Mary Pelotte, father, Shirley Thibeau, stepfather, Wilfred Pelotte; sisters Joan and Jeanette, and brother, Larry.
Geneva will be deeply missed by her family, friends, and all who knew her. She will be remembered for her kindness, generous heart, and the love she gave so freely to others. Her greatest joy was caring for her family and helping those around her, leaving behind a lasting legacy of love that will live on in the hearts of all she touched. Geneva’s caring spirit will never be forgotten.
We will gather together for an ice cream social to celebrate Geneva’s life on Sunday Oct. 25, from 1 to 3 p.m., at the Smithfield Grange Hall. We ask you to wear your favorite plaid shirt in honor of Geneva.

title: Family claims mother charged in Great Wolf Lodge murders ‘never wanted to get pregnant’
text:
(Gray News) - The family of a woman who is charged with killing her husband and 3-year-old son said she “never wanted to get pregnant” and resented her son because she lost time alone with her husband, according to WPVI.
Metallica Rose Harrison, 27, is accused of killing her husband, Charles Harrison, and her son at Great Wolf Lodge in Scotrun, Pennsylvania.
How the incident unfolded
Officials were notified of the “violent domestic tragedy” in a Great Wolf Lodge hotel room around 3 p.m. Monday.
Investigators said Metallica Harrison was suicidal when she called 911. Police found her at the resort with cuts on her wrists and neck. That is when they found Charles Harrison with several stab wounds to his chest. The couple’s son, who has not been identified, was found with a single stab wound through the chest.
A “large butcher kitchen knife” and a smaller knife were found in the bathroom, according to a criminal complaint. Great Wolf Lodge staff confirmed that the knives, which had teal handles, did not belong to the lodge, according to the complaint and WPVI.
Charges filed
The Monroe County District Attorney’s Office has charged Metallica Harrison with two counts of criminal homicide.
Harrison was taken to the hospital for self-inflicted injuries and is receiving treatment. She remains in police custody.
Investigation details
The family checked into the Great Wolf Lodge on Sept. 21, then on Oct. 5 they extended their stay with a checkout date of Oct. 13.
The Monroe County district attorney said this was just the start of a lengthy investigation. Investigators said they are still reviewing extensive evidence found at the scene. Autopsies will be done later this week.

title: Bruins beats Kings for 5th straight victory
text:
LOS ANGELES — Marat Khusnutdinov scored in the third period and the Boston Bruins beat the Los Angeles Kings 4-1 on Saturday night for their fifth straight victory.
David Pastrnak had a goal, Elias Lindholm and JJ Peterka scored empty-netters, and Jeremy Swayman made 25 saves. The Bruins swept the three California teams as part of a four-game trip that ends in Dallas on Tuesday.
Alex Laferriere scored for Los Angeles, and Anton Forsberg made 24 saves. The Kings remained winless through six games to start the season and were held to one goal for the fourth straight contest.
Khusnutdinov put the Bruins ahead 2-1 with 6:24 remaining, scoring on a backhander after Forsberg failed to cover up Morgan Geekie’s shot and Matt Poitras kept the puck alive.
The Kings got off to a quick start, scoring 31 seconds into the game. Laferriere was at the top of the crease to put in Adrian Kempe’s pass for his second goal of the season, making the most of his promotion to first-line center.
But the Bruins responded early in the second period, with Pastrnak tying it at 2:43. He pounced on a loose puck in the neutral zone and took it the other way to beat Forsberg on a wrist shot from the right circle for his fourth goal.
It was Pastrnak’s 289th goal at even-strength, tying Phil Esposito for third-most in Boston history.
Bruins center Pavel Zacha did not play because of an upper-body injury he sustained in the third period against the Ducks on Friday. He is day-to-day, coach Marco Sturm said before the game.
Up next
Bruins: At Dallas on Tuesday night.
Kings: At Washington on Tuesday night.
